name: Ordinances from other LGUs, kept as references
note: Ordinances that provinces, cities and municipalities outside BARMM have enacted, each read in full off the LGU’s own PDF (or the Internet Archive’s copy where the LGU has taken it down). They are kept so a BARMM council can see how others drafted a code before writing its own. None of them has force in the region, and a BARMM LGU drafts under the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code (BAA No. 49), not the 1991 Local Government Code these ordinances cite. Texts read from scans by OCR carry misread words; check the original PDF before quoting one.

ordinances.title: Provincial Environmental Protection and Management Code of La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Provincial Environmental Protection and Management Code of La Union (2002)
ordinances.summary: A provincial code that gathers La Union's environmental rules in 13 chapters: water resources, forests, air and vehicle pollution, wildlife, toxic substances, sewage, solid waste, caves, small-scale mining and mine safety. It sets rules for residents, businesses, quarry and mining operators and the cities and municipalities of the province, and lets the Governor issue implementing guidelines.
points: Quarry extraction needs a permit from the Provincial Governor; the quarry tax is shared 30% province, 30% city or municipality, 40% barangay
Bans slash-and-burn farming, cutting trees on public land without DENR clearance, and cutting coconut trees without a PCA permit and the mayor's approval
Bans smoking in cinemas, hospitals, classrooms, designated no-smoking areas and public utility vehicles; PUV drivers must carry a waste receptacle
Gold panning or sluicing needs a Bureau of Mines permit, the mayor's permit and the claim owner's written consent; minors may not be employed
Some articles, like anti-littering, apply only where the city or municipality has no ordinance of its own

provisions.title: One code for the province's environmental rules
provisions.text: The code gathers all general and special ordinances on environmental management and the protection of natural resources in La Union into 13 chapters, from water and forests to mining safety.

provisions.title: Sanitary permits for waterworks
provisions.text: No one may set up or run a waterworks system or deliver water to consumers without a sanitary permit from the city or municipal health officer, which must come before the mayor's permit.

provisions.title: Smoke-belching vehicles impounded
provisions.text: Vehicles must meet emission standards. One suspected of violating them is tested at a DENR-authorized centre and, if it fails, stays impounded until penalties are paid and repairs are made, with a pass of up to 7 days to fix it.

provisions.title: No slash-and-burn, tree or coconut cutting
provisions.text: Slash-and-burn farming is banned. Trees on public land need DENR clearance to cut, and coconut trees need a PCA permit and the mayor's approval, only if 60 years old, unproductive, diseased, storm-damaged, hazardous or on converted land.
provisions.section: Ch. VII, Arts. A to C

provisions.title: Quarry permits from the Governor
provisions.text: Extracting sand, gravel, stone or other quarry resources needs a permit from the Provincial Governor after paying the provincial tax. The tax is shared 30% province, 30% city or municipality and 40% barangay where it is extracted.

provisions.title: Flammables, garbage and premises
provisions.text: Storing flammable or explosive substances needs a mayor's permit through the fire station chief, except up to 100 litres of fuel in a vehicle tank. Garbage goes only to designated disposal areas, and every establishment and home cleans its own premises.

provisions.title: No smoking in cinemas, hospitals, classes and PUVs
provisions.text: Smoking is banned in cinema screening rooms, hospital rooms, classrooms, designated no-smoking areas and public utility vehicles, and those in charge must post signs.

provisions.title: Anti-littering, where no local rule exists
provisions.text: Littering in public places is banned, and every PUV driver, tricycles included, must carry a waste receptacle. The article applies only where the city or municipality has no ordinance of its own.

provisions.title: Gold panning rules
provisions.text: Panning or sluicing needs a Bureau of Mines permit, the mayor's permit and the claim owner's written consent. No minors, no night work, no drilling or blasting, and gold may be sold only to authorized Central Bank dealers.

provisions.title: Governor's guidelines and a general penalty
provisions.text: The Governor issues implementing guidelines for each chapter. Violations without a specific penalty draw a fine of up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both.

ordinances.penalties: Up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both, where no specific penalty is set
ordinances.caveat: Chapter XII, about half the text, reproduces national mine safety and health rules word for word, including their own final provisions.

sponsors: Hon. Ma. Annabelle S. de Guzman
details.covers: Water, forests, air, wildlife, caves, mines and waste across the Province of La Union
details.enforcers: Provincial Governor, with the DENR and other national agencies

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your province wants one code for quarrying, tree cutting, small-scale mining, pollution and waste instead of scattered ordinances. La Union's code shows how to lay that out in 13 chapters, and how to let a city or municipality ordinance prevail where it already covers the subject. It is from 2003, runs 212 pages, and about half of it copies national mine safety rules, so borrow its layout and a few clauses, not the text.

apply.if: If your province already issues quarry permits and collects a quarry tax
apply.then: you can replicate the quarry article by tying the Governor's permit to the tax paid and writing the 30% province, 30% city or municipality and 40% barangay split into the same article.

apply.if: If your province has no environment and natural resources officer in post yet
apply.then: start with the chapters a small staff can enforce, such as quarry permits, tree cutting and gold panning, and add the pollution and sewage chapters once the office is filled.

apply.if: If your cities and municipalities already have anti-littering or waste ordinances
apply.then: copy La Union's rule that the provincial article applies only where the city or municipality has no ordinance of its own, so the two never clash.

apply.if: If small-scale mining or gold panning happens in your province
apply.then: keep the written consent of the claim owner or landowner, the ban on minors and night work, and the ban on drilling, blasting and machinery, and refer to RA 7076 instead of copying Chapter XII.

apply.if: If your province has IP communities that farm by shifting cultivation
apply.then: consult them and MIPA before adopting the slash-and-burn ban as written.

change: Re-cite quarry rules to BLGC s. 161 and s. 162: the Governor's permit covers areas of up to 5 hectares, on the mayor's recommendation, for 5 years renewable to 25; areas over 5 and up to 20 hectares go to the Bangsamoro environment ministry, not DENR
Drop Chapter XII, the copied mine safety rules, and refer to the national small-scale mining law (RA 7076) and the province's BLGC s. 512 role in regulating small-scale mining instead

Rework the slash-and-burn ban where it reaches ancestral domains: if IP communities in the province practise shifting cultivation as custom, consult them and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs under BAA No. 64 and RA 8371 (IPRA) before banning it outright

Move the smoking rules out into a separate smoke-free ordinance under the national tobacco laws (RA 9211), and put solid waste rules under RA 9003 and the provincial solid waste board the province chairs under BLGC s. 512

Name the provincial environment and natural resources officer (BLGC s. 538) as the lead office, and require the sanggunian's prior approval for projects that may cause pollution or forest loss, as BLGC s. 32 does; keep penalties within the ₱5,000 and 1-year ceiling in BLGC s. 521
barmm.fits: Provinces where quarrying, upland farming or small-scale mining happen, and that have or plan an environment and natural resources office.

ordinances.title: Authorizing the collection and payment of solid waste management fees in the City of Bacoor, Cavite
ordinances.shortTitle: Solid Waste Management Fees Ordinance of the City of Bacoor
ordinances.summary: Levies a yearly solid waste management fee on households and on commercial, industrial and institutional establishments in Bacoor, tiered by type, location, waste volume and floor area. The money pays for garbage collection and disposal and for the city's solid waste plan, including a materials recovery facility, a waste-to-energy plant and a bio-digester. It also lists prohibited waste practices and their penalties.
points: Sets annual fees for 37 categories, from ₱1,000 for informal settler dwellings and ₱1,500 to ₱3,000 for titled homes up to ₱300,000 for large restaurants outside malls
Private haulers pay ₱10,000 a month and transporters ₱3,000 to ₱5,000 a month
Prohibits non-segregation at source; city and barangay collectors may not pick up unsegregated waste
The city must offer free scheduled collection of bulky waste and e-waste
Late fees carry a 1% surcharge plus 1% interest a month, capped at 12% a year
Enforced by the City Environment and Service Department with the finance, assessors and permits offices

provisions.title: A yearly fee on every waste generator
provisions.text: Every household and commercial, industrial and institutional establishment pays a yearly fee, tiered by type, location, waste volume and floor area. It funds collection and disposal and the city's solid waste plan, including a materials recovery facility, a waste-to-energy plant and a bio-digester.

provisions.title: Household rates
provisions.text: Titled homes pay ₱3,000 a year if they generate more than 4.64 kg a day and ₱1,500 if at least 2.32 kg a day; informal settler dwellings pay ₱1,000.

provisions.title: Business rates by size
provisions.text: 37 categories run from ₱3,125 for micro food stalls up to ₱300,000 for large restaurants outside malls. Malls pay ₱29,092.50 to ₱63,217.50, plus ₱18.65 per sq m over 50 sq m for larger malls; the Zapote public market is charged ₱5,358,251.10.

provisions.title: Fees on private haulers
provisions.text: Private haulers collecting waste in the city pay a waste contingency fee of ₱10,000 a month and transporters ₱3,000 to ₱5,000 a month, whatever their number of clients, and must hold all operating permits.

provisions.title: Free pick-up of bulky waste and e-waste
provisions.text: The City Environment and Service Department must set up scheduled collection of bulky waste and e-waste at no charge.

provisions.title: Segregate, or it is not collected
provisions.text: Households and establishments must segregate waste at source. City, barangay and contracted collectors may not pick up unsegregated waste, and the department head or punong barangay who lets them is in violation.

provisions.title: MRFs and oil collection points in every community
provisions.text: Every homeowners' association and barangay must set up a materials recovery facility and a hazardous waste area within 90 days of the implementing rules, and a used cooking oil collection area.

provisions.title: Duties of establishments
provisions.text: Establishments must secure an ECC or certificate of non-coverage before building, display colour-coded bins, keep separate storage for each type of waste, and follow collection schedules. Littering and dumping in public places get zero tolerance.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Each prohibited act draws a ₱5,000 fine. Violating businesses have their permit suspended for at least 30 days, and violators' waste is not collected until they comply. Paying the fine bars criminal prosecution; minors are not charged.

provisions.title: Late fees and where the money goes
provisions.text: Unpaid fees carry a 1% surcharge plus 1% interest a month, capped at 12% a year. Fines and surcharges go to the Bacoor Environment Fund, and the treasurer reports collections quarterly to the City Solid Waste Management Board.

ordinances.penalties: ₱5,000 per violation; businesses face at least 30 days of permit suspension and their waste is not collected until they comply

details.effect: Upon approval and publication in a newspaper of general circulation
details.covers: All residential, commercial, industrial and institutional establishments in Bacoor
details.enforcers: City Environment and Service Department, with Finance, Assessors and Permits
details.funding: City annual or supplemental budget; fines go to the Bacoor Environment Fund

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU collects garbage but pays for all of it from the general fund. Bacoor charges every household and business a yearly fee set by type of generator, location, waste volume and floor area, at about ₱1,317 a year for each kilogram of daily waste, and backs it with a 'no segregation, no collection' rule. The rates and the waste-to-energy plans fit a large, well-off city, so treat the fee table as a method, not a price list.

apply.if: If your LGU already runs regular collection and knows what it costs
apply.then: you can replicate this by pricing each category from your own cost per kilogram of waste, as Bacoor did, with a lower rate for informal settler homes.

apply.if: If you have no waste figures by type of generator yet
apply.then: start with a few broad categories, such as households, small stores, eateries, markets and larger businesses, with a flat yearly fee each, and refine the table after a year of weighing.

apply.if: If your barangays have no materials recovery facility yet
apply.then: skip Bacoor's 90-day deadline for every barangay to build one, and set a schedule your barangays can meet, or let neighbouring barangays share a facility.

apply.if: If your treasurer and business permits office already collect other fees
apply.then: tie payment to the yearly business permit and keep collection with the treasurer; don't copy the clause letting the mayor authorise any resident to collect, which BLGC s. 152 forbids.

apply.if: If you adopt the 'no segregation, no collection' rule
apply.then: pair it with free scheduled pick-up of bulky waste and e-waste, and fine violators rather than leaving their waste uncollected, so it is not burned or dumped.

change: Re-cite the legal basis to BLGC s. 148 (power to create sources of revenue) and s. 21, with RA 9003 as the national law on solid waste; a fee ordinance needs public hearings first under BLGC s. 212 and full publication under s. 213, and takes effect only 15 days after publication.

Rebuild the rate table from local collection costs and incomes; ₱1,500 to ₱3,000 a year per home and ₱300,000 for a restaurant would be oppressive where incomes are lower, and open to challenge under BLGC s. 152 (no unjust, excessive or confiscatory charges).
Bacoor's 1% surcharge plus 1% monthly interest is within BLGC s. 191, but BLGC s. 153 lets the council use a Shari'ah-compliant charge instead of interest; the council should decide which it wants.

Drop the waste-to-energy plant. Burning municipal waste runs into the national Clean Air Act (RA 8749) and RA 9003, and it is beyond most municipal budgets; a composting or bio-digester facility is a more realistic target.

Grade the flat ₱5,000 fine by offence and keep it within the cap: ₱5,000 or 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489), ₱5,000 or 1 year for a city (s. 509). Don't leave waste uncollected as a penalty, as it ends up burned or in the river. And don't let the mayor deputise 'any resident' to collect fees, which BLGC s. 152 forbids.
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities that already collect garbage on a schedule and can work out what it costs.

ordinances.title: Ordinance instituting an engagement with the 27 barangays of Naga in the management, collection, and disposal of solid wastes; appropriating funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay Solid Waste Management Volunteers Ordinance of Naga City
ordinances.summary: Sets up paid barangay volunteers who help the City run waste collection, segregation and disposal in each of Naga's 27 barangays. The City Solid Waste Management Office recruits, trains and equips them with the Punong Barangays, and they serve as the office's focal persons in their barangays.
points: The City Solid Waste Management Office sets how many volunteers each barangay needs, by population, area and waste volume; current Barangay Environment Monitors get preference
Volunteers keep roads, drainage canals and waterways clean, enforce segregation and run the barangay MRF, and move residual waste to the city sanitary landfill
Volunteers are deputised to issue citation tickets for violations of city and barangay ordinances
Honoraria of ₱3,000 a month per volunteer, plus a yearly awards scheme for barangays
The Solid Waste Management Board reports yearly to the Mayor and council by the first quarter; funding starts in FY 2026

provisions.title: Barangay volunteers to share the city's waste duties
provisions.text: The ordinance pays volunteer workers in each of Naga's 27 barangays to help the City manage, collect and dispose of solid waste, devolving part of the RA 9003 mandate to the barangays.

provisions.title: The SWMO sets how many volunteers each barangay gets
provisions.text: The City Solid Waste Management Office fixes each barangay's number of volunteers by population, area and volume of waste collected, and picks them with the Punong Barangay and the barangay kagawad on environment. Incumbent Barangay Environment Monitors get preference.

provisions.title: The city trains, contracts and equips them
provisions.text: The SWMO trains and orients the volunteers, prepares their engagement contracts, processes their accomplishment reports and time records, and supplies tools, equipment and safety gear.

provisions.title: What the volunteers do
provisions.text: As the SWMO's focal persons in their barangays, they keep roads, streets, drainage canals and waterways clean, enforce segregation, keep the barangay MRF working, move recyclables to the MRF and residual waste to the city sanitary landfill, and support composting.

provisions.title: Deputised to issue citation tickets
provisions.text: Volunteers are deputised to issue citation tickets to violators of city and barangay ordinances, and earn the incentives set in City Ordinance 2004-046.

provisions.title: ₱3,000 a month, plus yearly barangay awards
provisions.text: Each volunteer gets an honorarium of ₱3,000 a month. The SWMO also sets up an awards and incentives scheme that recognises well-performing, compliant barangays and communities every year.

provisions.title: A yearly report from the Solid Waste Management Board
provisions.text: The Solid Waste Management Board monitors and evaluates the ordinance and reports to the Mayor and the Sangguniang Panlungsod by the first quarter of every year.

provisions.title: Funded in the city budget from FY 2026
provisions.text: Funds go into the SWMO's investment plan and budget and the City's budget beginning FY 2026. The ordinance takes effect on approval and publication.

details.effect: upon approval and publication
details.covers: The 27 barangays of Naga and the solid waste volunteers they engage
details.enforcers: City Solid Waste Management Office, with punong barangays; monitored by the SWM Board
creates: Barangay Solid Waste Management Volunteers program (P3,000 monthly honoraria)
details.funding: Solid Waste Management Office budget and the city budget, from fiscal year 2026

barmm.why: Worth reading if waste collection and segregation in your LGU stop at the poblacion because barangays have no staff to run them. Naga pays a few trained volunteers in every barangay to enforce segregation, keep drains clear and run the barangay MRF, which is cheaper than hiring. It is 3 pages and easy to copy, but it assumes a working disposal site and a city waste office.

apply.if: If your LGU has a solid waste office or an environment officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by having that office set how many volunteers each barangay needs, by population, area and waste volume, and recruit and train them with the punong barangays.

apply.if: If your barangays have no materials recovery facility yet
apply.then: start the volunteers on collection, segregation and drain cleaning, and add MRF duties once a facility is built or shared among barangays.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot fund honoraria from the general fund
apply.then: begin with fewer volunteers in the barangays with the most waste, and say in the ordinance when funding starts and which budget it comes from, as Naga did.

apply.if: If you want volunteers to issue citation tickets
apply.then: first pass or check the penal ordinance they will enforce, and have the mayor deputise them in writing.

change: Replace the RA 7160 legal basis with BLGC s. 17 (general welfare), s. 480 (the municipal solid waste management board, plan and MRF; s. 496 extends this to cities) and s. 408 (barangay segregation and MRF), with RA 9003 cited as the national law

Base the city or municipality paying for barangay volunteers on BLGC s. 20 (augmentation of a lower unit's service) and s. 414 (volunteer community brigades), instead of the DBM position classification manual
Check the honorarium against the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17) on engaging non-plantilla workers, and against the 45% or 55% personal services cap in BLGC s. 349

Deputising volunteers to issue citation tickets needs a written designation by the mayor and must point to a penal ordinance that already exists; volunteers are not persons in authority under BLGC s. 416, so train them and limit them to ticketing
Say when funding starts and where it sits in the budget, since Naga deferred the money to the following fiscal year
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a working disposal site and a waste office to run the volunteers.

ordinances.title: The Gender and Development (GAD) Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: A comprehensive gender and development code that makes every municipal office mainstream gender in planning and budgeting and sets aside at least 5% of the budget for GAD programmes. It defines and prohibits violence, trafficking, harassment and exploitation of women and children, creates GAD bodies and support services, and sets local penalties for employers, establishments and offices that fail to comply.
points: Creates a Municipal GAD Council chaired by the Mayor (meeting at least quarterly), an Integrated Gender and Development Office under the Mayor, an inter-agency council for the protection of women and children, and a Council for Women.
At least 5% of the total budget for GAD programmes and at least 5% of the health budget for women's health; all GAD-funded plans must be reviewed and endorsed by the GAD Council.
Offers LGU employees extra maternity leave of up to 75 days (from 60) and paternity leave of up to 14 days (from 7), subject to a collective negotiation agreement.
Requires employers to provide women's seats, separate toilets, breastfeeding corners and diaper-changing stations; firms with more than 100 employees must provide reproductive health services.
Sets up a 24-hour women's desk at the PNP station, a medico-legal desk at the Municipal Health Office, barangay GAD committees and a committee on decorum and investigation.
All municipal departments must report compliance to the Sangguniang Bayan within 6 months and every 6 months after.

provisions.title: Gender mainstreaming in every office
provisions.text: All municipal offices must build gender into planning, budgeting and evaluation, set GAD performance indicators, and remove gender bias from their rules within 2 years. The municipality draws up a 3-year GAD Plan within its local development plan.

provisions.title: Local bans beyond national law
provisions.text: Internet shops must keep users visible, rows 1 metre apart, porn filters on and supervised units for minors. Forced marriage, sex tours, beauty contests that treat women as sex objects, using women as prizes in fund-raisers, and discrimination by sexual orientation are unlawful.
provisions.section: Ch. II, Art. I, Secs. 13 to 19

provisions.title: Women's desks at the police and health office
provisions.text: The PNP Loon station keeps a 24-hour women's desk where female officers trained in abuse cases handle complaints, and the Municipal Health Office has a medico-legal desk for women.

provisions.title: A GAD Council chaired by the mayor
provisions.text: The mayor chairs and the vice mayor vice-chairs a council of the SB secretary, budget, planning, health, social welfare and GAD offices, the Liga, the People's Council and women's NGOs. It meets at least quarterly and reviews every GAD program before it is carried out.

provisions.title: A council against abuse and a GAD office
provisions.text: An inter-agency council on abuse of women and children, chaired by the SB social welfare committee chair with DSWD, DOJ, PNP, NBI, DOLE and others, is created. An Integrated Gender and Development Office under the mayor serves as its and the GAD Council's secretariat.
provisions.section: Ch. III, Art. I, Secs. 8 to 11

provisions.title: Barangay GAD committees and a Council for Women
provisions.text: Every barangay forms a GAD committee that sets aside at least 5% of its budget for GAD. A municipal Council for Women, drawn from barangay women's organizations, is the GAD office's consultative assembly.

provisions.title: Longer maternity and paternity leave
provisions.text: Municipal employees with at least 1 year of service may get maternity leave of up to 75 days instead of 60, for breastfeeding, and paternity leave of up to 14 days instead of 7, if agreed in a collective negotiation agreement.

provisions.title: Workplace facilities and harassment rules
provisions.text: Employers must provide seats, separate toilets, a women's dressing room, breastfeeding corners and diaper-changing stations; firms with over 100 workers give reproductive health services. Every office runs harassment orientations, and the HRMO sets up a committee on decorum and investigation.
provisions.section: Ch. III, Art. IV, Secs. 4, 7, 8; Ch. IV, Art. III, Secs. 4, 5

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Sexual harassment draws 1 to 6 months in jail or ₱10,000 to ₱20,000. Cyber pornography costs ₱2,500 or 6 months. Employers without required facilities or health services pay ₱2,500 and lose their permit; government heads face 3 months' suspension without pay.

provisions.title: 5% for GAD and 5% of health for women
provisions.text: The municipality appropriates at least 5% of its total budget for GAD, and every plan charged to it needs GAD Council endorsement. At least 5% of the health budget goes to women's health. Offices report compliance to the SB within 6 months and every 6 months after.
provisions.section: Ch. III, Art. V, Sec. 2; Ch. V, Secs. 2, 3

ordinances.penalties: Mostly a ₱2,500 fine with suspension or cancellation of business permits; national-law penalties apply to trafficking, mail-order brides (6 to 8 years and ₱8,000 to ₱20,000) and sexual harassment (1 to 6 months or ₱10,000 to ₱20,000).
ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies all ordinances and local issuances inconsistent with it; no specific ordinance named.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU sets aside a GAD budget but has no code saying who plans it, who reviews it and which offices must report on it. Loon answers those questions with a GAD council chaired by the mayor, barangay GAD committees and a compliance report from every department every 6 months. It is a long 2008 code, so several of its national-law references and its leave clause are out of date.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a Gender Focal Point System
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving it Loon's council duties: meet at least quarterly, and review and endorse every plan that draws on the GAD budget before it is funded.

apply.if: If your LGU has no GAD body or focal point yet
apply.then: start with the council chaired by the mayor and the 6-month compliance report from each department, and leave the separate GAD office and Council for Women for later.

apply.if: If your health office runs women's health services
apply.then: earmark at least 5% of the health budget for them, as Loon does, and make gender-sensitivity training compulsory for health workers.

apply.if: If you issue business permits to employers with women workers
apply.then: attach Loon's workplace rules to the permit: separate toilets, breastfeeding corners and diaper-changing stations, with a ₱2,500 fine and permit suspension for violators.

apply.if: If your barangays have VAW desks but the police station has no women's desk
apply.then: copy the 24-hour women's desk at the police station and the medico-legal desk at the health office, so barangay referrals have somewhere to go.

change: Re-cite the 5% GAD allocation to BLGC s. 348 and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 (no GAD plan for 2 years, no accomplishment report or no Gender Focal Point System) and s. 584 (GAD budget used outside the plan)

Replace the integrated GAD office and the Council for Women with the Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8), and the women's development council required by BLGC s. 130

Drop the extra maternity leave clause: 75 days is now below the 105 days that national law (RA 11210) already gives. Check any extra paternity leave for LGU staff against the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17) first

Update the national-law penalties it repeats: the mail-order bride provisions it cites were replaced by RA 10906, and trafficking now runs under RA 9208 as amended. Refer to national law rather than copy penalty figures that go stale

Expect debate on the anti-discrimination section for LGBT people and on the reproductive health chapter. If your council drops or reframes them, keep a general non-harassment clause (national law, RA 11313) and maternal health services, and consult local ulama on birth-spacing language
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with a health office and a police station that can staff a women's desk.

ordinances.title: The Gender and Development Code of the Province of La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development Code of La Union
ordinances.summary: A 107-section provincial code on women's rights and gender equality, covering GAD programs, support services, political participation, work, health, education, livelihood, special sectors and violence against women and children. It creates a provincial Gender and Development Office to coordinate and monitor the code. Violations of the criminal provisions are prosecuted under national law.
points: Creates a provincial Gender and Development Office headed by a department head, with administrative, monitoring and training divisions
Creates a Pageant Regulatory Board and a task force against domestic violence
Declares March 8 of every year Provincial Women's Day and calls for a women's summit
Requires gender sensitivity orientation, registration of domestic workers and a gender-sensitive physical plan
Covers trafficking, sex trade, rape, sexual harassment, pornographic shows and surveillance of entertainment establishments
The Governor must form a committee to issue implementing rules within 60 days of publication

provisions.title: Gender sensitivity training for all officials
provisions.text: The province develops modules and a speakers' bureau to train barangay and municipal officials and employees, and all schools, offices and establishments in the province get gender sensitivity orientation, including men's role in the family.

provisions.title: A Pageant Regulatory Board at every level
provisions.text: Each municipality, city and the province creates a board, chaired by the governor or mayor, that sets rules for beauty contests; organisers need its permit, children may not join popularity contests, and violations draw ₱5,000 or 1 year in jail.

provisions.title: A crisis centre for women and children
provisions.text: A Women and Children Development Center, run by the PSWDO and the police women's desks, opens within 90 days as a temporary shelter with psychological services, with ₱1,000,000 from the GAD fund to start.

provisions.title: A coordinating council and an anti-trafficking task force
provisions.text: A Gender Multi-Sectoral Coordinating Council chaired by the governor forms within 60 days, and a Task Force Against Domestic Violence and Trafficking, co-chaired by the DOJ, runs prevention, counselling, referral and reintegration programs.

provisions.title: Provincial Women's Day and a yearly summit
provisions.text: March 8 is Provincial Women's Day, a special working holiday, and the coordinating council holds a Women's Summit at least once a year, with ₱800,000 from the GAD fund.

provisions.title: Women in governance and special bodies
provisions.text: The province backs women's organisations and their accreditation, and ensures women sit in the Provincial Development Council and all local special bodies at every level.

provisions.title: Workplace orientation, plans and kasambahay registration
provisions.text: Offices and businesses hold a yearly sexual harassment orientation and adopt a gender-sensitive physical plan; LGUs survey domestic workers yearly, households register them, and all must be enrolled in SSS.

provisions.title: Local penalties for battering and forced marriage
provisions.text: Husband and wife battering draws 1 month to 1 year in jail or ₱1,000 to ₱5,000; forcing a woman to marry draws ₱5,000 or 1 year, respecting indigenous customs; prohibited fund-raising draws ₱5,000 or 6 months.

provisions.title: A provincial GAD Office with 3 divisions
provisions.text: A Gender and Development Office headed by a department head, appointed by the governor with SP concurrence, has administrative, monitoring and coordinating, and training and special services divisions, and reports on compliance every 6 months.

provisions.title: Criminal acts prosecuted under national law
provisions.text: Trafficking, sex trade, sex tours, rape, sexual harassment, pornographic shows and other listed acts are prosecuted under national law; the governor's committee issues implementing rules within 60 days of publication.

ordinances.penalties: No local fines; violations of Sections 57 to 70, 73, 77, 79, 80 and 91 are prosecuted under existing national laws
ordinances.caveat: The ordinance number is partly illegible in the scan; 071-2015 is taken from the source file name.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has a GAD budget but no single law saying which office does what for women. La Union's code turns national women's laws into offices, programs and duties across work, health, education, livelihood and violence, and sends crimes to national law instead of setting local fines. It is a provincial code of 107 sections, and parts of it, such as the pageant board and the reproductive health sections, need rework with your women's council and religious leaders before adoption.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a gender focal point system or a women's development officer
apply.then: you can replicate the GAD office by giving that officer the 3 roles La Union splits into divisions: administration, monitoring and coordination, and training and special services.

apply.if: If you have no GAD office yet
apply.then: do as La Union did and let the social welfare office run the code in the meantime, with the existing programs and their funds, until the office is created.

apply.if: If your LGU has no crisis service for women and children yet
apply.then: set a deadline and an amount to open one, as La Union set 90 days and ₱1 million from the GAD fund, and run it with the social welfare office and the police women and children desk.

apply.if: If your barangays run day care or child development centres
apply.then: copy the floor on day care workers' honoraria, topped up from the GAD fund, and the yearly evaluation of their work.

apply.if: If you are a municipality
apply.then: take the GAD office, support services and livelihood chapters, and leave the pageant board and the task forces to the province.

change: Re-cite the legal basis from RA 7160 to BLGC s. 17 and s. 521, and build the office around the local women's development officer in BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8)
Tie the code's funding to the 5% GAD allocation in BLGC s. 348, and write in the sanctions BLGC s. 582 and s. 584 already set for a missing GAD plan or a misused GAD budget

Replace the domestic violence task force with the women's development council and the barangay VAW desk required by BLGC s. 130 and s. 408, and state that VAWC cases go to the courts, since BLGC s. 436 bars them from barangay settlement

Rework the reproductive health and pageant sections with the regional health ministry, the Women Commission and religious leaders instead of copying the Pageant Regulatory Board and the RH definitions word for word
Keep March 8 as an observance under RA 6949 (national law), not a holiday; any local holiday goes through the Chief Minister under BLGC s. 14 and BAA No. 39
barmm.fits: Provinces and cities with a GAD budget to program; municipalities can take the office and services chapters.

ordinances.title: An ordinance enacting the Gender and Development (GAD) Code of the City of Muntinlupa
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development (GAD) Code of the City of Muntinlupa
ordinances.summary: Muntinlupa's GAD Code is the main basis for all city policy on gender and development. It sets gender mainstreaming duties sector by sector: education, health, environment, labour, governance, trade, peace and order, and disaster risk reduction. It creates a GAD focal point system and a permanent GAD Office, and lists prohibited acts with penalties.
points: At least 5% of the city's total annual budget goes to GAD programs, projects and services
Creates the Muntinlupa City GAD Focal Point System and a GAD Office as a regular division under the Office of the City Mayor, replacing the office created by Executive Order No. 2 of 17 January 2014
City offices and barangays must act on reports of violence against women and children within 24 hours, or face neglect-of-duty charges
Bans fund-raising that uses men or women as prizes (₱2,500 and/or 6 months) and degrading beauty contests in schools and barangays
Disclosing the identities of victims or offenders is punished by 15 days in jail or ₱2,500; degrading media content by ₱2,500 or 1 month
Sets up a Muntinlupa Council of Women, a Women's Congress every March and a city GAD Center for women in especially difficult circumstances

provisions.title: A VAW desk in every barangay
provisions.text: The city ensures a Violence Against Women Desk in every barangay and trains barangay personnel to handle violence against women cases in a gender-responsive way.

provisions.title: A Council of Women and women's representation
provisions.text: Barangay women's organizations are encouraged and accredited, and a Muntinlupa Council of Women from their representatives advises the city council. Women must be represented in local special bodies and the city and barangay development councils.

provisions.title: A Women's Congress every March
provisions.text: During Women's Month the city holds a Women's Congress every March, where it reports on its work for women's economic empowerment, human rights and gender-responsive governance.

provisions.title: 24 hours to act on violence reports
provisions.text: City offices and barangays must act on complaints of violence against women and children within 24 hours. Failing to do so is neglect of duty, punished under the VAWC, anti-trafficking and other cited laws and the Civil Service rules.

provisions.title: No women or men as prizes, no degrading contests
provisions.text: Fund-raising that uses men or women as prizes draws a ₱2,500 fine, 6 months in jail, or both. Beauty contests that degrade women, men or children are banned in schools and barangays. Soliciting sexual services and prostitution are banned.

provisions.title: No deposits before emergency treatment
provisions.text: Hospitals and clinics may not demand a deposit or advance payment before treating emergency or serious cases, or refuse treatment needed to prevent death or permanent disability.

provisions.title: Protecting identities and banning degrading media
provisions.text: Disclosing the identities of victims or offenders draws 15 days in jail or ₱2,500, or both. Degrading reports, programs or ads draw ₱2,500 or 1 month, or both, and the court may suspend the permit or franchise.

provisions.title: A GAD focal point system led by the mayor
provisions.text: The Muntinlupa City GAD Focal Point System has an Executive Committee chaired by the mayor, with council committee chairs, department heads, the schools superintendent, the DILG, the police chief and an NGO representative, plus a technical working group.

provisions.title: A permanent GAD Office and a GAD Center
provisions.text: A GAD Office becomes a regular division under the Office of the City Mayor, replacing the office created by Executive Order No. 2 of 17 January 2014. A city GAD Center supports women in especially difficult circumstances.

provisions.title: At least 5% of the budget for GAD
provisions.text: The city council appropriates at least 5% of the city's total annual budget for GAD programs, projects, activities and services, which fund the code.

ordinances.penalties: ₱2,500 fines, or 15 days to 6 months in jail, for specific offences; other violations fall under national laws

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU sets aside the 5% GAD budget but has no code saying which office does what with it. Muntinlupa spells out duties sector by sector, from schools, health and labour to peace and order and disaster response, and creates a focal point system and a GAD office. It is 43 pages, written for a city with staff for a full office, and has only one short section on Muslim and Indigenous women.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a GAD focal point system
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the sector chapters and assigning each one to the office that already runs that sector, so the 5% is planned office by office.

apply.if: If you have no GAD office or women's development officer
apply.then: start by designating one officer under BLGC s. 547 and let the focal point system do the planning, instead of creating Muntinlupa's full division.

apply.if: If your barangays have a VAW desk
apply.then: adopt the 24-hour deadline to act on reports of violence against women and children, make missing it neglect of duty, and have the desk refer cases to the police and social welfare, not the lupon.

apply.if: If your LGU or its schools hold pageants and fund-raising contests
apply.then: add the bans on using people as prizes and on degrading contests, with fines set within your own cap.

apply.if: If you have no women's council yet
apply.then: set up the one BLGC s. 130 requires and hold a yearly women's congress in March, as Muntinlupa does.

change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the BLGC's own sanctions: failing to submit the GAD Plan or set up the focal point system is dereliction of duty (s. 582), and using GAD funds outside the plan is abuse of authority (s. 584).

Replace the GAD Office under the Mayor with the Local Women's Development Officer in BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8); an LGU near its personal services cap in BLGC s. 349 can designate an existing employee.

Route all VAWC reports to the barangay VAW desk (BLGC s. 408) and the police, never to the lupon: BLGC s. 436 bars amicable settlement of violence against women and their children; the basis stays national law (RA 9262 and the Magna Carta of Women).
Expand Muntinlupa's short section on Muslim and Indigenous women (s. 39) into articles covering Moro, Indigenous and settler women, and link the women's council to the one BLGC s. 130 requires.

Check penalties against your level: a municipality may set at most ₱5,000 or 6 months (BLGC s. 489), a barangay at most ₱3,000 (BLGC s. 419); drop the clause replacing Muntinlupa's Executive Order No. 2.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities that already set aside the GAD budget and want a code to spread it across offices; smaller LGUs can run it with one designated officer.

ordinances.title: Adopting the Marikina City Gender and Development Code of 2015
ordinances.shortTitle: Marikina City Gender and Development (GAD) Ordinance
ordinances.summary: This is a city gender and development code. It frames gender equality through protecting the family, and it covers gender violence, education, health, economic life, public participation and gender mainstreaming across city offices. It sets up the city's GAD focal point system, a GAD office and a GAD budget.
points: Prohibits physical, sexual, psychological and economic abuse against women, children, family members and LGBT persons.
Expands the Marikina Referral System to all victim-survivors of gender violence, with emergency shelter, medical aid and legal assistance.
Public officials who fail or refuse to help victim-survivors are held criminally and administratively liable under RA 3815, RA 6713 and RA 3019.
Reconstitutes the Marikina GAD Focal Point System with honoraria: ₱3,000 per semester for the chair, ₱2,500 per semester for ExeCom members and ₱2,000 a month for TWG members.
Creates a Marikina GAD Office with 12 positions, headed at SG-26, and funds it from the GAD budget.
The GAD budget must be at least 5% of the city's total budget appropriations.

provisions.title: Gender violence is prohibited
provisions.text: Bans physical, sexual, psychological and economic abuse against women, children, family members and LGBT persons, from rape, harassment and voyeurism to stalking, online abuse and controlling a victim's money or work.
provisions.section: Ch. II, Art. I, Secs. II, III

provisions.title: A wider referral system for victim-survivors
provisions.text: Extends the Marikina Referral System to victims of all gender violence, with shelter, medical, legal and psychological help, protection orders, counselling, livelihood training and scholarships, and screening and counselling for perpetrators.

provisions.title: Shelters, a legal fund and barangay VAW desks
provisions.text: The city sets up a Bahay Pag-asa, a women's shelter and a halfway house, keeps a legal assistance fund for indigent victims from the GAD budget, and gives plantilla posts and hazard pay to barangay VAW desk staff.

provisions.title: Liability of officials and penalties
provisions.text: Officials who fail or refuse to help victim-survivors are criminally and administratively liable under RA 3815, RA 6713 and RA 3019. Gender violence not covered by national law draws up to ₱5,000 in fines, up to 1 year in jail, or both.

provisions.title: Gender-fair schools and health care
provisions.text: The city trains teachers and health workers in gender sensitivity, promotes gender-sensitive curricula and family planning education, gives scholarships to women and children, and sets up a special education and rehabilitation centre.

provisions.title: Economic life and representation
provisions.text: Supports community child minding centres, socialized lending for solo mothers, persons with disabilities and seniors, tax incentives for firms giving care leave, and seats for marginalized groups, including Moro women and children, in special bodies.

provisions.title: Gender mainstreaming in every office
provisions.text: All city offices must mainstream gender, run gender analysis when drafting their yearly GAD plans and budgets, and report accomplishments.

provisions.title: A GAD focal point system with honoraria
provisions.text: Renames the GAD team the Marikina GAD Focal Point System, chaired by the Mayor with the women's committee chair as vice-chair. Honoraria: ₱3,000 a semester for the chair, ₱3,000 a month for the vice-chair, ₱2,500 a semester for ExeCom and ₱2,000 a month for TWG members.

provisions.title: A GAD office with 12 positions
provisions.text: Creates a Marikina GAD Office for admin, research and advocacy, crisis and livelihood services, and monitoring. It has 12 positions, headed at SG-26 with an assistant head at SG-24, funded automatically from the GAD budget.

provisions.title: A GAD budget of at least 5%
provisions.text: Programs under the code are funded from a GAD budget of at least 5% of the city's total appropriations, tracked by the budget and accounting offices. The code takes effect 15 days after publication.
provisions.section: Ch. III, Art. IV; Ch. IV

ordinances.penalties: Penalties under the national laws (RA 9262, RA 9208, RA 7877 and others). Where none applies, a fine of up to ₱5,000, up to 1 year in jail, or both.

sponsors: Councilor Thaddeus Antonio M. Santos, Jr.
Vice-Mayor Jose Fabian I. Cadiz, M.D.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has a GAD budget on paper but no working focal point system or referral path for survivors of violence. Marikina's code sets out the focal point structure, a referral system with shelter, medical and legal help, and a legal assistance fund paid from the GAD budget. It is 26 pages and city-scale: its 12-position office and honoraria for staff members will not fit most budgets as written.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a GAD focal point system
apply.then: you can replicate the duties Marikina gives its chair, executive committee and technical working group to plan, budget, monitor and report, and check your current members against them.

apply.if: If you have no shelter or crisis facility
apply.then: start with the referral part: list which office or agency gives shelter, medical aid, legal help and counselling, sign agreements with them, and pay for it from the GAD budget.

apply.if: If your LGU can fund only one GAD post
apply.then: skip the 12-position office and appoint a local women's development officer or designate a focal person to run the system.

apply.if: If your barangays have VAW desks
apply.then: copy the rule that barangay officials follow the RA 9262 steps for handling cases, and set aside GAD money for the desk personnel.

apply.if: If you want a legal assistance fund
apply.then: set it up as Marikina did, for indigent survivors' lawyers and documents, and say in the ordinance that it comes from the GAD budget.

change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the accountability rules: s. 582 (no GAD plan, accomplishment report or focal point system is dereliction of duty) and s. 584 (using GAD funds outside the plan is abuse of authority).

Replace the 12-position GAD office headed at SG-26 with a Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, qualified under Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8). If your LGU is 4th class or lower, BLGC s. 349 caps personal services at 55% of regular income, so check the cost first.
Drop or reword the honoraria for focal point members who are already LGU employees; BLGC s. 107 bars additional compensation unless a law authorises it, and auditors will question it.
Keep the residual penalty within the cap of the enacting LGU: ₱5,000 or 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509), but ₱5,000 or 6 months for a municipality (s. 489).

If the family planning and education articles are contested, rework them with local religious leaders and Indigenous elders. Keep protection from violence for every person, including LGBT persons; if the wording is contested, frame the clause as protection for everyone regardless of who they are, rather than leave anyone out.
barmm.fits: Cities and 1st to 3rd class municipalities that can staff a GAD unit; smaller LGUs can take the focal point and referral parts only.

ordinances.title: Promulgating the Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) Code of 2025 of the City of San Fernando, La Union
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender Equality and Social Inclusion Code of the City of San Fernando, La Union (GESI Code)
ordinances.summary: A city code that localizes the Magna Carta of Women, the anti-VAWC and anti-trafficking laws for San Fernando. It sets gender equality and inclusion duties across governance, health, education, labour, agriculture, trade and tourism, housing, disaster response, media and sports. It also penalizes sexual harassment in public spaces and sets up a GAD Office and focal point system.
points: Sexual harassment in public spaces is graded light, medium or severe, with fines of ₱2,000, ₱3,000 or ₱5,000 plus gender sensitivity training
Creates an Anti-Sexual Harassment Desk, with barangay VAW desk persons serving as ASH Desk officers
A Pageant Regulatory Board, chaired by the Mayor, regulates beauty contests
Creates a city GAD Office headed by a department head (Salary Grade 25) and a Gender Focal Point System
At least 5% of the city's annual budget goes to the GAD agenda; departments and barangays must report compliance to the council within 1 year and every year after
Bans sex trafficking, commodification of women and pornographic displays that treat women as sex objects

provisions.title: Gender mainstreaming in every city plan
provisions.text: The City adopts gender mainstreaming, writing gender equality and social inclusion goals into its whole planning and budgeting cycle, from the Comprehensive Development Plan and Annual Investment Program to the land use, disaster, health and waste plans.

provisions.title: Women make up a third of development councils
provisions.text: At least one third of the members of the City and Barangay Development Councils must be women, and women must be represented in the Lupong Tagapamayapa and peace and order councils.

provisions.title: Workplace duties for every employer
provisions.text: No one may be denied work, training or promotion for sexual orientation, gender identity, age, ethnicity, religion or civil status. Every office and company must offer support such as child-minding, lactation stations and flexible hours, and set up a committee on decorum and investigation on sexual harassment.

provisions.title: Protection for house helpers and informal workers
provisions.text: Households must enlist their house helpers with the barangay, and the CSWDO keeps a database to check work hours, days off and SSS and PhilHealth contributions. Women in entertainment jobs are wage earners entitled to at least the minimum wage.

provisions.title: Sexual harassment in public spaces fined
provisions.text: Catcalling and similar light violations draw ₱2,000, stalking and lewd gestures ₱3,000, and groping or public exposure ₱5,000, each with gender sensitivity training, or jail of up to 30 days (6 months for severe cases), or both.

provisions.title: An Anti-Sexual Harassment Desk, enforcers and hotline
provisions.text: An ASH Desk in the GAD Building takes and refers complaints, with barangay VAW desk persons as ASH Desk officers reporting quarterly. Traffic enforcers and tanods become ASH enforcers who can arrest offenders caught in the act; a hotline and a referral network support survivors.

provisions.title: Bans on trafficking, pornography and commodifying women
provisions.text: Sex trafficking, mail-order bride schemes, buying or selling women, luring women into prostitution, pornographic displays that treat women as sex objects, and activities that commodify women are prohibited and punished under national law.

provisions.title: A Pageant Regulatory Board
provisions.text: Beauty contests are strictly regulated by a board chaired by the Mayor, with the women and family committee chair as vice chair and members from the council, tourism, GAD, DepEd, CHED, the Liga, an NGO and the LGBTQIA+ community.

provisions.title: A GAD Office and Gender Focal Point System
provisions.text: A Gender Focal Point System with an executive committee, TWG, secretariat and M&E team is set up. A GAD Office of 12 staff, headed by a department head at Salary Grade 25, serves as its secretariat, with salaries charged to the GAD budget.

provisions.title: 5% of the budget and yearly compliance reports
provisions.text: At least 5% of the City's annual budget goes to the GAD agenda and plan. Every department and barangay reports its compliance to the council within 1 year and every year after.

ordinances.penalties: ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 plus gender sensitivity training, or up to 30 days in jail (up to 6 months for severe harassment), or both

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU spends its GAD budget without a plan that ties it to each office. San Fernando's 2025 code sets gender duties sector by sector, from health and labour to disaster response, and gives women harassed in public a local remedy through graded fines and an anti-sexual harassment desk. It is a recent city code with a department-level GAD office, so a smaller LGU will need to cut the structure down.

apply.if: If your LGU has a Gender Focal Point System
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving it the sector-by-sector duties and requiring every office and barangay to report compliance to the sanggunian within 1 year and every year after.

apply.if: If your barangays already have VAW desk persons
apply.then: name them as anti-sexual harassment desk officers, as San Fernando does, so no new barangay post is needed.

apply.if: If public-space harassment is not yet penalised in your LGU
apply.then: take the 3 grades (light, medium, severe) with fines of ₱2,000, ₱3,000 and ₱5,000 plus gender sensitivity training, and check each offence against the Safe Spaces Act first.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot fund a separate GAD department
apply.then: skip the SG 25 office and run the code through the focal point system and a women's development officer.

apply.if: If you keep lists of farmers, fisherfolk or entrepreneurs
apply.then: split them by sex, as the code requires, and seat women on the bodies that manage local resources.

change: Re-cite the 5% GAD budget to BLGC s. 348, and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 (no GAD plan or focal point system) and s. 584 (misuse of the GAD budget)

Replace the SG 25 GAD department with a Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8). Size the office to the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349, which is tighter for 4th to 6th class LGUs

Align the public-space harassment offences and fines with the Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313, national law), and keep jail terms within BLGC s. 489 (6 months for municipalities) or s. 509 (1 year for cities)

Drop the Pageant Regulatory Board. Expect objection to the SOGIE and reproductive health sections, so settle them early with the ulama and the Women Commission; the RH law and the Magna Carta of Women still apply as national law
Leave marriage and divorce among Muslims to the Code of Muslim Personal Laws and the Shari'ah courts, and keep VAWC cases out of barangay settlement as BLGC s. 436 requires
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a working Gender Focal Point System and offices that can each take on GAD duties.

ordinances.title: Ordinance enacting the Revenue Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.shortTitle: 1998 Revenue Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.summary: Pangasinan's provincial revenue code governing the levy, assessment and collection of provincial taxes, fees and charges. The available pages set the provincial taxes on printing and publication, franchises, quarry resources, professions, amusements and delivery vehicles.
points: Tax on printing and publishing and on franchises: 50% of 1% of gross annual receipts
Tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources: 10% of fair market value per cubic metre or metric ton, with permit and monthly reporting rules
Professional tax: ₱300 a year, due by 31 January; professionals in government service are exempt
Amusement tax: 30% of gross admission receipts, shared equally with the municipality; operas, concerts and exhibits are exempt except pop and rock concerts
Annual fixed tax of ₱500 on each delivery truck or van of liquor, soft drinks, cigarettes and other products

provisions.title: Covers every provincial tax, fee and charge
provisions.text: The Revenue Code governs the levy, assessment and collection of all provincial taxes, fees, charges and other impositions in Pangasinan, with rules for reading it, such as counting deadlines in days excluding weekends and holidays at the end.

provisions.title: Tax on printing and publishing
provisions.text: Printers and publishers pay 50% of 1% of the previous year's gross receipts, or 1/20 of 1% of capital for a new business, by 20 January. Receipts from DepEd-prescribed school texts and references are exempt.

provisions.title: Franchise tax
provisions.text: Businesses enjoying a franchise pay 50% of 1% of the previous year's gross receipts earned in the province, or 1/20 of 1% of paid-up capital for a new business, adjusted for branches in other provinces or cities.

provisions.title: 10% tax on sand, gravel and quarry resources
provisions.text: Extractors pay 10% of the fair market value per cubic metre or metric ton, set in a table from ₱25 a cubic metre for ordinary earth to ₱150 for gravel. Proceeds go 30% to the province, 30% to the municipality and 40% to the barangay where the materials are taken.

provisions.title: Quarry permit rules and fines
provisions.text: Permit holders file a monthly production report by the 5th of the next month. Hauling without an ENRO delivery receipt costs ₱100 per cubic metre or ton, and equipment used without a permit is fined ₱2,000 each or impounded; illegal quarrying is charged as theft of minerals.

provisions.title: Late quarry reports
provisions.text: Late reports are fined ₱1,000, ₱2,000 then ₱3,000 plus ₱10 to ₱30 a day; reports missing after a month ₱2,000, ₱3,000 then ₱5,000 plus ₱20 to ₱50 a day, capped at ₱10,000. Unpaid fines or missing reports can cost the permit.

provisions.title: ₱300 professional tax
provisions.text: Every licensed professional pays ₱300 a year to the provincial treasurer by 31 January, which lets them practise anywhere in the country. Employers must check it is paid; 2 years unpaid bars practice in the province. Professionals employed only by the government are exempt.

provisions.title: 30% amusement tax, shared with the municipality
provisions.text: Theatres, cinemas, concert halls, circuses, boxing stadia and other amusement places pay 30% of gross admission receipts, split equally between province and municipality. Operas, concerts, plays, recitals and exhibits are exempt, except pop and rock concerts.

provisions.title: ₱500 a year per delivery truck
provisions.text: Manufacturers, wholesalers, dealers and retailers pay ₱500 a year for each truck or van delivering liquor, soft drinks, cigarettes and other products in the province, and must list their vehicles and plate numbers with the treasurer.

ordinances.penalties: Quarry violations: late reports ₱1,000 to ₱3,000 plus daily fines, missing reports ₱2,000 to ₱5,000, capped at ₱10,000; ₱2,000 per unpermitted piece of equipment
ordinances.caveat: The PDF has only the cover (dated December 11, 1998), the contents and pages 1 to 7 of 31, ending at Section 9; the fees, collection rules, penal provisions and signatures are missing.

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your province is writing or updating its revenue code and wants a checklist of provincial tax bases with the quarry rules spelled out. Pangasinan publishes a fair market value for each quarry material and ties hauling, reporting and equipment to fines. But this is a 1998 fragment: only pages 1 to 7 of 31 survive, and its amusement tax and quarry tax base go beyond what the BLGC allows.

apply.if: If your province already collects a quarry tax
apply.then: you can replicate the enforcement rules: a delivery receipt for every load, a monthly production report due by the 5th of the next month, and fines for late or missing reports, with the amounts re-set under BLGC s. 576.

apply.if: If your province has no published fair market values for quarry materials
apply.then: start with a table like Pangasinan's, one value per cubic metre or metric ton for each material, and update it by ordinance.

apply.if: If you still charge amusement or delivery van taxes under an older code
apply.then: check your rates against BLGC s. 164 and s. 165 before reusing anything here; Pangasinan's 30% amusement tax is 3 times the BLGC cap.

apply.if: If you are a municipality in the Special Geographic Area
apply.then: borrow only the professional tax section, which BLGC s. 600 lets you levy until a province is formed for you.

change: Cut the amusement tax from 30% to no more than 10% of gross admission receipts, still shared equally with the municipality (BLGC s. 164)
Limit the quarry tax to resources taken from public lands and public waters, as BLGC s. 162 allows; Pangasinan's version also reaches private land. Quarry permits up to 5 hectares follow BLGC s. 161

Reset the professional tax (up to ₱1,300, BLGC s. 163) and the delivery van tax (up to ₱2,200, or ₱6,600 for liquor trucks, BLGC s. 165) to the BARMM ceilings. Drop the ban on bringing in quarry materials from outside the province, which BLGC s. 156 on taxing goods in transit makes risky
Re-set the quarry fines against BLGC s. 576 on penalties for tax ordinance violations, and decide whether to use Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rules in place of interest (BLGC s. 153)
Follow the public hearing and publication rules for tax ordinances (BLGC s. 212 and s. 213): full publication for 3 days and posting on the Bangsamoro register, with effect only 15 days after
barmm.fits: Provinces with quarrying to tax and regulate; SGA municipalities for the professional tax only.

ordinances.title: Revised revenue code of the Municipality of General Trias, Province of Cavite
ordinances.shortTitle: Revenue Code of the Municipality of General Trias
ordinances.summary: The municipality's full revenue code, setting the taxes, fees and charges General Trias may collect under the Local Government Code. It covers graduated business taxes, community tax, mayor's permit and regulatory fees, service fees, rentals, garbage and parking charges, and the rules on collection, remedies and penalties. It took effect on 1 January 2003.
points: Chapters on business taxes, community tax, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, municipal charges, administration and penalties
Taxes are due within the first 20 days of January or of each quarter
Late payment carries a 25% surcharge plus interest of up to 2% a month, for no more than 36 months
Annual garbage fees for businesses by floor area, e.g. ₱500 for manufacturers up to 100 sq. m. plus ₱1 per sq. m. beyond
Includes a special levy on lands and a socialized housing tax, to be collected only once an enabling ordinance is passed
Officers of a company that violates the code are held liable, and fines do not excuse unpaid taxes

provisions.title: Graduated business taxes on gross sales
provisions.text: Businesses pay yearly tax on the previous year's gross sales: manufacturers from ₱181.50 below ₱10,000 up to 41.25% of 1% above ₱6,500,000; banks pay 55% of 1% of gross receipts, and peddlers ₱55 each a year.

provisions.title: Taxes due in the first 20 days of the quarter
provisions.text: Business tax is paid within the first 20 days of January, or quarterly within the first 20 days of January, April, July and October; the SB may extend payment without penalty for up to 6 months.

provisions.title: A special levy on land that public works benefit
provisions.text: Land specially benefited by municipal public works pays a levy of 60% of the project cost, including land acquisition; government, church, charitable, cooperative land and owners who donated right-of-way are exempt.

provisions.title: A socialized housing tax on urban land
provisions.text: Urban land assessed above ₱50,000 pays a socialized housing tax of one-half percent of assessed value, collected with the real property tax for the municipal housing program; agrarian, park and institutional land is exempt.

provisions.title: Both levies wait for an enabling ordinance
provisions.text: The special levy and the socialized housing tax are collected only once the SB passes an enabling ordinance; market and slaughterhouse fees stay in force until a separate market code is enacted.

provisions.title: Community tax for residents and companies
provisions.text: Residents 18 and over who work, do business or own property pay ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income, up to ₱5,000; corporations pay ₱500 plus ₱2 per ₱5,000 of property or receipts, up to ₱10,000. It is due by the end of February, then 24% a year interest.

provisions.title: Mayor's permit and regulatory fees
provisions.text: Every business pays an annual Mayor's permit fee for each line and place of business, such as ₱7,500 for manufacturers and ₱2,000 for wholesalers, plus fees for building, cockpits, weights and measures, film-making, signs, water extraction and more.

provisions.title: Garbage fees by floor area
provisions.text: Businesses pay a garbage fee by floor area, such as ₱500 for manufacturers up to 100 sq. m plus ₱1 per sq. m beyond, and ₱300 for restaurants up to 50 sq. m; fees are paid by the 10th of each month.

provisions.title: 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest
provisions.text: Late taxes draw a 25% surcharge plus interest of up to 2% a month, for no more than 36 months; the SB may adjust rates only once every 5 years and by no more than 10%.

provisions.title: Penalties for officers, taxes still due
provisions.text: Violations draw a fine from ₱1,000 and/or imprisonment of 1 to 6 months; a company's president or manager is held liable, and paying a fine does not excuse the unpaid tax. The code took effect on 1 January 2003.

ordinances.penalties: A fine of at least ₱1,000 (the maximum is illegible in the scan), or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both
ordinances.caveat: The scan of the penal clause is partly illegible, and this copy has no signature block, only the line 'Enacted, 16 September 2002'.

details.enforcers: Municipal Treasurer

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU still collects under old or piecemeal revenue ordinances and wants to see what a complete code covers. General Trias puts business taxes, community tax, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, rentals, garbage and parking charges, collection and remedies in one 80-page text. It is from 2002, for a fast-growing Cavite municipality, and its rates and citations predate the BLGC, so use it as a checklist of chapters, not a draft. Part of the penal clause is illegible in the scan.

apply.if: If you already have a revenue code that predates the BLGC
apply.then: compare its chapters with General Trias's 9 and add only the fees you have a service to back, such as weights and measures sealing, garbage collection or parking.

apply.if: If you are writing your first full revenue code
apply.then: follow the chapter order but take every business tax rate from BLGC s. 167 and every fee from your own costs, and hold the public hearings BLGC s. 212 requires before enactment.

apply.if: If your LGU collects garbage from businesses
apply.then: you can replicate the floor-area scale: ₱300 to ₱500 a year for the first 10 to 100 sq. m., plus ₱1 for each sq. m. beyond.

apply.if: If your council prefers not to charge interest
apply.then: keep the 25% surcharge and replace the 2% monthly interest with a Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rule under BLGC s. 153.

apply.if: If you have no plan to pass the enabling ordinances
apply.then: drop the special levy on lands and the socialized housing tax rather than copying them as dead text.

change: Reset every business tax schedule to the ceilings in BLGC s. 167, including the half rate for dealers in essential goods and the exclusion of duly registered Islamic banks.

Rewrite the late-payment clause: BLGC s. 191 still caps the surcharge at 25% and interest at 2% a month for 36 months, but BLGC s. 153 lets the council replace interest with a Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rule, which the council should consider.
Raise the penal clause to the range in BLGC s. 576 (fines of ₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months in jail); the code's ₱1,000 floor falls below it.
Hold the public hearings and publication that BLGC s. 212 and s. 213 require, and note that rates can then be adjusted only once every 5 years by up to 10% under BLGC s. 216.
Drop the socialized housing tax and special levy unless the council will pass the enabling ordinances; the special levy must follow BLGC s. 266 (up to 60% of cost, 5 to 10 annual instalments).
barmm.fits: Municipalities writing their first full revenue code, or replacing one that predates the BLGC.

ordinances.title: Amending several provisions of City Ordinance No. 8182, entitled "An ordinance providing for comprehensive welfare for the children of the City of Manila, and for other purposes", enacted on December 16, 2008 and approved on March 13, 2009, and inserting several provisions thereto…
ordinances.shortTitle: Manila City Children's Welfare Code of 2023
ordinances.summary: This is a full children's code in 13 articles. It replaces Manila's 2009 children's welfare ordinance and covers children's survival, development, participation and protection rights, plus children in need of special protection. It sets up the Manila Council for the Protection of Children with district and barangay councils, and it penalises establishments and parents for listed acts.
points: Creates the Manila Council for the Protection of Children (MCPC), District Councils (DCPC), Barangay Councils (BCPC) and a Manila BCPC Federation. The city funds the councils with at least 1% of its IRA, and each barangay gives its BCPC at least 1% of its budget.
Computer shops and internet cafes may not let children game from 8 pm to 7 am, or from 7 am to 5 pm on school days, and must post child-abuse reporting signs.
Parents and guardians are barred from corporal punishment, from refusing a child's healthcare or intervention programs, and from letting children loiter or sleep in public places from 10 pm to 4 am.
Bans selling firecrackers to minors, overloading tricycles or pedicabs used as school service, and discriminating against a child in admission, enrolment or services.
Requires lactation stations, a children's desk in every police station, child-friendly buildings and a children's rights hotline. November is declared Children's Month.

provisions.title: A 6-year development plan for children
provisions.text: Within 180 days and every 6 years after, the MCPC drafts a Local Development Plan for Children covering 6 years, approved by the city council and built into the City Development Plan.

provisions.title: Lactation stations everywhere
provisions.text: All health and non-health facilities, establishments and institutions must set up lactation stations with a wash basin, cold storage for breastmilk, outlets and seats, never in a toilet, and with no promotion of infant formula.

provisions.title: November is Children's Month
provisions.text: November is Children's Month, ending on its last Monday, when the mayor issues a State of the Children Report. The city also holds an annual Children's Congress.

provisions.title: Children's desks, a hotline and safe buildings
provisions.text: Every police station has an officer trained in children's cases on duty 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The MCPC runs a children's rights hotline, and commercial buildings must be child-friendly, with stair balusters no more than 6 inches apart.

provisions.title: A city council for the protection of children
provisions.text: The Manila Council for the Protection of Children is chaired by the mayor, with city department heads, the police director, barangay and SK presidents, a judge, child representatives and at least 4 NGO representatives appointed for 5 years.

provisions.title: District and barangay councils and a federation
provisions.text: District councils (DCPC) and barangay councils (BCPC) are created below the city council, and BCPCs form a Manila BCPC Federation.

provisions.title: At least 1% of the IRA for the councils
provisions.text: The city regularly appropriates at least 1% of its IRA for the councils' programs, and each barangay at least 1% of its annual budget for its BCPC.

provisions.title: Bans on establishments
provisions.text: No discrimination against a child in admission, enrolment or services; no gaming for children in computer shops from 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. or 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on school days; no liquor, cigarettes, solvents or firecrackers sold to minors; no minors in bars, cockpits or casinos.

provisions.title: Bans on parents
provisions.text: Parents may not use corporal punishment, refuse a child's healthcare or intervention programs, let children loiter or sleep in public from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., or let them skate or bike on major thoroughfares.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Establishments pay ₱1,000, then ₱3,000, then ₱5,000 with closure and loss of permit. Adults face admonition and community service, then counselling, then up to 40 hours' service or up to 1 year in jail, with parenting seminars.

ordinances.penalties: Establishments: ₱1,000, then ₱3,000, then ₱5,000 with permit revocation and closure. Adults: community service of 16 to 40 hours, fines of ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 graded by the child's age, or up to 1 year in jail.
ordinances.amends: City Ordinance No. 8182 (2008), which it supersedes
ordinances.caveat: Section 118 on adult penalties has garbled cross-references (it cites Sections 120 and 121, which are the final clauses) and lists the age band of 15 to 17 years twice. It was approved by the Mayor on 1 June 2023.

sponsors: Hon. Benny Fog T. Abante III
Hon. John Marvin C. "Yul Servo" Nieto
