barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU or its barangays have councils for the protection of children on paper but no rules for them to enforce. Manila's 2023 code is a full, recent model: councils from city to barangay with a fixed budget share, duties on shops and schools, and graded penalties. It is 36 pages and written for a dense city, its adult penalty section has garbled cross-references, and some offences, such as fining parents for corporal punishment, need careful handling.

apply.if: If your LGU and barangays already have councils for the protection of children
apply.then: you can replicate Manila's structure by adding a federation of barangay councils and writing each council's budget share into the ordinance.

apply.if: If your barangays have no working council yet
apply.then: start with the barangay articles alone and the rule that each barangay sets aside at least 1% of its budget for its council.

apply.if: If your LGU has computer shops or internet cafes
apply.then: copy the gaming hours, the child-abuse reporting signs and the ₱1,000, ₱3,000, then ₱5,000 fines with permit revocation.

apply.if: If you have no police children's desk or hotline
apply.then: start with a named contact in the social welfare office and add the desk, hotline and lactation stations as budget allows.

apply.if: If you plan to sanction parents
apply.then: pair any fine with the parenting sessions and counselling the code requires, and refer children to the social welfare office rather than penalise them.

change: Re-cite the councils to BLGC s. 130 and s. 408, and replace '1% of the IRA' with the BLGC's own floor: at least 1% of the annual budget for the local council for the protection of children (BLGC s. 348)
Rename the Manila social welfare department as the social welfare and development officer, a licensed social worker under BLGC s. 537

Rewrite the rule on children loitering from 10 pm to 4 am so that only parents face sanctions and children are referred to the social welfare office, in line with the national Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act (RA 9344, as amended) on status offences
Pair the corporal punishment ban with positive-discipline sessions run with the social welfare office and religious leaders, and use fines only for repeat cases

Fix Section 118's garbled cross-references and duplicated age band, and cap penalties at ₱5,000 and 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509), 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489) and ₱3,000 for a barangay (BLGC s. 419)
barmm.fits: Cities and large municipalities for the full code; the barangay council articles suit any barangay.

ordinances.title: Ordinance providing for a comprehensive children's code in the City of Bacolod
ordinances.shortTitle: Bacolod City Children's Code of 2015
ordinances.summary: A local children's code in 66 articles that sets out children's rights to survival, development, protection and participation, and the duties of parents, the community and city offices. It puts in place health, nutrition, education, child protection and participation programmes, and funds them through a dedicated Children's Fund.
points: Children's Fund of at least 1% of the IRA, separate from the 1% already required under the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act
Local Council for the Protection of Children chaired by the Mayor, with a technical working group and the City Planning and Development Office as secretariat
Children's desks in all police stations; all government offices must adopt a child protection policy
The business permit office must start cancelling the permits of establishments using children in prostitution or lewd shows
Mandatory reporting of child abuse by heads of medical, school and other institutions; failure to report is punishable under RA 7610
Annual Children's Summit; implementing rules due within 90 days of approval

provisions.title: Birth registration, health centres and hospitals
provisions.text: The city aims for 100% birth registration. Barangays work toward exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months, newborn screening within 24 to 48 hours and full immunization, and run Sentrong Sigla health centres with a child health officer. Hospitals need child-friendly units.

provisions.title: Day care, school meals, libraries and scholarships
provisions.text: Every barangay has a day care centre and a children's library; undernourished pupils in public elementary schools and day care get at least 1 free meal a day; and at least 5% of the city scholarship program is set aside for children with disabilities.

provisions.title: A quick response system and protection network
provisions.text: The city sets up an integrated quick response to child abuse, trafficking, pornography, prostitution and child labour, and a multi-sectoral Bacolod City Child Protection Network, with accreditation for non-government members.

provisions.title: Children's desks and child protection policies
provisions.text: All police stations must have children's desks staffed 24 hours a day, 7 days a week by trained officers; at least 1 social welfare officer works on children's concerns; and all government offices adopt a child protection policy.

provisions.title: Street children, disasters and children in conflict
provisions.text: Street children are rescued under child-friendly protocols and reunited with family where possible, children get first priority in disasters, adults who use children in crimes are charged, and boys and girls are housed in separate youth homes.

provisions.title: Closing businesses that exploit children
provisions.text: The business permit office must start permanent cancellation of the permits of establishments using children in prostitution or lewd shows, or where child labour caused death or serious injury, and the city monitors internet cafes under the anti-child pornography law.

provisions.title: Children's participation and an annual summit
provisions.text: The city supports children's organizations with funding and training and holds a Children's Summit every October, planned with children.

provisions.title: A council for the protection of children
provisions.text: The Local Council for the Protection of Children, chaired by the Mayor with 2 councillors and the health, education, police and social services offices, plans children's programs, assisted by a technical working group led by social services. The planning office is secretariat.

provisions.title: Mandatory reporting of abuse
provisions.text: Heads of hospitals and clinics and attending doctors and nurses must report suspected abuse within 48 hours; teachers, police and barangay officials must also report. Failure to report is punishable under RA 7610, and good-faith reporters are immune.

provisions.title: A Children's Fund of at least 1% of the IRA
provisions.text: A Children's Fund of at least 1% of the IRA, separate from the 1% under the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, is allocated through an annual investment plan. Implementing rules are due within 90 days of approval.

Name the BARMM offices: the nutrition action officer (BLGC s. 548) with the Bangsamoro Nutrition Commission (BAA No. 83), and the social welfare officer (s. 537), who is the natural secretariat. Cover Madaris in the education, feeding and school board articles (BLGC s. 110 and s. 112, BAA No. 18).

Add articles Bacolod does not have: children in armed conflict under the national law RA 11188, displaced children under BAA No. 62, and child marriage under the national law RA 11596. Write that last one with Shari'ah court officials and ulama, not around them.

ordinances.title: The Child Welfare Code of Loon, amending for this purpose Municipal Ordinance No. 06-002, Series of 2006
ordinances.shortTitle: Child Welfare Code of Loon
ordinances.summary: A full child welfare code for Loon setting out children's rights and duties, the roles of families, schools, media, councils and businesses, and the municipality's programs for health, child development, emergencies and children in conflict with the law. It adds local prohibitions on top of national child protection laws and creates the municipality's child welfare councils and desks.
points: Prohibits children from betting in illegal numbers games and from being in gambling places
Video game shops and internet cafes serving children from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on school days or after 7:00 p.m. face a 15-day permit suspension, then 1 month, then confiscation and cancellation
Bars children 14 and below from using smartphones, tablets and computers except for authorised schooling or emergencies
Creates the Municipal Council for the Welfare of Children, Barangay Councils for the Protection of Children, a Desk for Children's Concerns and a Crisis Intervention Center
Sets a diversion system for child offenders at barangay and police level, including Katarungang Pambarangay conciliation
Hospital and clinic heads, teachers and government workers must report suspected child abuse

provisions.title: A children's programme every 3 years
provisions.text: Within 1 year of effectivity and every 3 years after, the municipality must draw up a comprehensive programme for children covering prevention, protection and rehabilitation, with parenting courses, primary health care and child development centers.

provisions.title: A Crisis Intervention Center and emergency plan
provisions.text: A Crisis Intervention Center serving abused children and other vulnerable groups, especially women, is funded through the MSWD's yearly budget. The MSWD also writes a Comprehensive Emergency Program for Children, and every barangay must provide a playground.

provisions.title: Local offences against children
provisions.text: On top of national child protection laws, it bans children betting on illegal numbers or being in gambling places, minors working as GROs, peonage, pre-arranged marriages, physical and degrading punishment, selling liquor, cigarettes or rugby to children, and using children in benefit dances.

provisions.title: Schools may not punish pregnancy or illegitimacy
provisions.text: Schools may not refuse to enrol illegitimate children or demand the parents' marriage contract, and may not expel, refuse to graduate or withhold clearances from a student because of pregnancy. Child passengers on motorcycles must meet set safety conditions.

provisions.title: Limits on video game shops and internet cafes
provisions.text: Shops serving children from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on school days or after 7:00 p.m. face a 15-day permit suspension, then 1 month, then confiscation of equipment and cancellation of the permit. Internet cafes may still serve college students.

provisions.title: No gadgets for children 14 and below
provisions.text: Children 14 and below may not use smartphones, tablets, laptops or computers except for authorised schooling or emergencies. Parents or adults who allow it pay ₱500, then ₱1,000, then ₱2,500, with cases filed before the Barangay Lupon.

provisions.title: Diversion for children in conflict with the law
provisions.text: Child offenders are diverted from the courts where possible, at barangay level through the Lupong Tagapamayapa and at police level through the Child and Youth Relations Unit. Katarungang Pambarangay conciliation applies to offences of up to 1 month in jail or ₱1,000.

provisions.title: Children's councils and a Desk for Children's Concerns
provisions.text: Creates the Municipal Council for the Welfare of Children and a Barangay Council for the Protection of Children in each barangay, which reports quarterly. A Desk for Children's Concerns under the MSWD serves as the council's secretariat and coordinates the code.

provisions.title: Mandatory reporting of child abuse
provisions.text: Heads of hospitals and clinics and attending doctors and nurses must report suspected abuse within 48 hours; teachers, police, barangay officials and other government workers dealing with children must also report. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability.

provisions.title: Penalties, with reform for first-time parents
provisions.text: Violations not punished elsewhere carry 6 months in jail and/or ₱2,500 (local offences not in national law: 1 year and up to ₱1,000). A first-time parent, teacher or relative who admits the offence may instead attend seminars, counselling or family therapy, with the child's consent.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your municipality's children's rules are spread across old ordinances, or its councils and desks exist only on paper. Loon's code puts the councils, a children's desk, a crisis centre, reporting duties and diversion for child offenders in one place. It is recent and complete, but it was written for a Visayan municipality, and some rules, such as the gadget ban for children 14 and below, cannot be enforced.

change: Re-cite the councils to BLGC s. 130 and s. 408 (the BCPC and child development centres), and fund the children's council with at least 1% of the budget under BLGC s. 348

Drop the ban on phones, tablets and computers for children 14 and below. It cannot be enforced, reaches into the home, and could cut off children who use phones for modular classes and madrasah lessons. Also drop confiscation of computer units, and cut the 1-year jail term for acts not covered by national law to the 6 months BLGC s. 489 allows; use permit suspension

Check barangay diversion and conciliation against BLGC s. 427 and s. 436, and against the juvenile justice law (RA 9344 as amended, national law). Add a chapter on children in armed conflict under RA 11188 (national law) and on displaced children under BAA No. 62

Rewrite the school rules, on pregnancy and on enrolling children born outside marriage, to fit the Bangsamoro Education Code (BAA No. 18) and to cover madaris. Name mosques, ustadz and imams alongside churches

A parenting course tied to the marriage licence will miss marriages solemnised under Muslim law or custom without a licence; if those are common in your LGU, also run it through the Shari'ah circuit registrar, imams and the social welfare office

ordinances.title: Enacting the revised 2022 La Union Investment and Incentives Code
ordinances.shortTitle: La Union Investment and Incentives Code of 2022
ordinances.summary: Sets the rules for attracting local and foreign investors to La Union through provincial tax breaks and other support. It creates an investment board and a one-stop promotion center, lists priority investment areas, and sets registration, reporting and sanction rules for registered enterprises. The tax incentives cover only the provincial share of taxes.
points: Creates the La Union Investment and Incentives Board (LUIIB) and the La Union Investment and Incentives Promotion Center (LUIIPC) as a one-stop processing center
Fiscal incentives: an extra 35% off the provincial share of basic real property tax and exemption from franchise, printing, amusement and annual fixed taxes, each for 1 year
Exemption from the Governor's permit and related business fees for 3 years, or at the Governor's discretion
Enterprises must apply within 6 months of getting their business permit; incentives may be availed only once and are non-transferable
Late reports are fined ₱3,000, ₱4,000 and ₱5,000, with cancellation of registration on the 4th infraction; appeals within 15 days
Sets an initial fund of ₱1,500,000 for the board and center

provisions.title: A provincial investment board
provisions.text: The La Union Investment and Incentives Board, chaired by the governor with the Chamber of Commerce president as vice-chair, has 13 members including 3 SP committee chairs, the DTI, Poro Point, business and banking groups, and the provincial treasurer, legal officer, ENRO and assessor. It meets quarterly.

provisions.title: A one-stop promotion centre
provisions.text: The La Union Investment and Incentives Promotion Center helps investors get local and national incentives and find partners, suppliers and sites. It is run by the Local Economic Enterprise and Investment Promotions Unit, which also serves as the board's secretariat.

provisions.title: Duties of registered enterprises
provisions.text: Enterprises must hire 70% of their semi-skilled and unskilled workers, including contracted workers, from the province, pay at least the DOLE minimum wage, prefer local suppliers and products, run at least 1 CSR project a year, and not discriminate or hire under-age workers.

provisions.title: Who qualifies
provisions.text: Enterprises must operate in La Union. New ones are small (₱3,000,001 to ₱15 million), medium (to ₱100 million) or large (over ₱100 million), must be in a priority area, file an environment plan and hire 80% of workers from the province. Expansions need the same minimum project cost.

provisions.title: Filing fees of ₱5,000 to ₱15,000
provisions.text: Applicants pay a non-refundable fee of ₱5,000 (small), ₱10,000 (medium) or ₱15,000 (large) and file a notarized form, a project study and registration papers. Applications are confidential; approved ones get a Certificate of Registration signed by the governor.

provisions.title: Priority investment areas
provisions.text: Areas range from COVID-19 medical supplies, agribusiness and fisheries, and tourism such as surfing in San Juan, to ICT and BPOs, transport, property and infrastructure, renewable energy, waste management and manufacturing. The board may add or remove areas with SP concurrence.

provisions.title: 1-year provincial tax breaks
provisions.text: On the provincial share only: an extra 35% off basic real property tax for 1 year, exemption from the real property transfer tax, and 1-year exemptions from franchise, printing, amusement and annual fixed taxes. The governor's permit fees are waived for 3 years.

provisions.title: Once only, and within 6 months
provisions.text: Incentives may be availed only once and cannot be transferred through mergers or joint ventures. Enterprises must apply within 6 months of getting their business permit.

provisions.title: Help with permits, power and labour
provisions.text: Registered enterprises get a one-stop documentation centre, help with local permits, labour recruitment and arbitration, utilities, sites and right of way, special power rates for loads of 1,000 kilowatts or more, and joint venture matching.

provisions.title: Fines, withdrawal and appeal
provisions.text: Late reports are fined ₱3,000, ₱4,000 and ₱5,000, and registration is revoked on the 4th. Other violations cost ₱5,000 or up to 1 year in jail. Appeals go to the board within 15 days. The province puts up an initial ₱1,500,000.

ordinances.penalties: ₱5,000 or up to 1 year in jail, or both; late reports ₱3,000 to ₱5,000, then cancellation of registration

sponsors: Hon. Maria Rosario Eufrosina P. Nisce
Hon. Maria Annabelle S. De Guzman

barmm.why: Worth reading if your province wants investors and has no single office to receive them. La Union sets up a board and a one-stop center, lists priority investment areas, and gives registered enterprises 1 to 3 years of breaks on the province's share of taxes in return for hiring local workers and filing reports. The province's share of tax is small, so the breaks matter less to an investor than fast permits and secure land; the hiring and reporting rules are the more useful part.

apply.if: If your LGU already runs a Business One-Stop Shop under BLGC s. 151
apply.then: you can replicate this by adding investor registration and records to that shop instead of opening La Union's separate promotion center.

apply.if: If your development council has not drawn up investment priority areas
apply.then: start there, since BLGC s. 121 gives it that job, and list only sectors your LGU can actually support with land, roads and power.

apply.if: If you want registered enterprises to hire locally
apply.then: copy the 80% resident rule for new enterprises and 70% for semi-skilled and unskilled jobs, and have your legal officer check it against national labour rules.

apply.if: If your province's own income is small
apply.then: cost the 35% property tax break against your 35% share under BLGC s. 297, scale down the ₱1,500,000 start-up fund, or begin with the one-stop service alone.

apply.if: If you are a city or municipality
apply.then: write the incentives around your own taxes and fees and leave out breaks on the province's share, which you cannot grant.

change: Fold the promotion center into the Business One-Stop Shop the BLGC already requires (s. 151) instead of running a second window, and staff it with the optional local economic and investment promotion officer.
Have the provincial development council draft the investment priority areas and incentives, since BLGC s. 121 gives it that job.

Make the incentives top up, not duplicate, the 6-year pioneer and 4-year non-pioneer exemptions for enterprises certified by the Bangsamoro Board of Investments (BLGC s. 156). Confirm in the full BLGC text that a sanggunian may grant tax exemptions by ordinance; that power is not in the summaries here.
Cost the real property tax break against the province's 35% share under BLGC s. 297; the municipality's 40% and the barangay's 25% cannot be waived by the province.
Keep the ₱5,000 or 1-year penalty (allowed for a province under BLGC s. 521), and scale the ₱1,500,000 start-up fund to the province's own income.
barmm.fits: Provinces, and cities, that want farm, fishery or processing investment and can staff a one-stop desk for investors.

ordinances.title: Enacting the 2018 Investments and Incentives Code of the City of San Fernando, Province of La Union, repealing City Ordinance No. 2006-03, otherwise known as the Investment Incentive Code of the City of San Fernando
ordinances.shortTitle: 2018 Investments and Incentives Code of the City of San Fernando
ordinances.summary: Sets San Fernando's investment policy and the local incentives it may grant to businesses that register. It creates an investments board and a one-stop investment centre, lists investment priority areas for 2018 to 2023, and sets the period of tax exemptions by enterprise size. Registered enterprises take on corporate social responsibility and environmental duties.
points: Creates the 19-member City of San Fernando Investments and Incentives Board (CSF-IIB) and the Investments Promotion and Assistance Center (CSF-IPAC) as a one-stop processing centre
Incentives apply only to activities on the Investment Priority Areas list for 2018 to 2023, which the board reviews periodically
Local tax exemption periods: large (above ₱100M) 6 years, medium (₱15M to ₱100M) 4 years, small (₱3M to ₱15M) 3 years, micro (below ₱3M) 2 years
Incentives never cover regulatory fees, service charges such as garbage and inspection fees, or utility charges; no double availment
5% of incentives availed must go to CSR projects; BOI pioneer-status enterprises are monitored from the 4th year
Refusing environmental compliance inspection is ground for forfeiting incentives and revoking registration or business permit

provisions.title: A 19-member investments and incentives board
provisions.text: The CSF-IIB, chaired by the City Mayor with the local chamber of commerce president as vice chair, includes 4 council committee chairs, DTI, DOT, DOTC and ICT representatives, city officers and private sector members; it meets at least monthly.

provisions.title: A one-stop investment centre
provisions.text: The CSF-IPAC, staffed by the Local Economic and Business Development Office, helps investors get permits and incentives, finds partners, suppliers and sites, and serves as the board's secretariat.

provisions.title: Investment Priority Areas for 2018 to 2023
provisions.text: Incentives go only to activities on the IPA list, chosen for jobs, local materials, dispersal, environment, PPP infrastructure and organic agriculture or eco-tourism; the board reviews the list at least every 2 years.

provisions.title: Who can register for incentives
provisions.text: An enterprise must be on the IPA list, operate in the city, hire a set share of residents, have pollution safeguards, and get NCIP free and prior informed consent if on ancestral domain; new, expansion, modernisation and diversification projects qualify.

provisions.title: A ₱2,000 filing fee and 15-day approval
provisions.text: Applicants pay a non-refundable ₱2,000 filing fee (half for micro enterprises); the board must act within 15 days or the application is deemed approved, and the certificate issues within 15 days after.

provisions.title: Tax exemptions by enterprise size
provisions.text: Business and real property tax exemptions run 6 years for large enterprises (above ₱100M), 4 for medium (₱15M to ₱100M), 3 for small (₱3M to ₱15M) and 2 for micro (below ₱3M).

provisions.title: No exemption from fees or utility charges
provisions.text: Incentives never cover regulatory fees, service fees such as garbage and inspection fees, or charges for water, power, tolls and use of city property; there is no double availment.

provisions.title: Non-fiscal help for registered enterprises
provisions.text: The board provides one-stop documentation, help with agencies, utilities and permits, mediation for industrial peace, TESDA links for training, site selection and trade fair slots for micro and small enterprises.

provisions.title: 5% of incentives to CSR projects
provisions.text: BOI pioneer enterprises must do CSR, monitored from the 4th year; local registrants with incentives of more than 2 years must from their 3rd year; 5% of incentives availed goes to greening, housing, education and similar projects.

provisions.title: Refusing environmental inspection forfeits incentives
provisions.text: Plants must run pollution, wastewater and solid waste facilities within capacity and allow periodic LGU-DENR monitoring; refusing inspection forfeits incentives and can revoke the registration or business permit.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants to offer investors local incentives but has no rules on who qualifies or for how long. San Fernando ties every incentive to a priority list, scales exemption periods by enterprise size, bars incentives on fees and utility charges, and withdraws them for refusing environmental inspection. Its legal basis rests on RA 7160 and the national Board of Investments, both of which change under the BLGC, and the power to grant local tax exemptions needs checking first.

apply.if: If your local development council already sets investment priorities
apply.then: you can replicate this by making that list the gate for any incentive and reviewing it at least every 2 years, as San Fernando does.

apply.if: If your LGU has a Business One-Stop Shop
apply.then: put the investment assistance desk there instead of creating a separate centre.

apply.if: If your LGU is a small municipality
apply.then: skip the 19-member board and give its work to a small committee of the mayor, treasurer, planning officer and an investment promotion officer or focal person.

Find the BLGC provision that lets a sanggunian grant local tax exemptions before drafting; the code cites RA 7160 s. 192, and BLGC s. 218 withdraws most existing exemptions, so the basis must be confirmed with the MILG or the Ministry of Finance
Have the investment priorities come from the local development council under BLGC s. 121, and fold the one-stop investment centre into the Business One-Stop Shop required by BLGC s. 151
Shrink the 19-member board for smaller LGUs, and staff the centre with the local economic investment promotion officer BLGC s. 481 allows
List the priority areas your own LGU actually has, such as halal processing, seaweed or marine products, and require that large projects consult affected communities before approval under BLGC s. 32

ordinances.title: Creating the Muntinlupa City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Muntinlupa City DRRM Office ordinance
ordinances.summary: This ordinance creates the Muntinlupa City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MCDRRMO) under the Office of the City Mayor, as RA 10121 requires. It lists the office's 26 functions, sets its staffing plan and sets up the city's DRRM fund.
points: The MCDRRMO is headed by a Department Head II with an Assistant Department Head II.

It has 3 divisions: Administrative and Training, Research and Planning, and Warning and Operation. Warning and Operation has a Rescue Operation Unit with medical, tactical and trauma sections, and a Warning and Communication Unit.

The Muntinlupa City DRRM Fund is at least 5% of estimated revenue from regular sources. 30% is a Quick Response Fund, and 70% goes to prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, rehabilitation and recovery.
Staff salaries go into the 2014 Executive Budget and every year after, following CSC and DBM rules.
Posts are filled first from existing city employees, with new hires only if none are available.

provisions.title: Plans, risk assessment and hazard data
provisions.text: The MCDRRMO sets the direction of the city's disaster risk programs, supports risk assessment and contingency planning, and consolidates hazard, vulnerability and climate risk information with the private sector, CSOs and volunteers.

provisions.title: Response teams, volunteers and relief
provisions.text: It organizes, trains and equips emergency response teams and accredited community disaster volunteers, and in emergencies ensures quick delivery of food, shelter and medical supplies, with a space for displaced mothers to breastfeed and care for babies.

provisions.title: Secretariat of the council and an operations centre
provisions.text: It serves as secretariat and executive arm of the city DRRM council, sets up a City DRRM Operations Center, and reports use of the DRRM fund to COA, the OCD and the DILG.

provisions.title: Headed by a Department Head II
provisions.text: The office sits under the Office of the City Mayor, headed by a Department Head II with an Assistant Department Head II.

provisions.title: 3 divisions
provisions.text: Administrative and Training, Research and Planning, and Warning and Operation. Warning and Operation has a Rescue Operation Unit with medical, tactical and trauma sections led by nurses, and a Warning and Communication Unit.

provisions.title: Duties set by the office heads
provisions.text: The department head, assistant and division heads define each staff member's duties based on the office's functions, subject to the mayor's approval.

provisions.title: A DRRM fund of at least 5% of revenue
provisions.text: At least 5% of estimated revenue from regular sources goes to the city DRRM fund: 30% as a Quick Response Fund and 70% for prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, rehabilitation and recovery. With council approval it may help other LGUs under a state of calamity.

provisions.title: Salaries from the 2014 budget on
provisions.text: Staff salaries and benefits go into the 2014 Executive Budget and every year after, following CSC and DBM rules.

provisions.title: Existing employees first

ordinances.title: An ordinance creating the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO) in the Province of Bataan
ordinances.shortTitle: Bataan PDRRMO Ordinance
ordinances.summary: A short ordinance that creates Bataan's Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office, as required by RA 10121 and its implementing rules. It lists the office's functions, fixes its staffing, qualifications and salary grades, and funds it from the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund.
points: Creates the PDRRMO with 15 listed functions, including risk assessment, a local risk map, early warning, drills and training, and preparing the provincial DRRM plan and budget.
Staffed by a PDRRM Officer and 3 staff for administration and training, research and planning, and operations and warning.
The PDRRM Officer needs a relevant bachelor's degree and 3 years of DRRM experience; each staff member needs a relevant degree and 2 years of experience.
Salary Grade 22 for the PDRRM Officer and Salary Grade 18 for the 3 staff; extra employees the Governor assigns cannot be paid from the LDRRMF.
The office's budget comes from the LDRRMF, endorsed by the Provincial DRRM Council to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan for appropriation.

provisions.title: A provincial DRRM office
provisions.text: Creates the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO), working with the national government and neighbouring provinces to design, program and coordinate disaster risk reduction to national council standards.

provisions.title: Risk assessment, risk map and early warning
provisions.text: The office supports risk assessment and contingency planning, consolidates hazard, vulnerability and climate change data into a local risk map, and runs an early warning system that reaches agencies, neighbouring provinces and residents by radio, telecoms and social networks.

provisions.title: Training, monitoring and a resource database
provisions.text: It runs seminars, training and drills, monitors disasters with the Metro Bataan Development Authority, civil society and other LGUs, and keeps a database of people, equipment and critical facilities such as hospitals and evacuation centres.

provisions.title: The provincial plan, budget and fund reports
provisions.text: It drafts the provincial DRRM plan with the Local Development Council, submits the yearly plan, budget and LDRRMF programming to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan, and reports fund use to COA, copying OCD and DILG. It serves as secretariat of the council.

provisions.title: Vulnerable sectors in planning
provisions.text: Women, children, senior citizens and persons with disabilities must be involved in risk assessment and planning, and the office raises public awareness of hazards and counter-measures.

provisions.title: An officer and 3 staff
provisions.text: The office is run by a PDRRM Officer with 3 staff for administration and training, research and planning, and operations and warning. Hiring follows Sec. 22 of the Local Government Code.

provisions.title: Qualifications for each post
provisions.text: The officer needs a relevant bachelor's degree and 3 years of DRRM experience. Each staff member needs a relevant degree and 2 years of experience in their field: office management and training, research and planning, or early warning and information work.

provisions.title: Salary Grade 22 and 18
provisions.text: The officer is paid at Salary Grade 22 and the 3 staff at Salary Grade 18 under RA 6758. Extra employees the Governor assigns to the office cannot be paid from the LDRRMF.

provisions.title: Funded from the LDRRMF
provisions.text: The office's budget comes from the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, endorsed by the provincial DRRM council to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan for an appropriation ordinance.

ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies all local ordinances and regulations inconsistent with it; no specific ordinance named.

ordinances.title: Ordinance revising and updating the "Bacoor City Disaster Management Code of 2012," institutionalizing the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management System of the City of Bacoor, aligning it with current national laws and policies on disaster risk reduction and management, climate change adaptation…
ordinances.shortTitle: City of Bacoor Disaster Risk Reduction and Management and Climate Change Adaptation Code of 2026
ordinances.summary: A full DRRM and climate adaptation code in 73 sections that rebuilds Bacoor's disaster system around the Incident Command System, an Emergency Operations Center and response clusters. It adds anticipatory action under RA 12287, damage and needs assessment rules, volunteer and amateur radio programmes, data privacy, no-build zones and a schedule of penalties.
points: Sets the City DRRM Council, the Bacoor DRRM Office, barangay DRRM committees and barangay clustering for mutual aid
The Mayor may recommend a State of Imminent Disaster after a pre-disaster risk assessment, unlocking anticipatory action, QRF use and emergency procurement
At least 5% of estimated regular revenue goes to the LDRRMF, with at least 30% of that held as the Quick Response Fund
Covers mandatory and pre-emptive evacuation, evacuation centre standards, early warning systems and a DRRM mobile app
Creates a disaster volunteer programme, a youth DRRM organisation for junior and senior high schools, and a role for amateur radio operators
Identifies no-build zones and danger areas; the council may adjust fines by resolution for inflation

provisions.title: A reorganised City DRRM Council
provisions.text: The old council becomes the City DRRM Council, chaired by the Mayor with the Vice Mayor as vice chair, and including department heads, DepEd, police, fire, AFP, Red Cross, the Liga and SK presidents, CSO and business seats, and at least 1 representative each of women, youth, older persons, PWDs and the urban poor.

provisions.title: The BDRRMO and barangay DRRM committees
provisions.text: The Bacoor DRRM Office, headed by an officer of department-head rank with 4 divisions, runs the EOC, the DRRM fund and the volunteer roster. Every barangay keeps a DRRM committee with hazard maps and trained responders, and barangays may be clustered for mutual aid.

provisions.title: Incident Command, an EOC and 14 response clusters
provisions.text: The City institutionalises its Emergency Operations Center under an EOC Manager the Mayor designates, uses the Incident Command System, and sets up 14 City Response Clusters copied from the national ones, each led by the city office closest to the national lead agency.

provisions.title: State of Imminent Disaster and anticipatory action
provisions.text: On the council's recommendation and a pre-disaster risk assessment, the Mayor may ask the council to declare a State of Imminent Disaster under RA 12287, for up to 15 days unless extended. It unlocks anticipatory action, use of the QRF and emergency procurement.

provisions.title: 5% of revenue to DRRM, 30% of it held for quick response
provisions.text: At least 5% of estimated regular revenue goes yearly to the LDRRMF, and at least 30% of that is the Quick Response Fund, released on a State of Calamity or Imminent Disaster. Unspent balances carry over as a trust fund instead of reverting.

provisions.title: Evacuation orders and evacuation centers
provisions.text: The Mayor may order mandatory or pre-emptive evacuation of threatened areas, announced through every channel, with transport, food, water and shelter provided. Evacuation centers must be hazard-resistant and give at least 3.5 sq. m per person, with water, sanitation and privacy.

provisions.title: People-centred early warning
provisions.text: The City runs multi-hazard early warning systems covering typhoons, floods, storm surge, landslides, earthquakes, tsunamis, fire and outbreaks, linked to PAGASA, PHIVOLCS and other national sources and issued in Filipino and English.

provisions.title: Volunteers, a youth DRRM group and radio operators
provisions.text: A City Disaster Volunteer Program keeps a registry of accredited volunteers, trains and insures them. A youth-led DRRM organisation for junior and senior high school learners feeds into it, and amateur radio operators support emergency communications.

provisions.title: No-build zones and danger areas
provisions.text: The City maps permanent danger zones and no-build areas such as fault lines, flood-prone areas, floodways and river and creek easements, writes them into the land use plan and zoning, bars new homes and critical facilities there, and relocates affected families.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Refusing to evacuate or entering danger zones: a warning or ₱1,000 or 8 to 24 hours of community service, rising to ₱4,000 to ₱5,000 and/or jail. Obstructing operations, building in no-build zones (plus demolition) or faking volunteer status: ₱5,000. The council may adjust fines by resolution.

ordinances.penalties: Refusal to evacuate: warning or ₱1,000 up to ₱4,000 to ₱5,000 and/or 1 to 30 days in jail for a 3rd offence; obstruction, hoarding, misuse of relief goods and false alarms: ₱5,000 and/or up to 1 year
ordinances.amends: Repeals and replaces City Ordinance No. 34, Series of 2012 (Bacoor City Disaster Management Code)

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU's disaster ordinance predates the Incident Command System or the anticipatory action law, RA 12287. Bacoor's 2026 code is current: an operations center, 14 response clusters, a pre-disaster risk assessment that can lead to a state of imminent disaster, damage assessment rules, volunteers, youth groups and amateur radio. It is 57 pages and written for a city with a full DRRM office, so most LGUs will take parts of it.

apply.if: If your LGU has a DRRM office with full-time staff
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the Incident Command System, an emergency operations center and the clusters your existing offices can lead.

apply.if: If your DRRM office is 1 or 2 people
apply.then: skip the full 14 clusters and start with the core ones: food and relief, camp management, health, search and rescue, and communications.

apply.if: If your LGU gets warnings ahead of floods, storms or landslides
apply.then: add the pre-disaster risk assessment and the state of imminent disaster, capped at 15 days unless the council extends it, so the quick response fund can pay for pre-emptive evacuation.

apply.if: If your LGU also hosts families displaced by armed conflict
apply.then: treat displacement as a hazard in the evacuation and camp chapters, and link it to BAA No. 62 and the IDP council in BLGC s. 130.

apply.if: If mobile signal is weak in parts of your LGU
apply.then: keep the amateur radio role and the emergency telecommunications cluster, and skip Bacoor's mobile app unless you can run it.

change: Re-cite the DRRM council to BLGC s. 129, which adds a 40% women membership target, with RA 10121 and RA 12287 kept as the national law.

Don't create separate barangay DRRM committees: under BLGC s. 121 the barangay development council acts as the barangay DRRM council. Re-cite the 5% calamity fund to BLGC s. 348, with the 30% quick response share kept from RA 10121.

Treat displacement from armed conflict as a hazard, and link evacuation, camp management and return to BAA No. 62 (IDPs), the IDP council in BLGC s. 130 and the property tax exemption for displaced owners in BLGC s. 260.

Keep penalties within BLGC s. 489 for municipalities (₱5,000 or 6 months) and s. 509 for cities (₱5,000 or 1 year); Bacoor's hoarding fine of double the value of the goods goes past the ₱5,000 cap, so set a fixed amount. Post the penal parts under BLGC s. 571, translated into the local language.

Name the health, social welfare and nutrition officers as frontline responders, since BLGC s. 532, s. 537 and s. 548 require those posts. Drop the Bacoor-only items such as the city app and the barangay clusters, unless the LGU can run them.

ordinances.title: A comprehensive municipal code providing for the sustainable management, development and conservation of the municipal waters and its coastal resources, harmonizing and integrating all ordinances pertinent thereto and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Coastal Resource Management Code of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: Loon's basic fisheries and coastal code. It brings the municipality's earlier fishery ordinances into one code under the Fisheries Code of 1998. It zones the municipal waters, governs licensing, marine sanctuaries, mangroves, fish corrals and aquaculture, and sets up the offices that enforce it. It applies to all fisherfolk, businesses and others who use the municipality's coastal and fishery resources.
points: Divides municipal waters into 6 zones: multiple use, rehabilitation, trade and navigation, tourism and recreation, protected (sanctuaries, no-take) and NIPAS

Closed season for danggit (siganid) during the 3rd to 5th rising of the new moon; catching, selling or possessing siganid fry is banned (₱1,000, ₱1,500, then ₱2,000 with confiscation, or 30 days in jail)
Bans trawl, compressor, lawag, electric shiner, liba-liba/hulbot-hulbot and beach seine fishing, sand extraction, mangrove conversion and anchoring in dive sites and sanctuaries
Fisherfolk registered in other municipalities pay double the license rate; marginal fisherfolk pay no other fee for the municipal fishery license
Creates a CRM Section under the Municipal Agriculturist, a Municipal FARMC and a Municipal Bantay Dagat Council
50% of fines collected go as cash incentives to the team that made the arrest and those who helped

provisions.title: Municipal waters in 6 zones
provisions.text: The waters are zoned for multiple use, rehabilitation, trade and navigation, tourism and recreation, protection (sanctuaries, no-take areas and mangrove reserves), and areas under the National Integrated Protected Areas System.

provisions.title: A free, public registry of fisherfolk
provisions.text: The CRM officer keeps a registry of municipal fisherfolk, updated yearly and posted in barangay halls, with no registration fee. Registered fisherfolk and their groups get priority in the municipal waters, and boats and gear are registered too.

provisions.title: Closed season for danggit and a ban on its fry
provisions.text: Danggit may not be caught during the 3rd to 5th rising of the new moon, and fish corral pocket nets stay out. Catching, selling or possessing siganid fry draws ₱1,000, ₱1,500, then ₱2,000 with confiscation, or 30 days in jail.

provisions.title: Sanctuaries, mangroves and fish corrals
provisions.text: No fishing in sanctuary core zones, and no fish corral within 200 metres of a sanctuary or another corral, with tails up to 100 metres and mesh of at least 3 centimetres. Sanctuary fees are split 60% municipality, 20% barangay, 20% managing group.

provisions.title: Licences from the mayor, double for outsiders
provisions.text: No one may fish or gather marine products without a licence from the mayor, renewed yearly. Fisherfolk registered in other municipalities pay double, and marginal fisherfolk pay no other fee beyond the licence.

provisions.title: Docking fees and lifeguards
provisions.text: Boats in dive sites and sanctuaries pay ₱50 a day and must use mooring buoys. Beach and dive resorts must keep a certified lifeguard on duty during business hours, or face ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 or 30 days to 6 months in jail.

provisions.title: Fishing revenue goes back to the coast
provisions.text: All revenue from use of the municipal waters funds coastal resource management, and 30% of the fees goes to the coastal barangay where the activity is allowed, remitted every quarter.

provisions.title: A CRM Section, a FARMC and a Bantay Dagat Council
provisions.text: A CRM Section under the Municipal Agriculturist runs coastal management. The FARMC has at least 11 elected fisherfolk representatives with government and NGO members. The Bantay Dagat Council includes the police chief, the agriculturist and fish wardens.

provisions.title: Destructive fishing banned
provisions.text: Banned: trawl, electric shiner, lawag, compressor, liba-liba or hulbot-hulbot and beach seine fishing, sand extraction, converting mangroves, and anchoring in dive sites and sanctuaries. Fines run ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 or 1 month to 1 year in jail, with boats and gear forfeited.

provisions.title: Half of fines to those who catch violators
provisions.text: 50% of fines collected goes as cash to the team that made the arrest and those who helped. Other violations draw ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 or 1 to 6 months. The SB reviews the code at least every 3 years.

ordinances.penalties: General penalty ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both; specific gear bans carry ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 and up to 1 year, with boats and gear forfeited
ordinances.amends: Harmonizes and integrates earlier Loon fishery ordinances (e.g. MO 1981-1, MO 1992-02, MO 1994-1, MO 1994-03, MO 1995-4) and repeals inconsistent ordinances

ordinances.title: Clean lifestyle ordinance prohibiting the use of e-cigarettes in certain places, imposing penalties for violations thereof and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Clean Lifestyle and Smoke-Free Bacolod Ordinance
ordinances.summary: Bans vaping in enclosed and public places, workplaces and public vehicles outside approved vaping areas, and restricts the sale, advertising and promotion of tobacco products and e-cigarettes in Bacolod City. It sets up a task force, a citation ticket system and a smoking cessation programme, with a yearly budget.
points: Bans selling tobacco or vapes to minors, within 100 metres of schools, playgrounds and health facilities, by street vendors, or without a permit
Bans tobacco and vape advertising where minors are allowed, open shelf display, and government officials' partnerships with the tobacco industry
Clean Lifestyle and Smoke-Free Task Force chaired by the Mayor, with the health and environment committee chairs as co-chairs
Citation tickets payable at the City Treasurer within 5 business days; a no-contest payment is allowed for 1st and 2nd offences; community service is allowed for those who cannot pay
At least ₱1,000,000 a year goes into a trust fund; 10% of each fine goes to the apprehending officer
Permits are suspended for 1 week to 1 month, or revoked, if violations are not fixed within 15 days

provisions.title: No vaping in enclosed and public places
provisions.text: Vaping is banned in enclosed or partly enclosed public places, workplaces, accommodation establishments and public or government vehicles, moving or parked, except in designated vaping areas that meet the ordinance's standards.

provisions.title: Sales limits for tobacco and vapes
provisions.text: No selling to or buying from minors, within 100 metres of schools, playgrounds and health facilities, inside government facilities, by street vendors, out of the original pack, or without a permit to sell.

provisions.title: Advertising and display bans
provisions.text: Cinema and outdoor ads, branded materials where minors may enter, promotions and sampling, and open-shelf display are banned; government officials may not join tobacco industry sponsorships or CSR.

provisions.title: Duties of persons in charge
provisions.text: Owners and managers must post No Smoking and No Vaping signs at least 8 x 11 inches, keep minors out of vaping areas, get a permit to sell, store products in closed opaque containers, and let inspectors in.

provisions.title: Fines from ₱2,000 to ₱10,000
provisions.text: Vaping and sales or advertising violations draw ₱2,000, then ₱5,000, then ₱10,000 or up to 3 months in jail; officials who partner with the tobacco industry face RA 3019 and RA 6713 sanctions.

provisions.title: Permits suspended or revoked
provisions.text: A seller's, establishment's or vehicle's permit is suspended for 1 week to 1 month, or revoked, if it does not comply within 15 days of a notice or pay within 7 working days.

provisions.title: Community service and a no-contest option
provisions.text: Violators who cannot pay may do community service, each hour cutting the fine by 3 times the hourly minimum wage; 1st and 2nd offenders may pay within 5 business days to avoid prosecution.

provisions.title: Citation tickets paid at the treasurer
provisions.text: The City Treasurer issues ticket booklets to enforcers within 90 days; a ticketed violator reports to the treasurer within 5 business days to pay or choose community service. Minors are referred to the CSWDO or their school.

provisions.title: A task force chaired by the Mayor

ordinances.title: Comprehensive anti-tobacco smoking control program ordinance for the Province of Bataan
ordinances.shortTitle: Smoke Free Ordinance of the Province of Bataan
ordinances.summary: Bans smoking in enclosed and partly enclosed public places, workplaces and public vehicles across Bataan, and restricts tobacco sales and advertising. It sets graduated fines, a citation ticket system, a smoking cessation program and a Smokefree Task Force chaired by the Governor. It applies to all persons and places in the province.
points: Bans tobacco sales to minors and within 100 meters of schools, playgrounds, hospitals and health offices
Bans cinema and outdoor tobacco ads and ad materials outside point-of-sale premises
Licences of establishments or vehicles can be suspended for 1 week to 1 month if a violation is not fixed within 15 days or a citation is unpaid within 7 working days
Violators who cannot pay may do community service, each hour reducing the fine by 3 times the hourly minimum wage
Allocates ₱500,000 at the start and at least ₱500,000 a year; fines go to a trust fund for the task force
Establishments are inspected starting 90 days after the ordinance takes effect

provisions.title: No smoking in public places and vehicles
provisions.text: Smoking is banned in enclosed or partly enclosed public places, workplaces and public conveyances, moving or stationary, and persons in charge may not allow or tolerate it.

provisions.title: Sales limits near schools and to minors
provisions.text: Tobacco may not be sold in or within 100 metres of schools, playgrounds and other places minors frequent, DOH offices, hospitals and health facilities. Selling to minors and buying from minors are banned.

provisions.title: Advertising bans
provisions.text: Cinema and outdoor tobacco ads are banned, as are leaflets, posters and similar materials outside point-of-sale premises, or inside them where the shop may not sell tobacco.

provisions.title: Duties of persons in charge
provisions.text: They post 'No Smoking' signs at least 8 by 11 inches at entrances and stickers in vehicles, remove ashtrays, post sales notices, ask violators to stop or leave and report those who refuse, and let inspectors in.

provisions.title: Graduated fines
provisions.text: Smoking in banned places: ₱500, ₱1,000, then ₱2,500 or up to 1 year. Sales violations: ₱1,500, ₱3,000, then up to ₱5,000 or 1 year. Ad violations: ₱2,000, ₱3,000, then up to ₱5,000 or 1 year. Repeat business offenders may lose their permit.

provisions.title: Licence suspension and community service
provisions.text: A business or vehicle that does not comply within 15 days or pay its citation within 7 working days is suspended for 1 week to 1 month or revoked. Those who cannot pay may do community service, each hour cutting the fine by 3 times the hourly minimum wage.

provisions.title: Citation tickets
provisions.text: The Treasurer issues ticket booklets to enforcers within 90 days. A violator must report to the Treasurer's Office within 3 business days to pay or opt for community service.

provisions.title: A task force chaired by the Governor
provisions.text: The Smokefree Task Force, chaired by the Governor with the Provincial Health Officer as vice chair, enforces the ordinance and deputizes enforcers. No one tied to the tobacco industry may sit on it or give it anything. A smoking cessation program is also set up.

provisions.title: Monthly inspections after 90 days
provisions.text: Starting 90 days after effectivity, a health, engineering and permits team inspects establishments, at least monthly after that. A ticket may issue for each day of non-compliance, with re-inspection within 10 days.

provisions.title: ₱500,000 a year and a trust fund
provisions.text: ₱500,000 is allocated at the start and at least ₱500,000 goes into the provincial budget every year, covering printing, enforcement, rewards for reporting and the cessation program. Fines go to a trust fund for the task force.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱5,000 depending on the act and offence; a 3rd offence can bring up to 1 year in jail and suspension or revocation of the business permit

It is from 2013, so it says nothing on vapes, and as a provincial ordinance it relies on cities and municipalities to suspend business permits.

Set the community service rate on the minimum wage that applies in BARMM under the Bangsamoro Labor Code (BAA No. 82), not Central Luzon's

ordinances.title: Prohibiting tobacco, cigar and cigarette smoking in public places, and providing penalties for violations therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Smoking ban in public places
ordinances.summary: Bans smoking in a list of public places in Naga City, including entertainment venues, government offices, shops and markets, public vehicles, schools, hospitals and places of worship. Owners, managers and drivers who allow smoking are liable along with smokers. Government offices must provide ventilated smoking areas; private businesses may choose to.
points: Covers bars, restaurants, cockpits, theatres, libraries, government offices, stores and markets, elevators, buses, jeepneys and trimobiles, classrooms, hospitals, clinics, churches and mosques
Bans smoking in warehouses for flammable materials and within 50 metres of them or of carriers of such materials
No smoking areas allowed in schools, public vehicles or fuel and explosives storage; where allowed, they must be well ventilated and are monitored by the city engineer
Owners, managers, heads of office and drivers who allow smoking: ₱500, ₱1,000, ₱1,500, then ₱2,000 with cancellation of the mayor's and business permit
Smokers: ₱200, ₱300, ₱500, then ₱1,000 and prosecution

provisions.title: Smoking banned in entertainment and eating places
provisions.text: No smoking in cocktail lounges, bars, nightclubs, discos, cafes, restaurants, eateries, video and amusement centres, or in cockpits, gyms, auditoriums, libraries, laboratories, theatres and cinemas.

provisions.title: Offices, shops, vehicles, schools and churches
provisions.text: The ban also covers all government offices, department stores, markets and shops open to the public, elevators, buses, jeepneys and trimobiles, school premises, hospitals and clinics, and churches, mosques and other places of worship.

provisions.title: No smoking near flammable materials
provisions.text: Smoking is banned in warehouses and storage for flammables, explosives and petroleum products, and within 50 metres of them or of vehicles carrying such materials.

provisions.title: Those who allow smoking are liable too
provisions.text: Owners, managers and heads of government offices and private businesses, and operators and drivers of public vehicles, may not allow or condone smoking in the covered places.

provisions.title: Smoking areas: required, optional or banned
provisions.text: Government offices must provide smoking areas; private businesses may choose to, and if they do not, the whole premises is covered. No smoking areas in schools, public vehicles, elevators or fuel and explosives storage.

provisions.title: Ventilation checked by the city engineer
provisions.text: Where allowed, smoking areas must be well ventilated so smoke does not reach non-smoking areas, and the city engineer regularly monitors compliance.

provisions.title: Fines for owners, managers and drivers
provisions.text: Those who allow smoking pay ₱500, ₱1,000 and ₱1,500 for the first 3 offences; a fourth brings a ₱2,000 fine, cancellation of the mayor's and business permits and prosecution.

provisions.title: Fines for smokers
provisions.text: Smokers pay ₱200, ₱300 and ₱500 for the first 3 offences, and ₱1,000 plus prosecution for a fourth.

provisions.title: Jail for unpaid fines
provisions.text: Anyone who does not pay the fine within 3 days of apprehension faces 6 months to 1 year in jail and a ₱3,000 to ₱5,000 fine, at the court's discretion. The ordinance repeals Ordinance No. 93-086.

ordinances.penalties: ₱200 to ₱2,000 administrative fines by offence; refusing to pay within 3 days brings 6 months to 1 year in jail and a ₱3,000 to ₱5,000 fine

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants to enforce smoking bans in markets, terminals, offices and public vehicles and has no local ordinance to do it with. Naga's 3-page text makes owners, office heads and drivers liable along with smokers, with fines that rise by offence. It is from 1995: it predates the national tobacco law, says nothing about vapes, and requires government offices to provide smoking areas, which national rules no longer allow.

apply.if: If your LGU has no smoking ordinance yet
apply.then: you can replicate this by listing the places Naga covers, including mosques, schools, clinics and public vehicles, and fining owners, office heads and drivers who allow smoking as well as smokers.

apply.if: If you want enforcement without a court case for every catch
apply.then: keep the fines by offence and the 3-day window to pay, and send only refusals to court, within your cap of ₱5,000 and 6 months for a municipality or 1 year for a city.

apply.if: If fuel is sold or stored along your roads
apply.then: keep the 50-metre ban around fuel, explosives and flammable stores and the vehicles carrying them.

apply.if: If your health office has sanitary inspectors
apply.then: name them, with barangay tanods, as enforcers instead of the city engineer Naga used.

apply.if: If you copy the section on smoking areas
apply.then: drop the rule that government offices must provide them, and add vapes under RA 11900.

change: Base it on the national tobacco laws (RA 9211 and the 2017 executive order on smoke-free places) and RA 11900 for vapes, which the 1995 text does not cover; drop the RA 7160 framing for BLGC s. 17 (general welfare).
Delete the rule that government offices must provide smoking areas; national rules now bar smoking in government premises, so the clause is unlawful.
Keep the jail term within the enacting LGU's cap: a city may go to ₱5,000 or 1 year (BLGC s. 509), but a municipality only to ₱5,000 or 6 months (s. 489).
Follow the penal ordinance rules: post for 6 consecutive weeks in 3 places, publish, translate into the local languages and send to the Bangsamoro Gazette within 12 days (BLGC s. 571).
Name an enforcer with real capacity, such as the health officer (BLGC s. 532) with barangay tanods, rather than the city engineer.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with busy markets, terminals and public transport; a barangay can pass a shorter version within its ₱3,000 cap.

ordinances.title: Enacting the Health, Sanitation, and Safety Code of the City of Bacoor and providing penalties for violations hereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Health, Sanitation, and Safety Code of the City of Bacoor
ordinances.summary: A 23-chapter code that gathers Bacoor's rules on public health, sanitation and safety into one document. It covers health certificates, City Health Office fees, food establishments and markets, schools, water, public restrooms, slaughterhouses, motels, laundries, swimming pools, cemeteries, sewage, garbage, livestock farms, salons, night clubs, spas, food vending and nuisances. It applies to every establishment and person in the city covered by its chapters.
points: No one may work in food establishments, water refilling stations, salons, clinics, funeral parlors or resorts without a City Health Office health certificate
Health certificate applicants need fecalysis, sputum test or chest X-ray and a drug test; lab results are valid 30 days, X-ray and drug test 6 months
Sets up the City Epidemiological and Testing Unit and the City Social Hygiene Clinic
Separate sub-codes for markets (with a Bacoor City Market Board), the city slaughterhouse, water, motels, pools, cemeteries and nuisance abatement
A food establishment that lets a sick person handle food pays ₱5,000 and loses its sanitary permit
The Mayor may form committees to write implementing guidelines for each chapter without Sanggunian approval

provisions.title: One code for health, sanitation and safety
provisions.text: The code gathers Bacoor's health, sanitation and safety rules into one document in 23 chapters, and creates the City Epidemiological and Testing Unit and the City Social Hygiene Clinic.

provisions.title: No health certificate, no job
provisions.text: No one may work in food establishments, food manufacturers, water refilling stations, salons, barber shops, clinics, funeral parlors, resorts and other covered establishments without a City Health Office health certificate, valid to the end of the year and renewed yearly.

provisions.title: Tests for a health certificate
provisions.text: Applicants need fecalysis, a sputum test or chest X-ray and a drug test. Lab results are valid 30 days, X-ray and drug test 6 months. Tests are free for residents at public health centers; staff who charge or refer residents to private labs are fined ₱3,000.

provisions.title: Free care for residents, set fees for others
provisions.text: Voters of at least 1 year and Special Bacoor Resident Card holders get free lab services, medicines and medical and dental check-ups at city facilities. Others pay listed fees, such as ₱25 for a urine exam and ₱120 for a chest X-ray; the health certificate itself costs ₱150 a year.

provisions.title: Yearly sanitary permits by type of business
provisions.text: Every business, building or house for rent needs a sanitary permit each year, with fees by type and size, from ₱50 per apartment door to ₱700 for hospitals, large hotels, malls and manufacturers. Employers whose staff lack exams pay ₱5,000 and lose their permits.

provisions.title: Food establishments inspected and closable
provisions.text: No food establishment gets a permit without a prior inspection, then one random inspection every quarter. The City Health Officer may order surprise inspections, cancel permits and temporarily close food places, markets or malls when disease may spread.

provisions.title: Sick workers may not handle food
provisions.text: A person with a communicable disease or carrying one may not handle or prepare food; their work permit is cancelled until cured. The establishment's owner pays ₱5,000 and loses its sanitary permit.

provisions.title: Sub-codes for each kind of place
provisions.text: Separate chapters cover schools, water, markets, the slaughterhouse, motels, vermin, laundries, swimming pools, cemeteries, sewage, garbage, livestock farms, salons, night clubs, spas, food vending and nuisances, most with fines rising to ₱5,000 for a 3rd offence.

provisions.title: A Bacoor City Market Board
provisions.text: Chaired by the Mayor with the Vice Mayor, council committee chairs, the treasurer, market administrator, vendors' association president and police chief. It awards stalls by lot or bid, sets market rates and rules, and hears grievances, meeting every first Wednesday.

provisions.title: The Mayor writes the guidelines
provisions.text: The Mayor may form committees to write implementing guidelines for each chapter, which need no council approval if they follow the code strictly. The council and information office run campaigns to explain it.

ordinances.penalties: Set chapter by chapter, typically ₱1,000, ₱2,000 and ₱5,000 for a 1st, 2nd and 3rd offence (some charged per day), with permit suspension, closure or cancellation of the sanitary permit

details.effect: immediately after publication in a Cavite newspaper and posting in 3 places
details.covers: All establishments and persons in Bacoor engaged in regulated activities
details.enforcers: City Health Office, with the City Legal Officer, BPLO and City Mayor
creates: Bacoor City Slaughterhouse (if a feasibility study favours it)

fine for letting a sick person handle food
renewal of every food handler's health certificate

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU enforces the national Sanitation Code (PD 856) with no local code behind it, so food stalls, water refilling stations and markets go uninspected. Bacoor turns PD 856 into local chapters with health certificates, permits, fees and graded penalties. It is 133 pages, written for a suburban city, and some chapters, such as motels, night clubs and spas, may not apply to you.

apply.if: If your LGU has a health officer and sanitary inspectors
apply.then: you can replicate the health certificate chapter: no one works in food places, water refilling stations, salons, clinics or funeral parlours without one, renewed every year.

apply.if: If your rural health unit has a laboratory
apply.then: copy the rule that residents get the required tests free at public health centres, with a ₱3,000 fine for staff who charge or refer them to private labs.

apply.if: If your inspectors are few
apply.then: start with the chapters on food establishments, markets, water and public toilets, and leave the rest for later.

apply.if: If your LGU runs a slaughterhouse
apply.then: rewrite that chapter for the animals you actually slaughter and for halal practice, under a veterinarian or a named inspector.

apply.if: If you charge City Health Office fees under an older revenue ordinance
apply.then: fold the new fees into it after a public hearing, rather than set them in the health code alone.

change: Re-cite the health officer and board to BLGC s. 532 and s. 114, and add the Minister of Health's power to take over during epidemics under BLGC s. 117

Rewrite the slaughterhouse chapter for halal slaughter, under the veterinarian's duties in BLGC s. 543 and the municipal slaughterhouse function in BLGC s. 480. Bacoor's text assumes hog slaughter; the meat inspection law still applies as national law

City Health Office fees are a revenue measure, so hold public hearings under BLGC s. 212 and publish under BLGC s. 213. Also streamline the health certificate through the Business One-Stop Shop under BLGC s. 151

Drop the mandatory drug test for every health certificate applicant; at most allow random testing under the drug law (RA 9165, national law). Drop the motel, night club and spa chapters if your LGU has no such establishments or does not permit them
Check that per-day fines cannot add up past ₱5,000, the cap in BLGC s. 489 and s. 509, and post the code as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571
barmm.fits: Cities and larger municipalities with a licensed health officer and sanitary inspectors; smaller LGUs can take the food, market and water chapters.

ordinances.title: Enacting the Health and Sanitation Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.shortTitle: Health and Sanitation Code of the Province of Pangasinan
ordinances.summary: This is a province-wide sanitation code built on PD 856 (the Sanitation Code of the Philippines) and the national environment laws. It sets health certificate and sanitary permit rules for food businesses and other establishments, and sanitation standards for a long list of facilities. The Provincial Health Office leads enforcement with city and municipal health and permit offices and the police.
points: Workers in food establishments, water resorts, beauty parlors, barber shops, clinics, funeral parlors and other covered places need a health certificate from the Local Health Office, after fecalysis and a sputum test or chest X-ray. The certificate is valid to the end of the year and renewed every year.
No food establishment may open without a sanitary permit posted in a conspicuous place. A new occupant must report a change of ownership within 14 days.

There are 25 chapters covering food establishments, schools, water supply, markets, hotels and boarding houses, ports and airports, vermin, laundries, swimming pools, cemeteries, sewage, solid waste, livestock farms, barber and beauty shops, night clubs, spas, caterers and ambulant vendors, and nuisances.
No provincial, city or municipal employee may deal directly with an establishment to facilitate a sanitary permit or health certificate.
Anyone who obstructs health officers or defaces posted notices faces up to 1 year in jail or a fine of not less than ₱5,000, or both.

provisions.title: Applies to every establishment in the province
provisions.text: The Health and Sanitation Code governs all establishments in Pangasinan and builds on PD 856, the Sanitation Code of the Philippines. National laws on solid waste, clean air, clean water, toxic waste and meat inspection fill any gaps.

provisions.title: Health certificates for workers
provisions.text: No one may work in food businesses, water resorts, beauty parlors, barber shops, clinics, funeral parlors or other covered places without a health certificate from the Local Health Office, after fecalysis and a sputum test or chest X-ray. It lasts to year's end and is renewed yearly.

provisions.title: Sanitary permits for food establishments
provisions.text: No food establishment may open without a sanitary permit from the Local Health Officer, posted in a conspicuous place. It needs a vermin control program, a water test and workers' health certificates; a new occupant reports a change of ownership within 14 days.

provisions.title: No animals or smoking in food places
provisions.text: Animals are not allowed inside food establishments, and smoking is strictly banned in all food establishments and food manufacturing plants.

provisions.title: Monthly tests for water refilling stations
provisions.text: Water retailers and refilling stations submit samples for unscheduled monthly lab tests, allow on-the-spot inspection, have operators take a 40-hour certification course, and get a Certificate of Water Potability from the Local Health Office.

provisions.title: Standards for 25 kinds of facilities
provisions.text: Chapters set sanitation rules for schools, markets, slaughterhouses (at least 300 metres from schools and churches), hotels, ports and airports, laundries, pools, cemeteries and funeral homes, sewage, night clubs (no private rooms), spas and caterers.

provisions.title: Segregation and no open burning
provisions.text: Businesses segregate waste into recyclable, residual, biodegradable and special, keep lidded bins and store garbage inside until collection. Open burning and dumping on streets, creeks or vacant lots are banned, and public utility vehicles must carry trash bins.

provisions.title: Rules for livestock farms
provisions.text: Piggeries and poultry farms need zoning or environmental clearance and a barangay permit, must stay away from homes, highways and watersheds, and commercial piggeries need a biogas digester. Backyard limits are 3 pigs for fattening, 1 sow and 25 poultry.

provisions.title: Fines and closure
provisions.text: Establishments are fined ₱2,500, then ₱5,000, then closed with their permit revoked. Individuals face ₱1,000 and up to 5 days, ₱2,500 and up to 15 days, then ₱5,000 and up to 30 days. Obstructing health officers draws up to 1 year in jail or at least ₱5,000.

provisions.title: Enforcement and no fixers
provisions.text: The Provincial Health Office leads enforcement with city and municipal health and permit offices and the PNP. No provincial, city or municipal employee may deal directly with an establishment to facilitate a permit or certificate.

ordinances.penalties: Establishments: ₱2,500, then ₱5,000, then closure and revocation of permit. Individuals: ₱1,000 and/or up to 5 days in jail, rising to ₱5,000 and/or up to 30 days for a 3rd offence.
ordinances.caveat: The OCR is garbled in places, and the governor's approval block cannot be read.

SP Member Von Mark R. Mendoza

barmm.why: Worth reading if your inspectors enforce PD 856, the national Sanitation Code, without a local ordinance that sets permits, fees and penalties. Pangasinan turns it into health certificate and sanitary permit rules across many kinds of establishments, from carinderias and markets to boarding houses and ports. It is a long provincial code and the copy is badly scanned, so redraft from it rather than paste it.

apply.if: If your health office already issues sanitary permits
apply.then: you can replicate this by adding Pangasinan's yearly health certificates for food handlers and other covered workers, after fecalysis and a sputum test or chest X-ray.

apply.if: If your LGU has no sanitation code yet
apply.then: start with the chapters for food establishments, markets, water supply and ambulant vendors, and add the rest as inspectors are trained.

apply.if: If you run a slaughterhouse or public market
apply.then: keep the market chapter and add halal handling and slaughterhouse sanitation, which the Pangasinan code does not cover.

apply.if: If permit fixers are a problem in your LGU
apply.then: copy the rule that no LGU employee may deal directly with an establishment to get it a permit or certificate.

apply.if: If your LGU is a municipality
apply.then: use the graded fines (₱2,500, ₱5,000, then closure for establishments) and cap any jail term at 6 months.

change: Name the provincial health officer as lead enforcer under BLGC s. 532, have the health board review the code and its budget (BLGC s. 114), and coordinate with the Ministry of Health (BLGC s. 117)
Fix the obstruction penalty: 'not less than ₱5,000' sets a floor, but BLGC s. 521 caps provincial fines at ₱5,000 and jail at 1 year. A municipal version must cap jail at 6 months (BLGC s. 489)
Drop or rewrite chapters that do not fit local rules, such as night clubs where the LGU bans them, and add halal handling and slaughterhouse sanitation, which municipalities run under BLGC s. 480
If your LGU runs evacuation centres, add sanitation rules for them and for water points used by displaced families, in line with BAA No. 62 on internally displaced persons
Post the penal ordinance for 6 weeks and translate it into local languages before it takes effect (BLGC s. 571)
