ordinances.title: The Transportation and Traffic Code of the Municipality of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Transportation and Traffic Code of the Municipality of Loon, Bohol
ordinances.summary: A full municipal traffic code covering every vehicle on public or private roads in Loon. It sets traffic rules, creates the bodies that manage and enforce them, regulates tricycle franchises and habal-habal motorcycles-for-hire, runs the transport terminal and cruise ship port traffic, and lists local fines for each violation.
points: Creates a Municipal Franchising and Regulatory Board, a Municipal Traffic Management Board, a Municipal Traffic Management Office under the Mayor, and Municipal Traffic Aides (MUTRA).
Requires helmets for motorcycle drivers and back-riders on every road, bans improvised mufflers, and sets speed limits, overtaking, right-of-way, parking and impounding rules.

Designates the Loon Bus Terminal at Mercado de Loon with daily parking fees, such as ₱10 for buses and jeepneys, ₱4 for tricycles and habal-habal, and ₱50 for 10-wheeler trucks; overnight parking is double.
Habal-habal operators pay a ₱300 Mayor's permit fee with sticker and ID, and drivers must wear an ID, shoes and a long-sleeve uniform.
At the Loon International Cruise Ship Port: 2 police outposts on 24-hour duty, vehicle users' charges from ₱2 to ₱350 a day, and a ₱2 environmental fee per passenger.
Violators have 7 days to pay a citation ticket before a court case is filed; fines are shared 75% to the general fund and 25% to MTMO and MUTRA operations.

provisions.title: A franchising board, a traffic board and a traffic office
provisions.text: A Municipal Franchising and Regulatory Board sets franchise rates; a Municipal Traffic Management Board chaired by the SB transportation chair reviews enforcement; a Municipal Traffic Management Office under the Mayor runs traffic.

provisions.title: Municipal traffic aides who issue tickets
provisions.text: Traffic aides (MUTRA) work under the traffic office, must be at least 20, high school graduates and residents for 6 months, and may issue citation tickets and enforce anti-littering and street ordinances.

provisions.title: Helmets, mufflers and speed limits
provisions.text: Motorcycle drivers and back-riders must wear standard helmets on every road; improvised loud mufflers are banned. Speed is capped at 60 km/h on open highways and 30 km/h through crowded streets, blind corners and school zones.

provisions.title: Impounding at a police-run depository
provisions.text: Vehicles in accidents, unregistered, carnapped, under litigation, with improvised mufflers or penalised for violations are impounded at a fenced Vehicle Depository Area, with the PNP liable for any loss or damage.

provisions.title: The Loon Bus Terminal and its parking fees
provisions.text: All franchised public transport loads at the terminal in front of Mercado de Loon; parking costs ₱10 a day for buses and jeepneys, ₱4 for tricycles and habal-habal, ₱20 to ₱50 for trucks, and double overnight.

provisions.title: Tricycle franchises from the SB
provisions.text: Tricycles need an SB franchise for ₱350 and a Mayor's Permit for ₱350, both valid 1 year; transfers or unit changes cost ₱300, and renewals late past January 20 draw a 25% surcharge, with cancellation if unpaid by March.

provisions.title: Habal-habal motorcycles for hire
provisions.text: Habal-habal operators pay a ₱300 Mayor's permit fee with sticker and ID by January 20, show 7 clearances including TPL insurance, and drivers wear an ID, shoes and a long-sleeve uniform; fines run ₱200 to ₱500.

provisions.title: Cruise ship port traffic and fees
provisions.text: 2 police outposts staff the Loon International Cruise Ship Port 24 hours; vehicles using the port road pay ₱2 to ₱350 a day, and each passenger pays a ₱2 environmental fee.

provisions.title: Local fines, capped at ₱2,500
provisions.text: Each violation has a local fine schedule, such as ₱500 to ₱1,500 for driving without a valid licence; LTO-listed violations default to ₱300, ₱500 and ₱1,000, and local penalties may not exceed ₱2,500.

provisions.title: 7 days to pay, and fines shared 75/25
provisions.text: A ticketed violator has 7 days to pay at the treasurer before a court case is filed; fines go 75% to the general fund and 25% to the traffic office and aides, and unpaid fines block licence and franchise renewals.

ordinances.penalties: A schedule of local fines by offence, for example ₱500, ₱1,000 and ₱1,500 for driving without a valid licence, capped at ₱2,500; the general penalty is ₱300, ₱500 and ₱1,000 for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd offences.
ordinances.amends: Repeals any inconsistent provision of previous ordinances; it carries over sections of Municipal Ordinance 1996-08 on tricycle franchising.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your municipality has tricycles, habal-habal and jeepneys but no written traffic code, or rules spread across old ordinances. Loon's code creates the boards and aides, franchises tricycles, permits habal-habal, runs a terminal and lists a fine for each violation. It runs 48 pages, has a cruise ship port chapter few municipalities need, and its 3 separate bodies may be too many for a small payroll.

apply.if: If your municipality already franchises tricycles under an older ordinance
apply.then: you can replicate Loon's approach by carrying those sections into the new code, as Loon carried over its 1996 tricycle ordinance, instead of starting over.

apply.if: If you have no traffic office
apply.then: start with a team of civilian traffic aides under the mayor, authorised to issue citation tickets, and merge the franchising and traffic boards into one.

apply.if: If habal-habal operate in your municipality
apply.then: copy the mayor's permit with sticker and ID, a number for each unit, and the driver ID and uniform rules.

apply.if: If your municipality has a terminal, market, ferry landing or pumpboat port
apply.then: use the terminal article as the model, with posted daily parking fees, double for overnight, and skip the cruise port chapter.

apply.if: If you want fines to fund the traffic aides
apply.then: set their share in the yearly appropriation, since earmarked fines still need one under BLGC s. 329.

change: Re-cite tricycle franchising to BLGC s. 480 and keep fees within BLGC s. 156, which bars LGUs from taxing common carriers or charging motor vehicle registration fees except for tricycles
Keep every fine within ₱5,000 or 6 months under BLGC s. 489, and post and publish the code as BLGC s. 571 requires

Leave police deployment to national law and the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BLGC s. 33); the code should create civilian traffic aides, not order police posts. Open the aide posts to women; Loon's code says aides shall be male
Drop the cruise ship port chapter; replace it with rules for the municipality's own market, ferry landing or pumpboat port where there is one

Merge the 3 bodies into 1 traffic and franchising board for 4th to 6th class municipalities; check the 25% fine share to the traffic office against BLGC s. 329, since earmarked fines still need an appropriation
barmm.fits: Municipalities with tricycles, habal-habal or a terminal to regulate, especially those on national highways.

ordinances.title: Adopting the 2015 Traffic Management Code of Marikina City
ordinances.shortTitle: The 2015 Traffic Management Code of Marikina City
ordinances.summary: This is a citywide traffic code covering all national and local roads in Marikina. It sets rules on signs and signals, general driving, giving way, speed, one-way streets, turns, stopping and parking, parking zones and fees, reckless driving and accidents. It is administered by the City Transportation Management and Development Office (CTMDO).
points: Motor vehicles may not drive or park on bicycle lanes or on the jogging lanes along the Marikina River.

Overnight parking is allowed only on listed streets. It costs ₱10 a night, collected by the barangay, or ₱750 a quarter or ₱1,500 a year paid to the City Treasurer. It is barred on roads under 3 metres wide and for buses, jeepneys, tricycles and trucks of 8 or more wheels.

Delivery vehicles entering the Marikina Public Market Zone pay ₱100 per entry for 6- to 10-wheelers, ₱50 for elf vans and ₱30 for jeepneys. Parking costs ₱10 for the first 2 hours and ₱20 per hour after, or ₱5 and ₱10 for motorcycles.
The Traffic Management and Enforcement Division may tow illegally parked vehicles at the owner's cost.
Repair shops must report to police within 24 hours any vehicle showing signs of an accident, crime or bullet strike, or face up to ₱5,000.

provisions.title: Covers every road in the city
provisions.text: The code applies to all national and local roads in Marikina and to every kind of vehicle, from buses and tricycles to bicycles and pedicabs, alongside RA 4136 and LTO rules, which it adopts.

provisions.title: No private sirens or flashing lights
provisions.text: No private person may use sirens, horns or similar gadgets, or dome, flashing or blinker lights, to bypass traffic, cross intersections or get ahead in congestion.

provisions.title: Bicycle and river jogging lanes kept clear
provisions.text: Motor vehicles may not drive or park on bicycle lanes or on the jogging lanes on both sides of the Marikina River, except at designated commercial and recreational areas and access lanes, and city peace-and-order vehicles.

provisions.title: Speed limits, seatbelts and no drag racing
provisions.text: Drivers keep to posted speed limits, drivers and front-seat passengers wear seatbelts under RA 8750, and drag racing or speed contests are banned without a special permit from the mayor.

provisions.title: Towing at the owner's cost
provisions.text: Enforcers may order illegally parked vehicles moved, and the Traffic Management and Enforcement Division may tow unattended ones to the city impound, with towing and impounding charged to the owner.

provisions.title: Market zone entry and parking fees
provisions.text: Delivery vehicles entering the Marikina Public Market Zone pay ₱100 per entry for 6- to 10-wheelers, ₱50 for elf vans and ₱30 for jeepneys. Parking is ₱10 for the first 2 hours and ₱20 an hour after, or ₱5 and ₱10 for motorcycles.

provisions.title: Overnight parking only where listed
provisions.text: Overnight parking is allowed only on listed streets, from midnight to 5:00 a.m., never on roads under 3 metres wide or PUV routes, and not for buses, jeepneys, tricycles or trucks of 8 or more wheels.

provisions.title: ₱10 a night, or ₱750 a quarter
provisions.text: Overnight parking costs ₱10 a night collected by the barangay, or ₱750 a quarter or ₱1,500 a year paid to the City Treasurer. Vehicles without receipts are towed and impounded.

provisions.title: No drunk or drugged driving
provisions.text: Driving with at least 0.06% blood alcohol, or impaired by drugs, is banned, including on bicycles, and violators must be tested.

provisions.title: Repair shops report suspicious vehicles
provisions.text: A repair shop must report to the nearest police precinct within 24 hours any vehicle showing signs of an accident, crime or bullet strike, or face the maximum ₱5,000 penalty.

ordinances.caveat: The text covers only pages 1 to 19 of 42 and ends at Section 76, so the penalty schedule, the later articles, the enactment date and the signatures are missing.

sponsors: Councilor Thaddeus Antonio M. Santos, Jr.
Vice-Mayor Jose Fabian I. Cadiz, M.D.
details.covers: All roads in Marikina and every motor vehicle, tricycle, bicycle and pedicab on them
details.enforcers: City Transportation Management and Development Office and its enforcement division

roads narrower than this can never be overnight parking

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your poblacion has traffic and parking problems and no written traffic code. Marikina's code is a clean outline: signs and signals, right of way, speed, one-way streets, turns, parking zones, reckless driving and accidents. The text stops at Section 76, on page 19 of 42, so it has no penalty schedule, enactment date or signatures, and some fees, such as per-entry charges on delivery trucks, are legally risky.

apply.if: If your LGU has a traffic office or traffic enforcers
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the chapter structure, naming that office as administrator, and writing your own penalty schedule within your cap.

apply.if: If you have no traffic office
apply.then: start with the parking, loading and towing rules around the market and terminals, enforced by the police and barangay tanods, and add the other chapters later.

apply.if: If cars park overnight on your residential streets
apply.then: copy the ₱10-a-night fee kept by the barangay, on listed streets only, from midnight to 5 a.m., and never on roads under 3 metres wide.

apply.if: If your LGU franchises tricycles
apply.then: add routes, terminals and franchise rules under BLGC s. 480, which Marikina's code leaves to other ordinances.

apply.if: If you want to charge delivery vehicles at the market
apply.then: tie the fee to parking or loading space you provide, since BLGC s. 156 bars taxes on goods passing through and on common carriers.

change: Write your own penalty schedule, since the text has none, within ₱5,000 and 1 year for a city (BLGC s. 509) or ₱5,000 and 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489), and post and publish it as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571.
Drop or rework the per-entry fees on delivery vehicles: BLGC s. 156 bars local taxes on goods passing through and on common carriers, so a fee must be tied to a real service such as market parking.
Add tricycle franchising and routes, which municipalities control under BLGC s. 480, and keep national roads and driver rules under the national Land Transportation and Traffic Code (RA 4136).
Use BLGC s. 24 for street closures for markets, fiestas and Friday prayers, and set parking fees by ordinance under BLGC s. 148.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with a congested centre, a public market and many tricycles.

ordinances.title: Ordinance enacting a market code of the Municipality of Trinidad, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Trinidad Market Code of 2007
ordinances.summary: A market code for the Trinidad Public Market covering its board, stall bidding and leases, vendor rules, rents and fees, weights and measures, and slaughterhouse fees. It is a compact model for a municipal public market.
points: Trinidad Public Market Board chaired by the Mayor, which runs stall bidding and sets rates subject to council approval; a Market Administrator runs the market day to day
Occupancy privilege fees of ₱4,000 to ₱10,000 for wet-market stalls and ₱30,000 in the main building, plus rent of ₱4 per sq m a day
Stalls idle for 3 months (90 days) are declared vacant and rebid
Bans selling outside assigned sections, short weighing, living in stalls, subleasing stalls and videoke machines
Transient vendors pay ₱300 for a Mayor's permit; porters register for ₱50 a year; entrance fees of ₱0.10 to ₱1.00 per kilo
Late payment: 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for up to 36 months; 20% discount for payment in the first 5 days of the month

provisions.title: A public market board chaired by the Mayor
provisions.text: Creates the Trinidad Public Market Board, chaired by the Mayor with the Vice Mayor, market administrator, treasurer, planning, engineering and health officers, police chief, 2 SB committee chairs and the vendors' association president. It meets every first Wednesday.

provisions.title: Board awards stalls; an administrator runs the market
provisions.text: The board runs stall draws and bidding, sets market rules, settles grievances, and sets rates so the market pays for itself, subject to Sangguniang Bayan approval. A Market Administrator runs the market day to day and reports to the board monthly.

provisions.title: Permits and vendor duties
provisions.text: No one may do business in or around the market without a business permit; food handlers also need a yearly sanitary permit and a health certificate with a check-up every 6 months. Vendors post their photo and permit, keep stalls clean and have scales sealed.

provisions.title: What vendors may not do
provisions.text: Bans selling outside assigned sections, extending stalls into pathways, short weighing, living in stalls, subleasing or transferring stalls, videoke machines, bringing vehicles inside, littering, and selling illegal goods.

provisions.title: Stall bidding and vacancies
provisions.text: Vacant stalls are posted for at least 10 days, then awarded by sealed bid run by the Bids and Awards Committee, announced 15 days ahead. Bidders must be adult Filipinos, local residents first, at most 2 stalls each. Stalls idle 3 months (90 days) are rebid.

provisions.title: Occupancy fees and rent
provisions.text: One-time occupancy fees run from ₱4,000 for vegetable and dried fish stalls to ₱10,000 for prime meat stalls, and ₱30,000 in the main building, plus rent of ₱4 per sq. m a day. Main building stalls facing the highway start bidding at ₱100,000.

provisions.title: Refund for surrendered stalls
provisions.text: A bidder who stops operating may surrender the stall for a refund of 80% of the winning bid after 1 year, falling to 5% after 9 years, paid from the rebid. Heirs may take over a stall if they notify the board within 30 days of the holder's death.

provisions.title: Transient vendors, porters and entrance fees
provisions.text: Transient vendors need a Mayor's permit for ₱300 and porters register for ₱50 a year. Goods brought in for sale pay entrance fees of ₱0.10 to ₱1.00 a kilo; selling without paying draws 3 times the fee or confiscation.

provisions.title: Slaughter fees
provisions.text: Slaughter fees per head are ₱200 for carabao and cattle, ₱100 for hogs and ₱70 for goats for commercial use, with lower rates for home use, plus permit, hauling, corral and meat inspection fees.

provisions.title: Discounts, surcharges and fines
provisions.text: Rent paid in the first 5 days of the month gets a 20% discount; late payment carries a 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for up to 36 months. Rule violations draw ₱1,000, ₱1,500, then ₱2,000 with revocation of permit and lease.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 for a 1st violation, ₱1,500 for a 2nd, ₱2,000 plus revocation of permit and termination of lease for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: This copy, posted by WIEGO, has no ordinance number, enactment date or signatures; the year comes from its short title.

barmm.why: Worth reading if you run a public market without a written code and stall awards, arrears and subleasing keep turning into disputes. Trinidad's code is a compact model for a small municipal market, from the board to sealed bidding, rents, weights and meat inspection. The copy is unsigned and undated, its 2007 rates are not a basis for yours, and its late-payment rules need changing under the BLGC.

apply.if: If your LGU runs its own public market
apply.then: you can replicate the market board chaired by the mayor, with the vendors' association president as a member, and a market administrator for daily operations.

apply.if: If stalls in your market are awarded informally
apply.then: start with sealed public bidding, priority for local bidders, a standard lease and a certificate of award, and rebid any stall idle for 90 days.

apply.if: If you collect market fees under an older revenue ordinance
apply.then: re-price every fee after a public hearing, and keep Trinidad's 20% discount for paying in the first 5 days.

apply.if: If you charge late-payment interest
apply.then: consider a fixed late charge instead, as BLGC s. 153 allows, rather than Trinidad's 25% surcharge and 2% a month.

apply.if: If your market sells meat
apply.then: name who inspects it, since a municipal veterinarian is optional, and give halal and non-halal meat separate sections, stalls and tools.

change: Trinidad's 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for 36 months are the maximum BLGC s. 191 allows; BLGC s. 153 lets the council use a Shari'ah-compliant fixed late charge instead. Keep the 20% early-payment discount.

Separate halal and non-halal meat: their own sections, stalls, tools and drainage, and pork kept away from the main meat line. Put meat inspection and slaughterhouse rules under the veterinarian (BLGC s. 543, optional for municipalities, so name who inspects).

Check the per-kilo entrance fees against BLGC s. 156, which bars taxing products sold by marginal farmers and fishers; exempt them or set a flat facility fee. Keep the transient vendor permit fee tied to regulation cost, since s. 167 caps the business tax on peddlers at ₱50 a year.
Run bidding through the Bids and Awards Committee under BLGC s. 387, hold public hearings on the rates (s. 212) and publish them (s. 213), and never let a private person collect market fees (s. 152).
Fill in the number, date and signatures yourself and re-price every fee; the 2007 Bohol rates are not a basis for your market.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a public market they run themselves, and cities with a small secondary market.

ordinances.title: Ordinance requiring businesses and establishments in Davao City which offer halal products and services to acquire halal certification from the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) accredited certifying bodies, prior to the posting of the word "halal" within their premises or to use the "halal" logo in their business name
ordinances.shortTitle: Halal Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Requires any business in Davao City that sells or serves halal food or non-food products to be certified by an NCMF-accredited halal certifying body before it uses the word or logo "halal". It covers hotels, restaurants, eateries, food stalls, school canteens, function halls and producers, manufacturers and suppliers.
points: Covers halal food served at any event in the city, including seminars, weddings and birthdays
Certified establishments must display the Philippine Halal logo at the front and keep their certification documents on the premises
Displaying the halal word or logo without certification from an NCMF-accredited body is prohibited
A 3rd offence can bring revocation of the business permit and closure, at the court's discretion

provisions.title: Halal claims need proper certification
provisions.text: Known as the Halal Ordinance of Davao City, it requires businesses offering halal products and services to get halal certification before posting the word 'halal' on their premises or using the halal logo in their business name, to protect Muslims' right to religiously sanctioned products.

provisions.title: What counts as halal and who certifies
provisions.text: Halal means food and non-food products Shari'ah permits Muslims to consume or use. Certification must come from a halal certifying body accredited by the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos under RA 9997.

provisions.title: Who is covered
provisions.text: Hotels, restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, food stalls and school or university canteens serving halal food; halal food served at any function in the city, from seminars and meetings to weddings and birthdays; and anyone producing, processing or supplying halal food and non-food products.

provisions.title: Duties of owners and managers
provisions.text: Owners, proprietors and managers must get halal certification from an NCMF-accredited body, display the Philippine Halal logo at the front of the business, and keep the certification documents on display on the premises.

provisions.title: No halal word or logo without certification
provisions.text: No business may display the halal logo or the word 'halal' on its premises unless an NCMF-accredited certifying body has certified it halal.

provisions.title: Fines, then closure on a 3rd offence
provisions.text: Fines run ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offence and ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd. A 3rd brings ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 plus revocation of the business permit and closure, at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Effect after publication
provisions.text: It takes effect after approval and publication in a newspaper of general circulation in Davao City.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd, ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 plus permit revocation and closure for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: The text is noisy OCR; it was deemed approved after the Mayor let 10 days lapse under Section 54 of the Local Government Code.

details.effect: upon approval and publication in a local newspaper
details.covers: Davao City businesses that serve, make or sell halal food and non-food products

highlights.label: minimum fine for a 1st offence
top fine on a 3rd offence, with permit revocation
duties: certify, display the logo, keep the papers

barmm.why: Worth reading if sellers in your LGU use the word or logo 'halal' on products or signs that no certifier has checked. Davao City's ordinance is short and easy to enforce: no certification, no halal sign. It is from 2015 and names only the NCMF, and where most food sellers already treat their food as halal, a strict version could fall first on small eateries that cannot afford certification.

apply.if: If your LGU has food processors, hotels, caterers or chain outlets
apply.then: you can replicate this by requiring them to be certified by an accredited body before they use the halal word or logo, and to display the logo and keep the certificate on the premises.

apply.if: If most of your food sellers are small eateries and stalls
apply.then: start with a certification drive and a grace period, and apply fines only to packaged goods and larger establishments at first.

apply.if: If you already check permits through a business one-stop shop
apply.then: add the halal certificate to the permit checklist for businesses that advertise halal.

apply.if: If you want to cover events
apply.then: limit it to commercial function halls and caterers, not food at private weddings, birthdays or family gatherings.

ordinances.title: Requiring restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, food stalls in moviehouses, school or university canteens and other food establishments which serve "halal" foods to acquire halal accreditation from the Davao City Muslim Ulama Halal Certifying and Monitoring Agency, prior to the posting of the word "halal"…
ordinances.shortTitle: Halal Ordinance
ordinances.summary: Food businesses in Davao City that serve halal food must get halal accreditation from the Davao City Muslim Ulama Halal Certifying and Monitoring Agency before they display the word "halal" or use the halal logo. It covers restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, cinema food stalls, school canteens and halal food served at events in function halls. The stated aim is to protect Muslims' right to religiously sanctioned food.
points: Covers restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, moviehouse food stalls, school and university canteens, and halal food served at seminars, weddings and other events in function halls
Establishments must get accreditation, display the halal logo in front and display their accreditation documents on the premises
Halal food must not be prepared with kitchenware or utensils used for haram food
Bans mixing pork or other haram meat with meat used in halal-processed food
Defines halal-processed meat, haram meat and the certifying agency

provisions.title: Accreditation before saying 'halal'
provisions.text: Food establishments that serve halal food must get halal accreditation from the Davao City Muslim Ulama Halal Certifying and Monitoring Agency before posting the word 'halal' on their premises or using the halal logo in their business name.

provisions.title: Halal, haram and the certifier defined
provisions.text: Halal-processed meat is from animals such as cow, chicken and goat slaughtered by Islamic ritual; haram meat is pork and animals killed by strangling, a violent blow or a headlong fall. The certifying agency is the office authorized by the National Halal Accreditation Board to accredit in Davao City.

provisions.title: Restaurants, canteens and function halls
provisions.text: It covers restaurants, fast-food chains, eateries, moviehouse food stalls, school and university canteens and other food establishments serving halal food, plus halal food served at seminars, meetings, weddings, birthdays and other events in any function hall.

provisions.title: Display the logo and the papers
provisions.text: Establishments offering halal food must display the halal logo in front and keep their accreditation documents on display inside the premises.

provisions.title: Separate utensils and sanitary preparation
provisions.text: Halal food must be prepared following proper sanitary procedures and never with kitchenware or utensils used for haram food.

provisions.title: No mixing haram meat
provisions.text: Meat from pigs or other forbidden animals may not be mixed with the meat used in halal-processed food.

provisions.title: Fines up to ₱5,000 and closure
provisions.text: Owners, managers or vendors who violate it are fined ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offense, ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd, and ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 for a 3rd, with revocation of the business permit and closure, at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Effect after publication
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation and posting for 3 consecutive weeks at City Hall.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 for a 2nd, and ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 with permit revocation and closure for a 3rd
ordinances.caveat: The approval stamp indicates the ordinance took effect by lapse without the mayor's signature under Section 54 of RA 7160; the scan's OCR is rough in places.

barmm.why: Worth reading if food sold as halal in your LGU comes from outlets no one checks, such as canteens, caterers, function halls or shops owned by non-Muslims. Davao ties the right to use the word 'halal' or the logo to accreditation, and bans shared utensils and mixed meat. It is 4 pages and easy to copy, but it names a single city certifier and defines haram narrowly.

apply.if: If your LGU already inspects food outlets when it issues business permits
apply.then: you can replicate this by adding halal accreditation to the checklist for any outlet that displays the word or the logo, through the Business One-Stop Shop.

apply.if: If there is no accredited halal certifier near you
apply.then: recognise any body accredited under RA 10817 instead of naming one, and give outlets time to get certified before fines apply.

apply.if: If you have religious authorities who can advise the council

apply.if: If nearly every eatery in your LGU is Muslim-run
apply.then: a shorter rule covering canteens, caterers and packaged food from outside may be all you need.

change: Don't name a single certifier in the ordinance. Recognize bodies accredited under national law (RA 10817), and check whether the Bangsamoro Government has issued halal rules; no halal BAA appears in the index
Widen the haram definition with local religious authorities: Davao's covers only pork and improperly killed animals and leaves out alcohol, blood and other ingredients

Re-cite the basis to the general welfare clause (BLGC s. 17, which covers preserving culture and public morals) and check halal status at business permit issuance through the Business One-Stop Shop (BLGC s. 151)
Keep fines within ₱5,000 (BLGC s. 509 for cities, s. 489 for municipalities), and replace the effectivity clause with the 6-week posting and translation rule in BLGC s. 571

ordinances.title: Recognizing the right of Muslim women to wear hijab, niqab, or burqa in school campuses, workplaces, commercial establishments and other private or public premises and prohibiting unlawful discrimination and unreasonable restriction thereof and providing penalties thereto
ordinances.shortTitle: The Hijab Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Protects the right of Muslim women in Davao City to wear the hijab, niqab or burqa in schools, workplaces, shops and other public or private premises. It bans refusing them entry, discouraging students from wearing them, or making their removal a condition of work. Institutions may still apply reasonable security checks, such as screening by a female guard.
points: Unlawful to refuse entry to a woman because she wears a hijab, niqab or burqa
Unlawful to discourage a female student from wearing one in class or in school activities such as contests and sports
Unlawful to bar it at work or make it a condition of work or ground for termination
Wearers must cooperate with reasonable security checks, such as screening by a female officer or uncovering for facial recognition
The Barangay Cultural Communities Affairs and Development office under the Mayor takes complaints and mediates, preferably within 7 working days

provisions.title: Covers every Muslim woman who wears a veil
provisions.text: The ordinance applies to all Muslim women in Davao City who wear the hijab, niqab or burqa, in school campuses, workplaces, commercial establishments and other public or private premises.

provisions.title: Reasonable security checks still allowed
provisions.text: Institutions keep the right to set security rules, and a woman wearing a veil must cooperate with reasonable checks on entry, such as screening by a female security officer or uncovering for facial recognition.

provisions.title: No refusing entry because of a veil
provisions.text: No person, group, organisation or institution may refuse a Muslim woman entry to a school, workplace, commercial establishment or other premises because she wears a hijab, niqab or burqa.

provisions.title: No discouraging students from wearing one
provisions.text: No one may discourage a female student from wearing a hijab, niqab or burqa on school days, in regular classes or in activities such as celebrations, contests and sports.

provisions.title: No barring it at work
provisions.text: No employer may discourage or prohibit wearing it on the job, or make its removal a condition of work or a ground for termination.

provisions.title: A city office takes complaints and mediates
provisions.text: The Barangay Cultural Communities Affairs and Development office under the Mayor spreads information, accepts complaints, notifies offenders, mediates preferably within 7 working days, and refers cases for formal investigation.

provisions.title: Penalties rise with each offence
provisions.text: A 1st offence draws a reprimand from the implementing office, a 2nd a ₱1,000 fine, and a 3rd a ₱3,000 fine and/or 20 days' imprisonment at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Takes effect 15 days after publication
provisions.text: It takes effect 15 days after publication in a local newspaper and posting for 3 consecutive weeks at City Hall and 2 other conspicuous places.

ordinances.penalties: Reprimand for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 for a 2nd, and ₱3,000 and/or 20 days in jail for a 3rd

details.effect: 15 days after publication and 3 weeks' posting
details.covers: Muslim women wearing hijab, niqab or burqa in Davao schools, workplaces and premises
details.enforcers: Barangay Cultural Communities Affairs and Development, Office of the City Mayor

highlights.label: acts banned, at school, at work and at the door
working days to mediate a complaint
fine, or 20 days in jail, for a 3rd offence
fine for a 2nd offence; the 1st draws a reprimand

barmm.why: Worth reading if women in your LGU are told to remove the hijab, niqab or burqa to enter a school, office, bank or shop, or to keep a job. Davao's 2018 ordinance is short and balanced: it bans 3 acts, lets institutions keep reasonable security checks such as screening by a female guard, and starts with mediation and a reprimand before any fine. It protects only Muslim women's dress, so consider widening it.

apply.if: If your LGU has a human rights action center or a legal officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving that office the job of receiving complaints and mediating within 7 working days, as Davao gave its cultural communities office.

apply.if: If you have neither office
apply.then: have the mayor designate an office to take complaints for now, with referral to the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission (BAA No. 4).

apply.if: If most respondents would be private schools, hospitals or companies
apply.then: keep complaints out of the lupon, since BLGC s. 436 excludes disputes with juridical entities, and send unsettled cases to the prosecutor.

apply.if: If your LGU has Christian or Indigenous residents
apply.then: widen the protection to their religious and cultural dress too, using the same 3 prohibited acts and the same security proviso.

change: Re-cite the enacting clause to BLGC s. 17 and s. 509 (or s. 489 for a municipality); the fines are already within both limits.

Give the complaint and mediation role to an office the BLGC provides for, such as the human rights action center in BLGC s. 480 or the legal officer in BLGC s. 535, with referral to the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission (BAA No. 4).
Do not route complaints through the lupon: most respondents are schools and companies, and BLGC s. 436 excludes complaints against juridical entities from barangay settlement.
Widen protection to the religious and cultural dress of Christian and Indigenous residents too (BAA No. 64); a one-sided rule is harder to defend and less fair in mixed communities.
Replace the effectivity clause with the 6-week posting, publication and translation BLGC s. 571 requires, and make the 1st-offence reprimand a written warning rather than a criminal penalty.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with schools, hospitals, banks or malls that serve more than one faith community.

ordinances.title: Ordinance providing for a Women's Development Code of Davao City and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Women Development Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: An early, wide-ranging women's code that defines women's rights and violence against women, and sets city duties on health, education, work, culture, rural, Indigenous and Moro women, and gender and development. A second book sets penalties for trafficking, sex tours, forced marriage and labour violations, and creates an Integrated Gender and Development Office to implement it.
points: Creates the Integrated Gender and Development Office as the city's coordinating, regulatory and monitoring body for the code
Sets aside 6% of the Annual Development Fund, plus official development assistance under RA 7192
Creates a Council for Women, a city Women's Summit, a Women Complaints Relation Section and women's representation in barangay and city development councils
Provides for the rights of Indigenous and Moro women, including culturally appropriate schools
Bans soliciting women's services for sexual purposes, sex tours and forced marriage; establishments offering sex tours lose their business permit
City departments must report on compliance every 6 months

provisions.title: Women's desks in police and city offices
provisions.text: A Women Complaints Relation Section with its own officer in every police station; abuse complaints handled by trained female officers; a Family Arbitration Committee in each barangay's Lupong Tagapamayapa; and a Medico-Legal Desk for Women at the social services office.
provisions.section: Bk. I, Ch. II, Secs. 20 to 23

provisions.title: Women's Day, a summit and a Council for Women
provisions.text: March 8 is declared a special holiday with barangay activities, a Women's Summit is held the first week of March each year, and a Council for Women is organized by district from barangay women's organizations.
provisions.section: Bk. I, Ch. II, Secs. 26 to 30

provisions.title: A third of development councils are women
provisions.text: At least 1/3 of the members of each Barangay Development Council and of the City Development Council must be women, and the women's sectoral representative to the council is elected by accredited women's organizations.
provisions.section: Bk. I, Ch. II, Secs. 31 to 33

provisions.title: Indigenous and Moro women
provisions.text: The cultural identity of Indigenous and Moro women is built into all city programs, with accessible, culturally appropriate schools and a survey of Indigenous and Moro areas within 2 years.
provisions.section: Bk. I, Ch. II, Secs. 36 to 39

provisions.title: Workplace, health and education duties
provisions.text: City offices hold sexual harassment orientations and set up grievance machinery; the city budgets for women's health and reproductive health care, offers Sunday classes and adult education, and promotes gender-sensitive curricula.
provisions.section: Bk. I, Ch. II, Secs. 40 to 54

provisions.title: No soliciting women, trafficking or sex tours
provisions.text: Soliciting a woman's services for sexual purposes, or deceiving women into prostitution or other jobs, draws ₱5,000 and 1 year in jail. Hotels, resorts and saunas used for sex tours lose their business permit, and the owner pays ₱5,000 and serves 1 year.
provisions.section: Bk. II, Ch. I, Secs. 1 to 4

provisions.title: No degrading beauty contests or fund-raisers
provisions.text: Beauty contests that treat women as sex objects are banned in schools, barangays and city celebrations, punished by ₱5,000 and loss of permit or 1 month's suspension. Fund-raising that uses women as prizes draws ₱5,000 or 6 months, or both.

provisions.title: No forced marriage, no women at checkpoints
provisions.text: Forcing a woman to marry draws ₱5,000 or 1 year, or both. PNP or military personnel who keep women or girls in detachments or checkpoints face summary dismissal proceedings.

provisions.title: An Integrated Gender and Development Office
provisions.text: The office is the city's coordinating, regulatory and monitoring body for the code: it keeps gender-disaggregated data, coordinates legal aid and advocacy, and sets standards for gender-sensitivity training.

provisions.title: 6% of the development fund and twice-yearly reports
provisions.text: The city appropriates 6% of its Annual Development Fund plus official development assistance under RA 7192. Every department reports its compliance to the council within 6 months and every 6 months after.

ordinances.penalties: Mostly a ₱5,000 fine and/or up to 1 year in jail; some labour and health provisions set fines of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 or permit cancellation
ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR of the session minutes (Resolution No. 12878), which record floor amendments; some figures are hard to read.

details.covers: Women of Davao City, and city offices, employers and establishments
details.enforcers: Integrated Gender and Development Office, with the CSSDO, police and barangays

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has Moro, Indigenous and settler communities and wants a women's code that speaks to all of them. Davao City's 1997 code has articles for Moro and Indigenous women, including culturally appropriate schools and access to schools and jobs for women whose births and marriages were never registered. But the text is OCR of session minutes, its budget and penalty rules predate national laws now in force, and some clauses reach beyond what an LGU can do.

apply.if: If your LGU has Moro or Indigenous communities whose births and marriages often go unregistered
apply.then: you can replicate the rule that women may enrol in schools and take jobs without a birth or marriage certificate, with another proof of status the ordinance names.

apply.if: If your LGU has no women's council or complaints desk
apply.then: start with a council for women, a yearly women's summit and a complaints desk where women's cases are handled by trained women officers.

apply.if: If your offices do not report on GAD
apply.then: copy the rule that every department reports to the sanggunian on compliance every 6 months.

apply.if: If your development councils have few women
apply.then: add women's seats in the barangay and municipal or city development councils, toward the 40% that BLGC s. 119 sets.

apply.if: If you want to address trafficking or forced marriage
apply.then: write referral and protection steps, not new offences; national law and the Shari'ah courts already cover them.

change: Replace the 6% of the Annual Development Fund with at least 5% of the annual budget under BLGC s. 348, and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 and s. 584
Replace the Integrated Gender and Development Office with the Local Women's Development Officer (BLGC s. 547) under Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8)
Drop the local penalties for trafficking and sex tours; national anti-trafficking law now covers them with much heavier penalties

Redraft the forced marriage clause with care: Muslim marriages fall under the Code of Muslim Personal Laws and the Shari'ah courts, and child marriage is now banned by national law (RA 11596); an LGU clause should focus on referral and protection, not new offences
Drop the sanctions on soldiers and police at checkpoints; under BLGC s. 33 control over the police is set by national law, so refer such cases to the proper bodies instead
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with mixed Moro, Indigenous and settler populations.

ordinances.title: Establishing Violence Against Women (VAW) Desk and protocol in handling VAW cases at the barangay level
ordinances.shortTitle: An Ordinance Establishing Violence Against Women (VAW) Desk and Protocol in Handling VAW Cases at the Barangay Level
ordinances.summary: This ordinance requires a Violence Against Women desk in every barangay of Davao City and sets a step-by-step protocol for barangay officials handling VAW cases. That protocol covers walk-in victims, cases reported by neighbours, protection orders and referrals.
points: Each punong barangay sets up a VAW desk in the barangay hall with furniture, a separate filing cabinet and logbooks. The desk person is trained in gender-sensitive case handling, preferably a woman kagawad or tanod.
The desk officer is on duty from 7 am to 7 pm, reachable by landline and mobile, and on call after hours.
Incidents must be reported to the PNP and the City Social Services and Development Office within 4 hours.

Victims are helped to file for a court TPO or PPO within 24 hours after a 15-day Barangay Protection Order is issued. Rape and trafficking cases go to the PNP Women and Children Protection Center or the NBI.
Funding comes from the GAD allocation of 5% of the annual barangay budget. Barangays file quarterly case reports with the City Mayor's Office through the Integrated Gender and Development Division.

provisions.title: A VAW desk in every barangay hall
provisions.text: Every punong barangay sets aside an area of the barangay hall for a VAW desk, with a table, chairs, a separate filing cabinet and logbooks, and keeps cases confidential and victims safe. The City Mayor makes sure every barangay has one.

provisions.title: A trained desk officer
provisions.text: The punong barangay names a desk officer trained in gender-sensitive case handling, preferably a woman kagawad or tanod; anyone untrained must take gender-sensitivity training and an orientation on anti-VAW laws.

provisions.title: On duty 7 am to 7 pm
provisions.text: The officer is on duty from 7 am to 7 pm, reachable by landline and mobile, and on call after hours.

provisions.title: What the desk does
provisions.text: It responds to gender-based violence cases, keeps records confidential, helps victims get Barangay Protection Orders and services, drafts the barangay's gender-responsive plan, refers cases to agencies and NGOs, and leads anti-VAW advocacy.

provisions.title: Protocol for walk-in victims
provisions.text: The officer gives the victim a safe private room, arranges medical care if needed, helps with a gender-sensitive investigation, explains her rights and the 15-day BPO, records the case on the Barangay Intake Sheet, and refers her to a shelter or the CSSDO if she wants.

provisions.title: Court orders within 24 hours, reports within 4
provisions.text: If she wishes, the victim is helped to file for a court TPO or PPO within 24 hours of a BPO, or directly. Every incident is reported to the PNP and the City Social Services and Development Office within 4 hours.

provisions.title: Cases reported by neighbours
provisions.text: When a community member reports a case, the officer verifies it, with PNP help if needed, arranges a rescue where necessary, informs the victim of her rights and the BPO, and refers her for medical care and shelter.

provisions.title: Rape and trafficking go to the police or NBI
provisions.text: For rape, trafficking and other cases outside barangay jurisdiction, the victim is helped to file a complaint with the PNP Women and Children Protection Center or the NBI.

provisions.title: Funded from the barangay GAD budget
provisions.text: The desk is funded from the gender and development allocation of 5% of the annual barangay budget.

provisions.title: Quarterly case reports
provisions.text: Barangays report setting up the desk, then file quarterly reports of all cases, the action taken and their status, to the City Mayor's Office through the Integrated Gender and Development Division.

details.covers: All barangays of Davao City
details.enforcers: Punong barangays and VAW desk officers, reporting to the City Mayor through the IGDD
details.funding: Barangay GAD budget, 5% of the annual barangay budget

highlights.label: to report a case to the police and social welfare
to help file for a court order after a BPO

barmm.why: Worth reading if your barangays have VAW desks on paper but no written protocol for handling a case. Davao City's 5-page ordinance sets it out step by step, for walk-in victims and for cases reported by neighbours, from first aid to protection orders and referrals. It costs little to run, but its deadlines assume a family court and police within easy reach.

apply.if: If your barangays already have VAW desk persons
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the protocol as written: safety and medical needs first, then rights, the intake sheet and the Barangay Protection Order, and help to file for a court order within 24 hours.

apply.if: If your barangays have no trained desk person
apply.then: have each punong barangay name one, preferably a woman kagawad or tanod, and require basic gender-sensitivity training before they take cases.

apply.if: If your barangays are far from a police station or family court
apply.then: allow the 4-hour report by call or text, and name the nearest court that can issue protection orders.

apply.if: If cases in your area tend to go to the lupon or to elders for settlement
apply.then: add a plain rule that VAW cases are never mediated or settled, at the barangay or by family or clan leaders.

apply.if: If your LGU wants to track cases
apply.then: require quarterly reports from each desk to the social welfare office, with the action taken and status of each case, kept confidential.

change: Re-cite the desk to BLGC s. 408 and the city's or municipality's role to its supervision over barangays (s. 37); RA 9262 and the Magna Carta of Women stay as the national law basis.
Add a plain rule that VAW cases are never brought to the lupon, mediation or settlement; BLGC s. 436 excludes them from amicable settlement. Say the same for settlement by elders or clan leaders.

Fund it from the 5% GAD budget in BLGC s. 348. Route reports to the social welfare officer (s. 537) and, where there is one, the Local Women's Development Officer (s. 547), with the Bangsamoro Women Commission (BAA No. 8) informed.

If some of your barangays are on islands or in the uplands, make the 4-hour report to the police and social welfare office realistic: allow a call or text, and name the nearest Regional Trial Court where there is no family court.
Publish the protocol in the local languages (BLGC s. 67) so desk officers and victims can use it.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities enacting it for all their barangays, or a sangguniang barangay acting on its own.

ordinances.title: The new comprehensive anti-smoking ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.shortTitle: The New Comprehensive Anti-Smoking Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: This ordinance bans smoking tobacco, e-cigarettes and shisha in public transport, government and company vehicles, workplaces, accommodation and entertainment establishments, enclosed public places, public buildings and public outdoor spaces, except in designated smoking areas. It puts duties on owners, managers and vehicle operators, and it creates an Anti-Smoking Task Force to enforce the ban.
points: A designated smoking area must be open-air with no roof or walls, at least 10 metres from entrances and places where people pass, no larger than 5 square metres, limited to 1 per place, and free of food or drink. It needs a certificate from the Anti-Smoking Task Force.
Establishments must post 8 x 16 inch "Non-Smoking Establishment" signs at entrances, remove ashtrays, brief staff, report violators and not sell cigarettes in non-smoking areas.
Jeepneys, taxis, buses and other vehicles must display "No Smoking" signs of set minimum sizes.
The Anti-Smoking Task Force is chaired by the City Administrator. It inspects places, certifies smoking areas, apprehends violators and recommends closures.
A first-time violator who does not contest may pay ₱500 within 3 days to avoid prosecution, once only, and must attend smoking-cessation counselling.
₱5,000,000 is appropriated for 2012 to 2016.

provisions.title: No smoking or vaping in public places
provisions.text: No one may smoke tobacco or use e-cigarettes, shisha and the like in public transport, government vehicles, accommodation and entertainment establishments, workplaces, enclosed or partly enclosed public places, public buildings or public outdoor spaces, except in designated smoking areas.

provisions.title: Strict rules for a designated smoking area
provisions.text: It must be open-air with no roof or walls, at least 10 m from entrances, exits and places people pass or gather, no larger than 5 sq. m, 1 per place, with no food or drink, and signed with health warnings and no tobacco branding. It needs a certificate from the Anti-Smoking Task Force.

provisions.title: Duties of establishments and buildings
provisions.text: The person in charge must post 8 x 16 inch 'This is a Non-Smoking Establishment' signs at all entrances, display 'No Smoking' signs, remove ashtrays, brief staff, report violators at once to the task force or police, and sell no cigarettes in non-smoking areas.

provisions.title: 'No Smoking' signs in vehicles
provisions.text: Jeepneys, taxis, vans, buses and other vehicles must show a sign of at least 3.5 sq. in at the windshield and another of at least 10 sq. in (14 sq. in for buses) facing passengers.

provisions.title: Who is liable
provisions.text: The smoker, the owner or manager of a covered place, and the operator, driver, conductor or inspector of a vehicle who allows smoking, fails to report violators or neglects the mandatory duties are all liable.

provisions.title: An Anti-Smoking Task Force
provisions.text: Created by the Mayor and chaired by the City Administrator, with the City Legal Officer, health, business bureau, building, tourism, information, environment offices, the police and a private sector seat. It inspects places, certifies smoking areas, apprehends violators and recommends closures.

provisions.title: Inspections and campaigns
provisions.text: Within 60 days of effectivity the task force inspects establishments with the Business Bureau, checks 'No Smoking' signs in public utility vehicles with traffic police, and runs awareness campaigns and cessation clinics with the City Health Office.

provisions.title: Fines, jail and permit cancellation
provisions.text: ₱1,000 or 1 month in jail for a 1st offence, ₱2,500 or 2 months for a 2nd, and ₱5,000 or 4 months for a 3rd, or both. An establishment's 3rd violation is ground to cancel its business permit; minors get counselling and diversion instead.

provisions.title: Pay ₱500 within 3 days to avoid prosecution
provisions.text: Police and deputised enforcers issue citation tickets. A smoker who does not contest may pay ₱500 to the City Treasurer within 3 days of apprehension, once only, and must then attend smoking-cessation counselling.

provisions.title: ₱5,000,000 for 2012 to 2016
provisions.text: ₱5,000,000 is appropriated to carry out the ordinance from fiscal year 2012 to 2016, with later years funded in the annual or supplemental budget.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 or 1 month in jail, ₱2,500 or 2 months, then ₱5,000 or 4 months for a 3rd offence. Business permit cancellation follows a 3rd violation, and minors go to counselling instead.

details.effect: immediately after approval and publication
details.covers: Smoking and vaping in vehicles, workplaces, establishments and public places in Davao City
details.enforcers: Anti-Smoking Task Force under the City Mayor, with the PNP
details.funding: P5,000,000 from the city treasury for 2012 to 2016, then the annual budget

highlights.label: minimum distance of a smoking area from entrances
maximum size of a smoking area, 1 per place
no-contest payment for a 1st offence, once only
budgeted for enforcement from 2012 to 2016

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants a smoke-free ordinance with strict rules on where smoking is still allowed. Davao's covers public vehicles, workplaces, public buildings and outdoor public spaces, sets tight standards for smoking areas, and lets a first offender settle for ₱500 with cessation counselling. Its 2012 text covers e-cigarettes and shisha but predates the national vape law, and its task force draws on city offices a small LGU may not have.

apply.if: If your LGU has an administrator and a health officer in post
apply.then: you can replicate the task force with the administrator as chair and the health officer as co-chair, joined by the legal, permits, building, information and police offices.

apply.if: If you do not have staff for regular inspections
apply.then: start with the duties on owners and vehicle operators to post signs, remove ashtrays and report violators, and inspect at permit renewal.

apply.if: If you want to keep minor cases out of court
apply.then: copy the no-contest rule: ₱500 paid within 3 days, once only, followed by cessation counselling.

apply.if: If your LGU has ports, landings or motorcycles for hire
apply.then: keep Davao's definition of public conveyances, which already names ships, tricycles and motorcycles, and name your terminals and landings as covered places.

apply.if: If minors are caught smoking
apply.then: send them to the social welfare officer and the BCPC for counselling, as Davao does, instead of fining them.

change: Re-cite the legal basis to BLGC s. 17 (health and general welfare) and keep RA 9211 as the national law. Check the e-cigarette and shisha rules against the 2022 national vape law (RA 11900), which came after this text

Chair the task force with the administrator, and have the health officer co-chair; both posts are mandatory for municipalities under BLGC s. 481. Send minors to the social welfare officer under BLGC s. 537
Keep jail terms within BLGC s. 489 for municipalities (6 months) and s. 509 for cities (1 year); Davao's 4-month maximum fits both
Replace the ₱5,000,000 appropriation for 2012 to 2016 with a current amount, and post and publish the ordinance under BLGC s. 571
Name the conveyances and terminals your LGU has, such as passenger boats, ferry terminals, landings and motorcycles for hire

ordinances.title: Providing for an ecological solid waste management, prohibiting certain acts and providing penalties for violations, and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Davao City Ecological Solid Waste Management Ordinance of 2009
ordinances.summary: This is Davao City's solid waste ordinance under RA 9003. It covers plastic bag and styrofoam limits, waste segregation and collection, composting, materials recovery and disposal. It requires certain establishments to hold a yearly Solid Waste Management Certificate, and it sets up an enforcement unit under the City ENRO with deputised community enforcers.
points: Stores and ambulant vendors may give out only paper, biodegradable, reusable or indigenous-material bags, or used boxes. Non-biodegradable plastic bags and styrofoam food containers are banned 2 years after approval.
Segregation at source is mandatory, and the city collects segregated waste on a schedule. Barangays, households and establishments must compost.
Industrial, agro-industrial and agricultural establishments and institutions such as schools, hospitals and clinics must secure a Solid Waste Management Certificate every year.
Bans littering, open burning, dumping outside the city disposal facility, and mixing health-care or hazardous waste with municipal waste.
The barangay whose enforcer catches a violator keeps 50% of the fine, and 50% of household garbage fees.
₱1,000,000 is appropriated on effectivity.

provisions.title: Only paper, reusable or biodegradable bags
provisions.text: All stores and ambulant vendors may give customers only recycled paper bags, biodegradable plastic bags, reusable bags, bags of indigenous materials such as buri, abaca or bamboo, or used boxes.

provisions.title: Plastic bags and styrofoam banned after 2 years
provisions.text: Only recyclable, biodegradable or reusable food and drink containers are allowed. 2 years after approval, non-biodegradable plastic bags and polystyrene foam containers are banned in the city.

provisions.title: Mandatory segregation in 4 bins
provisions.text: Households and establishments must segregate waste at source into biodegradable, recyclable, residual and special waste, in separate labelled, covered containers. Public utility vehicles must carry waste receptacles.

provisions.title: Segregated collection by barangay and city
provisions.text: Barangays designate collection points and bring residual and special waste there; the City ENRO collects it on a published schedule. Generators of 3 cubic metres or more, except public markets, haul their own waste to the landfill.

provisions.title: Composting and materials recovery
provisions.text: Barangays compost biodegradable waste and set up materials recovery facilities, alone or in clusters. Schools, hospitals, hotels, malls, food establishments, farms and other listed establishments must compost their own.

provisions.title: A yearly Solid Waste Management Certificate
provisions.text: Industrial and agricultural establishments, schools, hospitals, clinics, malls, hotels, restaurants, markets, junkshops, haulers, developers and national agencies must get one each year from the City ENRO, with a waste plan, a budget, a seminar and a ₱300 fee.

provisions.title: Half of fines and garbage fees to barangays
provisions.text: The barangay where a violation happened and whose enforcer made the arrest keeps 50% of the fine, and barangays get 50% of household garbage fees under the 2005 Revenue Code.

provisions.title: 16 prohibited acts
provisions.text: Banned are littering, abandoning debris on roads, dumping excreta or carcasses in garbage bins, open burning, non-segregation, mixing toxic or health-care waste with city waste, dumping outside the city facility, and operating without a certificate.

provisions.title: Fines from ₱300 to ₱5,000
provisions.text: Littering draws ₱300 to ₱1,000 or 1 to 15 days of community service; open burning and non-segregation ₱300 to ₱1,000 or up to 15 days in jail; illegal dumping and operating without a certificate ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 or 1 to 6 months. A 4th offense can cost a business its permit.

provisions.title: An enforcement unit and deputized enforcers
provisions.text: An Enforcement Unit under the City ENRO apprehends violators and issues citation tickets, helped by trained barangay officials, tanods and civic volunteers deputized by the mayor. The city appropriates ₱1,000,000 on effectivity.

ordinances.penalties: ₱300 to ₱1,000 or 1 to 15 days of community service or jail for minor acts, up to ₱2,000 to ₱5,000 or 1 to 6 months in jail for the gravest. Business permits are suspended or cancelled from the 4th offence.
ordinances.caveat: One penalty tier is printed inconsistently ("Three Thousand Pesos (P2,000.00)"), and the date of mayoral approval is unclear in the scan.

details.effect: 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation

details.enforcers: City ENRO and its Enforcement Unit, with barangays and deputized enforcers

Joint executive-legislative committee for the implementing rules

highlights.label: lead time before plastic bags and styrofoam are banned

yearly fee for the solid waste certificate

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU needs a full solid waste ordinance under RA 9003 and does not want to start from a blank page. Davao covers plastic and styrofoam limits, segregation, scheduled collection, composting, materials recovery, a yearly certificate for industries, schools and clinics, and community enforcers who earn their barangay half the fine. It is a large city's ordinance from 2010, with a misprinted penalty tier, so scale the office and budget to yours.

apply.if: If your LGU has an environment officer or a solid waste office
apply.then: you can replicate this by making it the enforcement unit, training and deputising community enforcers, and giving the barangay 50% of the fines they bring in.

apply.if: If you have no composting facility
apply.then: require each barangay to compost, alone or by arrangement with other barangays or private groups, as Davao allows.

apply.if: If your markets and small stores rely on plastic bags
apply.then: keep Davao's list of allowed bags (paper, reusable, buri, abaca, anahaw, bamboo, used boxes) and give at least the 2-year lead time, longer for small vendors.

apply.if: If your LGU has schools, hospitals, clinics or agro-industries
apply.then: copy the yearly solid waste certificate, with its waste plan, orientation and ₱300 fee.

apply.if: If you cannot fund ₱1,000,000 at the start
apply.then: appropriate what your budget allows and phase in the enforcement unit, starting with the barangays that make the most waste.

change: Re-cite the basis to national law (RA 9003, as amended by RA 11898 on extended producer responsibility) and to BLGC s. 480, which gives municipalities the solid waste board, plan and materials recovery facility. Cities hold those powers too under BLGC s. 496.
Give barangays their segregation and materials recovery duties under BLGC s. 408, and have the province chair the provincial solid waste board under BLGC s. 512.
Keep city penalties within ₱5,000 and 1 year (BLGC s. 509). A municipality must cap jail at 6 months (BLGC s. 489). Correct Davao's misprinted tier ('Three Thousand Pesos (P2,000.00)').
Scale the ₱1,000,000 start-up fund and the enforcement unit to the LGU's income, and give market and sari-sari vendors a longer plastic phase-out if alternatives are hard to find locally.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with scheduled collection and a disposal site, and barangays able to compost.

ordinances.title: Watershed protection, conservation and management ordinance hereinafter referred to as the Watershed Code
ordinances.shortTitle: Watershed Code
ordinances.summary: Davao City's Watershed Code protects the watersheds that recharge the city's drinking-water aquifers. It declares conservation and agro-forestry areas environmentally critical and bans a list of activities in them, and it regulates plantations in prime agricultural areas. It creates city and barangay bodies to monitor compliance and funds them through an environmental tax.
points: Declares 34,254 hectares of conservation areas and 12,240 hectares of agro-forestry/non-tillage areas environmentally critical, based on the city's Terrain Analysis Study

Conservation areas: bans land conversion, quarrying, water drilling except for household use, structures and businesses, and hunting or motorized equipment without a permit from the Watershed Management Council
Agro-forestry areas: bans aerial spraying and inorganic farm inputs, and phases out monocrop plantations within 3 years, with no new permits or expansion
Plantations in prime agricultural areas must keep a 40-metre buffer from water sources and critical areas, and a 30-metre buffer from homes, schools and chapels
Creates a Watershed Management Council under the Mayor, Watershed Multipartite Monitoring Teams and a Barangay Watershed Management Council in each covered barangay
₱5,000,000 initial fund, plus an annual environmental tax of ₱0.25 per square metre on undertakings of at least 50 hectares

provisions.title: Watersheds mapped by the Terrain Analysis Study
provisions.text: The code covers the Sibulan-Sirawan, Lipadas, Talomo, Tamugan, Cugan Creek and Suawan watersheds, with boundaries taken from the Terrain Analysis Study by the city planning office and the DENR's Mines and Geosciences Bureau.

provisions.title: 46,494 hectares declared environmentally critical
provisions.text: It declares 34,254 hectares of conservation areas, including 11,137 hectares of Mt. Apo Natural Park, and 12,240 hectares of agro-forestry/non-tillage areas environmentally critical.

provisions.title: What is banned in conservation areas
provisions.text: Land conversion, commercial tree farming except reforestation, water drilling except for household use, dumping, quarrying, squatting and mineral exploration, any structure or business, and hunting or motorised equipment without a Watershed Council permit are banned.

provisions.title: Monocrops phased out of agro-forestry areas
provisions.text: In agro-forestry areas, land conversion, quarrying, aerial spraying and inorganic fertiliser and pesticides are banned; existing monocrop plantations get a 3-year phase-out, may not expand, and no new monocrop permits are issued.

provisions.title: Buffer zones for plantations in prime farmland
provisions.text: Monocrops go only where a crop zoning plan allows, with a 40-metre buffer from water sources and critical areas and a 30-metre buffer from homes, schools, chapels and clinics; operators relocate residents in the buffer at their own expense.

provisions.title: No renewal of DENR tenure in critical areas
provisions.text: Existing DENR tenurial agreements are respected but not renewed on expiry; those areas then go under city-DENR co-management, and no new tenure is approved without the city's recommendation.

provisions.title: A Watershed Management Council under the Mayor
provisions.text: A council of 20 or more members chaired by the Mayor meets at least monthly; it can stop violating activities, clears every undertaking in critical areas before a DENR ECC, and rules on rezoning of prime farmland.

provisions.title: Monitoring teams and barangay councils
provisions.text: 3 Watershed Multipartite Monitoring Teams cover clustered watersheds and report monthly; a Barangay Watershed Management Council chaired by the barangay captain in each covered barangay marks boundaries on the ground and can recommend stoppages.

provisions.title: ₱5,000,000 fund and a ₱0.25 environmental tax
provisions.text: ₱5,000,000 from the general fund starts the program; an annual environmental tax of ₱0.25 per square metre on undertakings of at least 50 hectares in agro-forestry and prime agricultural areas is reserved for the code.

provisions.title: Up to 1 year in jail or a ₱5,000 fine
provisions.text: Violations draw imprisonment of up to 1 year, a fine of up to ₱5,000, or both; for a company, its officers are punished and the company pays an extra ₱5,000.

ordinances.penalties: Up to 1 year in jail or a fine of up to ₱5,000, or both; corporations pay an added ₱5,000 and their officers are liable

details.effect: 15 days after publication in a local newspaper
details.covers: Davao City watersheds: Sibulan-Sirawan, Lipadas, Talomo, Tamugan, Cugan, Suawan
details.enforcers: Watershed Management Council, with the monitoring teams and barangay councils
details.funding: P5,000,000 from the General Fund, an environmental tax, donations, grants and fees

highlights.label: hectares declared conservation areas
buffer between plantations and water sources
a sq m yearly tax on undertakings of 50 ha or more
initial fund to start the code

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU sits above a water source and is losing forest cover to conversion, quarrying or plantations. Davao City mapped its critical areas from a terrain study, banned listed activities in each zone, set buffers around plantations and funded monitoring with an environmental tax. Some parts were legally risky even in Davao, notably the aerial spraying ban, and the penalties run past the caps.

apply.if: If your LGU has a terrain, hazard or land use study that maps critical areas
apply.then: you can replicate this by declaring conservation and agro-forestry zones from it, each with its own list of banned activities.

apply.if: If you have no such map yet
apply.then: start with the buffers: 40 metres between plantations and water sources, and 30 metres from homes, schools and places of worship.

apply.if: If your environment officer has few staff
apply.then: copy the barangay watershed councils and multipartite monitoring teams so communities share the monitoring.

apply.if: If large plantations or other undertakings of 50 hectares or more operate in your watershed
apply.then: consider the ₱0.25 per square metre environmental tax, passed as a new tax after a public hearing, with the money kept for watershed work.

apply.if: If the watershed overlaps ancestral domains
apply.then: draft with the Indigenous communities concerned and seat their representatives on the council.

change: Base the code on BLGC s. 17 and s. 538, which tasks the environment officer with protecting watersheds, and require the sanggunian's prior approval for projects that threaten forest cover under BLGC s. 32

Drop or rewrite the outright aerial spraying ban: the Supreme Court struck down Davao City's separate aerial spraying ban in 2016 (Mosqueda v. Pilipino Banana Growers), so a copy invites the same challenge
Treat the ₱0.25 per square metre environmental tax as a new tax under BLGC s. 211, with a prior public hearing, and publish it under BLGC s. 213

If the covered areas include ancestral domains, bring them under BAA No. 64 and IPRA (national law), with the consent of the affected communities, and seat IP representatives where BLGC s. 132 requires them
Keep penalties within the city cap in BLGC s. 509 (₱5,000 or 1 year) or the municipal cap in BLGC s. 489 (₱5,000 or 6 months); the added ₱5,000 on corporations pushes past it
barmm.fits: Cities and upland municipalities above rivers, lakes or springs that supply drinking water or power.

ordinances.title: Regulating the tourism industry in the City of Davao
ordinances.shortTitle: The Tourism Development Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: This is a tourism code. It requires every tourism-related business in Davao City to register with the City Tourism Office and sets standards by type of business: accommodation, resorts, restaurants, tourist land and sea transport, malls, recreation, museums, homestays, events organisers, medical tourism and wellness, entertainment, theme parks, convention centres and marinas. It also covers inspections, upgrading and downgrading, and fines.
points: No tourism business may operate without a certificate of registration from the City Tourism Office and a Mayor's permit. The registration fee is paid once, unless the business stops operating for 6 months or loses its permit.
Accommodation establishments and resorts are classified and inspected every year. They must keep guest registers and submit tourist arrival reports.
An establishment that fails to fix defects found in inspection faces an administrative fine of ₱1,000 up to ₱5,000, then suspension or revocation of its registration.
Tourist sea transport (pumpboats) needs a certificate of public conveyance and seaworthiness from MARINA or the Coast Guard, plus a city accreditation valid for 1 year.
Resorts must provide lifeguards, security, medical services and fire-fighting equipment.

provisions.title: No tourism business without registration
provisions.text: No one may run a tourism-oriented or tourism-related business without a certificate of registration from the City Tourism Office, which also recommends business permits for tourism businesses to the mayor.

provisions.title: Inspection before registration
provisions.text: An inspection team checks each applicant, and the office acts within 7 working days of its recommendation. No certificate issues until the business meets this ordinance and the Fire and Building Codes.

provisions.title: Register once, pay once
provisions.text: Registration is applied for once, at the start of operations, and the fee is paid once. A new application is needed if the business stops for at least 6 months or loses its mayor's permit. Share transfers are reported within 10 working days.

provisions.title: Hotels classed from deluxe to budget
provisions.text: Accommodation is classed as hotels (deluxe, first class, standard, economy or budget), apartels, tourist inns, motels and pensions, each with its own standards.

provisions.title: Guest registers and monthly arrival reports
provisions.text: No guest may occupy a room until entered in the registry; motels also log the plate numbers of guests' vehicles. Every accommodation establishment submits a tourist arrival report each month.

provisions.title: Inspections at any time
provisions.text: The office may inspect at any time, including surprise night inspections when illegal activity is reported, with access to registers, premises and staff.

provisions.title: 2 weeks to fix defects, then fines
provisions.text: Defects found must be fixed within 2 weeks, extendable by at most 1 month. Hotels that fail face a ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 fine, resorts ₱100 a day up to ₱5,000, and then suspension or revocation of registration.

provisions.title: Lifeguards, doctors and fire equipment
provisions.text: Hotels with pools and all resorts must have accredited lifeguards and security; resorts also need an on-call or full-time physician, first-aiders and life-saving equipment, and all must follow the Fire Code.

provisions.title: Pumpboats need MARINA papers and accreditation
provisions.text: Tourist sea transport must carry identifying marks, passenger accident insurance, and a certificate of public conveyance and seaworthiness from MARINA or the Coast Guard, plus a city accreditation valid for 1 year.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Licensed violators face at least 6 months in jail or ₱5,000, or both, and automatic loss of their licence; unlicensed violators at least 1 year or ₱2,000 to ₱5,000. The mayor may also impose ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 administrative fines.

ordinances.penalties: Licensees: at least 6 months in jail or a ₱5,000 fine, or both, and the license is revoked. Unlicensed operators: at least 1 year in jail or ₱2,000 to ₱5,000. The Mayor may also impose administrative fines of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000.
ordinances.caveat: The OCR prints the number inconsistently (the first page reads "Series of 2007" and some page headers read "328-07"). The city legal office endorsement and the 8 December 2009 enactment confirm 0328-09, and it was approved on 6 April 2010.

ceiling on administrative fines
