barmm.why: Worth reading if resorts, homestays or boat operators in your LGU run without registration or inspection. Davao City's 2009 code shows how to register, classify and inspect them and how to fine those that do not fix defects. Much of it covers malls, theme parks, medical tourism and marinas, and its jail terms for unlicensed operators go past BLGC limits.

apply.if: If your LGU has resorts or other accommodation
apply.then: you can replicate this by requiring yearly classification and inspection, guest registers and tourist arrival reports, with lifeguards, security, first aid and fire-fighting equipment at resorts.

apply.if: If boats take tourists to islands, lakes or beaches
apply.then: require a MARINA or Coast Guard seaworthiness certificate plus a 1-year local accreditation before they carry tourists.

apply.if: If your LGU has no tourism office
apply.then: fold registration into the business permit and one-stop shop, and have the officer who handles tourism do the inspections.

apply.if: If you want an enforcement tool short of closure
apply.then: copy the ₱100-a-day fine for unfixed defects, capped at ₱5,000, with at most 1 month's extension before suspension.

apply.if: If your tourism is mostly homestays and heritage sites
apply.then: skip the chapters on malls, theme parks, convention centres and marinas, and write simple standards for homestays and site visits.

Fold registration into the business permit process and one-stop shop under BLGC s. 151 rather than a separate office visit

Fix the penalties: 'not less than 1 year' in jail for unlicensed operators exceeds the 1-year ceiling for a city (BLGC s. 509) and the 6-month ceiling for a municipality (BLGC s. 489); keep the ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 administrative fines
Cut the categories you do not have (malls, theme parks, medical tourism, convention centres, marinas) and add homestays, island-hopping operators and heritage sites

Add Muslim-friendly standards such as prayer spaces and clear halal labelling, but do not require every restaurant to be halal; keep national accreditation by the Department of Tourism under the national Tourism Act (RA 9593)

ordinances.title: Providing mandatory representation for Indigenous Peoples in the City Council of Davao and providing funds therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Indigenous Peoples mandatory representation ordinance
ordinances.summary: Gives Davao City's Indigenous Peoples a mandatory representative in the City Council, as allowed by the Local Government Code and the IPRA. The seat rotates each term among the city's 6 major IP groups. The representative has the same pay, powers and privileges as other council members.
points: The seat rotates per term among the Ata, Kalagan, K'lata, Matigsalog, Tagabawa and Ubo Manubo, in that order
The Mayor creates a Technical Working Group under RA 8371 and NCIP rules to design the selection process, subject to council approval
The representative serves 3 years
Pay, benefits, powers and duties equal those of regular council members, with a focus on the collective interest of IPs
Funds are appropriated every year from the General Fund

provisions.title: A mandatory IP seat in the City Council
provisions.text: Gives Davao City's Indigenous Peoples a mandatory representative in the City Council, under the Local Government Code and the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (RA 8371).

provisions.title: The seat rotates among 6 groups
provisions.text: The seat rotates each term among the city's 6 major IP groups in this order: Ata, Kalagan, K'lata, Matigsalog, Tagabawa and Ubo Manubo.

provisions.title: Purposes of the seat
provisions.text: Besides representation, the ordinance aims to protect IP rights, promote their customs and traditions, and strengthen their social, economic and political systems so they take part in development.

provisions.title: A working group designs the selection
provisions.text: On effectivity the Mayor creates a Technical Working Group, named under RA 8371 and NCIP Administrative Order No. 1 of 1998, to design how the representative is chosen. The City Council approves the process and the representative is then chosen at once.

provisions.title: A 3-year term
provisions.text: The representative serves for 3 years, as the Local Government Code provides.

provisions.title: Same pay and powers as other councillors
provisions.text: The representative gets the same compensation, benefits and privileges as regular council members, and has the same powers, duties, qualifications and disqualifications, with a focus on the collective interest of IPs.

provisions.title: Funded yearly from the General Fund
provisions.text: A sufficient amount is appropriated every year from the General Fund. The ordinance takes effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation.

ordinances.caveat: The Mayor did not sign it; the text records it as deemed approved after the period for her action lapsed.

details.effect: 15 days after publication
details.covers: Davao City's 6 major Indigenous Peoples, represented in rotation per term
details.enforcers: City Mayor, through a Technical Working Group

barmm.why: Worth reading if more than one Indigenous community lives in your LGU and they must share one mandatory seat on the sanggunian. Davao rotates the seat each term among 6 groups and funds it every year from the general fund. In BARMM the right to the seat comes from BLGC s. 132, so an ordinance like this only implements it, and Davao's NCIP-based selection process does not carry over.

apply.if: If IPs are at least 5% of your population but hold no more than 50% of elective offices, or a MIPA-recognised native title lies in your LGU
apply.then: you can replicate this as an implementing ordinance under BLGC s. 132: fund the seat every year and give the representative equal pay, powers and duties.

apply.if: If more than one IP community lives in your LGU
apply.then: agree on a rotation order with each community's elders before writing it in, rather than fixing one as Davao did for its 6 groups.

apply.if: If you are waiting on the joint MIPA and MILG selection guidelines
apply.then: state that selection follows those guidelines and the communities' own customs, instead of having a mayor-appointed working group design it.

apply.if: If you also have settler communities of 5% or more
apply.then: cover the settler seat under BLGC s. 133 and the IP seat on the development council under s. 119 in the same measure.

change: Base it on BLGC s. 132, which guarantees IP representation where IPs are at least 5% of the population but hold no more than 50% of elective offices, or where a native title recognised by MIPA lies in the LGU; for municipalities and barangays, also s. 488 and s. 418.

Replace the NCIP and RA 8371 selection process with the joint MIPA and MILG guidelines that s. 132 requires, following the communities' own customs, and cite BAA No. 64. A mayor-appointed technical working group should not design the selection.
Don't fix the rotation order in the ordinance without the groups' consent; have each community's elders agree on it, or it will be contested.
Add the settler seat under BLGC s. 133 where it applies, and the IP seat on the local development council under s. 119, so both are handled in one measure.
Re-cite the veto and deemed-approval rule to BLGC s. 62 (10 days for a city or municipality).
barmm.fits: Municipalities, cities and barangays where IPs meet the BLGC s. 132 thresholds, especially where several IP communities live side by side.

ordinances.title: Resorting to Indigenous Peoples' traditional way of conflict resolution, when invoked by disputing IP parties, in an Indigenous Cultural Community in Davao City
ordinances.shortTitle: IP Alternative Dispute Resolution in Davao City
ordinances.summary: This ordinance lets Indigenous Peoples in recognised Indigenous Cultural Communities settle disputes before their Council of Elders under customary law, when both parties choose to. It rests on Section 15 of the IPRA (RA 8371) and Section 399 of the Local Government Code. It also sets how that process links back to the Katarungang Pambarangay.
points: Applies to IP residents of ancestral domain areas in 81 listed barangays across Davao City's districts (per Resolution No. 02199-15), except disputes the law bars from compromise.
Both IP parties must voluntarily invoke the Council of Elders. Customary law may not involve cruel, degrading or inhumane punishment, the death penalty or excessive fines.
Each tribe's own justice system and customary law govern the procedure.
Agreements must be written, signed by the parties and the Council of Elders, and submitted to the Katarungang Pambarangay for confirmation. They then bind the parties.
If the Council of Elders does not act within 15 days, the dispute goes automatically to the Lupong Tagapamayapa.

provisions.title: Customary dispute settlement for IPs
provisions.text: Known as IP Alternative Dispute Resolution in Davao City, it protects the right of Indigenous Peoples to settle disputes through the Council of Elders of a recognised Indigenous Cultural Community, resting on Sec. 15 of the IPRA (RA 8371) and Sec. 399 of the Local Government Code.

provisions.title: Who it covers
provisions.text: IPs of a recognised tribe living in ancestral domain areas listed in Resolution No. 02199-15, in 81 named barangays across the city's districts, as a secondary mode of dispute resolution. Disputes the law bars from compromise are excluded.

provisions.title: Both parties must choose it
provisions.text: When 2 or more IP parties live in a recognised ICC, they may go to the Council of Elders, but only if both invoke it voluntarily. The customary law used may not involve cruel, degrading or inhumane punishment, the death penalty or excessive fines.

provisions.title: Each tribe's own procedure applies
provisions.text: The justice system, conflict mechanisms, peace-building processes and customary law of each tribe or ICC govern how the dispute is heard.

provisions.title: Written agreements confirmed by the barangay
provisions.text: Agreements are put in writing, signed by the parties and the Council of Elders, and submitted to the Katarungang Pambarangay for confirmation. They then bind the parties and are enforced under customary law, provided they break no law or public policy.

provisions.title: Inaction for 15 days sends it to the Lupon
provisions.text: If the Council of Elders does not act within 15 days of a dispute being brought to it, the case goes automatically to the Lupong Tagapamayapa.

provisions.title: Sanctions on both sides
provisions.text: Barangay officials who refuse without cause to refer a case to the elders after the parties chose the IP system face administrative charges. Elders who fail their duty are sanctioned under customary law, enforceable by the NCIP.

provisions.title: Effect 15 days after publication
provisions.text: It takes effect 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation and posting for 3 consecutive weeks at City Hall.

ordinances.penalties: There are no fines. Barangay officials who refuse to refer a case to the elders face administrative charges, and elders who fail to act are sanctioned under customary law, which the NCIP may enforce.
ordinances.caveat: The enactment date is read from poor OCR ("Bth day of January") and may be off.

details.effect: 15 days after publication and 3 weeks' posting
details.covers: Indigenous parties in disputes within recognized ancestral domain areas in 81 barangays
details.enforcers: Councils of Elders, with the Katarungang Pambarangay as fallback

highlights.label: for the elders to act before the case goes to the lupon
IP parties must choose the elders voluntarily
barangays with ancestral domains listed by name
fines; officials who block a referral face charges

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has non-Moro Indigenous communities whose disputes still go to the lupon even when both sides want their elders. Davao's 6-page ordinance sets the steps: both parties opt in, each tribe's own procedure applies, the settlement is written and confirmed through the katarungang pambarangay, and the case moves to the lupon if the elders do not act within 15 days. It rests on the 1991 Code and the NCIP, so the legal basis needs replacing.

apply.if: If most residents of a barangay are Indigenous
apply.then: you may not need the opt-in model there, since BLGC s. 427 already puts customary proceedings in place of the katarungang pambarangay; use the ordinance for the confirmation step and the 15-day fallback.

apply.if: If your barangays are mixed
apply.then: you can replicate this by letting IP parties opt in to their council of elders, and listing the covered barangays from MIPA-recognised ancestral domains.

apply.if: If your sanggunian has an IP mandatory representative
apply.then: have them help draw up the barangay list and consult the councils of elders on how settlements are written and recorded.

apply.if: If lupon members in your barangays tend to keep IP cases
apply.then: copy the administrative charge for officials who refuse to refer a case after the parties ask for the elders.

apply.if: If a dispute involves violence against women and children
apply.then: list it, with the other cases barred by BLGC s. 436, as outside both the elders and the lupon.

change: Replace Section 399 of the 1991 Code with BLGC s. 427, which is stronger: where most barangay residents belong to Indigenous communities, customary proceedings take the place of the katarungang pambarangay. The opt-in model is then needed only in mixed barangays.

Replace the NCIP with the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs under BAA No. 64. Build the list of covered barangays from MIPA-recognised ancestral domains or native titles (BLGC s. 132) and any tribal barangays under BLGC s. 406.
Spell out the cases that cannot go to settlement under BLGC s. 436, especially violence against women and children, instead of the general 'barred by law' wording.
Add the rules on written settlements in a language both parties know (BLGC s. 440) and on a settlement taking effect as a final judgment after 10 days (BLGC s. 445).
Keep this ordinance for non-Moro IP disputes. Handle rido between clans through the ad hoc bodies of the peace and order council under BLGC s. 128, and keep Shari'ah court matters out.
barmm.fits: Municipalities and barangays with non-Moro Indigenous communities and recognised councils of elders.

ordinances.title: Ordinance creating the City Peace 911 Council and Peace 911 sa Barangay, subject to all laws and existing legal rules and regulations
ordinances.shortTitle: City Peace 911 Council ordinance
ordinances.summary: Creates a City Peace 911 Council to advise the city on peacebuilding, and Peace 911 sa Barangay bodies in barangays the Mayor approves. It builds on Davao's Peace 911 programme and the Positive Peace framework, with Peace 911, The Center for Peacebuilding, as secretariat.
points: City council: the Mayor as chair, plus 2 government, 2 private sector, 1 faith-based, 1 education, 1 city councillor and 1 youth member; members are appointed by the Mayor and reconstituted each fiscal year
Barangay body: 1 kagawad, 1 barangay functionary as secretary and 5 sector members, appointed by the Punong Barangay with council concurrence
Farm, fisheries and Indigenous Peoples seats are required in agricultural, coastal and IPMR barangays
Barangay policies need approval by the City Peace 911 Council and adoption by barangay resolution
Both bodies meet at least once a quarter; honoraria are set by the Mayor, subject to funds
Renames the Peace 911 General Committee under Executive Order No. 08, s. 2021; automatic review every 3 years

provisions.title: Built on the 8 pillars of Positive Peace
provisions.text: The city adopts the Institute for Economics and Peace's 8 pillars of Positive Peace, from well-functioning government and low corruption to equitable resources and free flow of information, as the basis for its peacebuilding bodies.

provisions.title: A city council and barangay bodies
provisions.text: It creates the City Peace 911 Council and a Peace 911 sa Barangay in barangays the council recommends and the mayor approves. The mayor reconstitutes the city council every fiscal year; the punong barangay does the same for the barangay body with council concurrence.

provisions.title: The city council advises on peace
provisions.text: The City Peace 911 Council advises the city government on peace promotion, builds peace tables with the barangay bodies so communities can raise concerns, and plans and evaluates peacebuilding programs.

provisions.title: 9 members, chaired by the mayor
provisions.text: The mayor or a representative chairs, with 2 members from government, 2 from the private sector, and 1 each from faith-based groups, education, the city councillors and the youth. Members elect the vice-chair, and the mayor appoints all members.

provisions.title: Renames the Peace 911 General Committee
provisions.text: The Peace 911 General Committee created under Executive Order No. 08, s. 2021 becomes the City Peace 911 Council, and its earlier members form the council's first make-up. Peace 911, The Center for Peacebuilding, is the secretariat.

provisions.title: A peacebuilding plan in each barangay
provisions.text: Each Peace 911 sa Barangay draws up and carries out an integrated peacebuilding plan for the barangay, gathers information, organizes training, and gets the barangay council's concurrence for all its programs.

provisions.title: 7 members in each barangay body
provisions.text: 1 kagawad, 1 barangay functionary as secretary, and 5 members from 13 listed sectors, 1 per sector. Agricultural, IPMR and fishing barangays must seat farm, Indigenous Peoples and fisheries members.

provisions.title: Barangay policies need city approval
provisions.text: Every policy a Peace 911 sa Barangay adopts must be approved by the City Peace 911 Council and then adopted by the barangay council by resolution.

provisions.title: 13 city offices in support
provisions.text: City offices including health, agriculture, social welfare, tourism, engineering, planning, environment, DRRM and public safety support both bodies, and the mayor may hire technical advisers by contract of service or job order.

provisions.title: Quarterly meetings, honoraria and review
provisions.text: Both bodies meet at least once a quarter. Honoraria are set by the mayor, subject to funds, and the budget officer puts the cost in the annual budget. The council reviews the ordinance automatically every 3 years.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Davao City and the barangays chosen for Peace 911 sa Barangay
details.enforcers: City Peace 911 Council, with Peace 911 (The Center for Peacebuilding) as secretariat
details.funding: City annual budget; barangay honoraria from the barangay or Mayor's Office

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants a standing body for peacebuilding with seats for faith, youth, education and other sectors, matched in the barangays. Davao's council was built around its own Peace 911 programme and centre, which aimed mainly at the communist insurgency. If your conflicts are rido, land disputes or the return of former combatants, take the structure and leave the programme-specific text.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a peace and order council
apply.then: you can replicate this as a peacebuilding committee of that council, or as the ad hoc rido body BLGC s. 128 allows, rather than a separate council.

apply.if: If your barangays have farming, coastal or Indigenous communities
apply.then: copy the rule that agricultural, coastal and IPMR barangays must seat a farm, fisheries or Indigenous member.

apply.if: If your barangays settle disputes through customary or religious leaders
apply.then: link the barangay body to the lupon and to those systems instead of setting up a new venue.

apply.if: If you plan to pay members
apply.then: set the honoraria in the ordinance or the budget instead of leaving them to the mayor.

apply.if: If you want a light start
apply.then: begin with quarterly meetings and the 3-year review, and add barangay bodies where conflict is active.

change: Build it as a committee of the peace and order council or as the ad hoc rido body that BLGC s. 128 allows (traditional and religious leaders, women and others trusted by the parties), not as a parallel council under a programme name

Add required seats for women, and for Indigenous Peoples and settler communities where BLGC s. 132 and s. 133 call for them, and work with the lupon and customary dispute systems recognized in BLGC s. 427
Link the council to the regional transitional justice and reconciliation programme (BAA No. 89) and to displaced families' needs under BAA No. 62

Drop the rule that barangay policies need city council approval. Barangays act by ordinance or resolution under city or municipal review (BLGC s. 65), and a council appointed by the mayor should not hold a veto over them
Set honoraria in the ordinance or the budget instead of leaving them to the mayor
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with active rido, land disputes or post-conflict barangays.

ordinances.category: Senior citizens and persons with disability
ordinances.title: Creating the Persons with Disabilities Affairs Center (PDAC) – the Persons with Disabilities Affairs Office (PDAO) of Davao City, as a division under the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO), determining their duties, powers, and functions
ordinances.shortTitle: An Ordinance Creating the PDAC-PDAO DC
ordinances.summary: Creates Davao City's Persons with Disabilities Affairs Office, required by RA 10070, as a division of the City Social Welfare and Development Office. It sets the division's functions, its 2 sections, 15 plantilla positions with salary grades and qualifications, and requires sign language interpreters on staff.
points: The division is headed by a Disability Affairs Officer IV (SG 22) with a Disability Affairs Officer III (SG 18) as assistant head
Has an Operations Section and a Promotive Section, with 15 regular positions in total
Positions are appointed by the Mayor under Civil Service rules; the head needs 3 years of disability-affairs experience and 16 hours of training
At least 1 administrative officer, 3 promotive-section assistants and 1 staff member per congressional district must interpret sign language
The city must fund the office as required by RA 10070

provisions.title: A PWD affairs division under the CSWDO
provisions.text: The Persons with Disabilities Affairs Center, Davao City's PDAO under RA 10070, is created as a division of the City Social Welfare and Development Office.

provisions.title: Headed by an SG 22 officer, with 2 sections
provisions.text: A Disability Affairs Officer IV (SG 22) heads the division, with a Disability Affairs Officer III (SG 18) as assistant head; it has an Operations Section and a Promotive Section.

provisions.title: The division's functions under RA 10070
provisions.text: It makes and runs PWD welfare policies and programs, enforces RA 10070 and the Accessibility Law locally, represents PWDs in development councils, gathers PWD data, reports to the mayor, monitors fund-raising for PWDs and seeks donations.

provisions.title: What each section does
provisions.text: The Operations Section compiles PWD data and handles registration and PWD IDs; the Promotive Section trains barangay staff, monitors assistive devices and barangay PWD groups, and builds a community-based rehabilitation program.

provisions.title: 15 regular positions
provisions.text: Besides the head and assistant, it has 2 administrative staff, 5 in the Operations Section and 6 in the Promotive Section, ranging from Disability Affairs Officer II (SG 15) to Disability Affairs Assistant (SG 8), for 15 plantilla positions in all.

provisions.title: Duties of the head and assistant head
provisions.text: The head runs the office, ensures PWD representation in local special bodies, builds NGO and PO capacity, networks for partners and resources, and submits an annual work and financial plan to the mayor; the assistant supervises administration.

provisions.title: Appointed by the mayor on Civil Service standards
provisions.text: The mayor appoints all positions under Civil Service rules; the head needs a bachelor's degree, 3 years of disability-affairs experience, 16 hours of training and second-level eligibility. The mayor may also hire casual or contractual staff.

provisions.title: Sign language interpreters on staff
provisions.text: At least 1 Disability Affairs Officer I on the administrative staff, at least 3 Disability Affairs Assistants in the Promotive Section, and at least 1 regular staff member in each congressional district must translate and interpret sign language.

provisions.title: The city must fund the office
provisions.text: The city must appropriate funds for the office as RA 10070 requires, which points to a share of the 5% gender and development budget and the IRA for PDAO programs.

provisions.title: Takes effect on approval
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect upon approval.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU's persons with disability affairs office exists only as a designated focal person, or not at all. Davao City's 2022 ordinance is a clean template: functions, 2 sections, positions with salary grades and qualifications, and staff who can interpret sign language. The BLGC makes the office mandatory, so the real question is how big yours can be, and 15 positions is city-sized.

apply.if: If your LGU has a focal person but no office
apply.then: you can replicate this by creating the office with a head and 1 or 2 staff, using Davao's functions and its split between operations and promotive work.

apply.if: If your social welfare office already registers persons with disabilities and issues IDs
apply.then: place the new office under it as a division, as Davao did, and move that work to the operations section.

apply.if: If your LGU can afford a larger office
apply.then: follow Davao's staffing table and qualifications, and give priority to qualified persons with disabilities when hiring.

apply.if: If you have deaf residents and no interpreters on staff
apply.then: require that at least some staff can interpret Filipino Sign Language, as Davao does.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 480 and s. 481 (mandatory PDAO officer in municipalities; 4th to 6th class municipalities may name a focal person) or BLGC s. 513 for provinces, alongside RA 10070 (national law)
Size the plantilla to what the LGU can pay: 15 positions at SG 22 and below may not fit a municipality under the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349 (45% or 55% of regular income)
Fund programs from the 1% for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 348, and link the office to the council for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 130
Follow BLGC s. 87 and BAA No. 17 for the staffing pattern, and decide whether the office sits under the social welfare office (as in Davao) or stands alone
barmm.fits: Every province, city and municipality, with smaller LGUs adopting a 2 to 3 person version.

ordinances.title: Regulating the establishment, classification, administration and operation of government owned/operated public markets in the City of Davao, otherwise known as the "Market Code of Davao City"
ordinances.shortTitle: Market Code of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Davao City's market code governs city-owned and city-operated public markets: their administration, classification, stall rentals and fees, how stalls are leased, and rules for stallholders, sanitation and the slaughterhouse. It applies to stallholders, vendors, market personnel and cargadores in the city's public markets.
points: Classifies markets by average monthly income over the past 3 months: Class A ₱100,000 or more, Class B ₱50,000 to ₱100,000, Class C below ₱50,000
Sets stall rentals per square metre per day by section and class (e.g. meat section ₱5.88, ₱4.70, ₱3.92)
Vacant stalls are posted for at least 10 days and awarded by drawing of lots; lessees must run their stalls personally
Unpaid rent past 15 days (daily payers) or 20 days (monthly payers) is cause to revoke the lease and eject the stallholder
Unpaid occupancy pays 3 times the regular rate, extra space pays double, and late rent carries a 25% penalty plus 14% a year interest
Markets open 2:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.; stalls may not be used as dwellings; selling fish and meat outside the market is banned; covers slaughter permits and fees

provisions.title: City Administrator runs the markets
provisions.text: The City Administrator directly supervises city-owned and city-operated public markets and their staff, with a market superintendent and a market inspector for each market who checks receipts, sanitation and upkeep and reports daily.

provisions.title: Registered cargadores
provisions.text: Carriers in city markets must be Filipino citizens of good moral character certified by their barangay captain, registered with the Market Operations Officer and wear their ID while working.

provisions.title: Markets classed by income
provisions.text: Markets are Class A with average monthly income of ₱100,000 or more over the past 3 months, Class B with ₱50,000 to under ₱100,000 and Class C below ₱50,000. The City Treasurer may reclassify at most once a year.

provisions.title: Stall rent per square metre per day
provisions.text: Rent is set per square metre per day by section and class; the meat section pays ₱5.88 in Class A, ₱4.70 in Class B and ₱3.92 in Class C, and other sections pay less.

provisions.title: Vacant stalls by drawing of lots
provisions.text: A vacancy notice is posted at least 10 days before the award. Applicants must be 21 or older and pay a ₱20 application fee; where there is more than 1 applicant, the City Market Committee awards the stall by drawing of lots. Appeals go to the mayor.

provisions.title: Stallholders run their own stalls
provisions.text: The lessee must personally run the stall, helped only by family or registered helpers. Subleasing or selling the right is banned, and anyone else found selling at the stall is prima facie proof of subleasing, cause for revocation.

provisions.title: Market hours and banned uses
provisions.text: Markets open 2:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. daily. Stalls may not be used as dwellings, and peddling fish, meat and other perishable food outside the market is banned.

provisions.title: Revocation for unpaid rent
provisions.text: Failure to pay within 15 days for daily payers or 20 days for monthly payers is cause to revoke the lease and eject the stallholder after due process. An ejected stallholder may not apply for any stall in any city market.

provisions.title: Slaughter permits and fees
provisions.text: Animals for public consumption need a permit from the City Veterinarian, with fees paid to the City Treasurer, such as ₱7.50 per head of large cattle. They must be slaughtered at the city slaughterhouse; large cattle need proof of ownership.

provisions.title: Surcharges, fines and jail
provisions.text: Using space without paying costs 3 times the regular rate, extra space double, and late rent a 25% penalty plus 14% a year interest. Any violation carries a fine of up to ₱1,000, up to 6 months in jail, or both.

ordinances.penalties: Fine of up to ₱1,000, or up to 6 months in jail, or both, plus lease cancellation and ejectment
ordinances.caveat: The scan's OCR is poor in places, especially the rental rate table, so check figures against the original.

details.enforcers: City Administrator, with the City Treasurer for collections

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU runs a public market without written rules on how stalls are awarded, how rent is set, or what happens when rent goes unpaid. Davao's code covers all of that, plus market hours, sanitation and the slaughterhouse. It dates from 1989, its rent table is poorly scanned and decades out of date, and its late-payment interest needs rethinking under BLGC s. 153.

apply.if: If you collect market fees under an older revenue ordinance
apply.then: you can replicate Davao's classes by grouping your markets by average monthly collections and setting rent per square metre for each class in a new ordinance under BLGC s. 148.

apply.if: If stalls in your market are awarded informally
apply.then: copy the 10-day posting of vacant stalls and the award by drawing of lots, and require lessees to run their stalls personally.

apply.if: If unpaid rent is a problem in your market
apply.then: use Davao's 15-day and 20-day revocation rule and the 30-day abandoned stall rule, but replace the 14% interest with a Shari'ah-compliant rule or stay within BLGC s. 191.

apply.if: If your LGU runs a slaughterhouse
apply.then: put it under the veterinarian or the officer who regulates slaughter, and write in halal slaughter practice.

apply.if: If small fishers and farmers sell outside your market
apply.then: designate landing and trading areas instead of copying Davao's ban on selling fish and meat outside the market.

change: Replace the 25% penalty plus 14% a year interest: BLGC s. 153 lets the sanggunian adopt Shari'ah-compliant rules on late payment instead of interest (riba), and any surcharge must stay within BLGC s. 191 (25% plus at most 2% a month, for no more than 36 months)
Set new rents by ordinance under BLGC s. 148 from current costs; do not reuse the 1989 rates
Put the slaughterhouse under the veterinarian (BLGC s. 543) and require halal slaughter practice in line with local religious authorities

Soften the ban on selling fish and meat outside the market: it hits small fishers, and BLGC s. 156 bars taxing aquatic and farm products sold by marginal fishers and farmers; allow designated landing and trading areas
Keep penalties within ₱5,000 and 6 months for a municipality (BLGC s. 489); use BLGC s. 24 for night markets and street closures
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities that own and run a public market.

ordinances.title: Establishing and strengthening the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Volunteer Corps (CDRRMVC) and the Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Volunteer Corps (BDRRMVC) in Davao City, defining its composition, functions, trainings, support mechanisms, and for other purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Davao City DRRM Volunteer Corps Ordinance of 2025
ordinances.summary: Creates city and barangay disaster volunteer corps under the City DRRM Office and each barangay DRRM committee. It sets how volunteers and volunteer organizations are accredited, mobilised, insured and supported before, during and after disasters, following RA 10121 and NDRRMC guidelines.
points: The City DRRM Office accredits all volunteers and volunteer organizations and keeps a database of them
Barangay corps are organised by the barangay DRRM committee, with a volunteer coordinator named by the Punong Barangay and teams for rescue, first aid, relief, education and damage assessment
Volunteer organizations must insure their volunteers for at least ₱100,000 against accident, death, disability and hospitalisation
Deployed volunteers must be equipped and self-sustaining for 72 hours; post-activity reports are due within 7 days
Accredited volunteers get burial aid, free government hospital care for mission injuries, psychosocial support, ID cards and training
Funded from the City DRRM Fund, the General Fund or other sources

provisions.title: City and barangay volunteer corps
provisions.text: Creates a City DRRM Volunteer Corps under the City DRRM Office and a Barangay DRRM Volunteer Corps under each barangay DRRM committee, to help with risk mapping, early warning, drills, evacuation, relief, psychological first aid and recovery.

provisions.title: The City DRRM Office accredits volunteers
provisions.text: As RA 10121 requires, the City DRRM Office accredits all volunteers. Individuals register with a barangay unit where they live or work; organizations apply as volunteer-mobilizing organizations (VMOs) and the City DRRM Council approves them.

provisions.title: Who qualifies
provisions.text: Volunteers must be Filipino citizens, or resident foreigners with an ACR I-card, at least 18, with NBI or police clearance; those under 21 need parental consent. Organizations need 2 years of DRRM work; specialist roles need 1 year of experience and a medical certificate.

provisions.title: 5-year accreditation, renewed by yearly reports
provisions.text: Accreditation certificates run 5 years and may be revoked for fraud or poor vetting. Organizations file an annual report with an updated volunteer list by 31 January, and volunteers sign a code of conduct and data privacy consent.

provisions.title: National roster and ID cards
provisions.text: The City DRRM Office sends accredited organizations and volunteers yearly to the regional council for the national roster kept by the Office of Civil Defense, then issues each listed volunteer an ID card.

provisions.title: How barangay corps are organized
provisions.text: Barangay corps are residents endorsed by the barangay captain and overseen by the barangay DRRM committee, with a volunteer coordinator named by the Punong Barangay and teams for rescue, first aid, relief, education and damage assessment.

provisions.title: Mobilization rules
provisions.text: The City DRRM Office issues mobilization orders and briefs volunteers before deployment under the Incident Command System. Organizations bear deployment costs, must keep volunteers equipped and self-sustaining for 72 hours, and file post-activity reports within 7 days.

provisions.title: ₱100,000 insurance for each volunteer
provisions.text: Organizations must insure their volunteers for at least ₱100,000 against accident, death, dismemberment, permanent disability and hospitalization; the council may cover the cost for CSOs and private groups case by case.

provisions.title: Benefits for accredited volunteers
provisions.text: Listed volunteers get burial aid, free government hospital care for mission injuries, counselling and psychosocial support, free training, ID cards, uniforms and protective gear, food and transport on deployment, and awards.

provisions.title: Funding
provisions.text: Funds come from the City DRRM Fund, the General Fund or other sources, following COA Circular 2012-002 and NDRRMC Memorandum Circulars 64 and 110 of 2021. The City DRRM Office keeps a database of all volunteers.

sponsors: Councilor Luna Maria Dominique S. Acosta
Councilor Bai Hundra Cassandra Dominique N. Advincula
Councilor Diosdado Angelo Junior R. Mahipus
Councilor Kristine May John A. Mercado

barmm.why: Worth reading if the first responders in your floods and evacuations are neighbours, youth and faith groups with no training, insurance or ID. Davao turns them into accredited city and barangay corps with set teams, a database, and benefits such as burial aid and free government hospital care for injuries. It puts mobilisation costs and ₱100,000 insurance on the volunteer groups, which small groups may not afford.

apply.if: If your LGU has a DRRM office
apply.then: you can replicate this by having it accredit volunteers and groups, keep the database, and issue mobilisation orders.

apply.if: If your barangays have no DRRM committee
apply.then: have the barangay development council, which acts as the barangay DRRM council under BLGC s. 121, name a volunteer coordinator and form the 5 teams, or fewer to start.

apply.if: If your volunteer groups cannot pay ₱100,000 insurance per volunteer
apply.then: budget it from the 5% calamity fund under BLGC s. 348; Davao already lets its council cover the cost case by case.

apply.if: If many of your groups are not registered with the SEC, CDA, DOLE or DSWD
apply.then: accept registration with the LGU or a Bangsamoro ministry, so mosque, madrasah and youth groups can be accredited.

apply.if: If you shelter displaced families in evacuation centres
apply.then: add centre support under BAA No. 62 to the volunteers' duties, with women volunteers for women's spaces.

change: Re-cite: under the BLGC the barangay development council acts as the barangay DRRM council (BLGC s. 121), and the sangguniang barangay may form volunteer community brigades (s. 414); RA 10121 and RA 9418 stay as the national law basis.

Don't put the ₱100,000 insurance cost on volunteer organisations; many mosque, youth and women's groups cannot pay it. Budget it from the 5% calamity fund in BLGC s. 348, and link it to the insurance system for tanods and peacekeeping teams in s. 587.
Accept registration with regional ministries and Bangsamoro bodies, not only SEC, CDA, DOLE or DSWD, and allow madrasah, mosque and traditional leader groups to be accredited.

Add displacement: volunteers support evacuation centres under BAA No. 62 and the IDP councils in BLGC s. 130. Set the 40% women target from s. 129 for the corps too, with women volunteers for women's spaces in evacuation centres.
Name the Bangsamoro coordination line for regional mutual aid instead of the regional DRRM council; check BAA No. 13 for which regional office holds disaster response.
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with recurring floods or evacuations and many active community groups.

ordinances.title: Institutionalizing the programs, services, privileges, and benefits for solo parents and their children, appropriating funds thereof and for other purposes pursuant to Republic Act No. 8972, as amended by Republic Act No. 11861, known as the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act
ordinances.shortTitle: Solo Parents' Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Puts the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act into effect in Davao City and adds city-funded benefits for resident solo parents and their children. It sets who qualifies, how to register and get a Solo Parent ID, the discounts and subsidies available, and grounds for losing them. It creates a Solo Parent Division and a Solo Parents' Desk under the City Social Welfare and Development Office.
points: Registered solo parents earning minimum wage or below get a ₱1,000 monthly subsidy and ₱1,000 extra burial aid on top of the city's ₱2,000 when their child dies
10% discounts on basic necessities and medicines (up to ₱5,000 each), school supplies, laboratory and diagnostic fees, restaurant bills and medical bills
10% discount and VAT exemption on baby's milk, diapers, medicines and supplements up to the child's age of 6, for solo parents earning under ₱250,000 a year
Up to 7 working days of paid parental leave a year after 6 months of service, plus flexible work schedules; employers may not discriminate against solo parents
City-wide registration across 182 barangays; the Solo Parent ID is valid for 1 year, and termination of benefits takes effect 30 days after written notice
Solo Parents' Week every last week of April; funded from the city's General Fund

provisions.title: Who counts as a solo parent
provisions.text: Follows RA 11861: widows, parents left alone by a spouse's detention of 3 months, incapacity, separation or abandonment of 6 months, unmarried parents, guardians and relatives raising a child, certain OFW families, rape survivors raising the child, and pregnant women raising a child alone.

provisions.title: The national benefits made a city duty
provisions.text: The City binds itself and all government agencies in Davao to give solo parents the services RA 8972 as amended lists, such as livelihood help, counselling and parent effectiveness, and treats the Act's provisions as written into the ordinance.

provisions.title: No discrimination at work
provisions.text: No employer may treat a solo parent employee differently in terms and conditions of employment because of that status.

provisions.title: ₱1,000 a month and extra burial aid
provisions.text: Registered resident solo parents earning minimum wage or less get a ₱1,000 monthly subsidy, and ₱1,000 burial aid on top of the City's ₱2,000 when their child dies, if they get no other government cash aid.

provisions.title: 10% discounts on daily needs and care
provisions.text: 10% off basic necessities and prime commodities up to ₱5,000, medicines and vitamins up to ₱5,000, school supplies, private lab and diagnostic fees, restaurant bills and medical bills. Those earning under ₱250,000 a year also get 10% off and no VAT on baby's milk, diapers and medicines until the child turns 6.

provisions.title: Leave, flexible hours and disaster help
provisions.text: Solo parent employees with 6 months' service get up to 7 working days of paid parental leave a year and flexible arrival and departure times. In disasters and health emergencies they get food, medicine, repair aid and psychosocial support, and they have priority for livelihood aid.

provisions.title: A Solo Parent Division and city-wide registry
provisions.text: A Solo Parent Division under the CSWDO registers all solo parents and their children in the city's 182 barangays, recording income, number of children and circumstances.

provisions.title: Getting the Solo Parent ID
provisions.text: Applicants submit proof of 1 year's residence or voter registration, the children's PSA birth certificates, a barangay certification of solo status and the city form. After a social worker's assessment, the ID is issued within 15 days and is valid for 1 year, renewable; a free purchase booklet comes with it.

provisions.title: Losing the benefits
provisions.text: Marriage, adequate support from the other parent or a live-in partner, the spouse's release from detention, a child over 18 able to care for themselves, or income above the poverty threshold ends eligibility. Termination takes effect 30 days after written notice, with counselling.

provisions.title: A Solo Parents' Desk, a yearly week and funding
provisions.text: A Solo Parents' Desk under the CSWDO runs the programme and helps solo parents organise. Solo Parents' Week is the last week of April. Funds come from the General Fund; a 7-member Rules Committee led by the council's women and children committee chair writes the IRR.

details.effect: upon approval and publication in a Davao City newspaper
details.covers: Solo parents living in Davao City and their children
details.enforcers: City Social Welfare and Development Office, through its Solo Parent Division
details.funding: City General Fund

barmm.why: Worth reading if solo parents in your LGU rarely hold a Solo Parent ID or get the benefits of the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act. Davao turns that national law into a registration system down to the barangays, a desk, a monthly subsidy and a General Fund line. It is 12 pages and recent, but its separate division is city-scale.

apply.if: If your LGU has a social welfare and development officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by putting a Solo Parents' Desk in that office and registering solo parents barangay by barangay, with an ID valid for 1 year.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot add staff
apply.then: skip the Solo Parent Division and designate a focal person in the social welfare office instead.

apply.if: If your barangays keep a resident registry
apply.then: use it to find solo parents, under its data privacy safeguards.

apply.if: If many solo parents in your LGU are widows, divorced under Muslim law, or spouses of overseas workers
apply.then: list the proofs of status you will accept, such as Shari'ah court decrees and certifications from the MSSD or religious leaders.

apply.if: If you fund benefits from the General Fund
apply.then: budget the ₱1,000 monthly subsidy first, and restate the national discounts so shops and employers know them.

change: Re-cite funding to BLGC s. 348, which lists benefits for solo parents among items that must be funded. Put the desk under the mandatory social welfare officer in BLGC s. 537
A separate Solo Parent Division may break the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349 for 4th to 6th class LGUs; organise it under BLGC s. 87, or use a desk or focal person

Accept proof of status that fits your communities: Shari'ah court decrees, registered divorces under Muslim law, and certifications from imams or the MSSD for widows of conflict. Take the DSWD's role from the MSSD, which BLGC s. 512 names for social welfare
Check the parental leave and flexible work rules against the Bangsamoro Labor Code (BAA No. 82) for private employers, and cover the spouses of overseas workers with BAA No. 19
Use the barangay registry in BLGC s. 410 to find solo parents, under its data privacy safeguards
barmm.fits: Any city or municipality; the full version suits LGUs that can staff a desk, and a focal-person version suits small municipalities.

ordinances.title: Providing for prevention and intervention mechanisms in protecting children against all forms of sexual abuse and exploitation
ordinances.shortTitle: Anti-Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Against Children Ordinance of Davao City
ordinances.summary: Sets up a city-wide system to prevent and respond to sexual abuse and exploitation of children, including online abuse. It creates a multi-agency committee and assigns specific roles to the information office, DepEd, social welfare, barangay child protection councils, police, media, NCIP, civil society and the CHR. It creates no new penalties and relies on national laws for prosecution.
points: Creates a Committee on Children Protection against Sexual Abuse, chaired by the Special Office for Children's Concern with the CSWDO as vice-chair and 13 member agencies
Creates a city Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) to draw up a local cybersecurity plan against cybersex and child pornography
DepEd must run school-based awareness, referral systems and teacher training on spotting abuse
The CSWDO runs center-based programs, responsible parenting, life-skills training, and rescue, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims
Barangay councils for the protection of children must map high-risk areas and reach far-flung areas
The police Women and Children Protection Desk receives reports and must keep a child-friendly reception area

provisions.title: A city committee against child sexual abuse
provisions.text: The Committee on Children Protection against Sexual Abuse is chaired by the Special Office for Children's Concern, with the CSWDO as vice-chair, the Integrated Gender and Development Division as secretariat, and 13 members from bodies including the LCPC, BCPC, police, DepEd, NCIP, NCMF, CHR, media and private schools.

provisions.title: A city database and a yearly picture of risk
provisions.text: The committee builds a confidential master list and database of children, identifies those at high risk, such as children with disabilities, out-of-school youth and those in poor or far-flung homes, and sends a Local State of Children Report to the mayor.

provisions.title: Awareness campaigns by the information office
provisions.text: The City Information Office leads campaigns against child sexual abuse, prioritizing high-risk places, uses social media, observes the national awareness week and Safer Internet Day, and posts reporting hotlines in public places.

provisions.title: School programs and teacher training
provisions.text: DepEd sets child protection policies and a quick referral system, trains teachers to spot and handle abuse, adds age-appropriate lessons to the curriculum, keeps a confidential student database and posts hotlines in schools.

provisions.title: Parenting, life skills and centre programs
provisions.text: The CSWDO runs community and centre-based programs, parenting seminars and counselling, and life-skills training so children can recognize, refuse and report abuse and parents can spot the warning signs.

provisions.title: Rescue, rehabilitation and reintegration
provisions.text: The CSWDO gives child victims, including victims of child prostitution, therapy, shelter, counselling and livelihood help, and gives children in conflict with the law counselling and reintegration services.

provisions.title: Barangay councils map risks and set up quick response
provisions.text: Each BCPC runs local campaigns, maps high-risk areas, makes sure programs reach far-flung areas, keeps a confidential children's database, and sets up a quick-response team to take complaints and arrest perpetrators caught in the act.

provisions.title: Police desks for child victims
provisions.text: The police Women and Children Protection Desk takes reports in a child-friendly reception area, runs hotlines and social media reporting, and brings at least 1 social worker on every rescue. The SOCC trains police, barangay auxiliaries and the Lupon.

provisions.title: A local cybercrime centre
provisions.text: A Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center of the RACU, NBI, DOST and DOJ regional offices draws up a local cybersecurity plan against cybersex and child pornography, with an emergency response team, and monitors cases.

provisions.title: Media restraint and confidentiality
provisions.text: Sensationalized publicity of a case involving a child in conflict with the law violates the child's rights, and children in need of protection are not exposed to media without consent. All investigations respect the privacy of victims and perpetrators.

details.effect: upon approval and publication in a local newspaper
details.covers: Children in Davao City, against all forms of sexual abuse and exploitation
details.enforcers: Committee led by the Special Office for Children's Concern, with CSWDO and DCPO

barmm.why: Worth reading if child sexual abuse cases in your LGU, including online abuse, fall between offices with no one clearly in charge. Davao City's 2022 ordinance creates no new crimes; it gives each office a job in prevention, referral, rescue and reintegration and leaves prosecution to national law. It has no funding clause, and some bodies it names, such as a Special Office for Children's Concern and a city cybercrime centre, may not exist in your LGU.

apply.if: If your LGU has a local council for the protection of children
apply.then: you can replicate this by making the committee a part of that council, led by the social welfare officer, with seats for police, health, schools, media and civil society.

apply.if: If your barangays have councils for the protection of children
apply.then: have them map high-risk areas, keep a confidential list of children, post hotlines and set up a quick-response team with the tanods.

apply.if: If your police station has a women and children protection desk
apply.then: require a child-friendly reception area and training for its officers and for barangay officials.

apply.if: If your LGU has no cybercrime capacity
apply.then: skip the local cybercrime centre and refer online abuse cases to the police and national agencies, while schools and the information office run awareness campaigns.

apply.if: If you want the plan to be funded
apply.then: add the funding clause Davao left out, drawing on the 1% budget for the children's council.

change: Seat the committee in the local council for the protection of children (BLGC s. 130), funded from its minimum 1% budget share (BLGC s. 348). Unless your LGU has a Special Office for Children's Concern, make the social welfare officer the lead under BLGC s. 537

Rename the partner offices: the Ministry of Social Services and Development for DSWD, the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education for DepEd (and include madaris under the Education Code, BAA No. 18), the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs for NCIP (BAA No. 64), and add the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission (BAA No. 4)

Update the legal basis to the national laws now in force, especially RA 11930 (2022) on online sexual abuse of children, alongside RA 7610 and RA 9775. Don't call the local body a 'CICC', which is the name of the national cybercrime centre under RA 10175

If your LGU has evacuation centres or displaced families, add them to the risk mapping (BAA No. 62). Decide openly how the code will handle child marriage under national law (RA 11596), consulting Shari'ah court officials and ulama
barmm.fits: Cities and municipalities with a licensed social worker and a police women and children desk; the barangay duties suit any barangay with a children's council.

ordinances.title: An ordinance approving the 2005 Revenue Code of the City of Davao, as amended
ordinances.shortTitle: The 2005 Revenue Code of the City of Davao
ordinances.summary: Davao City's full revenue code, governing the levy, assessment and collection of every city tax, fee and charge. It runs 434 sections across 10 chapters: city taxes, permit and regulatory fees, service fees, city charges, the community tax, administrative provisions and remedies, and penalties. It is a complete model for a city council writing or updating its own revenue code under the Local Government Code.
points: Real property tax of 1.5% of assessed value plus 1% for the Special Education Fund, payable in 4 quarterly instalments, with a 10% discount for on-time payment and 20% for full payment before the end of the first quarter.
Idle land tax of 25% of 1% of assessed value, and a real property transfer tax of 80% of 1% of the consideration or fair market value, whichever is higher.
Graduated business tax schedules by gross sales (manufacturers, wholesalers and others), and a franchise tax of 82% of 1% of gross annual receipts.
Amusement tax on admissions: 30% for foreign films and cockpits, 15% for local films, concert halls, KTV clubs, theme parks and stadia, 5% for other amusement places.
Late payment draws a 25% surcharge and interest of up to 2% a month, capped at 36 months; the council may adjust rates once every 5 years by no more than 10%.
Long schedules of permit fees (mayor's permit, building, electrical, sign, zoning, tricycles, cockpits) and charges (garbage collection, parking, hospital, cemetery, slaughter).

provisions.title: Real property tax of 1.5% plus 1% for schools
provisions.text: Real property pays a basic tax of 1.5% of assessed value and an extra 1% for the Special Education Fund, due on 1 January or in 4 quarterly instalments by March 31, June 30, September 30 and December 31.

provisions.title: Discounts for prompt payment, 2% interest if late
provisions.text: Paying each instalment on time earns a 10% discount, and paying the whole year before the end of the first quarter earns 20%; unpaid real property tax draws 2% interest a month, for at most 36 months.

provisions.title: Idle land and transfer taxes
provisions.text: Idle land pays an extra 25% of 1% of assessed value a year; any sale, donation or other transfer of real property pays 80% of 1% of the price or fair market value, whichever is higher.

provisions.title: Franchise and professional taxes
provisions.text: Businesses with a franchise pay 82% of 1% of gross annual receipts (3/40 of 1% of capital in their first year), and every licensed professional pays ₱300 a year.

provisions.title: Amusement tax on admissions
provisions.text: Admissions are taxed 30% for foreign films and cockpits, 15% for local films, concert halls, KTV clubs, theme parks and stadia, and 5% for other amusement places; foreign live acts pay 15% and local acts 5%.

provisions.title: Graduated business taxes
provisions.text: Manufacturers pay from ₱272.25 a year on gross sales below ₱10,000 up to 41.5% of 1% above ₱6,500,000, with separate schedules for wholesalers, retailers and others; peddlers pay flat rates such as ₱500 for those selling from vehicles.

provisions.title: Permit fees and city charges
provisions.text: Long schedules set fees for mayor's permits, building, electrical and sign permits, zoning clearance, tricycles and cockpits, and charges for garbage collection, parking, the city hospital, cemeteries, fishery rentals and slaughter.

provisions.title: Community tax
provisions.text: Residents 18 and over who work, do business or own property pay ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income, up to ₱5,000; corporations pay ₱500 plus an additional tax of up to ₱10,000.

provisions.title: Late payment, protests and rate changes
provisions.text: Late taxes draw a 25% surcharge and up to 2% interest a month for at most 36 months; taxpayers may protest an assessment within 60 days, and the council may adjust rates only once every 5 years by up to 10%.

provisions.title: Fines of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000
provisions.text: Violations draw a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 and/or 1 to 6 months in jail; a company's president or manager is liable, and paying the fine does not excuse the unpaid tax.

ordinances.penalties: Violations not otherwise penalised draw a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both, without relief from the tax due.
ordinances.amends: Repeals all ordinances, rules and regulations inconsistent with it; no specific ordinance named.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your city is writing a full revenue code and wants a model that covers every tax, fee and charge a city can levy. Davao's 2005 code runs 434 sections across 10 chapters, and its long schedules of permit fees and service charges work as a checklist. Several of its rates exceed BLGC caps, and parts such as cockpit fees and interest on late payment may not fit your council's choices.

apply.if: If you are a city with an older revenue code
apply.then: you can replicate the 10-chapter layout and use the fee and charge schedules as a checklist of what your code leaves out.

apply.if: If you are a province
apply.then: borrow the real property tax chapters at your 1% ceiling under BLGC s. 258, and leave out the city mark-ups allowed by BLGC s. 174.

apply.if: If your council prefers no interest on late payment
apply.then: replace the 2% a month interest with a Shari'ah-compliant rule under BLGC s. 153; otherwise keep the 25% surcharge and the 36-month cap, which follow BLGC s. 191.

apply.if: If you want to reward early payment of real property tax
apply.then: copy the 10% on-time and 20% advance discounts, within BLGC s. 277.

apply.if: If your LGU has mosques, madaris or owners displaced from their property
apply.then: add the exemptions in BLGC s. 259 and s. 260, which Davao's code does not have.

change: Cut the amusement tax: BLGC s. 164 caps it at 10% of gross receipts, and BLGC s. 174 bars cities from exceeding that cap, so the 30% and 15% rates cannot be copied

Recompute the transfer tax (80% of 1%) and franchise tax (82% of 1%) from the base in BLGC s. 158 and s. 160 (50% of 1%) and the 50% city mark-up in BLGC s. 174; Davao's rates include past adjustments a new code cannot start from

Replace the interest provisions with a Shari'ah-compliant rule if the council chooses, under BLGC s. 153, and add the exemptions in BLGC s. 259 (mosques, madaris) and s. 260 (property left behind by displaced owners)
Raise the tax penal clause to BLGC s. 576 (₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months); keep the ₱5,000 and 1-year cap in BLGC s. 509 for non-tax violations
Drop the cockpit, KTV and similar fee schedules if your council does not license those businesses, and hold the public hearings in BLGC s. 212 before enactment
barmm.fits: Cities; provinces for the real property tax chapters.

ordinances.title: Ordinance to provide additional area of one-half hectare out of the city-owned public cemetery at Ma-a, for the exclusive use of the Muslim community as burial site in Davao City and appropriating funds for the construction of its perimeter fence
ordinances.shortTitle: Muslim burial site ordinance
ordinances.summary: Sets aside an extra half hectare of the city-owned public cemetery at Ma-a as a burial site for the exclusive use of Davao City's Muslims. It funds a perimeter fence and related development, citing the general welfare clause and the state's duty to provide a decent burial site.
points: Reserves an additional 5,000 sq m of the Ma-a public cemetery for Muslim burials
Appropriates ₱4,100,000 for the perimeter fence and other development of the area
Takes effect on approval and publication in a local newspaper 3 consecutive times

provisions.title: Half a hectare more for Muslim burials

provisions.title: ₱4.1 million for a perimeter fence

apply.then: you can replicate this by reserving a defined area for the community that needs it and appropriating a fixed sum for the fence and site works.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Enacting the Salay Comprehensive Fisheries Code of 2016 Providing for the Sustainable Management, Development and Conservation of the Municipal Waters and Its Coastal Resources, Harmonizing and Integrating All Ordinances Pertinent Hereto, and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Comprehensive Fisheries Code of Salay
ordinances.summary: Salay's fisheries and coastal code under the Fisheries Code of 1998 as amended by RA 10654. It maps the municipal waters, splits them into 8 zones, declares a marine sanctuary and a marine protected area, and sets the rules on registration, licensing, commercial fishing, payao, fish corrals and fish cages. It creates the offices that enforce it and lists prohibited acts with their fines, covering all fisherfolk, vessel owners, mariculture operators and fish traders in the municipality.
points: Municipal waters of 113.42 sq. km along an 8.2 km coastline, split into 8 zones; beach seines (baling) allowed only on sandy or muddy bottoms in parts of 4 barangays
A 3-hectare marine sanctuary off Looc and Casulog, a turtle nesting site in Casulog, and a 13.75-hectare marine protected area at Dinagsaan with a 4.18-hectare core zone

Registration of fisherfolk and vessels; yearly licences of ₱50 to ₱200 per boat and ₱100 to ₱150 per gear, double for fishers from other municipalities, and none for marginal fisherfolk certified by the social welfare office
Small and medium commercial vessels may fish only 10.1 to 15 km from shore, in water at least 7 fathoms deep, after an MFARMC hearing, for ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 a year
Fish cages of up to 25 sq. m per module, at most 4 modules at sea or 2 in rivers per licensee, and at least 200 m from the shore; fish corrals at least 200 m apart, one per permittee
Only fisherfolk associations and the LGU may install payao; 10% of fishery fees go to the barangays each quarter, and fishery revenues go to a coastal management trust fund

Creates a Fisheries Resource Management Officer (or a designated agricultural technologist), Fishery Law Enforcement Teams with a legal officer, and an MFARMC with at least 11 fisherfolk representatives

provisions.title: Municipal waters mapped and zoned
provisions.text: Fixes Salay's municipal waters at 113.42 sq. km along an 8.2 km coastline and splits them into 8 zones. Beach seines (baling) are allowed only on sandy or muddy bottoms in parts of Inobulan, Salay River Side 1 and 2, and Looc.

provisions.title: Waters reserved for registered fisherfolk
provisions.text: Municipal waters are for registered municipal fisherfolk and their accredited groups, Salay residents first. The agriculture office keeps a public registry, updated and posted in barangay halls, and registered boats follow a colour-coding scheme.

provisions.title: Licences for boats and gear
provisions.text: No one may fish without a municipal licence, valid 1 year. Boats pay ₱50 to ₱200 a year by horsepower and gear ₱100 to ₱150; fishers from other municipalities pay double, and marginal fisherfolk certified by the social welfare office pay nothing.

provisions.title: Commercial vessels only 10.1 to 15 km out
provisions.text: Small and medium commercial vessels may fish only 10.1 to 15 km from shore, in water at least 7 fathoms deep, after an MFARMC public hearing and a clean record. They pay ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 a year by tonnage.

provisions.title: A sanctuary, a turtle site and a protected area
provisions.text: Declares a 3-hectare marine sanctuary off Looc and Casulog, a turtle nesting site in Casulog, and a 13.75-hectare marine protected area at Dinagsaan with a 4.18-hectare core zone.

provisions.title: Fish corrals and payao
provisions.text: Fish corrals stay in designated areas, at least 200 m apart, with tails no longer than 100 m, mesh of at least 3 cm, and only 1 per permittee. Only fisherfolk associations and the LGU may install payao.

provisions.title: Fish cage limits
provisions.text: Cages only in mariculture zones, up to 25 sq. m a module, at most 4 modules at sea or 2 in rivers per licensee, and at least 200 m from shore. Licences run 3 years, renewable once, with no subleasing; residents get priority.

provisions.title: Where fishery money goes
provisions.text: Revenues from the municipal waters fund coastal management as a trust fund, and 10% of fishery fees go to the barangays before the end of each quarter.

provisions.title: A fishery officer, enforcement teams and an MFARMC
provisions.text: Creates a Fisheries Resource Management Officer, or designates an agricultural technologist, and Fishery Law Enforcement Teams. A Municipal FARMC of officials, sector representatives, 3 commercial fishers and at least 11 fisherfolk representatives advises on fisheries.

provisions.title: Banned practices and fines
provisions.text: Bans compressor fishing, motorized sudsud, reef seines, catching sardine fry, gathering sargassum, active gear in municipal waters and more. Most violations draw ₱2,500 fines or up to 6 months in jail; the Mayor may convert penalties to community service.

ordinances.penalties: Mostly ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 with up to 6 months in jail for banned gear and methods, superlights, coral and mangrove damage and fishing in sanctuaries; ₱300 to ₱2,500 by offence for fishing unregistered or in closed areas; catch, gear and in some cases the vessel confiscated, and the mayor may impose administrative fines of up to ₱2,500
ordinances.amends: Harmonizes and integrates earlier Salay fishery ordinances (none named) and repeals inconsistent ones
ordinances.caveat: The minutes date the session to 27 October 2016 but the closing line reads 'Enacted: 17 October 2017', and Section 13 on overfished areas is cut off mid-sentence in this copy.

details.effect: 10 days after posting in 3 conspicuous places
details.covers: Salay's municipal waters, coastal resources and the fisherfolk and vessels using them
details.enforcers: Mayor through the FRM Office or Municipal Agriculturist, with FLET, PNP and fish wardens
details.funding: Municipal Agriculture Office budget; fishery revenues held in trust for coastal work

highlights.label: zones in the municipal waters, named by barangay

fisherfolk seats, at least, on the MFARMC

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has municipal waters but no single fisheries code, or one written before the 2015 amendments to the Fisheries Code. Salay's 2016 code follows RA 10654 and covers mapped waters, zones, sanctuaries, licence fees, limits on commercial fishing, fish cages, an enforcement team and an administrative hearing process. It assumes delineated waters and a working agriculture office, its fee and fine provisions need checking against the BLGC, and one section is cut off in this copy.

apply.if: If your LGU is coastal and has a municipal agriculturist
apply.then: you can replicate this by setting up a fisheries resource management section in that office, or designating an agricultural technologist as the FRMO as Salay allows when funds are short, with an MFARMC that holds at least 11 fisherfolk seats.

apply.if: If your municipal waters have already been delineated
apply.then: copy Salay's practice of writing the boundary coordinates, area and coastline length into the code, naming the zones by barangay and describing each sanctuary by its corner points.

apply.if: If your municipal waters have not been delineated yet
apply.then: start with the free registry of fisherfolk and vessels, licensing and the list of banned gear, and add zones and sanctuaries once the boundaries are fixed.

apply.if: If small commercial vessels ask to fish in your waters
apply.then: copy the conditions: only 10.1 to 15 km out, at least 7 fathoms deep, after an MFARMC public hearing and with a clean record; if you do not want them, leave the clause out.

apply.if: If your waters have fish cages or seaweed farms
apply.then: copy the module size, the 200 m distance from shore, the 100 m between cages and seaweed lots and the 3-year licence, and designate the mariculture zones first.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 172 and s. 480 (exclusive municipal authority over fishery privileges and enforcement of fishery laws in municipal waters), with RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654 as the national law.

Make sure marginal fishers using nets, traps and traditional gear such as payao pay no charge, as BLGC s. 172 requires. Salay's exemption depends on a social welfare certification, and its rule that only associations and the LGU may set payao should not reach a marginal fisher's own traditional payao.

Keep every penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489). Most of Salay's do, but the ₱100 a day for an illegal cage and the ₱1 a kilo for missing auxiliary invoices can pass ₱5,000, so cap the total. Make the Fisheries Arbitration Committee's ruling open to appeal rather than 'final and executory'.

Replace BFAR, DENR and EMB with the Bangsamoro Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform and the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy where they carry those functions, and rebuild the technical committee (EMB, Coast Guard, NFARMC, NFRDI, academe) from offices you can actually call on.

Hold fishery revenues in a trust fund (BLGC s. 333), put the FRMO under the agriculturist and mangrove work with the environment officer (s. 536 and s. 538), and post the code for 6 weeks under s. 571 instead of Salay's 10 days.
barmm.fits: Coastal municipalities with delineated municipal waters, a municipal agriculturist and organised fisherfolk associations.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Strictly Prohibiting the Use of Mosquito Nets and Tiny-Holed Fishing Materials in the Rivers, Lakes and Streams in the Municipality of Bayog, Zamboanga del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Mosquito Net Fishing Ban of Bayog
ordinances.summary: A one-page ordinance banning the use of mosquito nets and other fine-meshed gear to catch fish and other aquatic species in Bayog's rivers, lakes and streams. It sets fines that rise with each offence and lets barangays enforce it and keep half of each fine.
points: Bans using mosquito nets and 'tiny-holed' fishing materials to catch or gather aquatic species in all rivers, lakes and streams in the municipality
₱1,000 for a 1st offence and ₱2,000 for a 2nd; a 3rd brings ₱2,500, 30 days in jail, or both
The barangay, through its punong barangay, enforces the ban and keeps 50% of each fine
Takes effect after 3 consecutive weeks of posting and publication in the municipal newsletter

provisions.title: Why the ban
provisions.text: Mosquito nets and fine-meshed gear have depleted freshwater species, and Bayog's rivers, lakes and streams no longer feed the people who depend on them.

provisions.title: No mosquito nets or fine-meshed gear in inland waters
provisions.text: No person or group may use mosquito nets or 'tiny-holed' fishing materials to catch or gather aquatic species in any river, lake or stream in the municipality.

provisions.title: Fines that rise with each offence
provisions.text: A 1st offence draws a ₱1,000 fine and a 2nd ₱2,000. A 3rd brings ₱2,500, 30 days in jail, or both, at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Barangays enforce it and keep half the fine
provisions.text: The barangay, through its punong barangay, enforces the ban and is entitled to 50% of the fine for every violation.

provisions.title: Effect after 3 weeks of posting
provisions.text: It takes effect after 3 consecutive weeks of posting in conspicuous places and publication in the municipal newsletter.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000, then ₱2,000, then ₱2,500 or 30 days in jail or both, at the court's discretion
ordinances.caveat: It does not define 'tiny-holed' by mesh size, so enforcement rests on the national fine-mesh rule or a later definition.

details.effect: after 3 weeks of posting and publication in the municipal newsletter
details.covers: Anyone fishing in the rivers, lakes and streams of Bayog
details.enforcers: Barangay chairmen, who keep 50% of each fine

highlights.label: of each fine kept by the barangay that enforces it
fine for a first offence, ₱2,000 for a second
in jail, ₱2,500 or both for a third offence

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has rivers, lakes or streams where people fish with mosquito nets and catches are falling. Bayog's ban fits on one page, keeps fines within municipal limits and gives barangays a reason to enforce it by letting them keep half of each fine. It does not define 'tiny-holed', say who seizes the nets, or allow for fry gathering.

apply.if: If your LGU has inland waters but no rule on fine-mesh nets
apply.then: you can replicate this almost as written, adding a mesh size (the Fisheries Code treats nets under 3 cm stretched mesh as fine mesh) so wardens and courts know what is banned.

apply.if: If your barangays have tanods or deputised fish wardens
apply.then: copy the 50% share of fines for the enforcing barangay, and say how the barangay receipts its share and remits the rest.

apply.if: If people in your LGU gather fry for fishponds or cages
apply.then: add an exception by permit for fry gathering, since marginal fishers may gather fry free of charge under BLGC s. 172.

apply.if: If you want the nets taken off the water
apply.then: add confiscation of the nets and say who keeps or destroys them.

apply.if: If your LGU is also coastal or has a fisheries code
apply.then: fold the ban into that code and extend it to all municipal waters instead of passing it alone.

change: Cite BLGC s. 480 (enforcement of fishery laws in municipal waters) and s. 489 as the basis, with RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654 for the fine-mesh rule.
Define 'tiny-holed' by mesh size and exempt fry gathering by permit, so the ban does not run against the free fry-gathering right of marginal fishers in BLGC s. 172.
Keep the fines and the 30-day jail term; they sit within the ₱5,000 and 6-month limit in BLGC s. 489.
Tie barangay enforcement to the punong barangay's duty to enforce ordinances (BLGC s. 417), and pay the barangay's 50% into its own funds with an official receipt.
Post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571, not Bayog's 3 weeks.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with rivers, lakes or streams fished for food, and barangays willing to enforce.
