ordinances.title: An Ordinance Enacting the Local Revenue Code for Taxes of Molave, Zamboanga del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Revenue Code for Taxes of Molave
ordinances.summary: Molave's tax code, covering the municipal taxes only: graduated business taxes, other business taxes, the community tax, and the rules on collection, civil remedies and taxpayer remedies. It adds a table of presumed incomes for 161 local lines of business that the treasurer uses to check what businesses declare.
points: Graduated yearly business taxes for manufacturers (₱34,125 for sales of ₱5 million to ₱6.5 million, then 37.5% of 1%), wholesalers (₱14,000 for ₱1 million to ₱2 million, then 50% of 1%) and contractors and service businesses (₱16,837.15 for ₱1 million to ₱2 million); half rates for exporters and essential goods
Retailers pay 2% on sales up to ₱400,000 and 1% above; barangays keep the power to tax stores with sales of ₱30,000 or less; peddlers pay up to ₱50 a year

Other taxes: 1% of gross receipts for mobile traders, ₱550 to ₱1,650 a year per public utility vehicle, ₱12,100 to ₱60,500 for sports exhibitions, fiesta rides and circuses, 2% on mining and forest concessions, and ₱192.50 to ₱2,420 for advertisements
A presumptive income level for 161 lines of business, from ₱40,000 for a load retailer to ₱1,000,000 for a fresh fish wholesaler, used to validate declared sales
Community tax of ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income (up to ₱5,000) for individuals and ₱500 plus up to ₱10,000 for corporations; half of what barangay treasurers collect stays with the barangay
25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest for up to 36 months on late payment; distraint and levy to collect; 60 days to protest an assessment
Rates may be adjusted only once every 5 years, by no more than 10%

provisions.title: Graduated tax on manufacturers
provisions.text: Manufacturers, processors, brewers and distillers pay a yearly tax on the previous year's domestic sales, from ₱231 on sales under ₱10,000 to ₱34,125 on ₱5 million to ₱6.5 million, then up to 37.5% of 1% above that.

provisions.title: Wholesalers, retailers and peddlers
provisions.text: Wholesalers pay from ₱25.20 up to ₱14,000 on ₱1 million to ₱2 million, then up to 50% of 1%. Retailers pay 2% on sales up to ₱400,000 and 1% above; barangays alone tax stores selling ₱30,000 or less. Peddlers pay up to ₱50 a year. Exporters and essential goods pay half.

provisions.title: Contractors, banks and service businesses
provisions.text: Contractors pay from ₱39.93 to ₱16,837.15 on ₱1 million to ₱2 million, then up to 60% of 1%. Banks pay 50% of 1% of gross receipts. Restaurants, amusement places and other services pay graduated rates, never less than ₱16,837.15 on ₱2 million or more.

provisions.title: Mobile traders and public utility vehicles
provisions.text: Mobile traders and rolling stores pay 1% of gross receipts. Public utility vehicle operators pay a yearly tax per unit: ₱1,650 for buses, ₱1,100 for mini buses, ₱880 for jeepneys, ₱770 for taxis and vans, ₱550 for multicabs.

provisions.title: Fiesta rides, mining, forests and ads
provisions.text: Circuses and fiesta rides pay ₱22,000 on private lots or ₱60,500 on public lots for up to 30 days; sports exhibitions ₱12,100 for up to 5 days. Mining and forest concessions pay 2% of gross receipts. Advertisements cost ₱192.50 to ₱2,420.

provisions.title: Presumptive income levels for checking sales
provisions.text: The treasurer keeps a schedule of minimum gross receipts by line of business, from ₱40,000 for a load retailer to ₱1,000,000 for a fresh fish wholesaler, used to check declared sales or set taxable receipts when no valid data exists.

provisions.title: Community tax
provisions.text: Adult residents who work, do business or own property pay ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income, up to ₱5,000. Corporations based in Molave pay ₱500 plus ₱2 per ₱5,000 of property or receipts, up to ₱10,000. Barangays keep 50% of what their treasurers collect.

provisions.title: 25% surcharge and 2% monthly interest
provisions.text: Late payment draws a 25% surcharge plus interest of up to 2% a month, for no more than 36 months. The municipality can collect by distraint of personal property and levy on real property.

provisions.title: 60 days to protest an assessment
provisions.text: A taxpayer has 60 days from a notice of assessment to protest to the treasurer, who decides within 60 days; a denied taxpayer then has 30 days to go to court.

provisions.title: Rate changes and penalties
provisions.text: The SB may adjust rates only once every 5 years and by no more than 10%. Most old tax exemptions are withdrawn. Violations draw ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 or 1 to 6 months in jail, and the tax is still owed.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both; company officers are liable, and paying the fine does not excuse the tax
ordinances.caveat: This code covers taxes only, not permit fees or service charges, and a few table entries look mistyped, such as a ₱75,000 minimum tax on a ₱70,000 presumed income for cafes.

details.effect: after posting for 3 consecutive weeks
details.covers: Business and community taxes levied within Molave
details.enforcers: Municipal Treasurer

highlights.label: lines of business with a presumed income
tax on a retailer's first ₱400,000 of sales

surcharge on taxes paid late

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU taxes businesses under an old revenue code and has no way to check what they declare. Molave's 2022 tax code is compact, and its table of presumed incomes for 161 local lines of business, from sari-sari stores to copra buyers, is the most useful part for a small municipality. Its business tax rates sit above the BLGC ceilings, its community tax uses the old ₱5, and its penalty clause is below the BLGC floor, so do not copy the numbers.

apply.if: If your LGU has a revenue code that predates the BLGC
apply.then: use Molave's chapters as a checklist for what yours is missing, such as situs of the tax, retirement of a business, distraint and levy, and protests.

apply.if: If your treasurer cannot check the sales businesses declare
apply.then: you can replicate the presumptive income table, building each figure from your own permit records by line of business and reviewing it every tax year.

apply.if: If your barangay treasurers collect community tax
apply.then: copy the 50% share for the barangay on what they collect, and bond them as Molave requires.

apply.if: If you are setting business tax rates for the first time
apply.then: start from the BLGC s. 167 schedules rather than Molave's figures, which include past increases, and hold the public hearing BLGC s. 212 requires.

apply.if: If your council prefers not to charge interest
apply.then: keep the 25% surcharge and replace the 2% monthly interest with a Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rule under BLGC s. 153.

change: Reset every business tax schedule to BLGC s. 167. Molave's top fixed brackets (₱34,125 for manufacturers, ₱14,000 for wholesalers, ₱16,837.15 for contractors) are above the s. 167 figures of ₱24,375, ₱10,000 and ₱11,500, and the bank tax must exclude duly registered Islamic banks.
Raise the community tax to BLGC s. 180 and s. 181: ₱20 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 for individuals, and ₱1,000 plus ₱5 per ₱5,000 for corporations. Molave's ₱5, ₱500 and ₱2 are the old amounts.
Raise the penal clause to the range in BLGC s. 576 (₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months); Molave's ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 falls below the floor.

Check the per-unit tax on public utility vehicle operators against BLGC s. 156, which bars taxes on transport contractors and common carriers, and the fixed tax on fiesta rides and circuses against the provincial amusement tax in s. 164. Re-cite investment incentives to the Bangsamoro Board of Investments (s. 156).
Hold public hearings and publish under BLGC s. 212 and s. 213, including the Bangsamoro Online Register of Ordinances; the code takes effect only 15 days after publication.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with many small businesses and a treasurer's office able to keep a table of presumed incomes up to date.

ordinances.title: Updated Market Code of 2017 of the Municipality of Bingawan, Province of Iloilo
ordinances.shortTitle: Updated Market Code of Bingawan
ordinances.summary: Bingawan's market code governs how the public market is run: stall and table rents, royalty fees and bonds, the award and lease of stalls, vendor conduct and sanitation, and terminal fees for the market parking area. The mayor runs the market through a Municipal Market Supervisor, while the treasurer's regular staff handle collections.
points: Rent of ₱1,200 a month (or ₱60 per sq. m) for stalls the municipality built and ₱45 per sq. m for stalls lessees built; tables ₱10 or ₱7 per sq. m a day
One-time royalty fees of ₱10,000 to ₱25,000 and application bonds of ₱2,000 to ₱5,000, paid before the certificate of award is issued
Vacant stalls are posted for 10 days and awarded by drawing of lots by a Market Committee chaired by the treasurer; appeals go to the council within 15 days
Leases run 5 years with the first option to renew; no subleasing or dummies, the lessee must run the stall in person, and rights pass to the spouse, children or parents on death
25% surcharge on late rent, and 3 months unpaid cancels the lease; extra space costs double, selling without paying costs triple, and an ejected lessee is barred for 2 years
No selling fish, meat, fruit, eggs or native delicacies within 100 m of the market except from private buildings; the market is open 4 a.m. to 9 p.m.
Toilet fees of ₱5 to ₱10, a ₱1,500 permit to renovate a stall, and terminal fees of ₱10 to ₱15 a trip for buses, jeepneys and cars and ₱10 a day for tricycles

provisions.title: Monthly stall rents and daily table rents
provisions.text: Stalls the municipality built rent for ₱1,200 a month or ₱60 per sq. m; stalls lessees built pay ₱45 per sq. m a month. Tables cost ₱10 per sq. m a day if municipal-built and ₱7 if lessee-built.

provisions.title: Royalty fees and application bonds
provisions.text: A one-time, non-refundable royalty fee of ₱25,000 or ₱20,000 for stalls and ₱15,000 or ₱10,000 for tables, plus an application bond of ₱5,000 for stalls and ₱2,000 for tables, both paid before the certificate of award is issued.

provisions.title: Rent due in the first 20 days, with surcharges
provisions.text: Stall rent is due within the first 20 days of each month, with a 25% surcharge if late; 3 consecutive unpaid months cancel the lease. Extra space costs double, and selling without paying costs 3 times the rate.

provisions.title: The mayor runs the market through a supervisor
provisions.text: The Municipal Market Supervisor runs the market for the mayor; the health office handles sanitation, the police chief handles order, and only regular staff of the treasurer's office may collect fees. The market opens 4 a.m. to 9 p.m.

provisions.title: Market rules for vendors
provisions.text: No selling fruit, fish, fowl, eggs, meat or native delicacies within 100 metres of the market except from private buildings; no cooking outside approved eateries, no animal pens, no vehicles inside, and no living in stalls.

provisions.title: Vacant stalls awarded by drawing of lots
provisions.text: Vacancies are posted for at least 10 days; Filipino applicants have preference, and a Market Committee chaired by the treasurer draws lots among several. Unhappy applicants may appeal to the SB within 15 days.

provisions.title: 5-year leases, run in person
provisions.text: Leases run 5 years and are renewable; the lessee must run the stall personally with Filipino helpers, and subleasing or using a dummy cancels the lease and ejects the holder, who is barred from any stall for 2 years.

provisions.title: Rights pass to family on death
provisions.text: On a stallholder's death or incapacity, the stall rights pass in order to the surviving spouse, legitimate children, parents, then relatives within the 4th degree.

provisions.title: Terminal and toilet fees
provisions.text: Buses and cargo trucks pay ₱15 a trip, mini-buses, jeepneys, vans and cars ₱10 a trip, and tricycles and pedicabs ₱10 a day, with a 25% surcharge if late; market toilets cost ₱5 to urinate and ₱10 for a bowel movement or bath.
provisions.section: Ch. II, Sec. 1B.02.04; Ch. IV, Secs. 1.01-1.03

provisions.title: Fines of up to ₱2,500
provisions.text: Any violation not given its own penalty is punished by a fine of up to ₱2,500, up to 6 months' imprisonment, or both, at the court's discretion.

ordinances.penalties: Up to ₱2,500, or up to 6 months in jail, or both, where no specific penalty applies; company officers are liable
ordinances.caveat: There is no Chapter III, the market entrance fee for transient vendors has no rate, and the code both lets foreigners lease a stall when no Filipino applies and says only citizens may lease.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU runs a public market and stall awards, arrears and subleasing keep turning into disputes. Bingawan's code comes with the forms you need: a notice of vacancy, a sworn application, a certificate of award and a 5-year lease contract. Its royalty fees of up to ₱25,000 are steep for a small market, a few provisions contradict each other, and it mentions the slaughterhouse without regulating it.

apply.if: If your LGU runs its own public market
apply.then: you can replicate the set-up: a market supervisor under the mayor for daily running, collections kept with the treasurer's regular staff, and a market committee chaired by the treasurer to award stalls.

apply.if: If stalls in your market are awarded informally
apply.then: start with Bingawan's forms: a 10-day notice of vacancy, a sworn application, drawing of lots among qualified applicants, a certificate of award and a written lease.

apply.if: If you collect market fees under an older revenue ordinance
apply.then: re-price rents, royalty fees and bonds from your own costs after a public hearing, and do not copy Bingawan's ₱25,000 royalty fee as it stands.

apply.if: If many of your vendors sell only on market days
apply.then: keep daily table and space fees low and copy the cash-ticket system, torn in half and checked against the collector's record each day.

apply.if: If your market sells both halal and non-halal meat
apply.then: add separate sections, stalls and tools for each, which Bingawan's meat rules do not cover.

change: Re-cite the authority from RA 7160 s. 447 to BLGC s. 489 and s. 480 (municipal markets), and keep collection with treasury staff, since BLGC s. 152 bars letting collection to private persons.

Bingawan's 25% surcharge is the most BLGC s. 191 allows; BLGC s. 153 lets the council use a Shari'ah-compliant late charge instead. Check the double and triple rates for extra or unpaid space against the rule in s. 152 that charges not be excessive.
Replace the National Meat Inspection Commission rules and the agriculturist's role with inspection by the veterinarian under BLGC s. 543, optional for municipalities, so name who inspects.
Settle the citizenship rule in one place, and fill in a rate for the market entrance fee or drop it.
Post the code for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571, since it carries penalties; Bingawan posted for 3 weeks.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Supplementing Municipal Ordinance No. 11th-33-2023, Otherwise Known as "An Ordinance Creating the Municipal Meat Inspection Service (MMIS) of the Municipality of Molave, Province of Zamboanga del Sur," by Prescribing Additional Rules and Regulations Governing the Operation of the Municipal Slaughterhouse, Providing for Tariff Rates and Butcher's Fees and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Supplemental Slaughterhouse Regulatory and Tariff Ordinance of Molave
ordinances.summary: Adds operating rules and price ceilings to Molave's 2023 ordinance creating a Municipal Meat Inspection Service. It covers butchers, helpers, meat dealers, transporters and anyone using the municipal slaughterhouse, and sets the most a licensed butcher may charge for butchering and lechon.
points: Butchers and helpers need a mayor's permit, wear white boots, may not work drunk, pay for damage to the facility, and may enter only from 12:01 a.m. (9 p.m. on fiestas and holidays)
No meat leaves without inspection; release times are set by animal: cattle and carabao 2:00 to 3:30 a.m., pigs 3:31 to 5:00 a.m., others from 5:01 a.m.
A barangay certification that the animals come from a barangay free of reported disease is required for pigs and goats, on top of the 2023 entry documents

Bans slaughtering pregnant cattle or carabao, slaughter without ante-mortem inspection except approved emergencies, burning rubber or plastic to heat the vat, littering and washing transport vehicles inside
Maximum butchering fees, paid to the butcher and not to the municipality: ₱5 a kilo for hogs, ₱1,000 per cow, ₱1,500 per carabao, ₱400 per goat, ₱40 to ₱60 per fowl
Lechon packages including the slaughter fee: ₱1,500 to ₱1,800 per pig by weight, ₱500 to ₱900 for pork belly, ₱5,000 per cow
Butchers must remit slaughter fees to the treasurer under the revenue code

provisions.title: Who it covers
provisions.text: It applies to all butchers, assistants, workers, meat dealers, transporters and anyone using the Molave Municipal Slaughterhouse, and adds to the 2023 ordinance that created the Municipal Meat Inspection Service.

provisions.title: Rules for butchers and helpers
provisions.text: Butchers and helpers need a mayor's permit, wear white boots, may not work drunk, keep clean and pay for damage to tiles, faucets or the boiling vat. They may enter from 12:01 a.m., or from 9:00 p.m. on fiestas, Christmas and other holidays.

provisions.title: Inspection and release times
provisions.text: No meat leaves without inspection by the meat inspector on duty. Cattle and carabao are released 2:00 to 3:30 a.m., pigs 3:31 to 5:00 a.m. and other animals from 5:01 a.m.

provisions.title: A barangay health certificate for pigs and goats
provisions.text: On top of the 2023 entry documents, pigs and goats need a barangay certification that they come from a barangay with no reported animal disease and were monitored before transport.

provisions.title: Banned practices at the slaughterhouse
provisions.text: No slaughter of pregnant cattle or carabao, no slaughter without ante-mortem inspection except approved emergencies, no burning rubber or plastic to heat the vat, no littering, and no washing of transport vehicles inside except the official meat van. It closes 8:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.

provisions.title: Maximum butchering fees
provisions.text: Licensed butchers may charge at most ₱5 a kilo for hogs, ₱1,000 per cow, ₱1,500 per carabao, ₱400 per goat, ₱40 per chicken and ₱60 per duck or turkey. These are paid to the butcher and are not municipal revenue.

provisions.title: Lechon package prices
provisions.text: Lechon, including slaughter fee, butchering, spices and firewood: ₱1,500 to ₱1,800 per pig by weight, ₱500 to ₱900 for pork belly, and ₱5,000 per cow, with the owner supplying spices and firewood for a cow.

provisions.title: Slaughter fees go to the treasurer
provisions.text: Butchers must remit the slaughter fee to the Municipal Treasurer under the revenue code, or face penalties under existing ordinances.

provisions.title: Suspension, then a permanent ban
provisions.text: A first offence suspends the mayor's permit or licence for up to 30 days. A second cancels it and bars the offender from working at the slaughterhouse for good.

ordinances.penalties: 1st offence: suspension of the mayor's permit for up to 30 days; 2nd: cancellation and permanent disqualification from working in the slaughterhouse
ordinances.amends: Supplements Municipal Ordinance No. 11th-33-2023, which created Molave's Municipal Meat Inspection Service
ordinances.caveat: The slaughter fees and the 2023 entry requirements are in other ordinances not included here, and the mayor's approval date is blank on this copy.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU runs a slaughterhouse and the complaints are about hygiene, late-night disorder or what butchers charge. Molave's 3-page supplement sets plain house rules, meat release times and a ceiling on butchers' fees, enforced through the butcher's permit rather than court cases. It builds on a 2023 ordinance and a revenue code that are not part of this text, and it handles pigs and cattle in the same facility.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a slaughterhouse ordinance or meat inspection service
apply.then: you can replicate this as a supplement, adding the house rules, release times and fee ceilings without re-enacting the whole ordinance.

apply.if: If butchers in your slaughterhouse work without a permit
apply.then: start by requiring a mayor's permit for every butcher and helper, since Molave's only sanction is suspending or cancelling that permit.

apply.if: If your slaughterhouse handles both halal and non-halal animals
apply.then: keep pigs on a separate line with their own tools, schedule and drainage, and have halal slaughter done by a qualified slaughterman; Molave's rules do not address this.

apply.if: If your LGU has no veterinarian
apply.then: name who does ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection and who approves emergency slaughter before copying the inspection rules.

apply.if: If you worry about disease in animals brought in from barangays
apply.then: copy the barangay certification for pigs and goats, and agree its form with the punong barangays.

change: Re-cite the basis from RA 7160 s. 16 to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare) and s. 480 (municipal slaughterhouses).
Put inspection and slaughterhouse regulation under the veterinarian (BLGC s. 543); the post is optional for municipalities, so name who inspects if you have none.
If halal meat passes through the facility, write halal slaughter and the separation of pigs into the rules, with separate tools, lines and release times.
Give a butcher notice and a hearing before suspension or cancellation, and consider a fixed period of disqualification instead of a permanent one.
Set the butchering fee ceilings after a public hearing and say how often they are reviewed; keep the slaughter fees themselves in your revenue code, and post under BLGC s. 67.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Prescribing Rules and Regulations in the Issuance of Franchise to Tricycles for Hire in the Municipality of Bingawan, Province of Iloilo
ordinances.shortTitle: Tricycle Franchise Ordinance of Bingawan
ordinances.summary: Sets the rules for franchising tricycles for hire in Bingawan through a Motorized Tricycle Operator's Permit (MTOP) granted by the Sangguniang Bayan. It covers who may operate, fares, operating conditions, 6 routes out of the poblacion and the yearly franchise fees.
points: The Sangguniang Bayan issues, renews, suspends and cancels MTOPs, sets fares after a public hearing, sets zones with the barangays, and may adjust fees no more often than every 3 years
Only Filipino citizens or firms with 60% Filipino equity may operate, with LTO-registered units and common carrier's insurance
Fares: ₱10 flat within a zone of up to 2 km, then ₱5 a km; students, PWDs and the elderly pay ₱7 for the first 2 km and ₱2 a km after
No tricycles on national highways used by trucks over 4 tons where speeds exceed 40 kph, unless there is no other route and the engineer clears it; one colour per zone and a unique body number
The MTOP runs 1 year; transfers of ownership or zone need council approval; drivers must hold LTO licences; no overloading
6 routes from the poblacion to the outlying barangays
Fees: ₱500 franchise fee a year, ₱500 one-time filing fee per unit, ₱200 privilege fee for new applicants, ₱100 inspection fee

provisions.title: The Sangguniang Bayan runs the franchise
provisions.text: The Sangguniang Bayan issues, amends, renews, suspends and cancels Motorized Tricycle Operator's Permits (MTOPs), sets fares after a public hearing, sets zones with the barangays, and adjusts fees no more often than every 3 years.

provisions.title: Who may operate
provisions.text: Only Filipino citizens and partnerships or corporations with 60% Filipino equity qualify, and only with LTO-registered units. MTOP holders must carry common carrier's insurance to cover liability to passengers in accidents.

provisions.title: Fares
provisions.text: ₱10 flat per passenger within a zone of under 2 km radius, then ₱5 a km beyond 2 km. Students, persons with disabilities and the elderly pay ₱7 for the first 2 km and ₱2 a km after. The fare table is posted at the terminal and in each unit.

provisions.title: No tricycles on fast national highways
provisions.text: Tricycles may not use national highways carrying vehicles over 4 tons where normal speed exceeds 40 kph, unless there is no other route and the traffic or highway engineer clears it. Zones crossing into another municipality need both councils' approval.

provisions.title: Colour, number and operating rules
provisions.text: Each zone has a common colour and each unit a unique number besides its LTO plate. Units run like taxis within a zone, may carry no more than they were designed for, and use only LTO-licensed drivers.

provisions.title: A 1-year permit
provisions.text: The MTOP runs 1 year, renewable, and may be suspended or cancelled after a hearing. A change of owner or zone counts as an amendment needing council approval; operators stopping service or suspending it over 1 month must report it.

provisions.title: 6 routes from the poblacion
provisions.text: Sets 6 routes: within the Poblacion, and from the Poblacion to Maldespina and Quinangyana, to Maganhop and Inamyungan, to Inaquigan, to Cubay and the barangays beyond them, and to Bulabog.

provisions.title: Franchise fees
provisions.text: Operators pay a ₱500 franchise fee and a ₱100 inspection fee each year, a one-time ₱500 filing fee per unit, and new applicants a ₱200 privilege fee.

provisions.title: Penalty for operating without an MTOP
provisions.text: Operating a tricycle for hire without a valid MTOP draws a ₱1,000 fine, 3 months in jail, or both, at the court's discretion.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000, 3 months in jail, or both, for operating without a valid MTOP

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has tricycles for hire but no franchise ordinance, or one that does not set fares or zones. Bingawan's is 4 pages and covers the essentials: who may operate, the permit, fares with discounts for students, PWDs and the elderly, highway safety limits, routes and fees. Enforcement is thin: the only penalty is for operating without a permit.

apply.if: If your LGU already issues tricycle permits without an ordinance behind them
apply.then: you can replicate this by putting the MTOP, its 1-year term and the council's powers over fares and zones into one ordinance, and carrying existing permit holders over.

apply.if: If tricycles in your LGU run on a national highway
apply.then: copy the rule barring them where trucks over 4 tons run and speeds pass 40 kph, and name the alternative routes.

apply.if: If you have a terminal or a poblacion zone
apply.then: set a flat fare inside the zone and a per-km fare beyond it, with lower fares for students, PWDs and the elderly, and post the fare table at the terminal and in each tricycle.

apply.if: If you want fares and loading enforced
apply.then: add penalties for overcharging, overloading and missing colours or body numbers, which Bingawan left out, within ₱5,000 and 6 months.

apply.if: If a route crosses into a neighbouring LGU
apply.then: get the joint approval of both councils, as Bingawan's operating conditions require.

change: Re-cite tricycle franchising to BLGC s. 480 (municipal transport, including franchising tricycles) and s. 489. BLGC s. 156 bars taxes on common carriers and motor vehicle registration fees except for tricycles, so keep the fees as regulatory charges tied to the cost of franchising and inspection.
Point the vehicle registration and driver's licence requirements to the Bangsamoro Ministry of Transportation and Communications where it handles land transportation in your area, instead of the LTO.
Hold the public hearing before setting or changing fares, as Section 2 requires, and keep the fare table and fees on a fixed review cycle.
Post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571, since it carries a penalty; Bingawan posted for 3 weeks.
barmm.fits: Municipalities where tricycles are the main public transport between the poblacion and the barangays.

ordinances.title: Adopting the Revised Comprehensive Municipal Ecological Solid Waste Management Program of the Municipality of Braulio E. Dujali, Davao del Norte and Providing for Fines and Penalties for Violations Thereof and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Revised Ecological Solid Waste Management Program of Braulio E. Dujali
ordinances.summary: Dujali's revised solid waste ordinance under RA 9003. It sets up a Municipal Ecological Solid Waste Management Board, requires segregation at source and materials recovery facilities, charges households a garbage fee shared with barangays, creates a trust fund, and lists prohibited acts with fines and community service. It covers households, businesses, institutions and transport operators.
points: A board chaired by the mayor with the MENRO as vice chair and over 20 members, from department heads to business, cooperative, farmer, women and purok representatives; it meets at least quarterly and must submit a waste plan within 3 months
Segregation at source in 4 classes in every barangay; unsegregated waste is not collected and the household is penalised; the MENRO collects from the MRFs
MRFs in all barangays, sitios, puroks, schools, churches, the public market and households; barangays collect and sort, the municipality hauls residual and special waste
₱10 garbage collection fee per household, 40% of it to the barangay; 80% of all waste fees, fines and charges go to a trust fund run by the board
Fines of ₱200, ₱300 and ₱500 plus 2, 3 and 5 hours of community service; 50% of fines go to the enforcers or informants
Certificates of waste orientation or compliance required for marriage applicants, graduating students and barangay and municipal clearances
Bans littering, open burning, open dumping, burying waste in rivers and flood-prone areas, and leaving fiesta and election posters up

provisions.title: Who is covered
provisions.text: It applies to households, shops, sari-sari stores, markets, vendors, restaurants, entertainment places, hospitals, clinics, funeral parlors, schools, churches, offices, slaughterhouses, piggeries, buses, jeepneys, tricycles, haulers and agro-industrial businesses in the municipality.

provisions.title: A solid waste board of over 20 members
provisions.text: The Municipal Ecological Solid Waste Management Board is chaired by the Mayor with the MENRO as vice chair, and includes council committee chairs, department heads, the police chief, school heads and business, cooperative, farmer, women and purok leaders' representatives.

provisions.title: What the board does
provisions.text: It writes the municipal waste plan and submits it to the council within 3 months, supports and oversees its implementation, coordinates barangays and allows them to cluster, sets incentives, reviews the plan yearly and meets at least quarterly.

provisions.title: Segregation at source in 4 classes
provisions.text: Every barangay must enforce segregation into compostable, recyclable, residual and special or hazardous waste, in labelled, colour-coded containers. Unsegregated waste is not collected and its owner is penalised. Waste goes out only on the scheduled day.

provisions.title: MRFs everywhere; who collects what
provisions.text: Materials recovery facilities are set up in all barangays, sitios, puroks, schools, churches, the public market and households. Barangays collect and sort waste in public spaces; the MENRO collects from the MRFs and the municipality hauls residual and special waste.

provisions.title: ₱10 garbage fee and a trust fund
provisions.text: Each household pays a ₱10 garbage collection fee, 40% of which goes to the barangay. 80% of all waste fees, fines and charges goes into a trust fund spent only on solid waste programs and run by the board.

provisions.title: Banned acts
provisions.text: Littering and dumping in public places, leaving fiesta and election posters up, not segregating, open burning, open dumping or burying waste in rivers, creeks and flood-prone areas, squatting in dumps, and mixing or taking recyclables set aside for collection.

provisions.title: Fines with community service
provisions.text: ₱200 and 2 hours of community service for a 1st offence, ₱300 and 3 hours for a 2nd, and ₱500 and 5 hours for later offences. Barangay enforcers issue citation tickets, and 50% of fines go to enforcers or informants.

provisions.title: Waste orientation tied to clearances
provisions.text: A certificate of ESWM orientation or compliance is required for marriage applicants, graduating students and barangay and municipal clearances, and for anyone transacting with the barangay or municipality. The Mayor issues the IRR within 90 days.

ordinances.penalties: ₱200 and 2 hours of community service, ₱300 and 3 hours, then ₱500 and 5 hours for later offences
ordinances.caveat: This is an OCR of a scan with some garbled words; the appropriation section (Section 34) is missing from this copy, and the garbage fee does not say how often it is paid.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your municipality needs a short RA 9003 ordinance that barangays can enforce with tickets. Dujali's sets up the board, segregation, barangay MRFs, a small household fee shared with barangays, a trust fund, and low fines paired with community service. Some sanctions go too far, such as withholding marriage and graduation papers, the shares of fines and fees overlap, and a section is missing from this copy.

apply.if: If your LGU has an environment officer or a solid waste board
apply.then: you can replicate Dujali's board, with the environment officer as vice chair and seats for business, cooperatives, farmers, women and purok leaders, meeting at least quarterly.

apply.if: If your barangays have no materials recovery facility yet
apply.then: start with segregation at source and pick-up points agreed with each barangay, and let barangays share or cluster MRFs as the board may allow.

apply.if: If you want to charge households for collection
apply.then: copy the small flat fee with a fixed share for the barangay, but say how often it is paid and charge only where collection reaches.

apply.if: If you want barangay enforcers to issue tickets
apply.then: train them through the board, adopt a citation ticket form, and decide what share of fines goes to enforcers before promising 80% to the trust fund.

apply.if: If you plan to tie clearances to waste compliance
apply.then: limit it to the barangay and municipal clearances you issue, and drop the marriage and graduation requirements.

change: Re-cite the board, plan and MRF to BLGC s. 480 (municipal solid waste management board, plan and MRF) and barangay segregation and MRFs to s. 408, with RA 9003 as the national law; name the environment officer's role under s. 538.
Hold the waste fund as a trust fund under BLGC s. 333, usable only for its purpose, and make the shares add up: Dujali promises 80% of fines to the fund and 50% of fines to enforcers.

Drop the waste certificate as a condition of marriage licences and school graduation. The first is set by the Family Code and the second falls under the Bangsamoro Education Code (BAA No. 18), and a municipal ordinance should not add conditions to either.
Keep the fines and community service; they sit within the ₱5,000 and 6-month limit in BLGC s. 489.
Post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571; Dujali's took effect on approval, which a penal ordinance cannot.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with an environment officer or waste office and barangays ready to run their own MRFs.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Implementing Forced Evacuation as a Last Resort When a Disaster or Emergency Has Been Declared in the Municipality and Danger of Loss of Lives Become Imminent
ordinances.shortTitle: Forced Evacuation Ordinance of Bayambang
ordinances.summary: Sets out how Bayambang orders residents out of danger when a disaster or emergency has been declared. The disaster risk reduction officer, as incident commander, can enforce pre-emptive evacuation and recommend forced evacuation, which the mayor declares along with orders on evacuation centres, transport, security and animals. It covers every resident in an affected area and lets the municipality use reasonable force on those who refuse to leave.
points: The municipal DRRM officer (LDRRMO V) is the incident commander and can enforce pre-emptive evacuation on their own assessment

Forced evacuation is declared by the mayor on the incident commander's recommendation, with orders on evacuation centres, standby vehicles, security, protection of homes from looting, and a stay until the danger is declared over
The municipal agriculture office takes custody of affected animals and moves them to a government facility
Before enforcement, residents must be told in a language they speak why they must leave and that there is no other safe option

Police, fire, social welfare, health, DRRM and agriculture personnel may be mobilised, and may use reasonable force on residents who refuse or go back, with attention to children, women, the elderly and persons with disabilities
The DRRM office runs training on pre-emptive and forced evacuation at least once a year
The mayor reports every declaration to the DRRM council and the Sangguniang Bayan within 24 hours

provisions.title: Forced evacuation as a last resort
provisions.text: Forced evacuation is an order given when a disaster or emergency has been declared, danger of loss of life is imminent and conditions critically endanger the people in a defined area. Pre-emptive evacuation moves residents out before they are exposed.

provisions.title: The DRRM officer is incident commander
provisions.text: The Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer V is the incident commander, responsible for all aspects of the emergency response, its priorities and its response teams.

provisions.title: Pre-emptive evacuation on the commander's call
provisions.text: When the incident commander judges that residents must be moved pre-emptively, the commander enforces the evacuation immediately.

provisions.title: The mayor declares forced evacuation
provisions.text: On the incident commander's recommendation, the mayor declares forced evacuation and orders evacuation centres, standby municipal vehicles, security in the centres, protection of homes from looting, and a stay until the danger is declared over.

provisions.title: Animals go to a government facility
provisions.text: The mayor mobilizes the Municipal Agriculture Office to take custody of affected animals and move them to a government animal control facility.

provisions.title: Residents told why, in their own language
provisions.text: After the declaration and before enforcement, the incident commander makes sure residents are told, in a dialect they speak, why they must leave and that there is no other way to keep them safe.

provisions.title: Who can be mobilized
provisions.text: The mayor may mobilize the Bayambang PNP station, the Bureau of Fire Protection, the MSWDO, Rural Health Unit II, the Municipal Health Office, the MDRRMO and the Municipal Agriculture Office.

provisions.title: Reasonable force on those who refuse
provisions.text: Residents who refuse to leave or go back without an order may be moved with reasonable force, with attention to children, women, the elderly and persons with disabilities. Those who defy the order release the mayor from liability, and those who comply go first.

provisions.title: Yearly evacuation training
provisions.text: The MDRRMO runs training and orientation on pre-emptive and forced evacuation at least once a year, in the local dialect, and puts out posters, newsletters and brochures on disaster risk reduction.

provisions.title: Report within 24 hours
provisions.text: Within 24 hours of declaring a pre-emptive or forced evacuation, the mayor reports it to the MDRRMC and the Sangguniang Bayan.

ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR from a scan; the first 2 pages are the provincial board's resolution finding the ordinance within the municipality's powers, and the signature page is partly illegible.

sponsors: SB Member Martin E. Terrado II
details.effect: Upon approval and publication
details.covers: Residents of Bayambang in areas under a declared disaster or emergency
details.enforcers: Municipal Mayor and the LDRRMO as incident commander, with PNP and BFP

highlights.label: to report each evacuation order to the council
orders the mayor issues with a forced evacuation
offices and agencies the mayor may mobilise

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has no written rule on who can order people out of a flood, landslide or storm zone and what happens when they refuse. Bayambang's 4-page ordinance names the incident commander, has the mayor declare forced evacuation, and requires a report within 24 hours. It sets no penalties, and 2 of its clauses, a waiver of the mayor's liability and priority for those who comply, should not be copied.

apply.if: If your LGU has a DRRM officer in place
apply.then: you can replicate this by naming that officer as incident commander, able to start pre-emptive evacuation and to recommend forced evacuation to the mayor.

apply.if: If your DRRM office is still a designated focal person
apply.then: name the position rather than a salary grade, so the rule still works when the post is filled.

apply.if: If you already have evacuation centres and transport assigned
apply.then: list them in the contingency plan the mayor's order points to, so the 6 orders can be issued the same day.

apply.if: If your residents speak more than one language
apply.then: require the warning before enforcement to be given in each of them, as Bayambang requires, and use the yearly training to rehearse it.

apply.if: If families in your LGU keep livestock
apply.then: keep the clause that has the agriculture office move animals to a safe facility, since owners often refuse to leave without them.

change: Re-cite the basis to the national DRRM law (RA 10121) with BLGC s. 17, the DRRM council in BLGC s. 129 and the mandatory DRRM officer in BLGC s. 481, in place of RA 7160 and DILG Memorandum Circular 2015-76

Drop the clause that releases the mayor from liability for anyone who defies the order; an ordinance cannot waive liability set by national law. Drop also the priority for residents who comply, and keep priority for children, women, the elderly and persons with disabilities
State who directs police officers when force is used: control over the police is set by national law, not by the LGU (BLGC s. 33)
If your LGU has had people displaced by armed conflict, cover that hazard too, and link evacuation and return to the council for internally displaced persons (BLGC s. 130) and BAA No. 62
Fund evacuation, transport and the yearly training from the 5% calamity fund in BLGC s. 348

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Enacting the Gender and Development (GAD) Code of the Municipality of Salay, Misamis Oriental
ordinances.shortTitle: Gender and Development Code of Salay
ordinances.summary: Salay's comprehensive gender and development code. It sets the municipality's duties on gender-based violence, women's health, women in governance, work, enterprise, education, justice, environment, disasters, infrastructure and special sectors, and creates a GAD council, office and resource centre. It applies to the municipal and barangay governments and to employers, establishments, schools and media in the municipality.
points: At least 5% of the municipal and barangay budgets go to GAD, and part of the 20% development fund may go to gender-related infrastructure
At least 3% of the municipal health budget goes to women's health care and nutrition
Reports of violence against women and children must be acted on within 24 hours; investigators endorse cases to the prosecutor within 36 hours, and the social welfare office runs a temporary shelter
The police station keeps a women and children's desk with at least 2 women officers

All offices and private establishments must hold an orientation on gender sensitivity and sexual harassment and set up a committee on decorum and investigation (₱1,000 fine for skipping the orientation)
A GAD council chaired by the mayor, with 4 committees, a GAD office and a GAD resource centre; a Women's Congress each March
Bans using women or men as door prizes in fund-raising, contests that degrade women, sex tours, and media that humiliate women, men or children

provisions.title: Support for survivors of violence
provisions.text: Investigators act within 24 hours and endorse cases to the prosecutor within 36 hours; survivors get counselling, legal and medical help, a private examination room, and a temporary shelter run by the social welfare office.

provisions.title: 3% of the health budget for women's health
provisions.text: At least 3% of the municipal health budget goes to women's health care and nutrition; the municipality promotes exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continued breastfeeding for 2 years.

provisions.title: Women in local bodies and the police
provisions.text: Women must sit on all mandatory and special bodies and the development councils, and at least 2 women officers of the Salay PNP staff the women and children's protection desk.

provisions.title: Gender sensitivity orientation for every office
provisions.text: All government offices and private establishments must hold an orientation on gender sensitivity and sexual harassment with the GAD office's help, or pay a ₱1,000 fine, and set up a committee on decorum and investigation.

provisions.title: Women's Month and a yearly Women's Congress
provisions.text: The GAD council leads International Women's Day on March 8 and Women's Month, and a Women's Congress of organised women's groups is held each March.

provisions.title: Act on violence reports within 24 hours
provisions.text: Municipal offices and barangays must act on reports of violence against women and children within 24 hours; failing to is neglect of duty.

provisions.title: Bans on sex tours and degrading events
provisions.text: Soliciting women's services as a gift, sex slavery, sex tours through resorts and lodging houses, using women or men as door prizes in fund-raising, and contests that degrade women, men or children are banned.

provisions.title: A GAD council, office and resource centre
provisions.text: A GAD council chaired by the mayor, with committees on violence, economic empowerment, reproductive health, and education and research, plus a GAD office in the municipal hall and a GAD resource centre.

provisions.title: At least 5% of budgets for GAD
provisions.text: The municipal and barangay governments put at least 5% of their annual budgets into GAD and may use part of the 20% development fund for gender-related infrastructure.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Soliciting and sex slavery are punished under national law; other violations draw 6 months' imprisonment and a fine, and a corporation's officers are liable, with its business permit open to revocation.

ordinances.penalties: General penalty of 6 months in jail and a fine written as ₱2,500 (the words say 2,000); specific offences carry ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, with 15 days, 1 month or 6 months in jail, and permits may be revoked
ordinances.caveat: The mayor's approval date is left blank on this copy, its first lines carry a stray header from Ordinance No. 14-12-2009, and the general penalty's amount differs between words and figures.

details.effect: 10 days after posting in 3 conspicuous places
details.covers: Women and men of Salay, municipal and barangay offices, and private institutions
details.enforcers: Salay GAD Council, chaired by the Mayor, with the GAD Office
creates: Salay GAD Council and its 4 committees

highlights.label: of the annual budget set aside for GAD

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU spends its 5% GAD budget without a code saying what it must cover. Salay's 34-page code runs from violence and health to work, disasters and buildings, and adds concrete rules such as 3% of the health budget for women and a 24-hour response to violence reports. Much of it restates national laws at length, its council and office are larger than a small municipality may need, and its penalty clause has a drafting error.

apply.if: If your LGU already prepares a GAD plan and budget
apply.then: you can replicate this by turning the plan's recurring items into code sections, such as the 3% of the health budget for women and the yearly Women's Congress.

apply.if: If your LGU has a local women's development officer or a women's council
apply.then: give them the GAD council's planning and reporting duties instead of creating a separate GAD office and resource centre.

apply.if: If your police station has a women and children's desk
apply.then: copy the 24-hour response rule and the 36-hour endorsement to the prosecutor, and have the social welfare office keep a list of shelter options.

apply.if: If your LGU has no shelter for women in crisis
apply.then: start with a separate counselling room and a referral agreement with the nearest shelter or hospital, as Salay's list allows.

apply.if: If you want employers to comply
apply.then: tie the gender orientation certificate and the decorum committee to the business permit, as Salay ties them to a ₱1,000 fine.

change: Re-cite the 5% GAD allocation to BLGC s. 348, and add the sanctions in BLGC s. 582 (no GAD plan, accomplishment report or Gender Focal Point System) and s. 584 (GAD budget used outside the plan)

Replace the GAD office and resource centre with the Local Women's Development Officer under BLGC s. 547, whose qualifications follow Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines (BAA No. 8), and make the women's council the one BLGC s. 130 requires
Fix the general penalty: state one amount, keep it within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489), and let the court impose a fine or jail rather than both every time
Add that violence against women and children is never settled before the lupon (BLGC s. 436), and drop the rule on handcuffing women, since police procedure is set by national law (BLGC s. 33)

Expand the short section on Muslims and other cultural communities to cover Moro, Indigenous and settler women, and expect debate on the reproductive health and sexual preference sections; settle them with the ulama and the Women Commission early
barmm.fits: Municipalities that already run a GAD plan and want one code for it, with a social welfare office and a police women's desk.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Providing for a Child Welfare and Protection Code of the Municipality of Nueva Era, Ilocos Norte
ordinances.shortTitle: Child Welfare and Protection Code of Nueva Era
ordinances.summary: Nueva Era's code for children's welfare and protection. It creates a municipal council for children with volunteers in every barangay, school and church, and requires a yearly action plan for children that must be built into the municipality's investment plan. It sets duties on birth registration, immunisation, nutrition, maternal health, early education and school aid, and covers parents, schools, barangays and municipal offices.
points: A Local Council for the Welfare and Protection of Children chaired by the mayor meets at least every quarter and has an executive officer from the permanent staff
The council deputises at least 1 child service volunteer in every barangay, school, church and other entity it names; volunteers must be at least high school graduates
An Annual Action Plan for Children is due each September, and the municipal investment plan cannot go to the development council until the plan is in it
Parents must register a birth within 1 week; the civil registrar holds barangay registration drives twice a year and issues the first copy of each birth certificate free
A Pregnant Women Health Day each month, with the LGU paying laboratory costs and newborn screening
Children aged 3 to 6 must attend a day care or pre-school programme, and the school board keeps an assistance and incentive fund for pupils
Fund drives for children are exempt from permit fees

provisions.title: A children's council chaired by the mayor
provisions.text: The Local Council for the Welfare and Protection of Children is chaired by the mayor and includes municipal department heads, the SK federation and ABC presidents, the chief of police and 4 religious sector representatives. It meets at least once a quarter.

provisions.title: An executive officer from permanent staff
provisions.text: On the council's recommendation the mayor names an executive officer holding a permanent post, who serves as secretary, runs projects and monitors the code.

provisions.title: Child service volunteers everywhere
provisions.text: The council deputizes at least 1 child service volunteer in every barangay, school, commercial establishment, church and other entity it names. Volunteers must be at least high school graduates, report cases and abuse, and may receive benefits the council sets.

provisions.title: An action plan built into the investment plan
provisions.text: By September each year the council adopts an Annual Action Plan for Children. The municipal investment plan cannot go to the development council until the action plan is integrated in it.

provisions.title: A quarterly count of children and pregnant women
provisions.text: The council keeps a quarterly inventory and profile of children and pregnant women, and barangays must pass ordinances requiring every birth and pregnancy to be reported to their volunteer.

provisions.title: Birth registration within 1 week
provisions.text: Parents must register a birth within 1 week, including non-residents who give birth in the municipality. The civil registrar holds barangay registration drives twice a year and issues the first copy of each birth certificate free.

provisions.title: A monthly Pregnant Women Health Day
provisions.text: Once a month the Municipal Health Office gives pregnant women prenatal check-ups, lectures and laboratory services. The LGU gives financial help for laboratory costs and for newborn screening.

provisions.title: Early education from 3 to 6
provisions.text: Parents must enrol children aged 3 to 6 in day care or a pre-school program, preferably the barangay's Child Development Center; volunteers report those not enrolled.

provisions.title: A school assistance and incentive fund
provisions.text: The Municipal School Board budgets a fund that buys supplies and textbooks for indigent pupils and rewards outstanding pupils and school staff. Fund drives for children are exempt from permit fees.

provisions.title: Prohibited acts and a ₱200 fine
provisions.text: Parents who let a child 3 or younger roam a street alone, or any child roam outside naked, are called in for child care orientation. Carrying a child 10 or younger not safely seated in a vehicle is fined ₱200.

ordinances.penalties: ₱200 for carrying a child aged 10 or below unsafely in a vehicle; parents who leave a child of 3 or below alone on the road, or let a child roam naked, are called in for child care orientation
ordinances.caveat: Section numbers skip and repeat (2 sections 3, no 4 or 22), the last page appears 3 times in the copy, and the file ends with the provincial board's resolution of 4 March 2019 declaring it valid.

details.effect: upon review by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and posting
details.covers: Children and pregnant women of Nueva Era, their parents, schools and barangays
details.enforcers: Local Council for the Welfare and Protection of Children, chaired by the Mayor

barmm.why: Worth reading if your children's council exists on paper but has no plan, no data and no one in the barangays. Nueva Era gives the council volunteers in every barangay and school, a September deadline for a yearly plan, and a rule that the investment plan waits until the children's plan is in it. It is mostly duties without a budget figure, and it is built on the Child 21 framework, which ran to 2025.

apply.if: If your LGU has a council for the protection of children
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving it the September deadline for a yearly action plan and the rule that the investment plan must include it.

apply.if: If your barangays have health workers or child development workers
apply.then: deputise them as child service volunteers who report births, pregnancies and unregistered children to the council.

apply.if: If many births in your LGU go unregistered
apply.then: copy the 2 barangay registration drives a year and the free first copy of the birth certificate, and check the fee waiver against your revenue code.

apply.if: If your health office already runs prenatal days
apply.then: fix them as a monthly Pregnant Women Health Day and state where the money for laboratory and newborn screening comes from.

apply.if: If your council has no data on children
apply.then: start with the quarterly inventory of children and pregnant women before adding the computer system the code asks for.

change: Seat the council in the council for the protection of children required by BLGC s. 130, funded from its minimum 1% share in BLGC s. 348, with the social welfare officer (BLGC s. 537) as executive officer

Replace Child 21, which ran from 2000 to 2025, with the current national plan for children, and name the Ministry of Social Services and Development and the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education where the text names DSWD or DepEd offices

Keep the 1-week registration as a target, not a deadline that makes later registration unlawful, and have the civil registrar (BLGC s. 533) run the barangay drives; if you waive the fee for the first copy, amend the revenue code to match

Add the Madaris superintendent and madrasah schools to the school fund and early education sections, as the local school board includes them (BLGC s. 110), and name the religious sector seats to fit your LGU's faiths
Post the ₱200 penalty as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571, translated into the local languages

ordinances.category: Senior citizens and persons with disability
ordinances.title: An Ordinance Creating the Persons with Disability Affairs Office (PDAO) in the Municipality of Bayambang, and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Persons with Disability Affairs Office Ordinance of Bayambang
ordinances.summary: Creates Bayambang's Persons with Disability Affairs Office (PDAO) under the mayor's office, as RA 10070 requires. Until a later ordinance sets its staff and budget, the municipal social welfare officer serves as focal person. It lists the office's duties, gives barangays the job of listing persons with disabilities, and sets how the yearly budget is worked out.
points: The PDAO sits under the Office of the Mayor, preferably within the municipal hall compound
Until the Sangguniang Bayan passes a staffing ordinance, the mayor designates the social welfare officer as PDAO focal person
Qualified persons with disabilities get priority for the post of PDAO head or focal person
The office plans and runs disability programmes, represents persons with disabilities in local councils, keeps data, monitors fund-raising for them and seeks donations
Barangay councils, through health workers and social welfare volunteers, list and profile all persons with disabilities, keep the list updated and release barangay funds due to them
Private groups helping a disability association must coordinate with the PDAO

The social welfare office drafts the first year's budget; later the PDAO proposes its own, weighed against the municipality's income, the number of persons with disabilities and the size of the programmes

provisions.title: A PDAO under the Mayor's office
provisions.text: Creates the Persons with Disability Affairs Office (PDAO) under the Office of the Municipal Mayor, as RA 10070 requires.

provisions.title: The social welfare officer stands in for now
provisions.text: A later ordinance will set the office's structure, staffing and yearly budget. Until then, the Mayor designates the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Officer as PDAO focal person.

provisions.title: Persons with disabilities get priority for the post
provisions.text: Qualified persons with disabilities get priority in appointment as PDAO head or focal person, subject to Civil Service Commission qualifications; the personnel-services cap is waived to fund the first year of the new post.

provisions.title: Duties of the head and the focal person
provisions.text: The head runs the office, develops and monitors disability programs, secures representation in local councils, builds NGO capacity, networks for resources and submits a yearly work and financial plan; the focal person carries out the same work and reports to the Mayor.

provisions.title: What the office does
provisions.text: Plans and runs programs with the National Council on Disability Affairs, enforces the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons and the Accessibility Law locally, represents persons with disabilities in local councils, compiles data with the barangays and publicises programs, training and jobs.

provisions.title: Fund-raising and donations
provisions.text: The office makes sure programs are funded nationally and locally, monitors fund-raising done for persons with disabilities, and seeks cash or in-kind donations from local and foreign donors for its approved work plan.

provisions.title: Barangays list every person with disability
provisions.text: Barangay councils, through health workers and social welfare volunteers, list, profile and regularly update all persons with disabilities, release barangay funds due to them under DSWD AO 13 of 2008, and help them access their legal benefits.

provisions.title: Private groups coordinate with the PDAO
provisions.text: NGOs, businesses, institutions and individuals are encouraged to support the PDAO, and any that help a disability association or its members must coordinate with the PDAO first.

provisions.title: How the budget is set
provisions.text: The social welfare office drafts the first year's budget; after that the PDAO proposes its own. The Sangguniang Bayan weighs the municipality's income, the number of persons with disabilities against the population, and the size of the programs.

ordinances.caveat: The scan's text layer is garbled in places, and some words are cut off at the page edges (the office location and enactment date were read from the page image); the staffing pattern is left to a later ordinance.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has not yet set up the disability affairs office that national law and the BLGC require. Bayambang's 5-page ordinance creates the office now and staffs it later, with the social welfare officer as focal person in the meantime, which suits an LGU that cannot fund new posts this year. It sets no budget figure, and its list of duties is copied from RA 10070 with little local detail.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot fund new positions this year
apply.then: you can replicate this by creating the office now and designating the social welfare officer as focal person until a staffing ordinance passes.

apply.if: If your LGU is 1st to 3rd class
apply.then: plan for a PDAO head in the staffing ordinance rather than a permanent focal person, and give qualified persons with disabilities priority as Bayambang does.

apply.if: If your barangays keep a registry of residents
apply.then: have them list and profile persons with disabilities through that registry and their health workers, and send the list to the office.

apply.if: If you want the budget to grow with need
apply.then: copy the 3 factors the council must weigh each year: income, the number of persons with disabilities and the size of the programmes.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 480 and s. 481, which make the PDAO officer mandatory for municipalities and let 4th to 6th class municipalities name a focal person, alongside RA 10070 (national law)
Fund programmes from the 1% for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 348, and link the office to the council for persons with disabilities in BLGC s. 130
Replace the waiver of RA 7160 s. 325 and s. 331 with a staffing plan under BLGC s. 87 that fits the personal services cap in BLGC s. 349

Name the Ministry of Social Services and Development where the text cites DSWD Administrative Order No. 13, and have barangays use the registry in BLGC s. 410 for the list of persons with disabilities

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Enacting the Health and Sanitation Code of Nueva Era, Ilocos Norte
ordinances.shortTitle: Health and Sanitation Code of Nueva Era
ordinances.summary: Nueva Era's general sanitation code, enforced by the municipal health officer. It sets rules for buildings, toilets, water supply, food establishments, markets and slaughter, barber shops, animal pens, places of assembly, and burials and funeral parlours, with sanitary permits and health certificates. It covers every household, business, vendor and transport operator in the municipality.
points: Every house must have a sanitary toilet approved by the health officer; places of assembly need at least 1 seat for every 50 women and 1 seat and 1 urinal for every 50 men
No washing or bathing within 15 metres of a drinking water source, no drinking well within 15 metres of a latrine, and public wells tested at least every 3 months
Food and other listed businesses need a yearly sanitary permit, renewed within the first 15 days of the year; workers need a health certificate every 6 months for ₱75
Restaurants must meet Grade A or B within 3 months; failing ones are suspended for up to 30 days, then closed
Burial grounds must be at least 25 metres from homes and 50 metres from rivers and water sources; remains of a dangerous communicable disease are buried within 12 hours
Pigpens and poultry houses in urban barangays must be 10 metres from any home, and commercial pigpens 20 metres
Sidewalk vendors need a ₱20 ID card renewed each year with a ₱10 sticker, and only portable containers

provisions.title: The health officer enforces it and may inspect
provisions.text: The municipal health officer enforces the code. No one may block the officer from entering and inspecting any house, building, vehicle or premises, or tear down a placard the officer posts.

provisions.title: Sidewalk vendors need a ₱20 ID
provisions.text: Vendors register with the Treasurer and wear a ₱20 ID, renewed each year by the last working day of February with a ₱10 sticker and reissued every 3 years. They may use only portable containers; fixed stalls must come down within 15 days. Food vendors also need a ₱20 health certificate.

provisions.title: A sanitary toilet in every house
provisions.text: Every dwelling needs a toilet of a type the health officer approves. Places of assembly and workplaces need separate facilities, at least 1 seat for every 50 women and 1 seat and 1 urinal for every 50 men; toilet rooms are at least 1.5 sq. m and 2.5 m high.

provisions.title: Safe water sources
provisions.text: New public water sources and wells need a sanitary permit and a lab test first. Washing or bathing within 15 m of a drinking water source is banned, no drinking well may be sunk within 15 m of a latrine, and public wells are tested at least every 3 months.

provisions.title: Yearly sanitary permits
provisions.text: Hotels, food businesses, stores, salons, funeral parlors, transport firms and other listed establishments need a sanitary permit every year, renewed within the first 15 days of the year. Ignoring the health officer's sanitary orders can mean revocation or closure.

provisions.title: Health certificates every 6 months
provisions.text: Owners, food handlers, vendors, drivers, conductors and employees of permitted establishments need a health certificate every 6 months at ₱75. Hospitality workers must be over 18, pass a ₱175 medical exam and pay a ₱100 yearly occupational licence.

provisions.title: Restaurants graded A or B
provisions.text: Food establishments display their grade. Within 3 months only Grade A or B restaurants may operate; one that fails is suspended for up to 30 days and closed permanently if it does not correct the defect within 30 days.

provisions.title: Market and slaughter rules
provisions.text: All animals for public consumption are slaughtered at the local abattoir after inspection, at least 2 hours before sale. Fresh meat, fish and milk are sold only in the public market, and selling spoiled or 'double dead' meat is banned.

provisions.title: Animal pens kept away from homes
provisions.text: Stables may not be built within 2 km of residential or commercial areas or 50 m of a dwelling. In urban barangays, pigpens and poultry houses must be 10 m from homes and streets, and breeding or commercial pigpens 20 m, and away from waterways.

provisions.title: Burials and penalties
provisions.text: Burial grounds must be 25 m from homes and 50 m from rivers and water sources; graves at least 1.5 m deep; victims of a dangerous communicable disease buried within 12 hours. Violations carry up to 6 months in jail, a fine up to ₱2,500, or both.

ordinances.penalties: Up to 6 months in jail or a fine of up to ₱2,500, or both, for any violation or for obstructing the health officer; permits may be suspended or revoked and restaurants closed
ordinances.caveat: Much of the text is copied from the Ilocos Norte provincial code and the national Sanitation Code (the vendor chapter still names the province and the governor), the autopsy section breaks off mid-list, and the file ends with the provincial board's review papers.

details.effect: After all procedures under the Local Government Code are met
details.covers: Food, lodging, market, water, waste and burial sanitation in Nueva Era
details.enforcers: Municipal Health Officer, with the Municipal Treasurer

highlights.label: no-washing zone around every drinking water source
months between tests of each public well, at most
health certificate for food workers, every 6 months
longest suspension before a restaurant is closed

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU enforces sanitation only through the national Sanitation Code and has no local rules or fees for it. Nueva Era's code gives the health officer clear distances, testing intervals, permits and a grading system for eateries in one place. It is long and partly copied from a provincial code, some chapters assume businesses a small municipality may not have, and a few rules, such as a dress code for drivers, do not belong in a health code.

apply.if: If your LGU has a health officer and a sanitary inspector
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the toilet, water and food establishment chapters first, with the yearly sanitary permit and the 6-month health certificate.

apply.if: If your households rely on wells or springs
apply.then: copy the 15-metre rules around water sources and latrines and the 3-month testing of public wells, and budget for the tests.

apply.if: If your municipality has eateries but no grading system
apply.then: copy the Grade A and B standards and the 30-day suspension, and give owners the 3 months Nueva Era gave to comply.

apply.if: If your LGU has no night clubs, cabarets or funeral parlours
apply.then: skip those chapters rather than regulate businesses you do not permit.

apply.if: If you already have a revenue code that sets health fees
apply.then: point to it instead of copying the ₱75, ₱20 and ₱10 figures here.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 and s. 480, and name the health officer under BLGC s. 532 as enforcer; the national Sanitation Code (PD 856) stays as national law, and the Ministry of Health replaces the Department of Health for funeral permits and early disinterment
The permit, certificate and ID fees are revenue measures, so pass them with a public hearing and publication (BLGC s. 212 and s. 213) or move them into your revenue code
Rewrite the slaughter rules for halal slaughter under BLGC s. 480 and s. 543, and make the burial rules allow burial on the day of death without embalming, as Islamic practice requires

Drop the gynaecological examination for hospitality workers, the dress code for drivers and the vendor ID signed by the governor; keep the penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489) and post it under BLGC s. 571
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a health officer, a sanitary inspector and a public market or eateries to inspect.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Requiring All Households in the Municipality of Maribojoc, Bohol to Comply with the Zero Open Defecation (ZOD) Policy, Providing Guidelines for Its Implementation, Prescribing Penalties for Violations, and Appropriating Funds Therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Zero Open Defecation Ordinance of Maribojoc
ordinances.summary: Requires every household in Maribojoc to have a sanitary toilet and bans open defecation and dumping human waste in open spaces or waterways. The municipality gives a free toilet bowl to households that dig their own septic pit, with purok leaders and barangay health workers listing homes without toilets and the sanitary inspector checking the work. Fines are shared equally between the municipality and the barangay where the violation happened.
points: Bans defecating in the open, leaving human waste outside toilets, and dumping it in rivers, creeks, drains or canals
Every household must have a sanitary toilet
The municipality gives a free toilet bowl; the household digs the septic pit, builds the toilet and buys other materials
Purok leaders and barangay health workers keep a master list of households without toilets; the sanitary inspector checks the pit before the bowl is given and the installation a few days after
The health office and sanitary inspector run information campaigns on typhoid, cholera and hepatitis A
Complaints go to the barangay council and then to the police station
50% of fines collected go to the barangay where the violation happened, released by the treasurer on the punong barangay's written request

provisions.title: Applies to everyone in the municipality
provisions.text: The Zero Open Defecation Compliance Ordinance applies to all persons, residents or not, within Maribojoc.

provisions.title: No open defecation or dumping of waste
provisions.text: It bans defecating in open places, disposing of human waste, including tissue and paper, outside toilets or in any open space, and dumping it in rivers, creeks, drains or canals.

provisions.title: Every household needs a sanitary toilet
provisions.text: Every household in the municipality must have a sanitary toilet at home to dispose of human waste properly and stop the spread of disease.

provisions.title: A free toilet bowl, the household builds the rest
provisions.text: The municipality gives a free toilet bowl. In return the household owner digs the septic tank pit, builds the toilet and supplies any other materials needed.

provisions.title: A master list of homes without toilets
provisions.text: Purok leaders and barangay health workers inspect and monitor households and keep a master list of those without sanitary toilets.

provisions.title: Information campaigns on water-borne disease
provisions.text: The Municipal Health Office and the Municipal Sanitary Inspector run information campaigns in the barangays on typhoid fever, cholera and hepatitis A caused by open defecation.

provisions.title: Two inspections per toilet bowl
provisions.text: The sanitary inspector checks that the septic pit is properly dug before the bowl is given, then returns a few days later to confirm the toilet is installed.

provisions.title: Complaints through the barangay to the police
provisions.text: On proof of a violation, a complaint goes to the barangay council and is forwarded to the municipal police station for investigation.

provisions.title: ₱200, ₱500, then ₱1,000
provisions.text: Anyone caught defecating outside a toilet is fined ₱200 for a 1st offense, ₱500 for a 2nd and ₱1,000 for a 3rd.

provisions.title: Half of each fine to the barangay
provisions.text: 50% of fines for violations in a barangay goes to that barangay and 50% to the municipality. The treasurer reports collections every 6 months and releases the share on the punong barangay's written request.

ordinances.penalties: ₱200, ₱500, then ₱1,000 for defecating outside a toilet
ordinances.caveat: The copy is the Sanggunian secretary's certified excerpt of the minutes and does not show the mayor's approval.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: All households and persons in Maribojoc, resident or not
details.enforcers: Municipal Health Office and Sanitary Inspector, with purok leaders, BHWs, barangays, police

highlights.label: toilet bowl for each household that digs its own pit
of fines go to the barangay where it happened
first-offence fine, rising to ₱1,000
sanitary inspections, before and after the bowl

barmm.why: Worth reading if some of your households still have no toilet and you want a simple rule plus help to build one. Maribojoc pairs a ban on open defecation with a free toilet bowl, a barangay master list and 2 inspections, and lets barangays keep half of each fine. It is 3 pages and recent, but it sets no deadline for households to comply and its funding clause is not spelled out.

apply.if: If your LGU has a sanitary inspector
apply.then: you can replicate this by having that inspector check each septic pit before the bowl is handed over and the installation a few days after.

apply.if: If your barangays have health workers and purok leaders
apply.then: have them keep the master list of households without toilets, and use it to plan how many bowls to buy each year.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot fund toilet bowls this year
apply.then: start with the master list and the information campaign, and add the free bowls once a budget line is set.

apply.if: If households in your area live over water or on flood-prone land
apply.then: say which toilet and pit types the health officer accepts there before copying the dig-your-own-pit rule.

apply.if: If you want barangays to keep 50% of fines
apply.then: write the release steps into the ordinance as Maribojoc did, and check them with your treasurer and auditor first.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 (sanitation and health) and s. 480, with the health officer in BLGC s. 532 leading enforcement; name the Ministry of Health's sanitation programme where the text cites DOH orders
Post and publish it as a penal ordinance under BLGC s. 571 before it takes effect, rather than 'upon approval', translated into the local languages
Add a compliance deadline and the budget line for the toilet bowls, which the title promises but the text does not give
Route complaints to the sanitary inspector and the barangay first, and reserve the police for refusals
barmm.fits: Municipalities with households still lacking toilets, a sanitary inspector, and barangay health workers to keep the list.
