ordinances.title: An Ordinance Requiring All Pregnant Women to Have Deliveries/Childbirth Attended by Skilled Health Professional or Trained Barangay Health Worker (BHW) and Penalizing Violations Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Skilled Birth Attendance Ordinance of Bayog
ordinances.summary: Requires every woman who gives birth in Bayog to be attended by a skilled health professional or a trained barangay health worker. Its aim is to cut maternal and newborn deaths and to increase births in health facilities. It penalises the mother, and on a 3rd offence withholds registration of the newborn.
points: Covers any pregnant woman who gives birth within the municipality
Aims to reduce maternal and newborn deaths, raise births attended by skilled professionals and increase facility-based deliveries
1st offence: reprimand for both the mother and the untrained birth attendant
2nd offence: a fine of up to ₱500
3rd offence: a fine of ₱500 to ₱1,000 and non-registration of the newborn

provisions.title: Covers every birth in the municipality
provisions.text: The ordinance applies to any pregnant woman who gives birth within the municipality of Bayog, Zamboanga del Sur.

provisions.title: Births must be attended by a skilled attendant
provisions.text: Every delivery must be attended by a skilled health professional or a trained barangay health worker (BHW); delivering without one is the offence the ordinance penalises.

provisions.title: Aims: fewer deaths, more facility births
provisions.text: It aims to cut maternal and newborn deaths and illness caused by poorly trained birth attendants, raise the share of births attended by skilled professionals, and increase deliveries in health facilities.

provisions.title: First offence: a reprimand for mother and attendant
provisions.text: On a 1st offence, both the mother and the untrained birth attendant are reprimanded.

provisions.title: Second offence: a fine of up to ₱500
provisions.text: On a 2nd offence, the mother is fined not more than ₱500.

provisions.title: Third offence: a fine and no birth registration
provisions.text: On a 3rd offence, the fine is ₱500 to ₱1,000, and the newborn child is not registered.

provisions.title: Takes effect after 3 weeks of publication
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect after 3 consecutive weeks of publication in a newspaper of general circulation in Zamboanga del Sur.

ordinances.penalties: Reprimand, then up to ₱500, then ₱500 to ₱1,000 and non-registration of the newborn
ordinances.caveat: It is a 1-page ordinance with no implementing rules, no health services or funding, and a penalty that falls on the mother and her child.

details.effect: after 3 weeks of publication in a provincial newspaper
details.covers: Pregnant women giving birth in Bayog, and their birth attendants

highlights.label: offences, from a reprimand to a fine
top fine for a birth without a skilled attendant
services or funds the municipality commits in return

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if births at home without a skilled attendant are common in your LGU and you are weighing an ordinance on it. Bayog's goal of facility-based delivery is sound, but it punishes the mother and threatens to leave the newborn unregistered, which harms the child and conflicts with the child's right to registration. A workable version pairs the rule with free delivery, transport and a list of who counts as a skilled attendant.

apply.if: If your LGU has a birthing facility or a rural health unit that handles deliveries
apply.then: you can take the idea by requiring facility delivery and backing it with free or PhilHealth-covered delivery and transport for women in far barangays.

apply.if: If your barangays still rely on traditional birth attendants
apply.then: give them a role in referring and accompanying women to the facility instead of fining them, and train barangay health workers to track pregnancies.

apply.if: If your LGU has no facility within reach of some barangays
apply.then: start with prenatal visits, a birth plan for each pregnant woman and an emergency transport arrangement before any penalty.

apply.if: If you want a penalty at all
apply.then: keep it light and never tie it to registering the child or to the mother's access to services.

change: Drop non-registration of the newborn: birth registration is the child's right under national law, and the civil registrar must accept registrable documents (BLGC s. 533)

Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 and the health officer's duties in BLGC s. 532, and define skilled attendants as national health policy does: doctors, nurses and midwives. A trained barangay health worker is not one

Add the services the LGU will provide, such as facility delivery, transport and prenatal care through the barangay health station (BLGC s. 408), and name the Ministry of Health's maternal health programme as partner
Let women choose a female skilled attendant where one is available, and replace the 3-week newspaper publication with posting and translation under BLGC s. 571
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a birthing facility or rural health unit and barangay health workers who can track pregnancies.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Prohibiting the Entry and Occupation of Forest Lands within Municipality of Carrascal, Surigao del Sur and Imposing Appropriate Penalties for Violations Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Forest Land Occupation Ban of Carrascal
ordinances.summary: Bans entry into and occupation of forest land in Carrascal without a lease or permit from the DENR, aimed at the informal settlers along the national road in Barangays Adlay and Bon-ot. It makes the municipal environment officer inspect the area with barangay officials, the CENRO and the police, and sets fines for violators.
points: Written for the forest land along the national road in Barangays Adlay and Bon-ot, where the CENRO counted at least 32 families selling gasoline and other goods
An illegal occupant is anyone who enters and occupies forest land without a DENR lease or permit
The MENRO inspects and monitors the area periodically with barangay officials, asks help from CENRO Cantilan and the PNP, and puts up 'DO NOT ENTER' signs
Mining companies must keep the trucks and equipment of their own and their haulers in motor pools or parking areas inside their MPSA, not on forest land along the road
Applies also to structures and establishments put up before the ordinance was approved
The municipality must appropriate funds to carry it out

provisions.title: Written for the roadside settlements
provisions.text: The council acted on informal settlers along the national road in Barangays Adlay and Bon-ot, where the CENRO counted at least 32 families selling gasoline and other goods.

provisions.title: Who counts as an illegal occupant
provisions.text: Anyone who enters and occupies forest land without a lease or permit from the DENR is an illegal occupant. Forest land covers the public forest, permanent forests or forest reserves, and forest reservations.

provisions.title: Aims: trees, waste and the roadside view
provisions.text: The ban is meant to stop the cutting of trees and other vegetation, keep the area from being polluted by settlers with no proper waste disposal, and keep the roadside green.

provisions.title: The MENRO inspects and posts signs
provisions.text: The MENRO inspects and monitors forest land periodically, especially along the national road in Bon-ot and Adlay, with barangay officials and help from CENRO Cantilan and the PNP, and puts up 'DO NOT ENTER' signs.

provisions.title: Mining trucks off the roadside
provisions.text: Mining companies must keep their own trucks and equipment, and those of their hauling contractors, in motor pools or parking areas inside their MPSA, not on forest land along the national road.

provisions.title: Fines from ₱1,000 to ₱2,500
provisions.text: A first offence brings a reprimand and a ₱1,000 fine, a second ₱2,000 and a third ₱2,500.

provisions.title: Covers structures already standing
provisions.text: The ordinance also applies to structures and establishments put up before it was approved, and the municipality must appropriate funds to carry it out.

provisions.title: Takes effect 10 days after posting
provisions.text: It takes effect 10 days after copies are posted at the entrance of the municipal hall and in at least 2 other conspicuous places.

ordinances.penalties: Reprimand and ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱2,000 for a 2nd and ₱2,500 for a 3rd; no jail term
ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances (general clause only)
ordinances.caveat: The scanned pages are out of order, one footer calls it 'Series of 2023', and the ordinance never states the prohibited act in a section of its own; the ban appears only in the title.

details.effect: 10 days after posting
details.covers: Forest lands in Carrascal, especially along the national road in Adlay and Bon-ot
details.enforcers: MENRO, with barangay officials, CENRO Cantilan and the PNP
details.funding: Municipal appropriation

highlights.label: families found living on the roadside forest land
fine and a reprimand for a first offence
fine for a third offence, the most it imposes
clauses on relocating the families who live there

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if families or roadside stalls have settled on forest land in your LGU and no office is clearly in charge of watching it. Carrascal gives the job to its environment officer, with the barangays, the forest office and the police, and tells mining firms to park their trucks inside their own permit areas. It is 4 pages and thin: it never spells out the prohibited act, does not say who pays the fine, and has no plan for the 32 families already there.

apply.if: If your LGU has an environment and natural resources officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by making regular inspection of named forest areas part of that officer's job, with the punong barangays and the MENRE field office, and by posting signs at the entry points.

apply.if: If families already live or trade on the forest land
apply.then: don't start with fines; list the households, plan relocation and livelihood help with your social welfare office, and set a date after which new entry is fined.

apply.if: If mining or quarrying firms haul through your LGU
apply.then: copy the rule that their trucks and equipment, and their contractors', must be parked inside their own permit areas and not on forest land.

apply.if: If you write your own version
apply.then: add what Carrascal left out: a section that names the prohibited acts, a map of the covered area, who is liable, and a written warning before the first fine.

change: Re-cite the basis from RA 7160 s. 447 to BLGC s. 489 and the general welfare clause in BLGC s. 17, and replace the DENR and CENRO Cantilan with the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and its field office (BAA No. 13)
Name the environment and natural resources officer under BLGC s. 538 as the lead office, since that post is mandatory for every municipality
Add relocation and mitigation for occupants before anyone is removed; BLGC s. 32 says occupants may not be displaced without them
Add a section stating the prohibited acts and who is liable, and fix the applicability clause (Section 9) and the double effectivity heading
Replace the 10-day effectivity with the posting and publication rule for penal ordinances in BLGC s. 571; the fines already fit the ₱5,000 cap in BLGC s. 489
barmm.fits: Municipalities with forest land along a road or near settlements and an environment officer who can inspect it.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Governing the Development, Management and Utilization of the Co-Managed Forests and Forestland of the Municipality of Opol, Misamis Oriental
ordinances.shortTitle: Co-Managed Forestland Ordinance of Opol
ordinances.summary: Governs the 15,362 hectares of forest and forestland that Opol manages jointly with DENR Region 10 under a co-management agreement and its forest land use plan. It gives occupants and investors tenure through 25-year management sub-agreements issued by a multi-sectoral council chaired by the mayor, sets fees that go to a special account, and lists the grounds for cancelling a sub-agreement.
points: No one may use, occupy or build in the co-management area without a management sub-agreement from the LGU
Open areas are grassland, bushland and cultivated land in production forest under 50% slope; strict protection zones and stands of natural forest cannot be converted
A family may hold only 1 sub-agreement of up to 5 hectares; cooperatives and corporations may hold more if they show financial and technical capacity
Filing fee of ₱1,000 per hectare; yearly user's fee of ₱1,000 per hectare for occupants, ₱5,000 for investors in agroforestry and ₱2,000 for monoculture plantations
Claims are mapped by sitio, verified with GPS and signed by the sitio leader and punong barangay; the council approves within 15 working days and certificates go out within 5
Sub-agreements run 25 years, are issued to both spouses, and cannot be sold or transferred without the council's approval
No sub-agreement over ancestral domain without the free and prior informed consent of the indigenous community

provisions.title: No use of the forest without a sub-agreement
provisions.text: No one may use, occupy or build anything in the Co-Management Area without a management sub-agreement from the LGU. Tenure is secured by recognizing individual property rights (IPR) or issuing sub-agreements.

provisions.title: Which areas are open
provisions.text: Grassland, bushland and cultivated land under 50% slope in production forest, plus multiple-use and sustainable use zones. Strict protection zones, stands of natural forest and titled land are excluded, and applications may be refused in the public interest.

provisions.title: Consent of indigenous communities
provisions.text: No sub-agreement may cover any part of an ancestral domain without first securing the free and prior informed consent of the affected indigenous community.

provisions.title: Up to 5 hectares a family
provisions.text: An individual or family may hold only 1 sub-agreement of up to 5 hectares. Cooperatives and corporations may hold more if they show financial and technical capacity, with the aggregate set by the council. Holders over the limit have 5 years to transfer the excess.

provisions.title: Who may apply and who may not
provisions.text: Filipino occupants in or next to the area get priority, then accredited cooperatives and corporations. Those with cancelled forestry permits, illegal logging or anti-dummy records, or existing forest tenure are disqualified.

provisions.title: Filing and user's fees
provisions.text: ₱1,000 per hectare to file. A yearly user's fee of ₱1,000 per hectare for occupants, starting a year after issue; investors pay ₱5,000 per hectare for agroforestry and ₱2,000 for monoculture plantations. All fees go to a co-management special account.

provisions.title: Mapping, approval in 15 days, certificates in 5
provisions.text: Claims are mapped by sitio, verified with GPS and signed by the sitio leader and punong barangay; applicants attend an orientation and draw up a farm plan. The council approves within 15 working days and certificates go out within 5.

provisions.title: A council and a project management unit
provisions.text: A multi-sectoral council (MENRC) chaired by the Mayor governs the area, with MENRO as secretariat. A Project Management Unit, appointed by the Mayor on the council's recommendation, handles applications, compliance and a public register of available areas.

provisions.title: 25-year sub-agreements in both spouses' names
provisions.text: Sub-agreements run 25 years or until the co-management agreement ends, are issued to both spouses if married, and cannot be sold, leased or transferred without the council's approval. Holders get priority for LGU incentives and help.

provisions.title: Grounds for cancellation
provisions.text: Not developing the area within 1 year, being a dummy, unapproved transfer or land-use change, cutting natural trees, abandonment for 1 year, unpaid fees, 3 years of unpaid real property tax, destructive farming, wildlife hunting, or inorganic pesticides.

ordinances.penalties: No fines; the council may cancel a sub-agreement on 19 listed grounds, such as 1 year of non-development or abandonment, cutting natural trees, illegal transfer, unpaid fees or 3 years of unpaid real property tax
ordinances.amends: Repeals inconsistent ordinances and issuances; holders of more than the new 5-hectare limit under earlier policies get 5 years to transfer the excess
ordinances.caveat: OCR copy; in places the text says 'Intellectual Property Rights' where it means individual property rights, item 8.1 and ground 13.19 are missing, and the application forms and the co-management agreement are not attached.

details.effect: 15 days after approval
details.covers: Opol's co-managed forests and forestland and the farmers who hold rights there
details.enforcers: Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Council and its Project Management Unit
creates: Project Management Unit for the Co-Management Area
details.funding: General fund and the co-management trust fund, plus donors

highlights.label: hectares of forestland co-managed with the DENR
most that 1 family may hold
term of each management sub-agreement
yearly fee per hectare for agroforestry investors

barmm.why: Worth reading if people already farm or live on forestland in your LGU and you want to give them tenure in exchange for protecting it. Opol sets the whole process: mapping claims by sitio, limits per family, 25-year agreements, fees kept in a special account, and clear grounds for cancellation. It only works on top of a forest land use plan and a co-management agreement with the regional environment office, which most LGUs will have to negotiate first.

apply.if: If your LGU has an approved forest land use plan and a co-management agreement with MENRE
apply.then: you can replicate this by creating a council chaired by the mayor to issue 25-year sub-agreements, with the environment officer as its secretariat and a small project unit to process claims.

apply.if: If you have no forest land use plan or co-management agreement yet
apply.then: start with those, and in the meantime map the claims and list the occupants by sitio as Opol's Section 9 describes, so the census is ready.

apply.if: If part of your forestland lies within an ancestral domain
apply.then: keep Opol's rule that no sub-agreement covers it without the community's free and prior informed consent, and run that consent through MIPA.

apply.if: If you want the program to pay for itself
apply.then: copy the per-hectare filing and user's fees, lower for resident families than for investors, and keep them in a special account for forest work.

apply.if: If some families already hold large areas under older arrangements
apply.then: copy the 5-hectare cap with Opol's 5-year period to transfer the excess.

change: Re-cite the basis from RA 7160 s. 17 and DAO 92-30 to BLGC s. 480 (communal forests of up to 50 square kilometres) and s. 538, and make the co-management agreement and forest land use plan approval with the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy instead of DENR Region 10 (BAA No. 13); confirm MENRE's current rules on LGU co-management first
Run free and prior informed consent under BAA No. 64 through the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs instead of the NCIP
Hold public hearings before setting the filing and user's fees, and keep them in a special fund under BLGC s. 333
Before cancelling a family's sub-agreement, provide for relocation and mitigation where they live on the land (BLGC s. 32)
Fix the drafting: 'Individual Property Rights' throughout, the missing item 8.1 and ground 13.19, and a clear definition of the ban on inorganic inputs before using it as a ground for cancellation
barmm.fits: Upland municipalities with a large area of occupied forestland, an environment officer, and a forest land use plan or the means to make one.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Regulating the Keeping of Dogs and Other Animals and Prohibiting Animals from Causing Harm, Injury, or Disturbance to People, Other Animals, or Residents within the Municipality of Maribojoc, Bohol
ordinances.shortTitle: Responsible Animal Ownership and Control Ordinance of Maribojoc
ordinances.summary: Makes owners responsible for dogs, cats, livestock and poultry in Maribojoc: they must confine, register and vaccinate them and pay for any harm they cause. It sets separate fines for pets and for livestock, lets the municipal agriculture office impound stray animals, and shares the fines with the barangay where the violation happened.
points: Bans letting animals roam in public places or on others' land, letting them attack or chase people, failing to vaccinate dogs against rabies, and abandoning or maltreating animals
Owners must register dogs with the Municipal Agriculture or Veterinary Office, clean up animal waste and report bites at once
Pets: ₱500 and a responsible ownership seminar, then ₱1,000, then ₱2,500 and/or impounding
Livestock and poultry: ₱1,000 and a written warning, then ₱2,000, then ₱2,500 and/or impounding
₱1,000 more when someone is hurt or killed, crops or property are damaged, a road is blocked or an accident results, or it is a repeat within the year
Unclaimed impounded animals may be adopted, transferred or humanely disposed of after 3 days
Fines split 60% to the municipality and 40% to the barangay, remitted every 6 months within 15 working days, for animal control and barangay livestock aides

provisions.title: What owners may not let their animals do
provisions.text: It is unlawful to let any animal roam in public places or on others' land, attack, bite or chase people or animals, or go unconfined; to leave dogs unvaccinated against rabies; to abandon or maltreat animals; to refuse to pay for harm they cause; or to keep them in a way that endangers health or peace.

provisions.title: Duties of every animal owner
provisions.text: Owners must give animals food, water, shelter and humane care, keep them confined or restrained, register dogs with the Municipal Agriculture or Veterinary Office, vaccinate them on time, report bites at once and clean up animal waste, especially in public places.

provisions.title: Fines for pets
provisions.text: For dogs, cats and similar pets: ₱500 and a Responsible Animal Ownership Seminar for a 1st offence, ₱1,000 for a 2nd, and ₱2,500 and/or impounding for a 3rd and later offences.

provisions.title: Higher fines for livestock and poultry
provisions.text: For pigs, goats, cattle, carabaos, horses, poultry and the like: ₱1,000 and a written warning, then ₱2,000, then ₱2,500 and/or impounding, because they pose greater risk to traffic, sanitation and property.

provisions.title: ₱1,000 more when there is harm
provisions.text: An extra ₱1,000 applies when a person or animal is hurt or killed, crops, fences or property are damaged, a road is blocked or a vehicle accident results, or the violation repeats within the calendar year. Owners also pay medical, veterinary and repair costs.

provisions.title: Impounding strays
provisions.text: The Municipal Agriculture Office captures stray or uncontrolled animals. Owners reclaim them by paying the fine, impounding and daily upkeep fees and meeting registration and vaccination rules; animals unclaimed after 3 days may be adopted, transferred or humanely disposed of.

provisions.title: 60% to the municipality, 40% to the barangay
provisions.text: Fines split 60% to the General Fund and 40% to the barangay where the violation happened, for animal control, Barangay Livestock Aides, information drives and supplies. The barangay share is remitted every 6 months within 15 working days after each semester, with a statement of collections.

provisions.title: Who enforces it
provisions.text: The Municipal Agriculture Office enforces it with barangays, the health office, the police and Barangay Livestock Aides, who monitor and respond in their barangays; tanods help apprehend. The office also runs regular seminars on responsible ownership and rabies prevention.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 to ₱2,500 for pets and ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 for livestock, plus ₱1,000 for aggravating circumstances, impounding, and liability for medical, veterinary and repair costs
ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, executive orders and rules (general clause only)
ordinances.caveat: OCR copy; the mayor's approval block on the last page is blank, and the impounding and daily maintenance fees are left for the agriculture office to set, so no amounts appear.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Owners and keepers of dogs, pets, livestock and poultry in Maribojoc
details.enforcers: Municipal Agriculture Office, with barangays, MHO, PNP and Barangay Livestock Aides
details.funding: Municipal annual budget, under the concerned offices

highlights.label: of fines go to the barangay where it happened
first fine for a pet, with a seminar for the owner
added when someone is hurt or crops are damaged

barmm.why: Worth reading if roaming goats, cattle, dogs or poultry cause bites, crop damage or road accidents in your LGU and there is no clear rule on who pays. Maribojoc's 2026 ordinance is short, separates pets from livestock, makes owners pay for the harm, and gives barangays a 40% share of fines to fund their own animal control. It leaves the impounding fees to the agriculture office and assumes there is somewhere to keep impounded animals.

apply.if: If your LGU has an agriculturist or a veterinarian and barangay livestock aides
apply.then: you can replicate this by making that office the lead, with the aides doing first response in each barangay and the tanods helping with enforcement.

apply.if: If roaming livestock, not dogs, cause most of the trouble
apply.then: use the livestock schedule and the extra ₱1,000 for crop damage, blocked roads and accidents, and drop the pet provisions you don't need.

apply.if: If you have no pound or impounding area
apply.then: start with the fines, the owner seminar and liability for damage, and add impounding once a barangay or the municipality has a place and a budget to keep animals.

apply.if: If you want barangays to share in enforcement
apply.then: copy the 60/40 split with remittance every 6 months, after your treasurer confirms it can be done under your accounting rules.

apply.if: If dogs in your LGU are not yet registered
apply.then: pair the registration rule with a free rabies vaccination drive before fining owners for unvaccinated dogs.

Replace 'effective upon approval' with the posting and publication rule for penal ordinances in BLGC s. 571

Check with your treasurer and COA that ordinance fines may be shared 40% with barangays; Maribojoc itself makes the split subject to treasury and audit rules

ordinances.title: The Revised Investment Incentive Code of Sta. Cruz, Davao del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Revised Investment Incentive Code of Sta. Cruz
ordinances.summary: Sta. Cruz's investment code. It creates a board chaired by the mayor to pick priority investment areas and register enterprises, and gives registered enterprises a business tax holiday that shrinks year by year, plus help with sites, permits and labour. In return they must hire 80% of their semi-skilled and unskilled workers locally, run a yearly community project and file regular reports.
points: 15 priority areas, from agri-business and food processing to tourism, renewable power, logistics, ICT and shipbuilding; the board may add or delist areas with SB approval
To qualify, a project needs at least ₱3 million in capitalisation (small ₱3M to ₱15M, medium to ₱100M, large above), excluding land

Business tax exemption from the start of operation: small new enterprises 100% in year 1 down to 20% in year 5; large new ones 100% for 3 years; large pioneers 100% for 4 years; expanding firms 100%, 50%, 30%
Filing fee of ₱5,000, ₱8,000 or ₱10,000 by size; an application not acted on within 15 days is deemed approved
Registered enterprises must hire at least 80% of semi-skilled and unskilled workers from residents and run at least 1 community CSR project a year
A PAIC Management Office of 5 staff serves as secretariat; the board meets quarterly and reviews the incentive package every 5 years

provisions.title: A PAIC Management Board under the mayor
provisions.text: The mayor chairs the board, with the governor as honorary chair and the vice mayor as vice-chair. Members include 3 SB committee chairs, DTI, TESDA, the planning officer, agriculturist, treasurer and engineer, and business and labour representatives. It meets every quarter.

provisions.title: 15 priority investment areas
provisions.text: From agri-business and food processing, tourism, light manufacturing and packaging to fuel depots, real estate, logistics, renewable power, rail, ICT, export industries, shipbuilding, health facilities and medium-sized malls. The board may add or delist areas with SB approval.

provisions.title: At least ₱3 million to qualify
provisions.text: A project must be in a priority area and capitalized at ₱3 million to ₱15 million (small), over ₱15 million to ₱100 million (medium) or over ₱100 million (large), excluding land. Existing firms qualify by expanding, diversifying or moving their main office to Sta. Cruz.

provisions.title: Filing fees and a 15-day deemed approval
provisions.text: Applicants pay a non-refundable ₱5,000, ₱8,000 or ₱10,000 by size. The secretariat reviews within 10 working days and the chair decides within 5 days; an application not acted on within 15 days is deemed approved.

provisions.title: 80% local hiring and a yearly CSR project
provisions.text: Registered enterprises must hire at least 80% of their semi-skilled and unskilled workers from qualified residents, give residents priority for skilled posts, run at least 1 community CSR project a year, and not discriminate by gender, age, faith or disability.

provisions.title: Annual and quarterly reports
provisions.text: Enterprises file a company profile and audited financial statements within 60 days after the fiscal year, and production and manpower reports within 15 days after each quarter.

provisions.title: A PAIC office of 5 as secretariat
provisions.text: The PAIC Management Office processes applications and supports investors, staffed by a PAIC manager, a senior tourism operations officer (SG 18), a tourism operations officer and a planning officer (SG 11) and an administrative assistant (SG 8).

provisions.title: A business tax holiday that tapers off
provisions.text: From the start of operation: small new firms 100% in year 1 down to 20% in year 5; medium 100% for 2 years; large 100% for 3 years; pioneers 1 year longer at each size; expanding firms 100%, 50%, 30%; distressed firms 100%, then 50%. Only 1 category applies.

provisions.title: Help with sites, permits and labour
provisions.text: All registered enterprises get one-stop investment assistance and help with site selection, regulatory compliance, product launches, raw material supply, manpower pooling, offsite infrastructure and labour disputes. The board reviews the package every 5 years.

provisions.title: Withdrawal of incentives and late-report fines
provisions.text: Incentives are withdrawn for breaking hiring or CSR duties, blocking inspections, violating the ECC, understating capital or giving false information. Late reports are fined ₱10 a day, then ₱20, then ₱50 a day.

ordinances.penalties: Late reports fined ₱10, ₱20, then ₱50 a day; other breaches lead to withdrawal of the incentives
ordinances.amends: Revises the earlier code, Municipal Ordinance No. 02, Series of 1998, and repeals inconsistent ordinances
ordinances.caveat: The mayor's approval line is unsigned in this copy, and the application form the code refers to is not attached.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: New and expanding enterprises in the priority investment areas of Sta. Cruz
details.enforcers: Sta. Cruz PAIC Management Board, with the PAIC Management Office as secretariat
details.funding: General fund, plus funds the PAIC Board secures

before an unanswered application is deemed approved
of full business tax exemption for a large pioneer
minimum capitalisation to qualify, excluding land

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants an investment code that asks something back from investors. Sta. Cruz ties its tax holidays to local hiring, a yearly community project and regular reports, and sets a 15-day deadline for deciding applications. It dates from 2014 and rests on the national power to grant local tax exemptions, which a BARMM council has to confirm under the BLGC before copying the tax schedule.

apply.if: If your LGU has a local economic and investment promotion officer or a Business One-Stop Shop
apply.then: you can replicate this by making that office the secretariat and having applications decided within the same 15 days, deemed approved if no one acts.

apply.if: If your development plan has no list of priority investments
apply.then: start by having the municipal development council draw one up from what your LGU can actually host, before granting any incentive.

apply.if: If you want to grant business tax holidays
apply.then: first confirm the legal basis, then copy the shrinking schedule and the rule that an enterprise may claim only 1 incentive category.

apply.if: If local jobs are the main goal
apply.then: copy the 80% local hiring rule, the quarterly manpower report and withdrawal of incentives for firms that fall short.

apply.if: If your LGU is small and expects few investors
apply.then: skip the board and the tax schedule, and keep the non-fiscal help: site identification, permit assistance and training of local workers.

change: Confirm that a sanggunian may grant local tax exemptions under the BLGC before adopting the tax schedule; the code relies on RA 7160, BLGC s. 218 withdrew most existing exemptions, and BLGC s. 156 already exempts enterprises certified by the Bangsamoro Board of Investments for 6 years (pioneer) or 4 years (non-pioneer), so local holidays should not stack on that

Have the municipal development council propose the priority areas (BLGC s. 121), run registration through the Business One-Stop Shop (BLGC s. 151), and staff it with the optional local economic investment promotion officer (BLGC s. 481) instead of a new 5-person office

Review the priority list in line with BLGC s. 152, which asks local taxation to consider Shari'ah principles: decide whether to keep brewing and liquor production, and add halal processing or other areas your LGU has

Replace DTI with the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism, TESDA with the Bangsamoro technical education office under the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education, and check which office issues the environmental compliance certificate in BARMM
Re-cite the Labor Code provisions on minimum working age and the duties to workers alongside the Bangsamoro Labor and Employment Code (BAA No. 82)
barmm.fits: Municipalities on a highway or near a port that expect medium or large investors and have a development plan with priority areas.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Institutionalizing the Municipal Gardening Program of Kalilangan to Promote Food Security and Address Malnutrition
ordinances.shortTitle: Municipal Gardening Program Ordinance of Kalilangan
ordinances.summary: Makes food gardening a standing program in all 14 barangays of Kalilangan: household backyard gardens, a community garden in every barangay and a garden in every public school. The municipal agriculture office leads it, with priority for malnourished and 4Ps families, pregnant and lactating mothers and children, and the LGU gives yearly cash awards to the best barangays.
points: Every barangay keeps a community garden of at least 200 square metres, for demonstration, training and extra food; it may use private land under a MOA that transfers no ownership
All public schools keep a garden under DepEd's Gulayan sa Paaralan, built into the curriculum
The agriculture office trains, distributes seeds, seedlings and tools first to at-risk and 4Ps households, and helps design gardens for small spaces
The MSWDO adds gardening and nutrition to 4Ps family development sessions without adding conditions to the cash grants
Quarterly training for households, coordinators and schools; barangays inspect household gardens monthly and the agriculture office reports quarterly to the SB
Best Barangay Garden Award: ₱20,000, ₱15,000 and ₱10,000, ₱3,000 consolation prizes, and special awards of at least ₱5,000, subject to funds

provisions.title: Priority for the most food-insecure families
provisions.text: The program covers all 14 barangays, public schools, households and partner groups, and puts first nutritionally at-risk families, 4Ps households, pregnant and lactating mothers and children, and areas that nutrition and poverty mapping flag.

provisions.title: A 200 sq. m community garden in every barangay
provisions.text: Every barangay keeps a community garden of at least 200 square metres for demonstration, training and extra food; it does not replace the household gardens 4Ps families must keep.

provisions.title: Household and school gardens
provisions.text: All households are encouraged and helped to keep backyard gardens, and every public school keeps a garden built into the curriculum under DepEd's Gulayan sa Paaralan.

provisions.title: Private land by agreement, without transfer
provisions.text: Barangay gardens may use private land with the owner's consent under a MOA or MOU on terms, duties and duration; this never transfers ownership or permanently encumbers the property.

provisions.title: The agriculture office leads the program
provisions.text: The Municipal Agriculture Office trains and advises on organic and space-saving gardening and gives seeds, seedlings and tools first to at-risk and 4Ps households; barangays name garden coordinators and report monthly.

provisions.title: Gardening in 4Ps family sessions
provisions.text: The MSWDO adds gardening and nutrition to 4Ps family development sessions and supports 4Ps households without adding conditions to their cash grants.

provisions.title: Quarterly training and community events
provisions.text: The LGU, through the agriculture office and the Municipal Nutrition Council, holds quarterly training for households, barangay coordinators and schools, and organises garden fairs and nutrition campaigns.

provisions.title: Measured by gardens kept and malnutrition cut
provisions.text: Success is measured by gardens established and sustained, falls in malnutrition, more vegetable consumption and dietary diversity, and the participation of partners and 4Ps leaders.

provisions.title: Cash awards for the best barangays
provisions.text: An annual Best Barangay Garden Award recommends ₱20,000, ₱15,000 and ₱10,000 for the top 3 and ₱3,000 consolation prizes, plus special awards of at least ₱5,000, subject to funds.

provisions.title: General fund money and quarterly reports
provisions.text: The program is paid from the general fund, augmented by nutrition and agriculture program funds; the agriculture office reports quarterly to the SB, and barangays inspect household gardens monthly.

ordinances.caveat: OCR copy; the attestation says the session was on January 26, 2025, while every page header and the number say 2026.

details.effect: as provided in Section 511(a) of the Local Government Code
details.covers: All 14 barangays, public schools, households and partner groups in Kalilangan
details.enforcers: Municipal Agriculture Office as lead, with barangays, schools and the MSWDO
details.funding: Municipal general fund, augmented by nutrition and agriculture program funds

highlights.label: minimum community garden in every barangay
barangays covered, with every public school
prize for the best barangay garden
training rounds a year for households and schools

barmm.why: Worth reading if malnutrition is a concern in your LGU and garden programs run by different agencies do not add up. Kalilangan's 2026 ordinance puts household, barangay and school gardens under one lead office, gives priority to at-risk and 4Ps families, and measures results by nutrition data rather than just gardens planted. It has no penalties and depends on yearly funding for seeds, training and the cash awards.

apply.if: If your LGU has an agriculturist and a nutrition action officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by making the agriculturist lead the program and the nutrition officer track the nutrition indicators it sets.

apply.if: If your barangays have no public land for a 200 m² garden
apply.then: copy the clause that lets them use private land under a MOA with the owner, for gardening only and with no transfer of ownership.

apply.if: If many households in your LGU are 4Ps beneficiaries
apply.then: have your social welfare officer add gardening and nutrition to family development sessions, without adding conditions to the cash grants.

apply.if: If you cannot fund the cash prizes
apply.then: start with certificates, seed packages and tools as awards; Kalilangan's prizes are only recommended and subject to funds.

apply.if: If your schools or madaris already have gardens
apply.then: bring them into the same reporting and training instead of starting new ones.

Rename the partner offices: the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform for DA, the Ministry of Social Services and Development for DSWD, and the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education for DepEd, including madaris under the Bangsamoro Education Code (BAA No. 18); check whether the MILG runs its own version of the HAPAG sa Barangay program
Put the nutrition indicators under the nutrition action officer (BLGC s. 548) and align them with the Bangsamoro Nutrition Commission (BAA No. 83)
Budget the cash awards in the annual appropriation and keep the 'subject to availability of funds' wording
barmm.fits: Any municipality with an agriculture office and a nutrition program; the community garden duty suits barangays with some public or lendable land.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Regulating the Selling, Serving and Drinking of Liquor in Places of Entertainment, Business Establishments and Public Places and Providing Penalties for Violation Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Liquor Regulation Ordinance of Carrascal
ordinances.summary: Regulates where and when liquor may be sold and served in Carrascal, and bans drinking in public places and in vehicles. It covers bars, restaurants, stores and sari-sari stores, bans sales to minors and drinking by minors, and fines both sellers and drinkers.
points: No new liquor licence within 100 metres of a school, church, clinic, hospital or public building; the MPDO must certify the distance
Existing sellers inside the 100 m zone may stay, but no new licence is given at that site once they close or change owners
Stores and sari-sari stores in the zone may sell liquor but not serve it for drinking on the premises
Liquor may be sold and served only until 12 midnight; places of entertainment must have at least 1 guard to search customers for weapons and drugs
Sellers must post a 2 by 3 foot notice that persons below 18 may not be sold or served liquor
Drinking in public places and in vehicles is banned, except during barangay fiestas, wakes and municipal celebrations
The Rural Health Unit and the treasurer's office enforce it with the PNP

provisions.title: Where it applies
provisions.text: It covers places of entertainment such as clubs, bars, videoke bars and beer gardens; businesses that sell or serve liquor, from restaurants and carinderias to sari-sari stores; and public places and buildings. Liquor includes local drinks such as tuba and lambanog.

provisions.title: No new licence within 100 metres
provisions.text: No new liquor licence is issued unless the MPDO certifies the place is more than 100 metres from any school, church, clinic, hospital or public building and complies with the zoning ordinance.

provisions.title: Existing sellers in the zone phase out
provisions.text: Sellers already inside the 100-metre zone may continue, but no new licence is given at that site once they close or change owner. The same applies when a new school, church, hospital or public building opens nearby.

provisions.title: Stores may sell but not serve
provisions.text: Convenience stores, bazaars, groceries and sari-sari stores in the zone may sell liquor if licensed, but may never serve it for drinking on the premises. Every seller must display an abstract of the ordinance.

provisions.title: Sales until midnight, a guard at the door
provisions.text: Liquor may be sold and served only until 12 midnight. Places of entertainment must have at least 1 guard to search customers for weapons, explosives and prohibited drugs during operating hours.

provisions.title: No liquor for minors, and a sign saying so
provisions.text: Liquor may not be sold or served to persons below 18, and minors may not drink it. Sellers must post a permanent 2 by 3 foot notice in bold letters saying so.

provisions.title: No drinking in public places or vehicles
provisions.text: Drinking is banned in public places such as plazas, markets, parks, streets and sidewalks, and inside vehicles, moving or parked, in public places. The ban does not apply during barangay fiestas, wakes and municipal celebrations.

provisions.title: Fines of ₱2,500 for sellers, ₱500 for drinkers
provisions.text: Owners and operators pay ₱2,500 for each violation of the licensing, hours, minors and guard rules. Public drinkers and drinking minors pay ₱500 an offence; parents pay for minors, and those who cannot pay do community service set by the mayor.

provisions.title: Enforced by health, treasury and police
provisions.text: The Rural Health Unit and the Municipal Treasurer's Office lead enforcement with the PNP. It takes effect 10 days after posting at the municipal hall and 2 other conspicuous places.

ordinances.penalties: ₱2,500 per offence for owners and operators; ₱500 per offence for drinking in public or in vehicles and for minors who drink (paid by parents), or community service for those who cannot pay
ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, rules and regulations (general clause only)

details.effect: 10 days after posting at the Municipal Hall and 2 other places

the latest liquor may be sold or served
fine per offence for a seller

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU allows liquor sales but has trouble with drinking near schools, on the street or by minors. Carrascal's 5-page ordinance keeps new sellers 100 m from schools, churches and hospitals, sets a midnight cut-off, bans public drinking and gives those who cannot pay a fine community service instead. It is short and clear, but it names health and treasury staff as enforcers without saying who issues tickets.

apply.if: If your LGU already bans the sale of liquor outright
apply.then: take only what your ban may lack, such as the ban on drinking in public and in vehicles and the community service option for those who cannot pay.

apply.if: If your LGU licenses liquor sellers
apply.then: you can replicate this by having the planning office certify the 100 m distance before any new licence and refusing a new licence at a site when the owner changes.

apply.if: If mosques, madaris or Islamic centres stand near stores that sell liquor
apply.then: add them to the 100 m list beside schools, churches and hospitals.

apply.if: If public drinking is the main problem
apply.then: copy the ₱500 fine and community service, and decide openly whether fiestas, wakes and celebrations should be exempt.

apply.if: If your barangay tanods will help enforce it
apply.then: name them and the police as the offices that issue citations, rather than the health unit and treasurer alone.

change: Re-cite the basis from RA 7160 s. 16 and 447 to BLGC s. 17 (public morals, peace and order) and s. 489; the ₱2,500 and ₱500 fines fit the ₱5,000 cap
Replace the 10-day effectivity with the posting and publication rule for penal ordinances in BLGC s. 571, with the text translated into the local language
Add mosques and madaris, and any other places of worship, to the 100 m list beside schools, churches, clinics, hospitals and public buildings
Run the distance certification through the Business One-Stop Shop (BLGC s. 151) so it is part of the business permit
Name who issues citations; tanods may help enforce but are civilians who may not carry firearms (BLGC s. 408)
barmm.fits: Municipalities that license liquor sellers and have bars, stores or roadside drinking near schools and places of worship.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Providing Monthly Honoraria to Recognized Barangay Tribal Chieftains, Municipal IP Women Representative and Municipal IP Youth Representative Not Holding IPMR Positions in the Municipality of Braulio E. Dujali, Defining Their Roles and Functions, and Appropriating Funds Therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Recognized IP Leaders Honorarium Ordinance of Braulio E. Dujali
ordinances.summary: Pays a monthly honorarium to the recognized tribal chieftain of each barangay and to the municipal IP women and IP youth representatives who do not hold an IPMR seat. It lists what these leaders are expected to do, from mediating disputes under customary law to acting as liaison with government, and charges the cost to the general fund. Sitting IPMRs are left out because they already draw government pay.
points: ₱1,000 a month for each recognized barangay tribal chieftain, the municipal IP women representative and the municipal IP youth leader representative
Only 1 tribal chieftain per barangay and 1 per municipality may be paid
Barangay chieftains must be certified by the NCIP on the recommendation of the municipal tribal chieftain, who must be certified first
Leaders are expected to uphold customary law, mediate intra-community conflicts, join consultations, act as liaison with government and protect ancestral domains
Customary law prevails: payment may not depend on duties that conflict with the community's own practices
The mayor's office, through the municipal administrator, runs the program; the yearly amount follows the updated list of certified chieftains

provisions.title: Support for IP leaders, not a salary
provisions.text: Sets up a monthly honorarium program for recognized tribal chieftains and the municipal IP women and IP youth representatives. The honorarium is support for their leadership, not a salary, wage or employment benefit.

provisions.title: Sitting IPMRs are left out
provisions.text: Leaders who hold Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representative seats are excluded, since they already draw government pay. Only 1 tribal chieftain per barangay and 1 for the municipality may be paid.

provisions.title: ₱1,000 a month each
provisions.text: Each barangay tribal chieftain, the municipal IP women representative and the municipal IP youth leader representative receive ₱1,000 a month.

provisions.title: NCIP certification first
provisions.text: A barangay chieftain qualifies only once the NCIP certifies them as a recognized tribal chieftain, on the recommendation of the municipal tribal chieftain, who must be certified first.

provisions.title: What the leaders are expected to do
provisions.text: Uphold customary law and traditions, mediate intra-community conflicts by indigenous dispute resolution, join community programs and provincial consultations, act as liaison with government, and protect ancestral domains and indigenous knowledge.

provisions.title: Customary law prevails
provisions.text: Payment may not be made to depend on any of these duties where it conflicts with the community's own customary practices.

provisions.title: Run by the mayor's office
provisions.text: The Office of the Mayor, through the municipal administrator, coordinates, monitors and pays out the honoraria.

provisions.title: Funded yearly from the General Fund
provisions.text: Funds are set aside every year from the General Fund or other sources; the amount follows the updated list of certified chieftains, which changes as leaders move into or out of IPMR seats. Takes effect on approval.

ordinances.caveat: Section 3 first says it covers leaders 'serving as' IPMRs and then excludes IPMRs, the text skips from Section 8 to Section 10, and the mayor's approval date is not shown.

sponsors: Hon. Donna Mae B. Bernadas, Ed.D.
Hon. Mikhael Julian III G. Dujali

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has indigenous communities whose traditional leaders settle disputes and speak for them with government, but receive nothing for it. Dujali's ordinance is 3 pages and simple: a flat monthly honorarium, 1 leader per barangay, certification before payment, and a clause that customary law prevails. Its coverage clause contradicts itself, a section is missing, and the certification runs through the NCIP.

apply.if: If your LGU already has an IPMR in the sangguniang bayan
apply.then: you can replicate this by paying the leaders who do not hold that seat, and stating plainly that the IPMR and any other paid official are excluded.

apply.if: If your indigenous communities have no certified leaders yet
apply.then: start by asking the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs to certify the municipal leader first, and let that leader recommend the barangay leaders, as Dujali does.

apply.if: If your budget cannot cover every barangay at once
apply.then: begin with the barangays where the indigenous community is largest and add the rest in later budgets, naming the appropriation each year.

apply.if: If your indigenous communities have women's or youth leaders outside the sanggunian
apply.then: copy the 2 municipal posts for IP women and IP youth so they are paid on the same terms.

apply.if: If you want the honorarium tied to work
apply.then: keep Dujali's list of duties but also its rule that customary law prevails where a duty conflicts with community practice.

change: Replace NCIP certification with certification by the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs (BAA No. 64). The IPMR seat itself follows BLGC s. 132 and s. 488 in the sangguniang bayan and s. 418 in the sangguniang barangay, under MIPA and MILG guidelines

Rewrite Section 3 so it covers only leaders who hold no IPMR seat or other paid government post, and add the missing section; no official may receive additional compensation without a law allowing it (BLGC s. 107)

Ground the honorarium in the general welfare duty to preserve culture (BLGC s. 17) and the power to give financial assistance to organizations of indigenous cultural communities (BLGC s. 39), and appropriate it in the annual budget
Define 'tribal chieftain' to fit the indigenous political structures of the communities in your LGU, and say who recommends when there is more than one community
Require a yearly list of certified leaders, posted with the budget, so the payroll can be checked
barmm.fits: Municipalities with indigenous communities whose traditional leaders are not in the sanggunian, and which can fund a small monthly honorarium from the general fund.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Creating the Committee on Indigenous Peoples a Regular Standing Committee in the Barangay Councils of Awang, Bagocboc, Tingalan, Nangcaon, Cauyonan and Limunda in the Municipality of Opol
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay Committee on Indigenous Peoples Ordinance of Opol
ordinances.summary: Makes a Committee on Indigenous Peoples a regular standing committee in the councils of 6 Opol barangays that have a sitting IPMR. Most of the text restates the NCIP's 2021 rules on how IPMRs are chosen, who qualifies and who is disqualified, and how long they serve. The provincial board declared it valid in December 2022.
points: Creates the committee in Awang, Bagocboc, Tingalan, Nangcaon, Cauyonan and Limunda, where an NCIP-affirmed IPMR sits
The committee handles IP development programs, the protection and welfare of IPs, IP rights, and all matters affecting IPs
Representation follows NCIP Administrative Order No. 1, series of 2021: mandatory where there is an ancestral domain or land, otherwise by population threshold
Resettled and migrant IPs living in the domain for more than 10 years may join the selection when they outnumber the domain owners
An IPMR in a legislative council must be at least 18, able to read and write, conversant with the culture, and a resident for 10 years
Disqualifies those in a political party or soliciting support from politicians, losing candidates within 3 years, and those who held government office in the past year
IPMR term of 3 years, up to 3 consecutive terms

provisions.title: A standing IP committee in 6 barangay councils
provisions.text: The Committee on Indigenous Peoples becomes a regular standing committee of the barangay councils of Awang, Bagocboc, Tingalan, Nangcaon, Cauyonan and Limunda, where an IPMR affirmed by the NCIP sits.

provisions.title: What the committee handles
provisions.text: Its jurisdiction covers IP development programs, the protection and welfare of IPs, IP rights, and all measures and matters affecting IPs.

provisions.title: When IP representation applies
provisions.text: Under NCIP Administrative Order No. 1, series of 2021, representation is mandatory where there is an ancestral domain or land. Elsewhere an IP population must reach the LGU's population divided by its number of council seats, or the LGU may still allow it at the IPs' initiative.

provisions.title: Resettled and migrant IPs
provisions.text: Resettled and migrant IPs living in the domain for more than 10 years who outnumber the domain owners may help draft the local guidelines and be nominated, after petitioning the community and a census, with the NCIP guarding the owners' rights.

provisions.title: Who may be an IPMR
provisions.text: A bona fide member of the community, able to read and write, fit, natural-born and at least 18. An IPMR in a council must also know the culture, have lived in the community for the last 10 years and be a registered voter there; one in a policy-making body must be a high-school graduate.

provisions.title: Who is disqualified
provisions.text: Those found by the IPs to have broken custom, convicted of moral turpitude or offences of 1 year or more, removed from office, fugitives, party members or those seeking politicians' support, those in government office in the past year, and losing candidates within 3 years of an election.

provisions.title: A 3-year term, at most 3 in a row
provisions.text: An IPMR serves 3 years from assumption, may be re-endorsed by the IP constituents, and may not serve more than 3 consecutive terms, unless IP groups agree to rotate the seat one term per community.

provisions.title: Effect and provincial review
provisions.text: It took effect on approval. The Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental declared it valid in Resolution No. 289-2022 on 19 December 2022.

ordinances.caveat: Two sections are numbered 3, much of the text copies NCIP rules rather than setting local ones, and the last pages are the provincial board's resolution declaring it valid.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Barangay councils of Awang, Bagocboc, Tingalan, Nangcaon, Cauyonan and Limunda
creates: Committee on Indigenous Peoples in 6 barangay councils

highlights.label: barangay councils given an IP committee
term of an IPMR, up to 3 in a row

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your barangays have indigenous representatives but no committee that gives their concerns a place on the agenda. The idea is simple: where an IP representative sits, make an IP committee a standing committee. Opol's text is mostly a copy of national NCIP rules on selecting IPMRs, and it has a municipality set committees inside barangay councils, which each council normally decides in its own rules.

apply.if: If your barangay councils already have an IP representative
apply.then: you can replicate this by having each of those councils add a Committee on Indigenous Peoples to its internal rules, with the IP representative as chair.

apply.if: If your sangguniang bayan has an IPMR but no IP committee
apply.then: start at the municipal level and add the committee to your own internal rules, with the same 4 areas of jurisdiction.

apply.if: If you are not sure which barangays qualify for an IP seat
apply.then: list them by the BLGC test (at least 5% of the population, or a recognized native title) rather than by name, so new qualifying barangays are covered.

apply.if: If your LGU also has settler representatives
apply.then: decide whether the committee covers their concerns too or whether each group needs its own.

apply.if: If you want rules on choosing representatives
apply.then: skip Opol's copied qualifications and point to the guidelines issued by the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the MILG.

change: Replace the NCIP Administrative Order No. 1 rules with the selection guidelines issued jointly by the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and the MILG (BLGC s. 132; BAA No. 64). The barangay IP seat and its 5% or native-title test are in BLGC s. 418

Each sanggunian sets its own standing committees in its internal rules (BLGC s. 58). Have each sangguniang barangay adopt the committee itself, with the municipal measure directing or encouraging it, and review those barangay ordinances under BLGC s. 65
Drop the copied qualifications, disqualifications and term rules unless the MIPA and MILG guidelines say the same; the 10-year residence and 1-year bar on prior government office are NCIP rules
Where settler communities hold a seat under BLGC s. 133 and s. 418, say whether the committee covers them
Define 'NCIP' and 'Certificate of Affirmation' again under the Bangsamoro terms, naming MIPA as the office that affirms representatives
barmm.fits: Municipalities with indigenous representatives in some barangay councils, and any sanggunian with an IP seat but no committee for it.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Creating the Office of the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts in the Local Government Unit of Alamada, Province of Cotabato, Defining Its Powers and Functions, and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts Office Ordinance of Alamada
ordinances.summary: Turns Alamada's tourism unit under the mayor's office into a full department, the Office of the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts. It sets the head's rank and qualifications, the office's powers, and 4 divisions covering planning, tourism services and promotion, cultural affairs and events, and administration. Staff of the old unit move over with no one separated.
points: The Tourism Officer is a department head at Salary Grade 24, appointed by the mayor
The officer must be a resident with a relevant bachelor's degree, first grade civil service eligibility and at least 4 years in the tourism industry, and must take DOT training
Powers include tourism plans and promotion, supervising cultural affairs and municipal tourism facilities, and monitoring standards and accreditation of tourism establishments
4 divisions: Technical Support Services, Tourism Services and Promotions, Cultural Affairs and Events, and Administrative and General Services
The cultural affairs division researches and documents local heritage and gives technical help to artists and cultural workers
Funds, staff, records and equipment of the old Tourism Development and Promotion Unit transfer, with no mandatory separation

provisions.title: Tourism, culture and the arts as policy
provisions.text: The municipality puts a tourism, culture and arts agenda into its local development plan, strengthens the Local Tourism Council and the Local Culture and Arts Council, and commits to eco-tourism, local products and preserving historical sites and heritage.

provisions.title: A new Office of Tourism, Culture and the Arts
provisions.text: The ordinance creates the Office of the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts, headed by a Tourism Officer whom the mayor appoints with the rank of department head, Salary Grade 24.

provisions.title: Who can be Tourism Officer
provisions.text: The officer must be a Filipino and a resident of Alamada of good moral character, hold a bachelor's degree preferably in tourism, planning, development studies, economics or public administration, be first grade civil service eligible, have 4 years in the tourism industry and take DOT training.

provisions.title: The lead office for tourism and culture
provisions.text: The office is the municipality's main planning, coordinating, implementing and regulatory office for tourism and cultural affairs under RA 9593, the Tourism Act of 2009.

provisions.title: Powers of the office
provisions.text: It sets tourism policy and plans, supervises cultural affairs and municipal tourism facilities, coordinates with barangays and national agencies, develops new products and investment, monitors standards and accreditation of tourism establishments, and runs integrated marketing.

provisions.title: 4 divisions
provisions.text: The office has a Technical Support Services Division for planning, product development and coordination, a Tourism Services and Promotions Division, a Cultural Affairs and Events Division, and an Administrative and General Services Division.

provisions.title: Standards, training and promotion
provisions.text: The Tourism Services and Promotions Division sets service standards for the industry, runs the accreditation program for tourism enterprises and manpower training, and carries out marketing through public relations, social media and special events.

provisions.title: Heritage research and help for artists
provisions.text: The Cultural Affairs and Events Division researches and documents Alamada heritage, gives technical help to artists, cultural workers and organizations, runs cultural education campaigns and stages special events.

provisions.title: Shared roles with the national government
provisions.text: Following RA 9593, the municipality prepares a tourism development plan, enforces standards and collects tourism statistics, and is primarily responsible for tourism facilities, attractions and their concessions and security.

provisions.title: Old unit's staff and funds move over
provisions.text: All funds, personnel, records, property and equipment of the Tourism Development and Promotion Unit under the mayor's office transfer to the new office, with no mandatory separation. It took effect on approval.

ordinances.amends: Converts the Tourism Development and Promotion Unit under the Office of the Municipal Mayor into a department; repeals inconsistent ordinances and orders
ordinances.caveat: The mayor's approval date is blank on this copy.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Tourism, culture and the arts in the Municipality of Alamada
details.enforcers: Office of the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts, under a Tourism Officer
creates: Office of the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts
details.funding: Funds and staff transferred from the Mayor's Tourism Development and Promotion Unit

highlights.label: rank of the tourism officer, a department head
divisions in the new office

barmm.why: Worth reading if tourism and culture in your LGU sit with one or two staff in the mayor's office and you want a department with a head and a budget. Alamada's ordinance is a clean template: mandate, powers, 4 divisions and a transition clause. It is written for a municipality with growing tourism; a smaller LGU may need only some of the divisions, and the qualifications must be raised to the BLGC standard.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a tourism unit or a designated tourism officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by converting it into a department and moving its staff, funds and records over with no separation, as Alamada did.

apply.if: If your LGU has major tourism industries
apply.then: note that the BLGC makes a tourism officer mandatory for you, so this ordinance is the way to create the post.

apply.if: If your tourism is small
apply.then: start with the officer and 2 divisions, tourism services and cultural affairs, and add planning and administration as staff allow.

apply.if: If your LGU has a local council for culture and the arts
apply.then: make the new office its secretariat so the culture work has one home.

apply.if: If your heritage sites are not documented
apply.then: give the cultural affairs division the first task of researching and listing them, before promotion.

change: Re-cite the basis from LGC s. 443 and s. 465 to BLGC s. 489 (the sangguniang bayan sets positions and salaries) and s. 546 (the tourism officer). Raise the qualifications to s. 546: a relevant bachelor's degree, second level eligibility and at least 5 years in tourism, not 4 years and first grade eligibility

Replace the Department of Tourism with the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism for standards, accreditation and training (BAA No. 13), and involve the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage for heritage sites, alongside national heritage bodies
Link the culture work to the local council for culture and arts that BLGC s. 130 requires, and fund it under the culture and heritage allocation in BLGC s. 348
Size the structure to your staff and budget; BLGC s. 87 lets each LGU design its own structure, and appointments follow the Bangsamoro Civil Service Code (BAA No. 17)
Cut Section 10, which restates national-local roles under RA 9593, to what binds the LGU
barmm.fits: Municipalities and cities with tourist sites or cultural events that already fund a tourism unit and can afford a department head.

ordinances.title: The Revised Internal Rules of Procedure of the Sangguniang Bayan of Sta. Cruz, Province of Davao del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Revised Internal Rules of Procedure of the Sangguniang Bayan of Sta. Cruz
ordinances.summary: The full internal rules of the Sta. Cruz sangguniang bayan, adopted by Resolution No. 205-14. It covers the presiding officer, sessions, quorum, order of business, the 3 readings, voting, debate limits, 21 standing committees, committee reports, minutes, motions and discipline. It applies to every member, including the vice mayor as presiding officer.
points: Regular sessions every Wednesday at 9:00 a.m.; a session may be held in a barangay by majority vote; special sessions need 24 hours' written notice
Speaking limits: 30 minutes for a sponsor or committee report, 20 minutes for other debate, 5 minutes on each amendment, 3 minutes to explain a vote
21 standing committees (10 mandatory and 11 others) of 7 members each; no member may chair more than 3
No tax or revenue measure may pass without a public hearing by the committee concerned
A measure a committee has not acted on within 30 days goes on the calendar for second reading
Abstention is allowed only for a member with a pecuniary interest; no member may vote where a relative within the 3rd degree has one
Fines are deducted from the erring member's salary into a trust fund that the whole council decides how to spend

provisions.title: Members must disclose, attend and vote
provisions.text: Every member discloses financial and business interests, attends every session unless sick or prevented and gives prior notice, and must vote on every question; abstaining is allowed only for a member with a pecuniary interest.

provisions.title: Regular sessions every Wednesday at 9:00 a.m.
provisions.text: Regular sessions are held every Wednesday at 9:00 a.m. at the legislative building; a majority of members present may move a session to a barangay hall. No 2 sessions may be held on the same day.

provisions.title: Special sessions on 24 hours' notice
provisions.text: The Mayor or a majority of members may call a special session with written notice served at least 24 hours before; only the matters in the notice may be taken up unless 2/3 of those present agree. Sessions are open to the public.

provisions.title: Every ordinance passes 3 readings
provisions.text: On first reading a measure is referred to committee without debate; on second reading it is sponsored, debated, amended and approved; on third reading it is put straight to a vote.

provisions.title: No vote where a relative has an interest
provisions.text: No member may vote on a measure in which he or a relative within the 3rd degree has a direct pecuniary interest; a member may explain a vote for up to 3 minutes.

provisions.title: Limits on speaking time
provisions.text: A sponsor or committee reporter may speak up to 30 minutes, other members up to 20 minutes on an issue, and up to 5 minutes on each amendment, unless a majority allows more.

provisions.title: 21 standing committees of 7 members
provisions.text: The council creates 10 mandatory and 11 other standing committees of 7 members each; the presiding officer sits on none, and no member may chair more than 3.

provisions.title: Public hearings and a 30-day committee deadline
provisions.text: No tax or revenue measure may pass without a public hearing by the committee concerned, and a measure a committee has not acted on within 30 days is calendared for second reading.
provisions.section: Rule XII, Sec. 4; Rule XIII, Sec. 7

provisions.title: Fines and suspensions for members
provisions.text: Penalties run from a reprimand for disorder to fines of ₱25 to ₱50 an hour for lateness, ₱1,000 to ₱3,000 for 4 straight unjustified absences, 15 days' suspension, and expulsion; suspension or expulsion needs 2/3 of all members.

provisions.title: Fines go into a trust fund
provisions.text: Fines are deducted from the erring member's salary into a trust fund in a savings account, and the council, as a committee of the whole, decides by majority how to spend it.

ordinances.penalties: Reprimand, then exclusion, for disorderly conduct; ₱50 to ₱200 per unjustified absence, ₱1,000 to ₱3,000 for 4 consecutive, ₱25 to ₱50 per hour late; 15 days' suspension without pay for refusing an assigned task; expulsion on conviction for moral turpitude
ordinances.amends: Revises the internal rules the Sangguniang Bayan adopted on July 3, 2013
ordinances.caveat: The rules are adopted through Resolution No. 205-14 and signed by an acting vice mayor as temporary presiding officer; no mayor's approval is shown.

details.effect: On the date of its adoption
details.covers: The Sangguniang Bayan of Sta. Cruz, its members, sessions and committees
details.enforcers: Presiding Officer and the Committee on Rules

highlights.label: standing committees, each with 7 members
before a stalled measure goes to second reading
top fine for 4 unjustified absences in a row
limit on each member's debate on a question

barmm.why: Worth reading if your sanggunian is due to update its internal rules and wants a complete, working set to start from. Sta. Cruz's rules are detailed on what usually goes unwritten: speaking limits, the 30-day rule against bills dying in committee, abstention, and a schedule of fines for absence and lateness. They predate the BLGC, so quorum, discipline and posting rules must be brought in line, and some fines are paid in unusual ways.

apply.if: If your sanggunian's rules are older than the BLGC or were never updated
apply.then: you can replicate this by using Sta. Cruz's structure, rule by rule, and replacing each LGC citation with the BLGC section that now governs it.

apply.if: If bills in your sanggunian stall in committee
apply.then: copy the 30-day rule that puts a measure on the calendar for second reading when the committee has not acted.

apply.if: If absences and late sessions are a problem
apply.then: copy the schedule of fines for absence and lateness, but follow the BLGC for 4 consecutive absences and pay fines to the treasury rather than through salary deduction.

apply.if: If your sanggunian has fewer members than committees need
apply.then: cut the 21 committees to the 6 the BLGC requires plus those your agenda needs, and size each to your membership.

apply.if: If your sanggunian holds sessions in a local language
apply.then: add the BLGC rule that minutes be translated into English or Tagalog, and set your own dress code in place of coat and tie or barong.

change: Re-cite the legal basis from RA 7160 and its IRR to BLGC s. 56 to s. 63, and adopt or update the rules within 90 days of the members' election (BLGC s. 58)

Make the 6 committees BLGC s. 58 requires mandatory: appropriations, women and family, human rights, youth and sports development, environmental protection, and cooperatives. Sta. Cruz lists environmental protection only as optional

Rewrite the quorum rule to BLGC s. 61: count sectoral and ex officio members and the vice mayor, and leave out members absent without cause for 4 consecutive sessions and those under preventive suspension. The presiding officer votes only to break a tie and may not chair a standing committee (BLGC s. 57)

For 4 consecutive unjustified absences, use the BLGC s. 58 sanctions of censure, suspension of up to 60 days or expulsion by two-thirds of all members. Route fines through the treasurer under the usual rules, not salary deduction into a trust fund in a named private bank

Add the BLGC steps after passage: transmittal to the province within 3 days (s. 64), posting and publication (s. 67 and s. 571), online posting (s. 68), and filing with the Bangsamoro Register of Ordinances (s. 69)
barmm.fits: Any sangguniang bayan or panlungsod updating its internal rules; the committee list suits councils with at least 7 regular members.
