ordinances.title: An Ordinance Adopting the Updated Zoning Regulations of the Municipality of Itogon, Province of Benguet and Providing for the Administration and Enforcement and Amendments Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Updated Zoning Ordinance of Itogon
ordinances.summary: Itogon's zoning ordinance, which puts into effect its comprehensive land use plan for 2015 to 2024 (SB Ordinance No. 34 of 2017). It divides an upland mining and forest municipality into base zones and sub-zones, adds 6 hazard and special overlay zones, and describes zone boundaries in each of its 9 barangays. It sets building, buffer and easement rules and the permits, appeals board and review committee that enforce them.
points: 3 base zones (forest, alienable and disposable, mineral land) with sub-zones down to small-scale mining, quarry, socialized housing and cemetery; 6 overlay zones for landslide, flood, faultline, heritage, ecotourism and ancestral domain
In the landslide overlay, buildings may cover at most 30% of a lot (20% for parks) and at least 60% must stay unpaved (70% for parks)
No permanent buildings in the flood overlay or within 5 m of either side of a fault; Water Code easements of 3, 20 and 40 m along rivers
Buffers of 4 m between commercial and residential zones, 1 km between industrial and residential or commercial zones, and 500 m to 1 km around poultry and piggery farms
Locational clearance is required before any activity or construction and before building, business and occupancy permits; it lapses if unused for 1 year
Non-conforming uses may continue but not expand, may be rebuilt only if damage is 50% or less of replacement cost, and must phase out within 10 years
A Local Zoning Board of Appeals chaired by the mayor decides variances and exceptions within 30 days; amendments need a public hearing and a three-fourths vote of the sangguniang bayan

provisions.title: 3 base zones with many sub-zones
provisions.text: The municipality is divided into a Forest Zone, an Alienable and Disposable Zone and a Mineral Land Zone, each with sub-zones ranging from watershed, agricultural and residential to quarry, small-scale mining, socialized housing and cemetery.

provisions.title: 6 overlay zones
provisions.text: Overlay zones for landslide, flood, faultline, heritage, ecotourism and ancestral lands add rules on top of the base zones.

provisions.title: Landslide overlay limits
provisions.text: Since the MGB rates the whole municipality landslide-prone, buildings may cover at most 30% of a lot (20% for parks), at least 60% must stay unpaved (70% for parks), and native vegetation and natural drainage must be kept.

provisions.title: No building in flood and fault zones
provisions.text: No permanent buildings in the flood overlay (Dalupirip, Poblacion and Tinongdan along the Agno and Ambalanga rivers) or within 5 m of either side of a fault, where only parks and easements are allowed. Sinking areas are non-buildable.

provisions.title: River and fault easements
provisions.text: Water Code easements of 3 m in urban, 20 m in agricultural and 40 m in forest areas along rivers and streams, a mandatory 5 m easement on both sides of PHIVOLCS fault traces, and no building under transmission lines.

provisions.title: Buffers between uses
provisions.text: 4 m between commercial and residential zones; 1 km between industrial zones and residential or commercial zones; 500 m between small poultry farms and built-up areas; and 1 km for medium poultry and piggery farms.

provisions.title: Locational clearance first
provisions.text: Every owner or developer needs locational clearance from the zoning officer, or from the LZBA for variances and exceptions, before any activity or construction, even in forest land. It lapses if not used within 1 year.

provisions.title: Non-conforming uses phase out in 10 years
provisions.text: Existing non-conforming uses may continue but not expand, cannot revive after 1 year idle, may be rebuilt only if damage is 50% or less of replacement cost, and must phase out within 10 years.

provisions.title: A zoning board of appeals chaired by the mayor
provisions.text: The Local Zoning Board of Appeals, chaired by the mayor with the SB land use chair, legal officer, assessor, engineer and planning coordinator, decides variances, exceptions and appeals within 30 days by absolute majority; its decisions go to the HLURB.

provisions.title: Amendments, fines and effectivity
provisions.text: Amendments need a public hearing and a three-fourths vote of the sangguniang bayan. Violations draw up to ₱2,500 or 1 year in jail, and continuing violators pay 100% of the clearance fee each month. It takes effect on SP or HLURB approval and publication.

ordinances.penalties: Fine of up to ₱2,500 or up to 1 year in jail, or both; continuing violators pay 100% of the locational clearance fee for every month the violation goes on
ordinances.amends: Updates the earlier zoning regulations and repeals conflicting ordinances; implements the CLUP adopted by SB Ordinance No. 34, Series of 2017
ordinances.caveat: This is an OCR of a scanned copy: the zoning and overlay maps (Annexes A and B) cannot be read, and the overlay list names an 'Ancestral Lands' zone that Section 13 calls 'Ancestral Domain'.

sponsors: Hon. Dante Alain Xavier D. Godio
details.effect: upon SP/HLURB approval and publication
details.covers: All land, buildings and land uses in the Municipality of Itogon
details.enforcers: Mayor through the Municipal Zoning Office, with the Local Zoning Board of Appeals

highlights.label: overlay zones, from landslide to ancestral domain
for non-conforming uses to phase out
buffer between industrial and residential zones
no-build strip on each side of a fault

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU is drafting a zoning ordinance for hilly, forested or mining land and wants to see how hazard overlays work in practice. Itogon's zone boundaries come from its own land use plan and cannot be copied, but its landslide, flood and fault overlays, its ancestral domain overlay, and its enforcement machinery are reusable. It follows the old HLURB model, and its penalty runs past what a municipality may impose.

apply.if: If your LGU has an approved comprehensive land use plan
apply.then: you can replicate the structure by drawing base zones from your plan and adding overlay zones for the hazards your maps show, with Itogon's site-occupancy and unpaved-area limits for landslide areas.

apply.if: If your LGU has no land use plan yet
apply.then: start with the plan; a zoning ordinance without one has no legal basis for its boundaries.

apply.if: If parts of your LGU are ancestral domain or have a native title
apply.then: copy the ancestral domain overlay, which defers to the community's own development plan and consent process, and name the BARMM office that handles it.

apply.if: If your LGU has a planning coordinator but no zoning staff
apply.then: assign zoning to that office first, and create Itogon's 3-person zoning office (zoning officer, GIS operator, inspector) once funded.

apply.if: If small-scale mining or quarrying goes on in your LGU
apply.then: map those areas as separate sub-zones with buffers, as Itogon did, instead of leaving them to permits alone.

change: Re-cite the authority from LGC s. 20 and s. 447 to BLGC s. 480 (the municipality adopts its land use plan and zoning ordinances) and s. 23 (reclassification of agricultural land: up to 10% for 1st to 3rd class municipalities and 5% for 4th to 6th class, after public hearings)
Cap the penalty at ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); Itogon's 1 year is over the limit. Recast the monthly 100% surcharge as an administrative fine within that cap, or drop it
Replace HLURB, now DHSUD, as the reviewer and appeal body with the national or Bangsamoro office that holds that role under your rules, and send the ordinance to the province for review (BLGC s. 64)

Replace NCIP, FPIC guidelines and the ADSDPP with the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs and its processes (BAA No. 64), and DENR with the Bangsamoro ministry that took over the function where BARMM law moved it

Make the municipal engineer the building official who must see the locational clearance (BLGC s. 531), and put the zoning office and the board's secretariat under the planning and development coordinator (BLGC s. 530)
barmm.fits: Upland, forested or mining municipalities with an approved land use plan and hazard maps to draw overlay zones from.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Prescribing Guidelines for the Declaration of Death and Regulating Funeral Home Procedures in the Municipality of Kalilangan
ordinances.shortTitle: Death Declaration and Funeral Home Regulation Ordinance of Kalilangan
ordinances.summary: Sets out who declares and certifies a death in Kalilangan for each kind of death, how deaths reach the civil registrar, and what funeral homes must do. It lets Muslims and indigenous communities bury their dead at once, with the death reported within 14 days after burial under the Philippine Islamic Burial Act. It covers all deaths in the municipality and every funeral home operating there.
points: Every death is declared by a licensed physician or the municipal health officer; a home death with no doctor is reported to the BHERT, health office or LDRRMO, which brings the health officer for an on-site exam
Separate rules for deaths in a facility, at home with or without a doctor, in the ER, in an ambulance, in a moving vehicle, fetal deaths and medico-legal cases referred to the PNP or NBI

Muslim and IP burials may proceed with or without a certificate; the death is reported within 14 days after burial to the health officer, or the mayor's office, with an imam's written confirmation as support
When no physician is available, the civil registrar may accept a certification of the fact of death signed by the mayor, the SB secretary or an SB member; the health officer adds the cause later
Funeral homes may not accept or embalm a body without a death declaration or medical certificate, must use licensed embalmers, keep a logbook and face quarterly inspections
No hospital, clinic or funeral home may withhold remains or death papers over unpaid bills; promissory notes are allowed
The health officer may use the SmartVA verbal autopsy tool and may issue a post facto certificate with the cause marked 'undetermined'

provisions.title: Every death declared by a doctor
provisions.text: All deaths must be declared by a licensed physician or the Municipal Health Officer. For a home death with no doctor, the family notifies the BHERT, health office or LDRRMO, and the health officer examines the body on site and issues a Certificate of Death Declaration.

provisions.title: Who certifies each kind of death
provisions.text: The last attending physician certifies facility deaths, the ER doctor on duty certifies ER deaths, and the health officer certifies unattended deaths, using verbal autopsy if needed. Deaths in moving vehicles are reported to the health officer where they occur.

provisions.title: Medico-legal cases go to the PNP or NBI
provisions.text: Deaths that meet medico-legal criteria, or that suggest injury, violence or poisoning, are referred at once to the PNP, the NBI or a medico-legal officer.

provisions.title: Immediate burial for Muslims and IPs
provisions.text: Muslims and indigenous communities may bury at once, with or without a certificate. Under RA 12160 the death is reported within 14 days after burial to the health officer, or the Mayor's office if none, with an imam's or cultural leader's written confirmation as support.

provisions.title: Officials may certify the fact of death
provisions.text: When no doctor is available, the civil registrar may accept a certification of the fact of death signed by the Mayor, the SB secretary or an SB member, backed by barangay papers or affidavits. The health officer adds the cause of death later.

provisions.title: Funeral home rules
provisions.text: Funeral homes may not accept, store or embalm a body without a death declaration or medical certificate, must use only licensed embalmers, meet DOH sanitation standards, and keep a logbook of each body, its papers, the embalmer's licence and its release.

provisions.title: Quarterly inspections and a hotline
provisions.text: The health office leads enforcement with the permits office, BHERTs and the LDRRMO, inspects funeral homes quarterly with spot checks on complaints, and sets up a hotline for violations and death reports.

provisions.title: Late registration and post facto certificates
provisions.text: For undeclared deaths, the registrar may require affidavits of 2 witnesses and a barangay certification. The health officer may issue a post facto certificate using verbal autopsy tools such as SmartVA, marking the cause 'undetermined' when evidence is thin.

provisions.title: No holding bodies over unpaid bills
provisions.text: No hospital, clinic or funeral home may withhold remains or death papers over unpaid bills; they may take a promissory note instead. Unclaimed and indigent remains are handled with the social welfare office.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: A first offence draws a warning and a compliance seminar; a second a fine of up to ₱2,000 and up to 3 days' permit suspension; a third or later a fine of up to ₱2,500 and a recommended permit revocation. Funded from the health office's budget.

ordinances.penalties: Written warning and a compliance seminar; then a fine of up to ₱2,000 and up to 3 days' permit suspension; then up to ₱2,500 and a recommendation to revoke the business permit
ordinances.caveat: OCR of a scanned copy: the number is garbled in some page headers, the civil registry step appears twice, and the effectivity clause cites RA 7160 s. 511.

details.effect: after posting and publication under RA 7160 Section 511
details.covers: All deaths in Kalilangan and the funeral homes operating there
details.enforcers: Municipal Health Office, with the BPLO, BHERTs and LDRRMO
creates: Hotline for reporting violations and death declarations
details.funding: Existing budget of the Municipal Health Office

highlights.label: after burial to report a Muslim death
top fine for repeat violations
funeral home inspections a year, plus spot checks
bodies held back for unpaid hospital or funeral bills

barmm.why: Worth reading if deaths in your LGU go unregistered because families bury at once, live far from a doctor, or cannot pay hospital bills. Kalilangan's 2026 ordinance fits immediate burial into civil registration, gives home deaths a clear reporting path, and stops facilities from holding bodies over unpaid bills. Its penalties are within the municipal limit, but it names national health and interior offices throughout.

apply.if: If your LGU has a municipal health officer or rural health unit physician
apply.then: you can replicate this by making that physician the certifier for home deaths and the reviewer of every death certificate before it goes to the civil registrar.

apply.if: If families in your LGU bury their dead within the day
apply.then: copy the 14-day post-burial report, the imam's or cultural leader's written confirmation, and the post facto certificate.

apply.if: If your LGU has no doctor available in remote barangays
apply.then: start with the reporting chain through barangay health teams and the disaster office, and the rule letting named officials certify the fact of death for registration.

apply.if: If there are funeral homes in your LGU
apply.then: add the document check, licensed-embalmer rule, logbook and quarterly inspections, enforced with the business permits office.

apply.if: If hospitals or funeral homes have held bodies over unpaid bills
apply.then: copy the ban on withholding remains and death papers, with promissory notes allowed.

change: Rename the Department of Health to the Ministry of Health and the DILG to the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government where they set or check local rules; keep national bodies such as the PSA, PNP and NBI

Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare, including health and sanitation) and name the health officer (BLGC s. 532) and civil registrar (BLGC s. 533). A health officer is mandatory only for provinces and cities, so if your municipality has none, name the physician who will act
Replace the effectivity clause's 'RA 7160 Section 511' with BLGC s. 571: posting in 3 places for 6 weeks, publication, and transmittal to the Bangsamoro Gazette within 12 days
Keep penalties within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); Kalilangan's ₱2,500 top fine already fits

Say which imams, ulama or cultural leaders may sign the post-burial confirmation, and check the rule letting the mayor, SB secretary or an SB member certify the fact of death against current PSA rules before copying it
barmm.fits: Municipalities with Muslim or indigenous communities that bury at once, or with home deaths far from a doctor, and any LGU with funeral homes to regulate.

ordinances.title: Revised Revenue Code of the Municipality of Magsaysay
ordinances.shortTitle: Revised Revenue Code of Magsaysay, Davao del Sur
ordinances.summary: Magsaysay's full municipal revenue code under the Local Government Code of 1991. It sets the graduated business taxes, the mayor's permit and regulatory fees, service fees, charges for markets, parking, waterworks, cemeteries and the slaughterhouse, and the community tax. It also adds 7 earmarked fees, from a scholarship fee to an archival fee, to transactions with municipal offices, and lays down collection, civil remedies and taxpayer remedies for everyone doing business or dealing with the municipality.
points: Retailers pay 2.2% of yearly sales up to ₱400,000 and 1.1% above; manufacturers pay ₱184.80 to ₱29,676.90 a year by bracket, then 41.25% of 1% above ₱6.5 million; stores selling ₱30,000 or less are left to the barangays
1% of gross receipts on mobile traders and on forest concessions, 2% on mining operations, and a yearly tax of ₱500 to ₱1,500 per unit on bus, jeepney, taxi and multicab operators

7 earmarked add-on fees (scholarship, environment, road maintenance, security, sanitation, garbage, archives), each to be spent only on its listed purpose, such as scholarships for local students and LGU midwife scholars

Mayor's permit fee by enterprise size, from ₱100 for micro to ₱2,000 for large businesses (₱1,000 to ₱5,000 for banks), based on assets or workers, whichever gives the higher fee, plus the scholarship and environment fees
Market stalls at ₱35 to ₱50 per sq. m. a month; parking from ₱2 a day for tricycles to ₱25 for buses and trucks, with 15% of overnight parking fees going to the barangay that helps enforce it
Community tax of ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income (up to ₱5,000) for individuals and ₱500 plus up to ₱10,000 for corporations; 50% of what barangay treasurers collect stays with the barangay
Late payment draws a 25% surcharge and 2% a month interest for at most 36 months; the council may adjust rates once every 5 years by no more than 10%

provisions.title: Graduated tax on manufacturers and retailers
provisions.text: Manufacturers and similar businesses pay ₱184.80 to ₱29,676.90 a year by bracket of gross sales, then 41.25% of 1% above ₱6.5 million. Retailers pay 2.2% of yearly sales up to ₱400,000 and 1.1% above; stores selling ₱30,000 or less are left for the barangays to tax.

provisions.title: Taxes on traders, transport, mining and forests
provisions.text: Mobile traders pay 1% of gross receipts, mining operations 2% and forest concessions 1%. Public utility operators pay a yearly tax per unit, from ₱500 for multicabs and ₱600 for jeepneys and taxis to ₱1,500 for air-conditioned buses.

provisions.title: 7 earmarked fees on municipal transactions
provisions.text: Anyone transacting with a municipal office pays a scholarship, environment, road maintenance, security, sanitation, garbage and archival fee. Each may be spent only on its listed purpose, such as scholarships for local high-school and college students and LGU midwife scholars.

provisions.title: Mayor's permit fee by enterprise size
provisions.text: Businesses pay a yearly permit fee by size, from ₱100 for micro to ₱2,000 for large firms, plus ₱10 to ₱30 each in scholarship and environment fees. Size is set by assets or workers, whichever gives the higher fee; banks pay ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 and cell sites up to ₱25,000.

provisions.title: Parking charges, with a barangay share
provisions.text: Day parking runs from ₱2 for tricycles to ₱25 for buses and cargo trucks; overnight parking is ₱10 a day or ₱3,600 a year. Barangays that help enforce night-parking rules keep 15% of the fees from their area. Towing costs ₱300 and impounding ₱100 a day.

provisions.title: Market stall rentals
provisions.text: Fixed stalls in the public market rent for ₱35 to ₱50 per sq. m a month depending on the section, and fish and meat stalls in the wet section ₱300.

provisions.title: Community tax, half kept by barangays
provisions.text: Individuals pay ₱5 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 of income, up to ₱5,000; corporations ₱500 plus ₱2 per ₱5,000 of property or receipts, up to ₱10,000. Half of what barangay treasurers collect stays with the barangay.

provisions.title: Surcharge and interest for late payment
provisions.text: Taxes are due within the first 20 days of January or of each quarter. Late payment draws a 25% surcharge and up to 2% interest a month, for no more than 36 months.

provisions.title: Rate changes and penalties
provisions.text: The council may adjust rates no more than once every 5 years and by no more than 10%. Violations carry a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both, without excusing the unpaid tax.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 to ₱5,000, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both; the president or manager answers for a juridical entity, and the tax stays due
ordinances.amends: Repeals ordinances in conflict with it; no earlier revenue code is named
ordinances.caveat: Parts of the code are carried over from a model template and were not tidied: blanks around the mining and forest tax rates, an 'alternative' parking schedule, a note that 'a separate Market Code is recommended', and pauper-litigant rules that refer to Metro Manila.

details.effect: 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation
details.covers: Everyone doing business, transacting with municipal offices or using municipal facilities
details.enforcers: Municipal Treasurer, with the mayor's office, municipal engineer and barangay treasurers

tax on a retailer's first ₱400,000 of yearly sales

of community tax a barangay collects stays with it

barmm.why: Worth reading if your municipality is revising an old revenue code and wants a complete, recent model built for a small municipality rather than a city. Magsaysay's 2019 code covers business taxes, permit and service fees, municipal charges, the community tax and collection remedies in one place, and shows how to earmark fees for scholarships, waste management and roads. Several of its rates sit above or below what the BLGC now sets, its penal clause is below the BLGC floor for tax ordinances, and template leftovers remain in the text.

apply.if: If your revenue code predates the BLGC
apply.then: you can use Magsaysay's chapter order (business taxes, permit fees, service fees, municipal charges, community tax, collection and remedies) as the outline, and fill each schedule from the BLGC ceilings rather than copying Magsaysay's figures.

apply.if: If you want fees that pay for scholarships, waste management or road upkeep
apply.then: copy the idea of naming each add-on fee and listing what it may be spent on, and keep the proceeds in a trust fund so they cannot be used for anything else.

apply.if: If your barangays help collect the community tax or police night parking
apply.then: copy the shares: 50% of the community tax collected by a bonded barangay treasurer and 15% of overnight parking fees from its area go to the barangay.

apply.if: If your LGU does not run a waterworks system, slaughterhouse, toll road or cockpit
apply.then: skip those articles; drafting charges for facilities you do not operate only invites confusion.

apply.if: If you have no records of business gross sales
apply.then: start with the sworn statement of gross sales and the yearly submission of a certified income tax return by 30 April, which Magsaysay uses to check declared sales.

change: Reset every business tax schedule to BLGC s. 167. Magsaysay's top manufacturer bracket (₱29,676.90, then 41.25% of 1% above ₱6.5 million) and its 2.2% and 1.1% retail rates exceed the s. 167 figures of ₱24,375, 37.5% of 1%, 2% and 1%; add the half rate for dealers in essential goods and exclude duly registered Islamic banks from the bank tax.
Raise the community tax to BLGC s. 180 and s. 181: ₱20 plus ₱1 per ₱1,000 for individuals, and ₱1,000 plus ₱5 per ₱5,000 for corporations. Magsaysay's ₱5, ₱500 and ₱2 are the old amounts.

Raise the penal clause to the range in BLGC s. 576 (₱40,000 to ₱1,200,000 and 1 to 6 months); Magsaysay's ₱1,000 to ₱5,000 falls below the floor. Keep the surcharge and interest within BLGC s. 191, or replace interest with a Shari'ah-compliant late-payment rule under s. 153.

Hold each earmarked fee in a trust fund used only for its purpose (BLGC s. 333), and check that each is a reasonable charge for a service; if it is really a tax, levy it under s. 211 after a public hearing. Check the per-unit tax on bus and jeepney operators against the bar on taxing common carriers in s. 156, and re-cite pioneer exemptions to the Bangsamoro Board of Investments.

Remove the template leftovers, then hold public hearings and publish under BLGC s. 212 and s. 213, including the Bangsamoro Online Register of Ordinances; the code takes effect only 15 days after publication.
barmm.fits: Municipalities rewriting a pre-BLGC revenue code that want a complete small-municipality model to work from.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Institutionalizing the Damgo sa Kabukiran Program of the Municipality of Magsaysay, Davao del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Damgo sa Kabukiran Program Ordinance of Magsaysay
ordinances.summary: Magsaysay's short ordinance making the mayor's Damgo sa Kabukiran program permanent. Any barangay that opens a farm access road joins the program, and farmers along it are required to plant perennial crops, fruit trees and forest trees. The municipal engineer and agriculturist deliver it for barangays that ask the mayor's office for help.
points: Institutionalizes Damgo sa Kabukiran in the Office of the Mayor as a long-running program for opening an access road in every barangay
A barangay that opens an access road takes part in the program automatically
Farmers are required to carry out massive planting of perennial crops, fruit-bearing trees and reforestation in return
The Municipal Engineer's office facilitates the road work once the mayor approves
The Municipal Agriculturist's office distributes the planting materials
Policy aims include farm tourism, sustainable farm practices and upland biodiversity; funds are to be appropriated, with no amount set

provisions.title: Trees and farms as municipal policy
provisions.text: The municipality commits to massive reforestation and perennial crops to keep upland biodiversity, to environment-friendly and sustainable farm practices, and to farm tourism combining agriculture and recreation.

provisions.title: Open to every barangay that asks
provisions.text: The ordinance covers every Sangguniang Barangay in Magsaysay that wants to avail of the program from the Office of the Municipal Mayor.

provisions.title: Damgo sa Kabukiran made permanent
provisions.text: The program is institutionalized in the Office of the Municipal Mayor as a long-running program for opening an access road in every barangay.

provisions.title: Farmers plant trees in return
provisions.text: Farmers served by the program are required to carry out massive planting of perennial crops, fruit-bearing trees and reforestation.

provisions.title: Opening a road means joining the program
provisions.text: A barangay that undertakes the opening of an access road takes part in Damgo sa Kabukiran automatically.

provisions.title: The engineer handles the road work
provisions.text: The Office of the Municipal Engineer facilitates the program once the mayor approves it.

provisions.title: The agriculturist hands out seedlings
provisions.text: The Office of the Municipal Agriculturist facilitates the distribution of the planting materials the program covers.

provisions.title: Funding left to the budget
provisions.text: The funds needed to run the program are to be appropriated for it, with no amount set. The ordinance takes effect on approval.

ordinances.caveat: This copy numbers its sections 1 to 5 with repeats, sets no budget or planting quota, and leaves the mayor's approval date blank.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Barangays of Magsaysay that open an access road and avail of the program, and their farmers
details.enforcers: Office of the Mayor, with the Municipal Engineer and Municipal Agriculturist
details.funding: Funds to be appropriated, amount not set

highlights.label: enrolment for any barangay opening an access road
kinds of planting: perennial crops, fruit trees, forest trees
municipal offices that deliver it, engineer and agriculturist

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU opens farm-to-market or access roads into upland barangays and wants each road to bring tree planting with it. Magsaysay ties road opening to a duty on farmers to plant perennial crops, fruit trees and forest trees. The text is 2 pages and only states the idea: it sets no planting quota, no budget, no selection rules and no way to check that the planting happens.

apply.if: If your LGU already opens barangay access roads with a municipal engineer
apply.then: you can replicate this by making every road request carry a planting plan, signed by the farmers served, that the agriculturist approves before work starts.

apply.if: If your agriculturist runs a nursery or receives seedlings from a ministry program
apply.then: name that source in the ordinance and set how many seedlings go to each road, per kilometre or per farmer.

apply.if: If you want the planting to be checked
apply.then: add what Magsaysay leaves out: a planting quota, a survival count after 1 year by the agriculturist or environment officer, and what happens to a barangay that does not comply.

apply.if: If an access road would pass through forest land, a watershed or ancestral domain
apply.then: require clearance from the environment officer and consultation with the community first, and plant native species there rather than fruit trees.

apply.if: If your LGU has no fund for road opening
apply.then: start with the planting half of the idea, tied to roads the barangays build with their own funds, and add municipal road support when it is budgeted.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 and s. 480 (municipal agriculture, infrastructure and environment services) and s. 408 (barangay farm-to-market roads), instead of the general welfare policy alone.
Spell out the funding: which budget pays for road opening and planting materials, and how much, rather than 'shall be appropriated for the purpose'.

Give the duties to the officers the BLGC names: the engineer (s. 531) for the road, the agriculturist (s. 536) for planting materials, and the environment officer (s. 538) for reforestation and watersheds.

Where planting materials or reforestation sites come under the Bangsamoro Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform or the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy, name them as partners and get their sign-off.
Fix the numbering, add a quota and a monitoring rule, and state what the farmers' planting duty means for those who do not plant.
barmm.fits: Upland and farming municipalities that open barangay access roads and have an agriculturist with planting materials to give out.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Shortening the Processing Time in Granting Municipal Business Permits and/or Licenses to Clients/Applicants Consistent with Republic Act No. 9485, Otherwise Known as Anti-Red Tape Act (ARTA) of 2007
ordinances.shortTitle: Business Permit Streamlining Ordinance of Catarman, Camiguin
ordinances.summary: A short ordinance that sets how Catarman processes business permits under the Anti-Red Tape Act of 2007. It fixes 5 standard steps, a one-stop shop, a single joint inspection and a ceiling of 10 days for new permits and 5 days for renewals. It covers every applicant for a new or renewed municipal business permit and the municipal offices that process them.
points: 5 standard steps for new and renewal permits: get the form, file it with the requirements, one-time assessment, one-time payment, then release of the Mayor's Permit on showing the receipts
New permits take no more than 10 days, aiming for 5 or less; renewals no more than 5 days, aiming for 1 day or less
A barangay clearance comes first and must be acted on within 7 working days; the sangguniang barangay may charge a reasonable fee

A joint inspection team of 6 (business permit officer, engineer, health officer, planning or zoning/environment officer, treasurer and fire marshal) inspects once and signs one Joint Certificate of Compliance
All staff who process business permits sit together in a one-stop shop
Only 2 signatories on the permit: the mayor and the treasurer, or their deputies
The permit may be released before SSS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth clearances are in, if they follow within 1 month; otherwise it is revoked or not renewed

provisions.title: 5 standard steps for every permit
provisions.text: New and renewal applicants get the form, file it with the requirements, have taxes and fees assessed once, pay once, and receive the Mayor's Permit on showing the official receipts.

provisions.title: Barangay clearance first, within 7 working days
provisions.text: No business permit is issued without a clearance from the barangay where the business is; the sangguniang barangay may charge a reasonable fee and must act on it within 7 working days of filing.

provisions.title: One joint inspection, one certificate
provisions.text: A joint inspection team inspects each business once instead of each office separately, and all members sign a single Joint Certificate of Compliance.

provisions.title: A 6-member joint inspection team
provisions.text: The team is the business permit and licensing officer, the municipal engineer, the municipal health officer, the planning and development coordinator or zoning/environment officer, the municipal treasurer and the municipal fire marshal.

provisions.title: A one-stop shop for business permits
provisions.text: All staff who process business permit applications sit together in one common site to receive and process applications through a streamlined procedure.

provisions.title: 10 days for new permits, 5 for renewals
provisions.text: A new permit takes no more than 10 days, aiming for 5 or less; a renewal takes no more than 5 days, aiming for 1 day or less.

provisions.title: Only 2 signatures on the permit
provisions.text: The business permit needs only the signatures of the municipal mayor and the municipal treasurer, or their authorised representatives.

provisions.title: Release before SSS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth clearances
provisions.text: Once fees are paid, the permit may be released even without SSS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth clearances, which must follow within 1 month or the permit is revoked or not renewed.

provisions.title: A ₱500 fine or a week in jail
provisions.text: Violating any prohibitory provision is punished by a ₱500 fine, 1 week's imprisonment, or both, at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Takes effect 1 January 2016
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect on 1 January 2016, after approval and the publication or posting required by the Local Government Code.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 or 1 week in jail, or both, at the court's discretion, for violating any prohibitory provision
ordinances.caveat: This is an unsigned typed copy, and it follows the 2007 Anti-Red Tape Act, whose processing limits the 2018 Ease of Doing Business Act (RA 11032) has since shortened.

details.effect: January 1, 2016, after posting or publication
details.covers: Every applicant for a new or renewed municipal business permit in Catarman
details.enforcers: Business permit and licensing staff, the joint inspection team, the mayor and the treasurer

highlights.label: at most to issue a new business permit
at most for a renewal, aiming for 1
signatories on the permit: mayor and treasurer
to bring SSS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth papers

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if business permits in your LGU pass through several offices, each with its own inspection and signature. Catarman's 2015 ordinance cuts this to 5 steps, one joint inspection, one shared site and 2 signatures, and lets a permit go out before the national agency clearances arrive. It is 5 pages and simple, but it follows the 2007 Anti-Red Tape Act: its 10-day and 5-day limits are longer than the 2018 Ease of Doing Business Act allows, and its penalty clause names no offence.

apply.if: If your LGU already runs a business one-stop shop
apply.then: you can replicate the joint inspection team and the single Joint Certificate of Compliance, so the engineer, health officer, zoning officer, treasurer and fire marshal inspect once and sign one form.

apply.if: If your permit staff still sit in separate offices
apply.then: start by seating them in one place, as Catarman's section 8 requires, before buying any software.

apply.if: If applicants wait weeks on SSS, Pag-IBIG or PhilHealth clearances
apply.then: copy the rule that releases the permit on payment and gives the business 1 month to bring them, with revocation or non-renewal if it does not.

apply.if: If your business permit carries many signatures
apply.then: cut them to the mayor and the treasurer or their deputies.

apply.if: If you want deadlines and penalties in the ordinance
apply.then: use the working-day limits of the Ease of Doing Business Act instead of Catarman's 10 and 5 days, and list the offences (extra requirements, unreceipted fees, fixing) that its penalty clause leaves out.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 151, which requires a Business One-Stop Shop and a standardised permit system, and to RA 11032 (Ease of Doing Business Act of 2018) in place of RA 9485, which RA 11032 amended.
Replace the 10-day and 5-day limits with the RA 11032 limits of 3 working days for simple and 7 for complex transactions, and set the barangay clearance time to match.
Write out the prohibited acts before keeping a penalty clause, keep any penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489), and post and publish it as a penal ordinance under s. 571.
Name the fire station that serves your LGU on the inspection team, and use the environment and natural resources officer (BLGC s. 538) where Catarman names a zoning/environment officer.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a small business permit office that want a short streamlining rule before a full ease-of-doing-business ordinance.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Protecting Coconut Producers and Farmers from Thievery of Coconuts, namely: Matured (Tibuok Lubi) and Young Coconuts (Butong)
ordinances.shortTitle: Anti-Coconut Thievery Ordinance of Catarman, Camiguin
ordinances.summary: A short ordinance against the theft of mature and young coconuts. It requires every coconut, copra and young-coconut producer to get a permit from the punong barangay where the plantation is before each harvest. Each permit costs ₱20 per parcel, paid to the barangay.
points: Coconut, copra and butong (young coconut) producers must get a permit from the punong barangay of the plantation's barangay just before harvesting
The barangay collects ₱20 per parcel of coconut plantation for every permit, and the money goes to barangay funds
Covers both mature coconuts (tibuok lubi) and young coconuts (butong)
Violations carry a fine of up to ₱2,000, or up to 60 days in jail, or both, at the court's discretion
Takes effect after a public hearing and posting in conspicuous places in the municipality

provisions.title: A barangay permit before every harvest
provisions.text: Every coconut, copra and butong (young coconut) producer must get a permit from the Office of the Punong Barangay where the plantation is, just before harvesting.

provisions.title: Covers mature and young coconuts
provisions.text: The rule is aimed at the theft of both mature coconuts (tibuok lubi) and young coconuts (butong).

provisions.title: ₱20 a parcel, kept by the barangay
provisions.text: The barangay may charge ₱20 per parcel of coconut plantation for every permit it issues, and the money goes to barangay funds.

provisions.title: Fine of up to ₱2,000 or 60 days
provisions.text: A violation is punished by a fine of up to ₱2,000, jail of up to 60 days, or both, at the court's discretion.

provisions.title: Takes effect after hearing and posting
provisions.text: It takes effect after a public hearing and after it is posted in conspicuous places in the municipality.

ordinances.penalties: Fine of up to ₱2,000, or up to 60 days in jail, or both, at the court's discretion
ordinances.caveat: The ordinance never defines the offence beyond harvesting without a permit, says nothing about buyers or checks at the point of sale, and its second page is headed 'Resolution No. 12' although it is the ordinance.

details.effect: after a public hearing and posting in conspicuous places
details.covers: Coconut, copra and young-coconut producers harvesting in Catarman
details.enforcers: Punong barangays, who issue the harvest permits
details.funding: ₱20 permit fee per parcel, credited to barangay funds

highlights.label: per plantation parcel for each harvest permit
maximum fine for harvesting without a permit
maximum jail term, with or without the fine

barmm.why: Worth reading if coconut farmers in your LGU lose nuts to people who harvest and sell them without the owner knowing. Catarman's answer is simple: no harvest without a barangay permit, so anyone harvesting can be asked to show one. It is 2 pages and easy to copy, but it does not say who checks permits, does nothing about buyers of stolen nuts, and lets a municipal ordinance set a barangay fee.

apply.if: If your barangays already keep a register of farmers
apply.then: you can replicate this by tying the harvest permit to that register, so the punong barangay can confirm quickly that the applicant owns or tends the parcel.

apply.if: If most theft ends with copra buyers or traders
apply.then: add what Catarman left out: require buyers to ask for the harvest permit or a barangay certificate before buying, and keep a simple log of purchases.

apply.if: If you want the barangays to keep the permit fee
apply.then: have each sangguniang barangay set the fee by its own ordinance, since barangay fees come from the barangay's own taxing power, and keep the fee low so small farmers are not burdened.

apply.if: If your tanods patrol farm areas
apply.then: name them as the ones who may ask harvesters for the permit and report violators, and say what happens to coconuts taken without one.

change: Let each barangay levy the harvest permit fee by its own ordinance under BLGC s. 175, or turn the ₱20 into a municipal fee with a stated share to the barangay; a municipal ordinance should not fix a barangay's fee for it.

Keep the penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); Catarman's ₱2,000 and 60 days already fit. Define the offence clearly, and leave the theft itself to the Revised Penal Code, which treats coconuts taken from a plantation as qualified theft.
Name the punong barangay as issuer and the tanods as enforcers (BLGC s. 417 and s. 408), and involve the municipal agriculturist in the farmer list (s. 536).
Post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571, in the local language, instead of Catarman's open-ended 'after public hearing and posting'.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with coconut farms where harvesting by outsiders is a common complaint.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Levying Fees, Charges, Rentals, Fixing Price of Pasalubong Items for Sale and Other Facilities Likewise for Rent to Any Person Who May Avail the Facilities Herein Above Referred to and Providing Penalties Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Coastal Eco-Tourism Center Fees Ordinance of Catarman
ordinances.summary: Catarman's fee schedule for its Coastal Eco-Tourism Center at Bonbon, run by the Municipal Economic Enterprise Development Office (MEEDO). It sets rates for snorkelling and diving gear, boats, dive packages, a cliff trail, comfort rooms and showers, charges private guides and boats working in the marine protected areas, and fixes the mark-ups at the center's pasalubong shop. It applies to anyone who uses the center or its tours.
points: Snorkel set ₱50 a person; dive gear ₱100 to ₱250 an item a day; air tank refill ₱200
Dive boat ₱500 a day at Bonbon Pasil or ₱1,000 to other dive sites; intro dive lesson ₱2,500 and fun dive ₱1,700, of which ₱150 goes to the municipality and the rest to the dive service provider
Pump boat for up to 10 people ₱2,500 a trip for dolphin or whale watching and ₱4,000 for an inter-municipal tour; glass boat for up to 6 people ₱300 a trip
Legaspi Trail entrance ₱10, split ₱5 and ₱5; comfort room ₱10 or ₱5; shower ₱10, free for snorkel, swim and dive customers
Private operators in the MPAs pay ₱150 a batch of up to 3 for snorkel guiding, ₱20 a person for boat service and ₱300 a trip for a glass boat
Goods consigned to the pasalubong center carry a 20% mark-up kept by MEEDO; MEEDO's own goods carry 5%; licensed snorkel and swim guides pay ₱150 a year for a mayor's permit
Fees are paid before the service to center staff, who issue official receipts; the Local Finance Committee and the SB committee on economic enterprise oversee the center

provisions.title: Snorkel and dive gear rental
provisions.text: A full snorkel set (flotation device, mask, snorkel, flippers and boots) is ₱50 a person. Dive gear rents by the day: ₱150 each for a buoyancy control device or regulator, ₱100 for a mask, snorkel, boots or flippers; a filled air tank is ₱250 and a refill ₱200.

provisions.title: Dive boats and dive packages
provisions.text: A dive boat is ₱500 a day at Bonbon Pasil or ₱1,000 to other dive sites. An intro dive lesson is ₱2,500 and a fun dive ₱1,700 with all gear; ₱150 of each goes to the municipality and the rest to the dive service provider.

provisions.title: Boat tours
provisions.text: A pump boat for up to 10 people costs ₱2,500 a trip for dolphin or whale watching and ₱4,000 for an inter-municipal tour; a glass boat for up to 6 is ₱300 a trip around the mapped Bonbon Pasil route.

provisions.title: Trail, comfort rooms and showers
provisions.text: Entrance to the Legaspi Trail along the Lawigan cliffs is ₱10, split ₱5 to the municipality and ₱5 to the service provider. Comfort rooms are ₱10 or ₱5 for urinal use; showers are ₱10, free for snorkel, swim and dive customers.

provisions.title: Charges on private operators in the MPAs
provisions.text: Private snorkel guides pay ₱150 a batch of up to 3 people in the Bonbon Pasil, Catibac, Lawigan and Poblacion marine protected areas; private boats pay ₱20 a person to the Bonbon Pasil MPA and private glass boats ₱300 a trip.

provisions.title: Pasalubong center mark-ups
provisions.text: Goods consigned by private sellers to the Municipal Tourism Center carry a 20% mark-up kept by MEEDO as revenue; goods MEEDO buys itself for display carry a 5% mark-up.

provisions.title: A permit for snorkel and swim guides
provisions.text: Trained guides operating in the marine protected areas pay ₱150 a year for a Mayor's permit as licensed guides.

provisions.title: Pay first, get a receipt
provisions.text: Fees are paid to the center's authorized staff before the service, and they issue an official receipt.

provisions.title: Run by MEEDO, overseen by the council
provisions.text: The Municipal Economic Enterprise Development Office runs the Coastal Eco-Tourism Center, overseen by the Local Finance Committee and the Sangguniang Bayan committee on economic enterprise.

provisions.title: Penalty
provisions.text: Violators are fined ₱2,500 or jailed for up to 2 weeks, and must pay the fees for the services they used. The ordinance takes effect on approval.

ordinances.penalties: ₱2,500 fine or up to 2 weeks in jail, plus payment of the unpaid fees
ordinances.caveat: The minutes date the special session to 19 September 2014 but the ordinance says it was enacted on 18 September, and despite its title it fixes mark-ups rather than prices for pasalubong items.

details.effect: immediately upon approval
details.covers: Users of the Coastal Eco-Tourism Center at Bonbon, its tours and the municipality's MPAs
details.enforcers: MEEDO, overseen by the Local Finance Committee and the SB Committee on Economic Enterprise

highlights.label: mark-up kept on goods consigned to the pasalubong center
a trip for a pump boat tour of up to 10 people
a year for a licensed guide's permit in the MPAs
fine for not paying, on top of the fee owed

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU runs, or plans, a beach, dive or river tourism facility and needs a fee schedule for it. Catarman prices each service, splits dive and trail fees with private service providers, and charges private guides and boats that work inside its marine protected areas. It is short and easy to copy, but it was written for one coastal center, its rates date from 2014, and it skipped the steps a revenue measure needs before taking effect.

apply.if: If your LGU already runs a tourism facility as an economic enterprise
apply.then: you can replicate this by listing each service with its rate, unit and who keeps the money, as Catarman's table does, and naming the enterprise office that collects.

apply.if: If private dive shops, boatmen or guides deliver the services
apply.then: copy the split, such as ₱150 of each dive package to the municipality, and put the rest of the terms in a written agreement with each provider.

apply.if: If your waters or rivers have protected areas that visitors use
apply.then: copy the charges on private guides and boats working inside them and the yearly permit for trained guides, so only licensed guides take visitors in.

apply.if: If you sell local products at a visitor center
apply.then: copy the consignment rule, a fixed mark-up such as 20% kept by the enterprise, instead of fixing each item's price in the ordinance.

apply.if: If your LGU has no tourism facility yet
apply.then: skip the schedule for now and keep the structure: rates by service, payment before service, official receipts and a finance committee check.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 21 (fees and property held in a proprietary capacity) and s. 480 (municipal tourism services), and hold a public hearing before enactment as s. 212 requires for revenue measures.
Replace 'effective immediately upon approval' with publication under s. 213: published or posted within 10 days of approval and in force 15 days after publication.

Keep the penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); Catarman's ₱2,500 or 2 weeks fits. If your council treats the schedule as a tax ordinance, s. 576 sets a ₱40,000 minimum fine, which is out of proportion to ₱10 to ₱4,000 fees, so frame these as charges for the use of municipal facilities.
Have fees collected by the treasurer's deputised collectors, since s. 152 bars letting collection to a private person, and state in a contract how the providers' shares are paid out.

Fix the drafting before copying: the title promises fixed prices for pasalubong items that the schedule does not set, the table does not say clearly which column receives each share, and there are two sections numbered 7.
barmm.fits: Coastal and river municipalities with a tourism facility or protected area they run themselves, ideally with a tourism officer or economic enterprise office.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Regulating the Operation and Management of Piggery, Poultry and Other Livestock Raising in the Municipality of Camaligan
ordinances.shortTitle: Piggery, Poultry and Livestock Ordinance of Camaligan, Camarines Sur
ordinances.summary: Regulates where and how piggery, poultry and other livestock farms may operate in Camaligan, to cut foul odour, flies and water pollution. It sets distances from homes, roads, water sources and other farms, requires biogas digesters or septic tanks, and makes a municipal task force's certificate to operate a condition of the business permit. It covers new, expanding, revived and existing commercial and backyard farms.
points: A backyard piggery is 1 sow and up to 10 heads, a backyard poultry up to 500 fowls; both are allowed in rural areas only
Commercial farms at least 500 m from built-up areas in the land use plan, backyard farms 200 m, and all farms 25 m from any drinking-water source
Commercial piggeries 500 m and commercial poultry farms 200 m from the national highway and major roads; commercial farms 1 km apart, backyard farms 500 m
Every piggery, backyard ones included, needs a watertight concrete biogas digester or septic tank sized to the herd

A Municipal Task Force chaired by the mayor, with the agriculture officer as vice-chair and seats for hog and poultry raisers, inspects farms and issues the certificate to operate needed for a business permit

The agriculture officer runs a census of all farms; commercial farms register with the agriculture and health offices, every farm with its barangay, and new or expanding farms need a zoning development permit
Discharging animal waste into canals, rivers, riverbanks or any water body is banned; a farm idle more than 1 year applies as new

provisions.title: New, expanding and revived farms are covered
provisions.text: It applies to every application to set up or expand a piggery or poultry farm, and existing farms must comply. A farm idle for more than 1 year that restarts is treated as a new application.

provisions.title: What a backyard farm is
provisions.text: A backyard piggery is 1 sow and up to 10 heads, and backyard poultry up to 500 fowls. Both are allowed in rural areas only, outside the poblacion, business district and other built-up areas.

provisions.title: A Municipal Task Force issues the certificate to operate
provisions.text: Chaired by the Mayor with the Municipal Agriculture Officer as vice-chair, plus the planning officer, sanitation officer, police, CADRRESMO, the punong barangay and a hog raisers' and a poultry raisers' representative. It inspects farms and issues the certificate to operate required for a business permit.

provisions.title: A census, permits and registration
provisions.text: The agriculture officer takes a census of all farms. New or expanding farms need a zoning development permit, building plans approved by the Municipal Engineer and biogas plans approved by the task force. Commercial farms register with the agriculture and health offices, and every farm with its barangay.

provisions.title: Distances from homes, water and roads
provisions.text: Commercial farms must be 500 m from built-up areas and backyard farms 200 m; all farms 25 m from any drinking-water source. Commercial piggeries must be 500 m and commercial poultry farms 200 m from the national highway and major roads.

provisions.title: Farms kept apart, on suitable land
provisions.text: Commercial farms must be at least 1 km from each other and backyard farms 500 m, to limit pests and air pollution. Farms avoid flood-prone and wet soils, and commercial farms are ringed by a planted buffer zone.

provisions.title: Biogas digester or septic tank for every piggery
provisions.text: Every piggery, backyard ones included, must build a watertight concrete biogas digester or standard septic tank sized to its herd, not under a building and not within 25 m of the nearest groundwater.

provisions.title: No waste in waterways, less odour and flies
provisions.text: Discharging animal waste into irrigation canals, rivers, riverbanks or any water body is unlawful. Farms must control fly larvae chemically and feed their animals a diet that cuts the odour of their waste.

provisions.title: Fines, closure or jail
provisions.text: ₱1,000 for a 1st offence, ₱2,000 for a 2nd, and ₱2,500 and/or closure of the farm or up to 6 months in jail for a 3rd, at the court's discretion.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 for the 1st offence, ₱2,000 for the 2nd, and ₱2,500 and/or closure of the farm or up to 6 months in jail for the 3rd
ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR from a scan and reads clearly, but the ordinance sets no permit or registration fees and leaves them to other municipal and barangay ordinances.

details.effect: Upon approval and publication in a local newspaper for 2 consecutive weeks
details.covers: New, expanding, revived and existing piggery, poultry and livestock farms in Camaligan
details.enforcers: Municipal Task Force, with the agriculture office, zoning officer, engineer and barangays
creates: Municipal Task Force on piggery, poultry and livestock

highlights.label: between commercial farms and built-up areas
between one commercial farm and the next
fowls at most for backyard poultry
from any drinking-water source

barmm.why: Worth reading if complaints about pig or poultry smell, flies or waste in creeks reach your council and you have no farm siting rules. Camaligan's 2020 ordinance defines backyard and commercial farms, sets buffer distances, requires biogas digesters or septic tanks and ties the business permit to a task force inspection. Its distances assume a land use plan that marks built-up areas, it sets no fees, and it says nothing on animal disease.

apply.if: If your LGU has a land use plan that marks built-up areas
apply.then: you can replicate the distance rules as written: 500 m for commercial farms and 200 m for backyard ones, measured from those areas.

apply.if: If your land use plan is old or missing
apply.then: start with the 25 m from water sources, the ban on dumping animal waste into water and the biogas or septic tank rule, which need no map.

apply.if: If your LGU has a municipal agriculturist
apply.then: have that office run the farm census first, so you know how many farms already sit inside the new buffers before you enforce them, and give those farms a deadline, which Camaligan does not.

apply.if: If many households keep a few animals
apply.then: copy the backyard limits (1 sow and 10 heads, 500 fowls) so small raisers register with the barangay instead of applying as commercial farms.

apply.if: If pig raising is rare or not practised in your LGU
apply.then: write the scope around poultry, goats, cattle and carabao, and keep the waste, water and distance rules for them.

change: Re-cite the basis from LGC s. 447 to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare and sanitation) and s. 489; Camaligan's top penalty of ₱2,500 and 6 months already sits within the ₱5,000 and 6-month municipal cap.

Replace DENR and DA with the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform where they hold those functions, and check which office now carries the old HLURB's land use role in your area.

Put the census and registry under the agriculturist (BLGC s. 536), add the veterinarian (s. 543) to the task force if your LGU has one or shares one with the province, and give the environment officer (s. 538) the water-pollution checks.
Swap Camaligan's disaster and environment office (CADRRESMO) for your own offices, and post and publish the ordinance under s. 571, since it carries penalties.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with piggery or poultry farms growing near homes or water sources, and a land use plan that marks built-up areas.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Prohibiting Any Person or Entity to Close, Hinder, Obstruct, Suspend, or Cause the Delay of the Free Flow of Rain or Flood Waters in Any Canal, Creek or Any Existing Waterways within the Jurisdiction of Camaligan, Camarines Sur by Whatever Manner Including the Construction of Any Structure, Putting Any Materials Therein or on Its Banks, and Parking or Docking Any Vehicle (Land and Water Vessel)
ordinances.shortTitle: Waterways Protection Ordinance of Camaligan
ordinances.summary: Bans anything that blocks the flow of rain or flood water in Camaligan's creeks, canals and drainage waterways, natural or man-made, whether on public land or inside private property. It forbids building on or dumping in them, parking or docking vehicles and boats in them, and building drainage at the wrong elevation. Violators must remove the obstruction and restore the waterway at their own cost, and owners of existing obstructions were given 30 days to clear them.
points: Covers all creeks (including those on the cadastral map), roadside and boundary canals, and drainage channels in the municipality
Bans closing, obstructing or slowing the flow of rain or flood water by any means, even inside one's own property
Bans building any structure on, or putting or dumping any material in, creeks, canals and waterways
Bans parking, docking or abandoning land vehicles or boats on waterways, including covered sidewalks, and building drains at the wrong elevation
Violators must demolish obstructions and restore the waterway at their own expense on receiving a notice of violation
Obstructions built before the ordinance had to be removed within 30 days
Enforced by the mayor, the rural health unit, the police and the barangay captains

provisions.title: Every creek, canal and waterway, natural or man-made
provisions.text: The Waterways Protection Ordinance covers all creeks, canals and waterways in Camaligan, natural or man-made, to keep rain and flood water flowing freely.

provisions.title: What counts as a creek, canal or waterway
provisions.text: Creeks are natural streams that exist or appear on the municipality's cadastral map; canals are man-made roadside or property-line drains; waterways are any channel built as part of the drainage system.

provisions.title: No blocking the flow, even on your own land
provisions.text: No person or entity may close, hinder, obstruct or slow the flow of rain or flood water in any canal, creek or waterway by any means, whether it is inside or outside their property.

provisions.title: No building or dumping in waterways
provisions.text: No one may build any structure on, or place or dump any material in, creeks, canals or waterways.

provisions.title: No parking, docking or abandoned vehicles
provisions.text: No one may park, dock or abandon a land vehicle or boat on creeks, canals and waterways, including covered sidewalks, or build a drain or waterway at the wrong elevation for water to flow.

provisions.title: ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 or up to 6 months in jail
provisions.text: Violators face a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both, at the court's discretion. For an entity, its highest official or the head of the family answers for the penalty.

provisions.title: Remove it and restore the waterway at your cost
provisions.text: On a notice of violation, the violator must also demolish the obstruction and restore the canal, creek or waterway to its original condition at their own expense.

provisions.title: 30 days to clear old obstructions
provisions.text: Anyone who built or placed an obstruction before the ordinance was given 30 days to remove it, or face the same penalties.

provisions.title: Enforcement
provisions.text: The mayor, the Rural Health Unit, the PNP, the barangay captains and other agencies enforce the ordinance, which took effect on approval.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 to ₱2,500, or 1 to 6 months in jail, or both, at the court's discretion; for an entity, its highest official or the head of the family answers for it
ordinances.caveat: Two sections are numbered 5, and the ordinance took effect on approval although it carries penalties.

details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: All creeks, canals and drainage waterways in Camaligan, public or private
details.enforcers: Municipal mayor, rural health unit, PNP and barangay captains

highlights.label: to clear obstructions built before the ordinance
maximum fine, or up to 6 months in jail
kinds of act banned on creeks, canals and drains

barmm.why: Worth reading if flooding in your LGU is made worse by fences, extensions, fill or parked boats in creeks and canals. Camaligan's ordinance is 3 pages, reaches waterways on private land, and makes the violator pay to restore the channel. It sets no easement width, names no office to inspect, and took effect at once although a penal ordinance must first be posted.

apply.if: If your LGU has a municipal engineer
apply.then: you can replicate this by having the engineer inspect the waterways, issue the notices of violation and set the right elevation for new drains.

apply.if: If your creeks and canals have never been mapped
apply.then: start by listing them by barangay with the help of the punong barangays, and attach the list or map to the ordinance so owners know which channels are covered.

apply.if: If houses already stand over or beside your waterways
apply.then: give a longer and staged period than Camaligan's 30 days, and coordinate with your social welfare and housing programs before any demolition.

apply.if: If boats are moored in your canals or rivers
apply.then: keep the ban on docking in drainage channels, and name places where boats may be tied up instead.

apply.if: If your LGU has a disaster risk reduction office
apply.then: have it list the channels that flood first and inspect them before each rainy season.

change: Re-cite the basis to the municipality's drainage, environment and disaster duties (BLGC s. 480) and the engineer's duties over public works (s. 531); add the easements along banks under the national Water Code.

Keep penalties within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489). Replace the rule that the 'head of the family' suffers the penalty for an entity with liability for the person who did the act, while the owner or occupant must still remove the obstruction.
Post it for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571, in the local language, before it takes effect, instead of 'immediately upon approval'.
Name the engineer and the environment officer (BLGC s. 538) as inspectors alongside the barangays, and fix the double Section 5.
barmm.fits: Low-lying and river or coastal municipalities whose drainage canals and creeks run through built-up areas.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Strengthening Participatory Governance in the Municipal Government of San Roque, Northern Samar through the Empowerment of Civil Society Organizations, Establishing a People's Council, Prescribing Its Powers and Functions, and Providing for Their Participation in the Local Legislative Process, and Local Boards, Councils, Committees, Task Forces and Similar Work Groups
ordinances.shortTitle: People's Council Ordinance of San Roque
ordinances.summary: San Roque's ordinance on civil society participation. It sets how civil society organizations are accredited by the Sangguniang Bayan, makes every accredited group a member of a municipal People's Council, and lets that council choose the CSO representatives on local special bodies, boards, committees and task forces. It covers all CSOs, NGOs and people's organizations working in the municipality.
points: A CSO must have operated in San Roque for at least 1 year and apply to the SB with 8 documents: application letter, form, board resolution, registration or accreditation (NCIP certification for IP groups), list of officers, minutes, annual report and financial statement
The SB Committee on Awards, Citations and Accreditations processes applications and monitors compliance; the People's Council gets a seat on it once organized
Every accredited CSO is automatically a member of the People's Council, which the committee convenes within 90 days
The People's Council elects the CSO representatives to all local special bodies, boards, committees and task forces, up to 25% of each body's membership
It may propose legislation, take part at SB committee level and elect a representative to the Sangguniang Bayan; members serve without pay and the municipality provides office space and equipment
A help desk with a desk officer tracks CSO participation in municipal programs
The SB may withdraw recognition only on petition, for example for partisan activity, and stays out of internal disputes

provisions.title: An open partnership with people's organizations
provisions.text: The municipal government declares itself open to partnership with accredited San Roque-based people's organizations in conceiving, implementing and evaluating all its activities.

provisions.title: CSO accreditation by the Sangguniang Bayan
provisions.text: A CSO must have operated in San Roque for at least 1 year and apply to the SB with a letter, an application form, a board resolution, its registration or accreditation (NCIP certification for IP groups), and its officers list; older groups add last year's minutes, accomplishment report and financial statement.

provisions.title: Existing accreditations carry over
provisions.text: Approved CSOs receive a certificate stating the terms of accreditation; groups already accredited before the ordinance need not register again unless their accreditation was withdrawn.

provisions.title: An SB committee processes accreditation
provisions.text: The SB Committee on Awards, Citations and Accreditations receives and evaluates applications, monitors compliance and proposes measures; the People's Council gets a seat on it once organised.

provisions.title: A People's Council of all accredited CSOs
provisions.text: Every accredited CSO is automatically a member of the People's Council; the committee convenes all accredited CSOs within 90 days of effectivity to organise it, and the council elects a representative to the Sangguniang Bayan.

provisions.title: The council sets its own rules
provisions.text: The council decides its own structure and rules but must consult political parties, government employees' groups and non-member CSOs; none of these may be nominated to special bodies or get accredited CSOs' privileges.

provisions.title: Recognition by SB resolution
provisions.text: The council petitions the SB for recognition through its elected representative; the SB may withdraw it only on petition, on grounds such as partisan activity, and does not take up internal conflicts.

provisions.title: Up to 25% of seats on local bodies
provisions.text: Once recognised, the council elects its representatives to all local special bodies, boards, councils, committees and task forces, up to 25% of each body's membership.

provisions.title: Unpaid participation, with office space
provisions.text: The council takes part in municipal activities, proposes legislation and joins SB committee work without pay; the municipality provides office space, facilities and equipment, and a help desk officer monitors CSO participation.

provisions.title: Strictly non-partisan
provisions.text: The council may not engage in, or let its members be used for, partisan politics, meaning any activity that mainly campaigns for or against a party or candidate.

ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, orders and issuances (none named)
ordinances.caveat: The scan's OCR garbles some words, and the text does not say whether the People's Council representative in the Sangguniang Bayan votes or only takes part.

details.effect: upon approval and posting at the public market, municipal hall lobby and Super RHU
details.covers: CSOs, NGOs and people's organizations operating in San Roque for at least 1 year
details.enforcers: Sangguniang Bayan, through its Committee on Awards, Citations and Accreditations
details.funding: Municipality provides office space, facilities and equipment

highlights.label: cap on People's Council seats in any local body
of local operation before a CSO can be accredited
to convene accredited CSOs into a People's Council
documents a CSO files for accreditation

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU accredits CSOs one by one for the development council and other local special bodies, with no standing body to choose their representatives. San Roque lists the accreditation papers, gathers every accredited group into a People's Council and lets it pick the CSO seats. It is 5 pages and simple, but its 25% ceiling and its seat in the Sangguniang Bayan need rewriting under the BLGC.

apply.if: If your Sangguniang Bayan already accredits CSOs for local special bodies
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting San Roque's 8-document list and the 1-year operating rule, and giving the accreditation committee a deadline of 90 days to convene a People's Council.

apply.if: If your LGU has never accredited CSOs
apply.then: start with the accreditation rules and the committee, and convene the People's Council once enough groups are accredited to fill the seats.

apply.if: If your municipality has IP organizations, cooperatives or women's and youth groups
apply.then: keep San Roque's rule that accepts certification from the agency that registers them, and name the Bangsamoro offices that now issue it.

apply.if: If you want CSOs heard in the Sangguniang Bayan
apply.then: let the People's Council propose measures and take part in committee hearings, and give its representative a speaking seat without a vote.

apply.if: If your LGU has no space or budget for a CSO desk
apply.then: start with a desk officer designated from an existing office, as the ordinance allows, and add office space later.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 39, which requires LGUs to promote independent people's and non-governmental organizations as partners in local autonomy.

Turn the 25% ceiling into a floor for the development council: BLGC s. 119 requires NGOs to hold not less than one fourth of the seats of a fully organized council. Keep a ceiling only for bodies where the law sets none.

Make the People's Council representative a non-voting participant. The membership of the Sangguniang Bayan is fixed by BLGC s. 488, including its 3 sectoral representatives, and an ordinance cannot add a member.

Replace the NCIP certification for IP organizations with the Bangsamoro Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs where it carries that function, and accept registration with the Cooperative and Social Enterprise Authority for cooperatives (s. 541).
State who issues the rules on withdrawal of recognition, since the ordinance refers to implementing rules it never assigns to anyone.
barmm.fits: Municipalities that fill development council and special body seats with CSOs and want one accredited body to choose them.
