ordinances.title: An Ordinance Promoting Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Delivery of Government Services in the Local Government Unit of San Francisco, and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Ease of Doing Business Ordinance of San Francisco, Cebu
ordinances.summary: San Francisco's local version of the Ease of Doing Business Act of 2018 (RA 11032), enacted through SB Resolution No. 008-2020. It sets citizen's charters, processing limits of 3, 7 and 20 working days, automatic approval when an office misses its deadline, a business one-stop shop in the Negosyo Center and a complaints route through the SB Committee on Rules. It covers municipal and barangay offices and the national offices stationed in the municipality.
points: Every office posts a Citizen's Charter listing requirements, steps, responsible staff, maximum time, fees and the complaint procedure; asking for anything not on it is a violation
Processing limits of 3 working days for simple, 7 for complex and 20 for highly technical or risky transactions, extendable once; the SB gets 45 working days plus 20 when its approval is needed
An application with complete papers and paid fees is deemed approved if the office misses the deadline, and a renewal is automatically extended
A unified business application form and a business one-stop shop in the Negosyo Center, with the treasury, permits, zoning and fire offices together; the permit system to go electronic within 3 years
No more than 3 signatures on any document; staff serve applicants inside before closing time, including over lunch; every office has a public assistance and complaints desk
Barangay business clearances are applied for, issued and paid at the municipality, with the barangay's share remitted
Fire safety certificates within 7 working days; if the fire office has not acted 3 working days after a renewal application, the business holds a temporary valid FSIC

provisions.title: Covers municipal, barangay and national offices
provisions.text: It applies to all offices of the municipality and its barangays, and to the national government offices and agencies stationed in the municipality, which must review and reengineer their procedures.

provisions.title: A citizen's charter in every office
provisions.text: Every office posts a citizen's charter at its entrance and online listing requirements, steps, the person responsible for each, the maximum time, fees and how to complain. Staff have no contact with applicants beyond assessing their papers.

provisions.title: 3, 7 or 20 working days
provisions.text: Applications are acted on within 3 working days for simple, 7 for complex and 20 for highly technical or risky transactions, extendable once with written notice. Where SB approval is needed, it has 45 working days plus 20.

provisions.title: Receipts, written denials and 3 signatures
provisions.text: Every application gets a tracking number and receipt; any denial is explained in writing. No document needs more than 3 signatures, staff serve everyone inside before closing, even over lunch, and every office has a complaints desk.

provisions.title: Automatic approval when an office is late
provisions.text: An application with complete papers and paid fees is deemed approved if not acted on in time; the receipts serve as the permit. A renewal not acted on in time is automatically extended.

provisions.title: A business one-stop shop
provisions.text: A unified business application form, a one-stop shop in the Negosyo Center with the treasury, permits, zoning and fire offices together, and an electronic permit system within 3 years. Business permits are valid 1 year.

provisions.title: Barangay clearances at the municipality
provisions.text: Barangay clearances for business are applied for, issued and paid at the municipality within the same processing times, with the barangay's share remitted to it.

provisions.title: Fire safety certificates within 7 days
provisions.text: FSEC and FSIC issue within 7 working days. If the fire office has not acted 3 working days after a renewal application, the business holds a temporary valid FSIC. Fire officers may not sell or recommend extinguisher brands.

provisions.title: Acts that are violations
provisions.text: Refusing complete applications, asking for requirements or costs not in the charter, missing deadlines, not serving those inside before closing, not issuing receipts, and fixing or colluding with fixers.

provisions.title: Complaints to the SB Committee on Rules
provisions.text: Complaints are notarized and filed with the SB Committee on Rules, which investigates within 7 working days. A first offence draws a warning, a second an SB investigation, a third a case before the Ombudsman or Sandiganbayan.

ordinances.penalties: 1st offence a warning before the SB, 2nd an SB investigation in session, 3rd a case before the Ombudsman or an administrative or criminal case; no fines are set
ordinances.caveat: This copy is unsigned, with the mayor's approval line and date left blank, and much of it repeats RA 11032 word for word, including duties of the DICT and the fire bureau that a municipal ordinance cannot impose.

details.effect: 10 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation
details.covers: Municipal and barangay offices, and national offices stationed in San Francisco
details.enforcers: Heads of offices and the mayor, with the SB Committee on Rules for complaints
creates: Business One-Stop Shop in the Negosyo Center
Public assistance and complaints desk in each office

highlights.label: working-day limit for simple transactions
the most for highly technical applications
signatures at most on any document
to put business permits online

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has no local rules on processing times, citizen's charters or fixers, and wants one ordinance that brings the Ease of Doing Business Act down to municipal and barangay offices. San Francisco's 2020 ordinance does that and adds a complaints route through the SB. It copies large parts of RA 11032 verbatim, including duties of national agencies the municipality cannot bind, its penalties are warnings and referrals rather than fines, and this copy is unsigned.

apply.if: If your offices already post citizen's charters
apply.then: you can replicate the processing limits and the automatic approval rule, and make the charter the only list of requirements and fees staff may ask for.

apply.if: If your LGU has no business one-stop shop yet
apply.then: start with the unified application form, the 3-signature limit and seating the treasury, permits, zoning and fire staff together, and set your own date for going electronic.

apply.if: If a Negosyo Center operates in your LGU
apply.then: house the one-stop shop there as San Francisco did; if not, use the municipal hall.

apply.if: If your barangays issue business clearances separately
apply.then: copy the rule that the municipality accepts and collects them at the one-stop shop and remits the barangay's share.

apply.if: If you copy the text
apply.then: drop sections 13 to 15 on the national business portal, databank and telecom towers, and keep only what your own offices must do.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 151 (streamlined licensing and the Business One-Stop Shop) and, for barangays, s. 411 on citizens' charters, alongside RA 11032.
Delete the clauses that only restate duties of national agencies (sections 13 to 15) and the lines that claim to amend the Local Government Code and the Fire Code, which an ordinance cannot do.
If the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism runs the Negosyo Center in your area, name it, and name the fire station that serves your LGU.

An SB warning or investigation is not a penalty a council can impose on employees; route discipline through the mayor under the civil service rules (BAA No. 17), and if you add fines for fixers who are not employees, keep them within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489) and post and publish under s. 571.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a business permit office and frontline services busy enough that delays and fixers are a common complaint.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Regulating Diggings and Excavations on Existing Roads within the Municipality of San Francisco
ordinances.shortTitle: Road Digging and Excavation Regulation Ordinance of San Francisco, Cebu
ordinances.summary: Regulates digging and excavation on roads, streets, pathways and similar places in San Francisco, Camotes. Anyone digging, including water, power and telecom utilities and contractors of government agencies, needs a permit, must post a bond of 150% of the cost of restoring the road, and must restore it on schedule. It sets the permit fees by type of work and road surface, with fees for poles and cables.
points: No digging for pipes, cables, poles or drainage without a permit and barangay clearance; emergency repairs may start first, with notice to the engineer within the next working day

A bond of 150% of the restoration cost, set by the municipal engineer, is forfeited if restoration does not start within 10 days of finishing the dig; it is released within 5 days of the engineer's acceptance
The engineering office evaluates any temporary road closure, with a timetable and safety measures to keep traffic moving
On busy main roads, work is done at night until dawn and on Saturdays and holidays, never on Sundays; signs must name the agency doing the work
Restoration fees per sq. m.: ₱173 for gravel shoulder, ₱542 for concrete sidewalk, ₱571 for concrete pavement, ₱653 for asphalt; ₱90 a day inspection and ₱75 clearance
Poles pay ₱20 each plus ₱500 a year; fiber optic lines ₱2 per four-core per km and copper lines ₱1 per pair per km
The utility and its contractor are jointly liable to anyone injured by an unrestored excavation

provisions.title: Covers every road dig, utilities included
provisions.text: Applies to digging and excavation on any road, street, passageway or pathway in the municipality, including by public and private water, power, gas and telephone utilities and contractors of national or local agencies.

provisions.title: No digging without a permit
provisions.text: Installing pipes, telecom lines, poles or drainage under roads needs an excavation permit. Applicants submit the requirements, a timetable approved by the Municipal Engineer that includes restoration, a barangay clearance, the fees and the bond.

provisions.title: Emergency repairs may start first
provisions.text: Emergency repairs to leaking pipes, faulty connections and damaged facilities may begin without a permit, with notice to the Municipal Engineer by the next working day and the permit secured within 3 working days.

provisions.title: A bond of 150% of restoration cost
provisions.text: Diggers post a bond of 150% of the cost of restoring the road, set by the Municipal Engineer. It is forfeited if restoration does not start within 10 days of finishing the dig, and released within 5 days of the engineer accepting the work.

provisions.title: Road closures, signs and debris
provisions.text: Temporary road closures are first evaluated by the Engineering Office for a timetable and traffic safeguards. Diggers must post warning signs and barricades and may not leave debris on the road.

provisions.title: Night and weekend work on busy roads
provisions.text: On busy main roads, work is done at night until dawn and on Saturdays and holidays where practicable, never on Sundays, and signboards must name the agency doing the work.

provisions.title: Restoration on schedule, or joint liability
provisions.text: The permit holder restores the road to standard on schedule. If not, the agency and its contractor pay the penalty and are jointly liable to anyone injured by the unrestored dig. The Municipal Engineer certifies completion.

provisions.title: Restoration fees per square metre
provisions.text: Water, drainage and sidewalk works pay ₱172 to ₱173 for gravel shoulder, ₱542 for concrete sidewalk, ₱571 for concrete pavement and ₱653 for asphalt per sq. m., plus ₱90 a day for inspection and ₱75 for clearance.

provisions.title: Fees for poles and cables
provisions.text: Telecom and power poles pay ₱20 each plus ₱500 a year per pole; fiber optic lines pay ₱2 per four-core per km and copper lines ₱1 per pair per km.

provisions.title: Penalties
provisions.text: Any violation draws a fine of ₱2,000 to ₱2,500, forfeiture of the bond, and a court case where warranted. The ordinance takes effect on approval.

ordinances.penalties: ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 and forfeiture of the bond, with a case in court where warranted
ordinances.caveat: This copy is unsigned and names no sponsor or mayor's approval, and it is internally inconsistent: Section 4 has the treasurer issue permits and allows 3 working days for emergency permits, while Sections 5 and 6 give the permit to the engineer and require notice the next working day.

details.effect: immediately after approval
details.covers: Anyone digging on roads or paths, including utilities and government contractors
details.enforcers: Municipal Engineering Office, with the Municipal Treasurer's Office

highlights.label: of the restoration cost posted as a bond
to start restoring the road after the dig ends
per sq. m. of asphalt pavement dug up
a year for each utility pole

barmm.why: Worth reading if water, power or telecom works in your LGU leave roads dug up and unrepaired. San Francisco's answer is a permit, a bond larger than the repair cost, a deadline to restore, and fees per square metre by road surface. It is short and practical, but this copy is unsigned and contradicts itself on which office issues permits and on the emergency rule.

apply.if: If your LGU has a municipal engineer
apply.then: you can replicate this by making the engineer the single office that issues the permit, sets the bond and accepts the restored road, with the treasurer only collecting the fees and holding the bond.

apply.if: If utilities in your area are mostly cooperatives or small water systems
apply.then: copy the list of requirements per type of work (water line, drainage, sidewalk, poles) so applicants know what to bring.

apply.if: If roads through your municipality belong to the province or the Bangsamoro Government
apply.then: limit the ordinance to municipal and barangay roads, and coordinate with the agency that owns the other roads.

apply.if: If telecom and power lines are being strung in your LGU
apply.then: copy the yearly per-pole fee and the per-kilometre cable fee, after checking them against your own costs of inspection.

change: Re-cite temporary closures for public works to BLGC s. 24, and the permit and inspection role to the engineer and building official (s. 531). Settle the conflict between Sections 4 and 5 so one office issues the permit.
Keep the penalty within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); the ₱2,000 to ₱2,500 fits, but say that forfeiture of the bond is separate from the fine.
Hold a public hearing on the fee schedule as BLGC s. 212 requires for fees and charges, and keep forfeited bonds and restoration fees for road repair.

Post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under BLGC s. 571 instead of 'immediately after approval', and coordinate pole and cable fees with the municipality's permitting of telecommunication towers (s. 480).
barmm.fits: Municipalities where utilities or contractors regularly dig up municipal roads and have a municipal engineer to inspect the work.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Enacting the Municipal Environment Code of Bayog, Zamboanga del Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Municipal Environment Code of Bayog
ordinances.summary: Bayog's environment code, which gathers its earlier environmental ordinances into one text and adds new rules. It sets up a municipal environment office and solid waste board, and covers land use and tree cutting, solid waste, hazardous materials, sanitation, water, air and noise. It applies to all residents, businesses, barangays and agencies in the municipality.
points: Mayor appoints a Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Officer heading a regular office; the SB keeps a permanent environment committee and reviews the code every 3 years
Agricultural land reclassification capped at 15%; a MENRO permit and 5 replacement seedlings for every tree of 10 cm DBH or more that is cut
Piggeries and poultry farms 500 to 1,000 m from built-up areas and 200 m from highways; backyard piggeries up to 3 heads in rural areas, banned in urban areas
Segregation at source with 'no segregation, no collection'; schools give 30 minutes a week to waste lessons and the MENRO campaigns 1 day a week until 80% of households segregate
Garbage fees for households, businesses and institutions go to a trust fund; no waste kept at the transfer station beyond 24 hours

Easements of 3 m in urban areas, 20 m on farmland and 40 m in forests along rivers and creeks; burial grounds 25 m from houses and 50 m from rivers and water sources; no factory within 1 km of the poblacion; noise capped at 60 decibels
Polluters pay clean-up costs plus a ₱100,000 environmental damage fee for every 24 hours they fail to clean up; half of every fine goes to whoever reported the violation or made the arrest

provisions.title: A MENRO and a permanent environment committee
provisions.text: The Mayor appoints a Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Officer, who heads the office and leads implementation of the code. The Sangguniang Bayan keeps a permanent Environment Committee of a chair and at least 2 members and reviews the code every 3 years.

provisions.title: Limits on land conversion and tree cutting
provisions.text: No more than 15% of agricultural land may be reclassified, and never prime farmland, only with a DA certification and the council's land use committee's endorsement. Cutting a tree of 10 cm DBH or more needs a MENRO permit and 5 replacement seedlings per tree.

provisions.title: Where piggeries and poultry farms may go
provisions.text: Farms need locational clearance and environmental permits and must be 500 to 1,000 m from built-up areas and 200 m from major roads. Backyard piggeries are capped at 3 heads in rural areas and banned in urban areas; farms of 2 ha or more plant trees on 10% of the land.

provisions.title: A solid waste board and 'no segregation, no collection'
provisions.text: A Municipal Solid Waste Management Board headed by the Mayor prepares and runs the waste plan. Waste is segregated at source into compostable, recyclable, non-recyclable and special waste, and unsegregated waste is not collected.

provisions.title: Waste lessons in schools and weekly campaigns
provisions.text: Schools devote at least 30 minutes a week to ecological waste management, and the MENRO campaigns on segregation at least 1 day a week until at least 80% of households comply.

provisions.title: Garbage fees go to a trust fund
provisions.text: Households, businesses, market stalls and institutions pay garbage fees into a trust fund, part of it for barangay waste operations. No waste may be kept at the transfer station beyond 24 hours, and it may never be used as a disposal site.

provisions.title: Hazardous materials and sanitation
provisions.text: Repair shops, terminals and fuel sellers are regulated, extremely toxic chemicals are banned, chemical manufacturers are inspected quarterly, clinics must dispose of clinical waste properly, and untreated sewage and septage may not be discharged.

provisions.title: Easements along rivers and creeks
provisions.text: Setbacks along rivers and creeks are 3 m for urban uses, 20 m for farmland and 40 m for forests and ecological parks, open to public use. No construction along waterways or well drilling without a permit.

provisions.title: Air and noise limits
provisions.text: No factory may be built within 1 km of the poblacion. Smoking in public places, smoke belching, open burning and foul odours are banned, and sound is capped at 60 decibels.

provisions.title: Polluters pay, and informants share the fines
provisions.text: Polluters pay clean-up costs plus ₱100,000 for every 24 hours they fail to clean up. Fines range from ₱300 to ₱1,000 with community service, up to at least ₱2,500 or 6 months in jail with closure for serious offences; half of each fine goes to whoever reported or arrested.

ordinances.penalties: 4 tiers: ₱300 to ₱1,000 with community service or up to 15 days; ₱500 to ₱1,500 or 15 to 30 days; ₱1,000 to ₱2,000 or at least 30 days; at least ₱2,500 or at least 6 months with immediate closure; solid waste offences follow RA 9003 and other violations get administrative sanctions from the mayor
ordinances.amends: Restates and absorbs Bayog's earlier environmental ordinances (among them MO 10-72-10 on dumping, MO 12-142-14 on burning garbage and MO 9-19-06 on pyrotechnics) and repeals inconsistent ones
ordinances.caveat: The garbage fee table lists the categories but leaves every peso amount blank, and the land use table's percentages do not add up.

details.covers: All residents, businesses, barangays and agencies in Bayog
details.enforcers: Municipal Mayor through the MENRO, with barangay officials and the Solid Waste Management Board
creates: Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Office
details.funding: Environmental and garbage fees, fines, and the MENRO budget

highlights.label: of each fine goes to the reporter or arresting officer
seedlings to replace every tree cut

damage fee per 24 hours a polluter fails to clean up

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has scattered environmental ordinances and wants one code with an environment office to enforce it. Bayog covers land, trees, waste, chemicals, sanitation, water, air and noise in 145 sections, with distances, setbacks and permit rules you can lift. It dates from 2016, its garbage fees are blank, and its heaviest penalties have no ceiling, which a municipality cannot impose.

apply.if: If your LGU already has an environment officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving that office the permit, inspection and business permit roles Bayog gives its MENRO, including recommending non-renewal for establishments that fail inspection.

apply.if: If you have no environment officer yet
apply.then: start with the appointment clause and the SB environment committee, and adopt the other chapters as the office is staffed.

apply.if: If you already have a solid waste board and plan
apply.then: take only the land, water, sanitation and air chapters, and cross-refer to your existing waste ordinance instead of copying Chapter IV.

apply.if: If you want the garbage fees
apply.then: fill in your own amounts after a public hearing, since Bayog's table is blank, and keep its rule that they go to a trust fund.

apply.if: If your municipality has farms near rivers, piggeries or upland forest
apply.then: copy the setbacks (3, 20 and 40 m), the piggery distances and the permit to cut with 5 replacement seedlings.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 and s. 480 (municipal environment services, including the solid waste board, MRF and communal forests) and appoint the officer under s. 538, which makes an environment and natural resources officer mandatory.

Cap every penalty at ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489). Bayog's top tiers say 'not less than ₱2,500', 'not less than 30 days' and 'not less than 6 months' with no ceiling, and the ₱100,000 damage fee every 24 hours and the RA 9003 fines go well past what a municipality may impose; leave those to national law or recast them as recovery of actual clean-up costs.

Rewrite the quarry clause: under BLGC s. 161 the governor issues quarry permits of up to 5 hectares on the mayor's recommendation, so a municipality can set conditions on its recommendation but not bar quarrying itself. Use s. 162's sharing of the quarry tax (30% province, 30% municipality, 40% barangay).

Replace DENR, EMB and DA with the Bangsamoro Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform where they carry those functions, hold garbage fees in a trust fund (s. 333), and post the code for 6 weeks under s. 571 instead of 10 days.
Make the mayor's decisions open to appeal rather than 'final and executory', and set rules of proof before half a fine is paid to an anonymous texter.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with an environment officer, farmland and forest to protect, and several older environmental ordinances to consolidate.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Declaring the Watershed Protection Areas within the Municipality of Nueva Era, Ilocos Norte
ordinances.shortTitle: Watershed Protection Ordinance of Nueva Era, Ilocos Norte
ordinances.summary: Declares 26 rivers, falls, springs and a lake in 10 barangays of Nueva Era as watershed protection areas. It bans dumping and discharges into the water bodies and groundwater, tampering with the water supply, and building houses, pig pens or any structure near the watersheds, and makes the punong barangays monitor them. It applies to everyone living or working in and around the listed areas.
points: Lists 26 watershed areas in 10 barangays: 9 falls, 14 river listings (Tibangran River appears in 2 barangays), 2 springs and Dan-aw Lake
Poblacion and Barangobong have 4 areas each, from Cacanan and Abot Falls to Pia-aw and Masian Falls
Bans discharging or depositing anything into the water bodies, or on their banks where floods or storms can wash it in, and letting any substance seep into groundwater
Bans booster pumps on the distribution line and any tampering that impairs water quality
Bans development without local permission and any structure, such as houses or pig pens, in the vicinity of the watersheds
Each punong barangay designates pollution control officers, monitors the areas and reports to the mayor

provisions.title: Covers every listed watershed area
provisions.text: The ordinance applies to all the watershed areas it identifies in Nueva Era, under a policy of promoting environmental strategies to protect water resources.

provisions.title: Key terms defined
provisions.text: It defines watershed protection, environmentally critical areas, contamination, discharge, dumping, hazardous waste, pollutant and groundwater, so that spilling, pumping, pouring or releasing any material into a water body counts as discharge.

provisions.title: 26 watershed protection areas in 10 barangays
provisions.text: It declares 26 falls, rivers, springs and Dan-aw Lake as protected, in Poblacion, Barikir, Acnam, Caray, Cabittauran, Sto. Nino, Naguilian, Bugayong, Uguis and Barangobong. Poblacion and Barangobong have 4 each.

provisions.title: No discharges into the water or onto the banks
provisions.text: No one may discharge or deposit any material directly or indirectly into the water bodies, or along their margins where tides, storms or floods can wash it in, polluting the water or blocking its flow.

provisions.title: No polluting the groundwater
provisions.text: No one may discharge, inject or let seep into the soil any substance that would pollute groundwater.

provisions.title: No booster pumps or tampering with supply
provisions.text: No one may use booster pumps directly on the distribution system or tamper with the water supply in a way that alters or impairs water quality.

provisions.title: No structures near the watersheds
provisions.text: No activity, development or project expansion may proceed without permission from local authorities, and no structure such as a house or pig pen may be built in the vicinity of the watershed areas.

provisions.title: Punong barangays monitor the areas
provisions.text: Every punong barangay designates pollution control officers, monitors the declared areas regularly and sends a monitoring report to the mayor.

provisions.title: ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 fine
provisions.text: Violators are fined ₱1,000 to ₱2,500. The ordinance took effect on approval.

ordinances.penalties: ₱1,000 to ₱2,500 per violation
ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR from a scan but reads cleanly; the ordinance draws no boundaries for the areas and sets no distance for the 'vicinities' where building is banned.

details.effect: Upon approval
details.covers: 26 listed rivers, falls, springs and a lake in 10 barangays of Nueva Era
details.enforcers: Punong barangays and their pollution control officers, reporting to the mayor

highlights.label: rivers, falls, springs and a lake declared
barangays with a protected watershed
prohibited acts, from dumping to building
top fine for a violation

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU draws its water from rivers, springs or falls that no ordinance protects. Nueva Era's 2022 ordinance names each one by barangay, bans dumping and building near them, and puts the punong barangays in charge of watching them. It is 3 pages and easy to copy, but it draws no boundaries, leaves 'vicinity' undefined and says nothing about structures already there.

apply.if: If your LGU has an environment and natural resources officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by having that office list each river, spring, falls and lake that supplies water, by barangay, as Nueva Era's section 5 does, and map them.

apply.if: If you have not mapped your water sources yet
apply.then: start with the barangays that draw drinking water from springs or rivers, and add the rest by amendment.

apply.if: If you want the building ban to hold up
apply.then: set a buffer in metres around each listed area instead of 'vicinities', and decide what happens to houses and pens already inside it.

apply.if: If your punong barangays will do the monitoring
apply.then: copy the rule that each designates a pollution control officer and reports to the mayor, and say how often, which Nueva Era leaves open.

apply.if: If any listed area lies in ancestral domain or a declared protected area
apply.then: consult the community and the ministry concerned before declaring it, and leave the national park rules to the protected-area law.

change: Re-cite the basis from LGC s. 16 to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare, clean water and ecological balance) and s. 480, and give the monitoring to the environment and natural resources officer, who under BLGC s. 538 protects communal forests and watersheds.
Keep the fine within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489) and drop the reference to the Revised Penal Code; post and publish the ordinance under s. 571, since Nueva Era's took effect on approval.

Replace DENR and DA with the Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform where they hold those functions, and check that no listed area overlaps forest land or a protected area the ministry manages.
If a listed area lies within ancestral domain, consult the community and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs first (BAA No. 64).
barmm.fits: Upland and rural municipalities whose barangays draw water from named rivers, springs or falls.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Prescribing Regulation on Certain Movement of Minors (17 Years of Age and Below) During the Prescribed Hours (10:00 PM to 4:00 AM) for Reasons of Public Safety and Security
ordinances.shortTitle: Curfew Ordinance for Minors of Bingawan
ordinances.summary: Sets a curfew from 10 PM to 4 AM for minors aged 17 and below in Bingawan, Iloilo, for public safety. Minors found out during those hours are taken to the barangay hall for recording, then to a curfew centre and on to their parents or guardians. Police, barangay officials and tanods enforce it, and the social welfare office writes the rules for repeat offenders and runs programs for young people.
points: Curfew for minors 17 years old and below from 10 PM to 4 AM
Minors found violating it are brought to the barangay hall for verification and recording, turned over to the curfew centre within a reasonable time, and then to their parents or guardians
Police, punong barangays, barangay kagawads and appointed tanods may apprehend violators; the police chief makes the force available to the punong barangays
The barangay secretary keeps a permanent list of each minor's name, address, birth date, and time and place of apprehension
The mayor may suspend the curfew in a barangay on the barangay council's recommendation
The social welfare office sets rules for repeat offenders and provides recreational, educational, religious, anti-drug and anti-gang programs
Copies posted at barangay halls, chapels, churches, schools, public utility vehicles and terminals, with schools discussing it in class

provisions.title: A curfew for minors from 10 PM to 4 AM
provisions.text: Minors aged 17 and below may not be out from 10:00 PM to 4:00 AM, for reasons of public safety and security.

provisions.title: Violators go to the barangay hall, then home
provisions.text: A minor found violating the curfew is brought to the barangay hall for verification and recording, turned over within a reasonable time to the curfew centre, and then to the parents or guardians.

provisions.title: Police, barangay officials and tanods enforce it
provisions.text: Members of the municipal police station, the punong barangay, sangguniang barangay kagawads and appointed barangay tanods may apprehend violators and hold them safely at the barangay hall or curfew centre.

provisions.title: A permanent record of every minor caught
provisions.text: The barangay secretary keeps a permanent list of each apprehended minor's name, address, date of birth, time and place of apprehension and other circumstances.

provisions.title: The mayor may suspend it in a barangay
provisions.text: On the barangay council's recommendation, the mayor may suspend the curfew in a barangay or specific area for as long as public interest requires.

provisions.title: Police resources for the punong barangays
provisions.text: The chief of police of the Bingawan Municipal Police Station makes the police force's resources available to punong barangays to enforce the curfew.

provisions.title: Posted widely and discussed in schools
provisions.text: Copies are posted at barangay halls, chapels, churches, schools, public utility vehicles, bus terminals and other conspicuous places, and public and private schools discuss the ordinance in class.

provisions.title: Social welfare rules for repeat offenders
provisions.text: The Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office issues the implementing rules, including procedures for repeat offenders, and provides recreational, educational, religious, anti-drug and anti-gang programs.

provisions.title: Takes effect after 3 weeks of posting
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect the day after it has been posted for at least 3 consecutive weeks at the municipal hall entrance and at least 2 other conspicuous places.

ordinances.caveat: The copy skips page 2, so Sections 3 to 6 (likely the definitions, the curfew rule itself, its exemptions and any sanctions) are missing; this entry describes only what survives.

details.effect: the day after 3 consecutive weeks of posting
details.covers: Minors 17 years old and below in Bingawan between 10 PM and 4 AM
details.enforcers: Bingawan police, punong barangays, kagawads and tanods, with the MSWDO
details.structure: 16 sections (Sections 3 to 6 missing from this copy)

barmm.verdict: Take the idea, not the text
barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU is drafting a curfew for minors and wants the procedure after a child is found out late: who may pick the child up, where the child is taken, who records it and who designs programs for repeat cases. Bingawan's version puts the barangay at the centre and gives the social welfare office the follow-up. The page with the curfew rule, its exemptions and any sanctions is missing from this copy, so the core of the ordinance must be written fresh.

apply.if: If your LGU has a licensed social welfare officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by giving that office the rules for repeat cases and the programs for young people, as Bingawan does, and by having it receive every child who is picked up.

apply.if: If your barangays have tanods and a children's protection council
apply.then: let the tanods bring children to the barangay hall, have the barangay secretary keep the confidential log, and have the council follow up with the families.

apply.if: If you have no curfew centre
apply.then: skip it and have the child taken straight home or released to a parent at the barangay hall, which the national juvenile justice law prefers anyway.

apply.if: If you are writing the missing curfew rule
apply.then: list clear exemptions, such as children with a parent or guardian, going to or from school, work, religious activities or an emergency, since curfews without them have been struck down in court.

change: Ground it in the general welfare clause (BLGC s. 17) and the local council for the protection of children (s. 130), with the social welfare officer's duty to prevent juvenile delinquency (s. 537).

Follow RA 9344 as amended by RA 10630: no penalty may be imposed on a child for a curfew violation, and the child must be released to the parents or a barangay official, so keep any 'curfew centre' a short, child-friendly stop and not detention.
Write the exemptions the Supreme Court required in its 2017 ruling on Manila, Navotas and Quezon City curfews, and protect the barangay log as confidential.
Remember that tanods are civilians who may not carry firearms (BLGC s. 408), and post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under s. 571 instead of Bingawan's 3 weeks.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a social welfare officer and active barangay tanods that want a curfew built around barangay follow-up rather than punishment.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Granting Hazard and Subsistence Allowances, and a One-Time Gratuity Pay to Registered and/or Accredited Barangay Health Workers (BHWs), Appointed Barangay Nutrition Scholars (BNSs), and Appointed Barangay Sanitary Inspectors (BSIs) in the Municipality of Braulio E. Dujali, Davao del Norte
ordinances.shortTitle: BHW, BNS and BSI Benefits and Gratuity Ordinance of Braulio E. Dujali
ordinances.summary: Braulio E. Dujali's ordinance granting municipal allowances to barangay health workers, nutrition scholars and sanitary inspectors. It pays a monthly hazard allowance, a daily subsistence allowance for those posted at isolated health stations, and a gratuity after 5 years of continuous service. It covers registered or accredited BHWs and appointed BNSs and BSIs certified by their punong barangays.
points: Hazard allowance of not less than ₱1,000 a month, paid quarterly, once certified by the punong barangay and endorsed by the health board
Subsistence allowance of ₱50 a day for those serving in isolated barangay health stations or other designated areas
One-time gratuity of ₱5,000 after 5 continuous years, plus ₱1,000 for each further year; rehired workers under 60 can earn it again after a new 5 years

Registered BHWs need 1 year of service and a passed exam and practical demonstration; accredited BHWs need 3 years of registered service and listing with the Local Health Board and Provincial Health Office
BNSs and BSIs need appointment by the punong barangay, 1 year of service and endorsement by the Municipal Health Office

Half the hazard allowance and all of the subsistence allowance and gratuity come from the general fund; the other half of the hazard allowance from the PhilHealth Konsulta trust fund, if PhilHealth rules allow
The Municipal Health Office issues implementing rules within 60 days and the Local Health Board monitors payments

provisions.title: Who is covered
provisions.text: Registered or accredited barangay health workers, and appointed barangay nutrition scholars and sanitary inspectors, certified by their punong barangays and actively serving in the municipality.

provisions.title: Hazard allowance of at least ₱1,000 a month
provisions.text: Covered workers certified by the punong barangay and endorsed by the Municipal Health Board get at least ₱1,000 a month, paid quarterly. The Local Health Board validates exposure to risk under RA 7883.

provisions.title: ₱50 a day for isolated stations
provisions.text: Those serving at isolated barangay health stations or other designated areas, available at all times, get a subsistence allowance of ₱50 a day.

provisions.title: ₱5,000 gratuity after 5 years
provisions.text: A one-time gratuity of ₱5,000 after 5 continuous years, plus ₱1,000 for each further year. Rehired workers under 60 can earn it again after a new 5 years; it depends on available funds and verified service records.

provisions.title: Registered and accredited health workers
provisions.text: A registered BHW needs 1 year of continuous service, a passed exam and practical demonstration, and validation by the Municipal Health Office and Local Health Board. Accreditation needs 3 years of registered service and listing with the Local Health Board and Provincial Health Office.

provisions.title: Nutrition scholars and sanitary inspectors
provisions.text: A BNS or BSI must be appointed by the punong barangay, have 1 year of continuous service and be endorsed by the Municipal Health Office as an active provider.

provisions.title: Split funding with PhilHealth
provisions.text: Half the hazard allowance, all of the subsistence allowance and the gratuity come from the general fund. The other half of the hazard allowance comes from the PhilHealth Konsulta trust fund, only if PhilHealth rules allow it.

provisions.title: Rules within 60 days, board monitoring
provisions.text: The Municipal Health Office issues implementing rules within 60 days of approval, and the Local Health Board monitors payments and beneficiaries' continued service.

provisions.title: Takes effect 15 days after publication
provisions.text: It takes effect 15 days after publication in a local newspaper or posting in at least 3 conspicuous places.

ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, resolutions and issuances (none named)
ordinances.caveat: Half the hazard allowance depends on PhilHealth allowing the Konsulta trust fund to be used, which the ordinance leaves unresolved, and the gratuity is subject to available funds.

sponsors: Hon. Donna Mae B. Bernadas, Ed.D.
Hon. Mikhael Julian III G. Dujali
details.effect: 15 days after publication in a local newspaper or posting in 3 conspicuous places
details.covers: Registered or accredited BHWs and appointed BNSs and BSIs serving in the municipality
details.enforcers: Municipal Health Office, with the Local Health Board monitoring

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU wants to add a municipal top-up to what barangays pay their health workers, nutrition scholars and sanitary inspectors. Braulio E. Dujali sets clear amounts, clear eligibility by years of service and a gratuity that rewards staying on. It is 5 pages and recent, but half its hazard pay rests on PhilHealth Konsulta money that may not be usable for this.

apply.if: If your LGU has a Local Health Board and a health office that keeps a BHW registry
apply.then: you can replicate this by tying each allowance to registered or accredited status, as Braulio E. Dujali does, so the registry decides who is paid.

apply.if: If you have no BHW registry or accreditation process
apply.then: start with the eligibility rules (1 year of service for registered, 3 for accredited) and have the health office build the list before the first payment.

apply.if: If your health stations are far from the poblacion
apply.then: copy the ₱50 a day subsistence allowance for workers posted there, and list the stations that qualify.

apply.if: If you want to use PhilHealth Konsulta funds
apply.then: get a written opinion from PhilHealth and the health ministry first, and budget the full amount from the general fund until it comes.

apply.if: If your budget is tight
apply.then: start with the gratuity, which costs nothing until workers reach 5 years, and phase in the hazard allowance.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 424, which already sets at least ₱1,000 a month for barangay health workers and nutrition scholars from barangay funds, and to s. 480 for municipal health services; make clear the municipal allowance is on top of that.
Name the Local Health Board under BLGC s. 114, which includes a Ministry of Health representative, instead of the 'Municipal Health Board' the text also uses.
Replace the Provincial Health Office in the accreditation rule with whatever registry the Bangsamoro Ministry of Health or your province keeps, and keep RA 7883 as the national law on BHW benefits.
Define barangay sanitary inspectors, who are not among the barangay personnel listed in BLGC s. 413, and have nutrition scholars endorsed with the nutrition action officer (s. 548).
State the general fund amount for the first year rather than leaving the gratuity 'subject to availability of funds'.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a health office and Local Health Board that keep a list of their barangay health workers.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Providing for the Prevention, Control, Reduction and Mitigation of the Mosquito Vector of Dengue in the Municipality of Calamba, Misamis Occidental, Penalizing Violations Thereof and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Anti-Dengue Vector Ordinance of Calamba, Misamis Occidental
ordinances.summary: Makes every owner, manager or caretaker of a house, establishment, school or vacant lot in Calamba responsible for clearing mosquito breeding sites, and lists the minimum steps. It requires health office clearance for chemical spraying and accreditation of pest control operators, creates an Anti-Dengue Task Force with a monitoring team for the 19 barangays, and fines repeat violators through citation tickets.
points: Owners and caretakers of houses, schools, vacant lots, abandoned houses, tire dealers and buildings under construction must remove stagnant water; larvae (kiti-kiti) found on the premises presume a violation

Minimum steps: cover drums and pails, puncture or store old tires, collect tins and bottles, keep gutters clear of rainwater, treat abandoned pools with larvicide, and check plant pots, bamboo poles, tree holes and leaf axils
Spraying and other chemical interventions need clearance from the Municipal Health Office, and pest control operators must be accredited by it first
The health office, the environment office and the Liga ng mga Barangay run the information campaign, ovi-larvitrapping and 'Oplan Linis' clean-ups
An Anti-Dengue Task Force sets policy, and a monitoring team tracks dengue cases in all 19 barangays and reports monthly
Citation tickets are paid at the treasurer within 72 hours; fines go 60% to the municipality, 30% to dengue programs and 10% to the enforcers who caught the violator

provisions.title: Owners must clear breeding sites
provisions.text: Owners, managers and caretakers of houses, schools, vacant lots, abandoned houses, tire businesses and other buildings must get rid of stagnant water; buildings under construction may not collect it. Larvae (kiti-kiti) found on the premises presume a violation.

provisions.title: Containers, tires and gutters
provisions.text: Water drums and pails must be covered at all times; old tires punctured, cut or stored; unused cans, jars and bottles collected or disposed of; and gutters and roofs kept free of rainwater.

provisions.title: Pools, empty buildings and plants
provisions.text: Abandoned swimming pools must be treated with larvicide, uninhabited buildings kept free of waste and stagnant water, and plant pots, open bamboo poles, tree holes and leaf axils checked as breeding places.

provisions.title: Chemical spraying needs health office clearance
provisions.text: Chemical interventions other than for research need clearance from the Municipal Health Office first, and pest control operators must be accredited by it before working in the municipality.

provisions.title: A public awareness campaign
provisions.text: The health office, with the environment office, the Liga ng mga Barangay and the barangays, runs health education, ovi-larvitrapping and 'Oplan Linis' clean-ups. The health office issues implementing rules, subject to the Mayor's approval.

provisions.title: An Anti-Dengue Task Force and monitoring team
provisions.text: A task force sets dengue policy and monitors clean-ups; its monitoring team tracks dengue cases in all 19 barangays and reports monthly to the task force and the health office.

provisions.title: Warning, then fines
provisions.text: A first offence draws a written warning from the health office; a second a ₱500 fine and a third a ₱1,000 fine, each payable instead as community service (pahina).

provisions.title: Citation tickets payable in 72 hours
provisions.text: Violators who do not contest are issued a citation ticket and pay at the Municipal Treasurer within 72 hours, or face a court case. Enforcers are oriented and deputized by the Mayor.

provisions.title: How the fines are split
provisions.text: Fines go 60% to the municipality, 30% to dengue prevention programs and 10% to the deputized enforcers who caught the violator.

ordinances.penalties: 1st offence a written warning from the health office; 2nd ₱500 and 3rd ₱1,000, each payable instead by community service (pahina)
ordinances.caveat: The text is OCR from a scan with councillors' signatures over each page; it reads clearly, but it does not say who sits on the Anti-Dengue Task Force.

details.covers: Owners and caretakers of houses, establishments, schools and vacant lots in Calamba
details.enforcers: Municipal Health Office, its deputised enforcers and the Anti-Dengue Task Force
details.funding: 30% of fines collected, for dengue prevention programs

barmm.why: Worth reading if dengue cases rise in your LGU each rainy season and clean-up drives depend on goodwill. Calamba's 2020 ordinance puts the duty to clear breeding sites on each owner or caretaker, lists the steps, controls who may spray chemicals and pays for enforcement from the fines. It is 4 pages and its fines are low, but it leaves the task force's members and the enforcers' names to later orders.

apply.if: If your LGU has a municipal health officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by having that office issue the warnings, clear any spraying, accredit pest control operators and train the enforcers before the mayor deputises them.

apply.if: If your barangays have health workers or tanods
apply.then: make them the monitoring team in each barangay, reporting dengue cases monthly to the task force.

apply.if: If many residents cannot easily pay fines
apply.then: keep Calamba's option of community service (pahina) for the 2nd and 3rd offence, and the written warning for the 1st.

apply.if: If you have no anti-dengue task force yet
apply.then: name its members in the ordinance (health officer, environment officer, DRRM officer, Liga president), which Calamba left out.

apply.if: If you want to reward enforcers from fines
apply.then: copy the 60%, 30% and 10% split only after your treasurer and accountant confirm the enforcers' share can be paid that way.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 (general welfare, health and sanitation) and the health officer's duty to enforce sanitation laws (s. 532), and name the Ministry of Health as the partner for case data and outbreak response; in an epidemic the Minister may step in under s. 117.
The fines already sit within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489); post and publish the ordinance under s. 571, since it carries penalties.

Name the task force members, with the health officer, the environment and natural resources officer (s. 538), the DRRM office and the Liga ng mga Barangay, and fund the program from the health-emergency allocation that s. 348 requires, not only from fines.
barmm.fits: Any municipality with a health office and barangays able to run regular clean-ups.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Regulating or Setting Guidelines for Availing the Medical and Death Assistance of Senior Citizens Who Are Members of the Federation of Senior Citizen, Camaligan Chapter, Camaligan, Camarines Sur
ordinances.shortTitle: Medical and Death Assistance for Senior Citizens of Camaligan
ordinances.summary: Sets the rules for medical and death assistance to senior citizens of Camaligan who are members of the municipal Federation of Senior Citizens. It fixes the amounts, the documents needed and the yearly budget, and fines anyone who falsifies papers to get the benefit. Assistance stops for the year when the appropriation runs out.
points: Covers residents 60 and above who are members of the Federation of Senior Citizens, Camaligan Chapter, a federation accredited by the sangguniang bayan
₱1,000 once a year for a senior citizen confined in hospital, and ₱500 once a year for outpatient care
Medical assistance needs a barangay certificate of indigency, a DSWD certificate of eligibility, the senior citizen ID and a doctor's prescription
₱2,000 death benefit for the family, claimed with the senior citizen ID, a death certificate and a certification from the barangay senior citizens' association president
Family is ranked: spouse, children, parents, brothers and sisters, then close relatives
₱100,000 appropriated in the yearly budget; releases stop when it is used up unless the council re-appropriates

provisions.title: Who qualifies
provisions.text: The assistance covers residents 60 and above who are members of the Federation of Senior Citizens, Camaligan Chapter, a municipal-wide federation with a full set of officers and accredited by the sangguniang bayan.

provisions.title: Medical assistance of ₱1,000 or ₱500 a year
provisions.text: A senior citizen confined in hospital gets ₱1,000 once a year. One treated as an outpatient may get ₱500 once a year.

provisions.title: Papers needed for medical assistance
provisions.text: The claimant brings a certificate of indigency from the barangay captain, a certificate of eligibility from the DSWD office, the senior citizen ID and a doctor's prescription.

provisions.title: ₱2,000 death benefit for the family
provisions.text: The family of a deceased senior citizen may claim ₱2,000, with the senior citizen ID, a death certificate from the Local Civil Registrar and a certification of membership from the BASCA president.

provisions.title: Which relative claims first
provisions.text: Family means, in order of priority, the legal spouse, children, parents, brothers and sisters, then close relatives.

provisions.title: Fines for falsified papers
provisions.text: Anyone, public or private, who falsifies documents to get or to give the benefits is fined ₱500 for a first offence and ₱1,000 for each later one.

provisions.title: ₱100,000 a year, until it runs out
provisions.text: ₱100,000 is appropriated in the yearly budget. Releases stop once it is used up, unless the executive certifies funds and the council re-appropriates. It took effect on approval, 13 February 2008.

ordinances.penalties: ₱500 for a first offence and ₱1,000 for later offences of falsifying documents to obtain or grant the benefits

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU gives medical or burial help to older residents case by case, with no rules on who qualifies or how much. Camaligan's 3-page ordinance sets fixed amounts, a short list of documents, a family order for the death benefit and a yearly cap. Its amounts date from 2008, it cites the senior citizens law that has since been amended, and it limits help to federation members.

apply.if: If your LGU has an Office of Senior Citizens' Affairs or a social welfare officer
apply.then: you can replicate this by having that office receive claims, check the documents and release the money, with amounts set at today's costs.

apply.if: If not every older resident in your LGU belongs to a senior citizens' organization
apply.then: drop the federation membership rule and use the senior citizen ID and residency instead, so no one is left out.

apply.if: If families in your LGU bury their dead within a day
apply.then: let them claim the death benefit after the burial, within a set period, with the death certificate and the ID.

apply.if: If your budget for senior citizens is small
apply.then: copy the rule that releases stop when the appropriation is used up, and post the remaining balance so claimants know where they stand.

change: Fund it from the at least 1% of the budget the BLGC sets aside for senior citizens' programs (s. 348), and run it through the Office of Senior Citizens' Affairs (s. 480) and the council for the elderly (s. 130).

Replace the DSWD certificate of eligibility with an assessment by the municipal social welfare officer (BLGC s. 537) or the Ministry of Social Services and Development, and update RA 9257 to RA 9994, the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010.
Keep the falsification fines within ₱5,000 and 6 months (BLGC s. 489), and post the ordinance for 6 consecutive weeks under s. 571 since it carries penalties.
Raise the 2008 amounts to current costs, and set how many claims a person may make if the budget allows more than one a year.
barmm.fits: Municipalities that already give medical or burial aid to older residents and want written rules, amounts and a yearly cap.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Granting Monthly Incentives to Barangay Tanods in the Municipality of Arteche, Eastern Samar, to Augment the Honorarium Provided by Their Respective Barangays, and Appropriating Funds Therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay Tanod Incentives Ordinance of Arteche
ordinances.summary: Arteche's ordinance paying a monthly municipal incentive to barangay tanods on top of their barangay honorarium. It caps each barangay's brigade at 20, creates an accreditation board that keeps the master list, and commits the municipality to regular training. It covers appointed and accredited tanods actively serving in every barangay of Arteche.
points: ₱200 a month from the municipality to each accredited tanod, on top of the barangay honorarium, rising after 2 years until it reaches ₱500
Each barangay brigade has no more than 20 tanods
A Tanod Accreditation Board, chaired by the SB chair on public order and safety with the Liga president, MLGOO, police chief and HRMO, validates appointments and keeps the master list
Eligible tanods are appointed by the punong barangay on the BPOC's recommendation, confirmed by barangay resolution, served during the month and are not suspended
Regular training in self-defense, blotter writing, fire suppression, surveillance and reporting, first aid and the incident command system
₱1,000,000 initially, from the Peace and Order and Public Safety Fund of the Office of the Mayor, and in each year's budget

provisions.title: Covers accredited tanods actively on duty
provisions.text: The ordinance applies to every duly appointed and accredited member of a Barangay Tanod Brigade in Arteche who is actively keeping the peace in their barangay.

provisions.title: At most 20 tanods a barangay
provisions.text: Each barangay keeps a Barangay Tanod Brigade of no more than 20 tanods, who are entitled to insurance coverage and other benefits during their term under Section 393(d) of the Local Government Code.

provisions.title: Accreditation before any incentive
provisions.text: Only tanods endorsed by their punong barangay and confirmed by a barangay resolution get the incentive, and only once the Tanod Accreditation Board accredits them. The board keeps the master list and submits it to the Sangguniang Bayan.

provisions.title: A Tanod Accreditation Board
provisions.text: Chaired by the SB chair of the Committee on Public Order and Safety, with the Liga ng mga Barangay president, the MLGOO, the chief of police and the municipal HRMO. It validates papers, keeps numbers within the cap, recommends approval, renewal or revocation, and coordinates training with the DILG and PNP.

provisions.title: ₱200 a month from the municipality
provisions.text: Every accredited tanod gets an initial monthly incentive of ₱200 from the municipality on top of the barangay honorarium, subject to available funds and auditing rules.

provisions.title: Who qualifies each month
provisions.text: A tanod must be appointed by the punong barangay on the Barangay Peace and Order Committee's recommendation, have actually served during the month, and not have been suspended or terminated in that period.

provisions.title: Regular training
provisions.text: The municipality runs regular trainings and seminars for tanods on self-defense, blotter writing, fire suppression, surveillance and reporting, basic life support and first aid, and the incident command system.

provisions.title: ₱1,000,000 to start, then every year's budget
provisions.text: An initial ₱1,000,000 comes from the General Fund under the Peace and Order and Public Safety Fund of the Office of the Mayor, and the cost goes into each year's annual budget.

provisions.title: Rising to ₱500 after 2 years
provisions.text: The incentive starts at ₱200 a tanod. After 2 years from effectivity it is raised step by step until it reaches ₱500 a tanod, built into later annual budgets.

provisions.title: Carried out by the mayor's office
provisions.text: The mayor implements the ordinance through the municipal treasurer and HRMO, working with the Liga ng mga Barangay and the Accreditation Board. It takes effect on approval and posting in 3 conspicuous public places.

ordinances.caveat: This is an OCR scan with two sections numbered 5, and the mayor's handwritten approval date reads 12/09/2025, taken here as 9 December 2025 since the council enacted it on 24 October.

details.effect: after approval and posting in 3 conspicuous public places
details.covers: Appointed and accredited barangay tanods actively serving in every barangay of Arteche
details.enforcers: Municipal Mayor through the Treasurer and HRMO, with the Liga and the Accreditation Board
details.funding: ₱1,000,000 from the Peace and Order and Public Safety Fund of the Office of the Mayor

highlights.label: a month from the municipality for each tanod at the start
a month once the incentive is fully phased in
set aside in the first year
tanods at most in each barangay's brigade

barmm.why: Worth reading if your barangays pay their tanods little and you want the municipality to add a regular amount without paying for unchecked appointments. Arteche pays ₱200 a month per tanod, routes payment through an accreditation board and a master list, and pairs the money with training. It is 4 pages and clear; you need to set your own amounts and the brigade size the BLGC allows.

apply.if: If your LGU has a peace and order fund under the mayor's office
apply.then: you can replicate this by charging the incentive there, as Arteche does, and naming the first-year amount.

apply.if: If your barangays appoint tanods without a common list
apply.then: start with the accreditation board and the master list, so the incentive goes only to tanods confirmed by barangay resolution and serving that month.

apply.if: If your budget cannot cover ₱200 for every tanod
apply.then: start with a smaller amount or a lower cap per barangay, and write in when it rises, as Arteche's 2-year step to ₱500 does.

apply.if: If your police station or fire office can give training
apply.then: copy the training list (blotter writing, first aid, fire suppression, incident command) and schedule it through the accreditation board.

apply.if: If you already provide group insurance for tanods
apply.then: keep it separate from the incentive and say so, so the two are not confused in the budget.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 414 and s. 424 instead of RA 7160 s. 389, 391 and 393: barangays have 1 tanod for every 200 inhabitants and no more than 30, and each tanod receives at least ₱1,000 a month from the barangay. Set the cap per barangay from population rather than a flat 20.
Make clear the municipal incentive is on top of the honorarium the barangay must pay under s. 424, not a substitute for it.

Replace the MLGOO and DILG memorandum circulars with the Bangsamoro Ministry of the Interior and Local Government's local officer and issuances, and coordinate training through the peace and order council (s. 128).
If you add insurance, cite BLGC s. 489, which lets the sangguniang bayan provide group insurance for tanods where finances allow, and s. 587 on the insurance system for barangay officials and tanods.
barmm.fits: Municipalities that want to support barangay tanods from a municipal peace and order fund and can keep a master list of them.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Providing Guidelines for the Registration and Accreditation of Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) in the Municipality of Arteche, Eastern Samar, and Granting of Performance Incentives to Qualified BHWs, Appropriating Funds Thereof and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay Health Workers Ordinance of Arteche, Eastern Samar
ordinances.summary: Sets how barangay health workers in Arteche are registered and accredited under RA 7883 and pays a one-time cash incentive when an accredited worker leaves the service. It creates a registration and accreditation committee under the local health board, sets qualifications, protects workers from removal without notice and hearing, and funds the incentive from the gender and development budget.
points: A BHW Registration and Accreditation Committee under the local health board, chaired by the municipal health officer, with an NGO representative, the BHW federation president, the DOH representative, the BHW coordinator, the SB health committee chair and the RHU public health nurse
Registration: age 18 to 59, at least high school level, 1 year's residence in the barangay, 1 year of voluntary service certified by the midwife, and basic BHW training
Accreditation: registered and actively serving for at least 3 years immediately before applying
Barangay officials cannot remove a BHW on their own; the local health board decides, after notice and hearing, on 6 grounds such as 3 months' inactivity or moving away
On separation, ₱2,000 after 5 years' service plus ₱200 for each extra year, or ₱4,000 after 10 years plus ₱200 for each year beyond 10
Claims need the accreditation certificate and a service record from the health centre or RHU, and the local health board reviews every incentive
Paid from the gender and development fund in the annual budget

provisions.title: Benefits only for registered and accredited BHWs
provisions.text: Barangay health workers get the benefits and incentives in the ordinance only once registered and accredited by the local health board, under RA 7883.

provisions.title: A registration and accreditation committee
provisions.text: The local health board creates a BHW Registration and Accreditation Committee chaired by the municipal health officer, with an NGO or PO health representative, the BHW federation president, the DOH representative, the BHW coordinator, the SB health committee chair and the RHU public health nurse.

provisions.title: Who can register as a BHW
provisions.text: An applicant must be 18 to 59 years old, at least high school level, a resident of the barangay for at least 1 year, have given 1 year of voluntary health service certified by the rural health midwife, have completed basic BHW training, and be mentally and physically fit.

provisions.title: Accreditation after 3 years of active service
provisions.text: To be accredited, a BHW must be registered and have actively given voluntary primary health services in the locality for at least 3 years immediately before applying.

provisions.title: No removal without notice and hearing
provisions.text: Barangay officials supervise BHWs but cannot remove one by mere order; removal needs valid cause and the local health board's notice and hearing.

provisions.title: 6 grounds for termination
provisions.text: The local health board may terminate a BHW for insubordination, 3 months of inactive service, failure to submit reports, transfer of residence, unethical behaviour, or conviction of a criminal offence.

provisions.title: A cash incentive on separation
provisions.text: Accredited BHWs who served continuously get, on separation and regardless of age, ₱2,000 after 5 years plus ₱200 for each year beyond 5, or ₱4,000 after 10 years plus ₱200 for each year beyond 10.

provisions.title: Claims need 2 documents
provisions.text: A claim needs the certificate of registration or accreditation and a service record from the barangay health centre or RHU.

provisions.title: Paid from the GAD fund, reviewed by the health board
provisions.text: The incentives are funded in the annual budget under the gender and development fund, and the local health board reviews and approves every incentive so only qualified BHWs receive one.

ordinances.caveat: Section 2 and the definitions speak of a 10-year minimum while section 10 pays from 5 years, and the copy is an OCR scan, though the incentive table reads clearly.

details.effect: 15 days after posting in 3 conspicuous places
details.covers: Barangay health workers serving in the barangays of Arteche
details.enforcers: Local Health Board and its BHW Registration and Accreditation Committee
details.funding: Gender and Development Fund in the annual budget

highlights.label: on leaving after 5 years, plus ₱200 a year
on leaving after 10 years, plus ₱200 a year

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU relies on barangay health workers but has no rules on who counts as one or what they get when they stop. Arteche's 2025 ordinance sets registration and accreditation under RA 7883, protects workers from removal at a barangay official's word and pays a modest one-time incentive on separation. The amounts are small, its 5-year and 10-year minimums contradict each other, and charging the incentive to the gender and development fund may not hold.

apply.if: If your LGU has a working local health board
apply.then: you can replicate this by having it form the registration and accreditation committee, chaired by the health officer, with the BHW federation and the SB health committee chair.

apply.if: If your BHWs are not yet listed anywhere
apply.then: start with registration (age, schooling, 1 year of residence and service, basic training), and accredit those with 3 years of active service.

apply.if: If BHWs are often replaced when barangay officials change
apply.then: copy section 7: removal only by the health board, on listed grounds, after notice and hearing.

apply.if: If you can fund an end-of-service incentive
apply.then: copy the table (₱2,000 at 5 years, ₱4,000 at 10, plus ₱200 a year), fix one minimum, and pay it from the health or general fund unless your GAD plan lists it.

apply.if: If your barangays already pay BHWs an allowance
apply.then: say in the ordinance that this incentive comes on top of it and of the RA 7883 benefits, so it is not read as replacing them.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 408 and s. 413, which make barangay health workers part of the barangay's health service, and to the local health board in s. 114, which seats a Ministry of Health representative in place of the DOH.
Fund the incentive from the health or general fund, or list it in the GAD plan first; using the GAD budget for purposes outside the plan is abuse of authority under BLGC s. 584.
Fix the contradiction between the 10-year minimum in sections 2 and 3 and the 5-year minimum in section 10 before copying.
Replace the DOH-DILG joint circular with any Ministry of Health or MILG issuance on BHWs, and check whether a newer national or Bangsamoro law sets higher benefits.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a functioning local health board and an organised BHW federation.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Creating the Municipal Youth Development Office and the Municipal Youth Development Council of the Municipality of Arteche, Eastern Samar, Providing Funds for the Purpose Thereof
ordinances.shortTitle: Youth Development Office and Council Ordinance of Arteche
ordinances.summary: Creates Arteche's Local Youth Development Office and Local Youth Development Council under the SK Reform Act of 2015. The council, led by the SK federation and youth sector representatives, plans and coordinates youth programs, while the office registers youth organizations, trains SK officials and serves as the council's secretariat. It sets ₱72,000 for the office's operations.
points: Youth are those aged 15 to 30, grouped as child youth (15 to 17), core youth (18 to 24) and adult youth (25 to 30)
Youth and youth-serving organizations with at least 10 members register with the office and renew every 3 years; registration is required to sit on the council

The council is headed by the SK federation president and vice president, with 2 representatives from each youth sector; it meets at least once a quarter, and its sectoral chair serves 1-year terms, up to 3
The council adopts a 3-year Local Youth Development Plan, drafted by the SK federation, covering scholarships, sports, livelihood, health, environment, culture and peace building

The office is housed in a youth centre or the municipal building; its officer should be 30 or younger, with 3 years in youth work and 1 year's residence, and not related to the mayor within the 4th degree
The office may have policy and planning, administration and finance, and programs and operations units if funds allow
₱72,000 is set aside for the office's operation

provisions.title: Who counts as youth
provisions.text: Youth are those aged 15 to 30, grouped for programming as child youth (15 to 17), core youth (18 to 24) and adult youth (25 to 30).

provisions.title: Youth groups must register
provisions.text: Every youth and youth-serving organization with at least 10 members in good standing registers with the Local Youth Development Office, which verifies it and sends the list to the National Youth Commission. Registration is renewed every 3 years.

provisions.title: Registration is the ticket to the council
provisions.text: Only registered and verified organizations may take part in the Local Youth Development Council. A group refused locally may seek special registration from the National Youth Commission.

provisions.title: A youth council led by the SK federation
provisions.text: The council is headed by the president and vice president of the SK Pambayang Pederasyon, with 2 representatives from each youth sector. It plans and coordinates youth programs, raises funds, takes donations and may set up youth centres.

provisions.title: Quarterly meetings and 1-year sectoral terms
provisions.text: The council meets at least once a quarter. Organization representatives elect a sectoral chairperson for a 1-year term, up to 3 terms, with an annual election.

provisions.title: A 3-year youth development plan
provisions.text: The SK federation drafts and the council finalizes a 3-year Local Youth Development Plan, approved by the mayor and endorsed to the council. It covers scholarships, sports, livelihood, training, cooperatives, culture, adolescent health, environment, inclusion and peace building.

provisions.title: A youth development office
provisions.text: The office is housed in a youth centre, or the municipal building if there is none. It registers youth groups, runs council elections, serves as the council's secretariat and trains SK officials and council members.

provisions.title: Who can be youth development officer
provisions.text: Preferably 30 or younger, with at least 3 years in youth work, a registered voter and 1-year resident of Arteche, appointed by the mayor and not related to the mayor within the 4th civil degree.

provisions.title: Units if funds allow
provisions.text: If funds allow, the mayor may add staff on the officer's recommendation, in policy and planning, administration and finance, and programs and operations units.

provisions.title: ₱72,000 for the office
provisions.text: The municipality sets aside ₱72,000 for the office's operation. The ordinance takes effect on approval.

ordinances.amends: Repeals other municipal policies creating councils or boards with similar youth programs, and inconsistent ordinances
ordinances.caveat: The OCR copy is rough, one page (Sections 5 to 8) was scanned twice, and the mayor's handwritten approval date cannot be read.

sponsors: Hon. Athena Erika C. Ocfemia, CPA
details.effect: upon approval
details.covers: Youth aged 15 to 30 and youth and youth-serving organizations in Arteche
details.enforcers: Local Youth Development Office and Council, with the SK federation
details.funding: ₱72,000 from the municipal budget

highlights.label: set aside to run the youth development office
ages counted as youth, in 3 age groups
members needed to register a youth organization

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has an SK federation but no youth development office, or a youth council that exists only on paper. Arteche's ordinance sets up both, says who sits on the council, how organizations register and what the 3-year youth plan must cover, and gives the office a small budget. The ₱72,000 covers little more than operations, the scan is rough, and its references to the National Youth Commission and DILG need updating for BARMM.

apply.if: If your LGU has no youth development officer post yet
apply.then: start by designating an existing employee to run the office, as the DILG guidance quoted in Arteche's preamble allows, and create the post once the budget permits.

apply.if: If your SK federation is active
apply.then: you can replicate this by having it convene the council and draft the 3-year youth plan, with the office as secretariat.

apply.if: If few youth organizations in your LGU are registered
apply.then: copy the 10-member minimum and the 3-year renewal, and have the office run a registration drive in schools, madaris and barangays.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a youth or sports council
apply.then: fold it into the new council, as Arteche's repealing clause does, so there is one body.

change: Re-cite the office to BLGC s. 480, which lists the Local Youth Development Office among municipal social services, and the council to s. 130 on councils for youth development.
Replace the National Youth Commission with the Bangsamoro Youth Commission (BAA No. 10) for registration, training and the youth plan, and DILG with the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government.
Tie the 3-year plan to the SK's own 3-year barangay youth plans and funds under BLGC s. 456 and s. 457, and to the pambayang pederasyon in s. 471.
Create the officer's post within your staffing pattern (BLGC s. 87) and set the appropriation by need rather than copying Arteche's ₱72,000.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with an organised SK federation that have not yet set up a youth development office and council.
