ordinances.title: An Ordinance Providing for a Community-Based Mental and Neurologic Health Program and Delivery System in the Municipality of San Roque, Northern Samar and Appropriating the Necessary Funds Therefor
ordinances.shortTitle: Community-Based Mental and Neurologic Health Program of San Roque
ordinances.summary: San Roque's ordinance setting up a community-based mental and neurologic health program under the Mental Health Act of 2018. It creates a municipal mental health board, a barangay mental health board and barangay mental health teams, lists the services the health center is to offer, and restates the rights of service users. It covers the residents of all 16 barangays, with attention to vulnerable groups.
points: An LGU Mental Health Board chaired by the mayor, with 15 members including the health officer, MSWDO, youth, senior citizen and PWD offices, the Liga and BHW presidents, the schools district supervisor and NGO and CSO representatives; it meets at least monthly and is appointed within 90 days
A barangay mental health board of the BHWs and officials of all 16 barangays, which picks a head within 30 days to sit on the municipal board
Barangay mental health teams of community health workers and barangay and youth council members, trained to assess, respond to and refer cases

Health center services: an observation room for acute cases, day care, outpatient consultations including telemedicine, psychotropic medicines in stock, screening and psychological first aid on home visits or a helpline
School-based and workplace mental health programs, and training such as mhGAP and MHPSS for health workers, teachers and others
Service users' rights to informed consent, the least restrictive treatment, confidentiality and access to their own records
₱100,000 appropriated from LGU funds

provisions.title: A municipal mental health board
provisions.text: Creates an LGU Mental Health Board as the policy body for mental and neurologic care. It recommends ordinances, maps resources, allocates funds and sets up monitoring. It meets at least monthly, and the Mayor appoints its members within 90 days.

provisions.title: 15 members, chaired by the Mayor
provisions.text: The Mayor chairs and the Vice Mayor is vice-chair, with the health committee chair, the health officer, MSWDO, youth office, OSCA, Liga, BHW and PDAO presidents, the schools district supervisor, NGO and CSO representatives and a barangay board representative.

provisions.title: A barangay board for all 16 barangays
provisions.text: BHWs and officials of all 16 barangays form a barangay mental health board to bring services to the grassroots; within 30 days they choose a head who sits on the municipal board.

provisions.title: Barangay mental health teams
provisions.text: Teams of community health workers and barangay and youth council members are trained to promote mental health, assess and respond to cases in the community, and refer them to proper experts.

provisions.title: A shift to community-based care
provisions.text: Mental health care is folded into primary health care, with mhGAP and MHPSS training for health workers, teachers, nurses and midwives, support groups for families, public awareness, and research with partners such as the Philippine Mental Health Association.

provisions.title: School and workplace programs
provisions.text: Targeted campaigns reach families, schools and vulnerable groups. Schools get a mental health program with trained focal teachers and referral pathways, and government offices a workplace program under the Mental Health Act of 2018.

provisions.title: Services at the health center
provisions.text: An observation room for acute cases instead of a psychiatric ward, day care, outpatient consultations and counselling including telemedicine, psychotropic medicines in stock, screening and psychological first aid on home visits or a helpline, and links to drug rehabilitation.

provisions.title: Rehabilitation and support for carers
provisions.text: Service users get psychosocial rehabilitation through sports, art therapy, life skills and livelihood; carers get support groups and psychoeducation; vulnerable people with mental conditions get basic needs in disasters or abuse.

provisions.title: Rights of service users
provisions.text: Service users have the right to free informed consent, care equal to other patients, treatment in the least restrictive setting, discharge on the psychiatrist's advice unless at serious risk, confidentiality and access to their own records.

provisions.title: ₱100,000 appropriated
provisions.text: ₱100,000 is appropriated from LGU funds. The ordinance takes effect on publication in 3 conspicuous places or a newspaper of general circulation.

ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, rules and regulations (none named)
ordinances.caveat: The OCR of the opening pages is badly garbled and the board's member list is misnumbered, but the sections from Article I onward read clearly in the scan.

details.effect: after publication at 3 conspicuous places or in a newspaper of general circulation
details.covers: Residents of San Roque's 16 barangays, especially service users and vulnerable groups
details.enforcers: LGU Mental Health Board, the health center and barangay mental health teams
creates: Community-Based Mental and Neurologic Health Program
details.funding: ₱100,000 from LGU funds

highlights.label: members on the municipal mental health board
barangays joined in a barangay mental health board

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has no mental health program and wants one that starts in the barangays and the health center rather than a hospital. San Roque sets up a board, barangay teams and a list of services the Mental Health Act expects at community level. It is recent and complete in structure, but ₱100,000 will not pay for most of the services it lists, and parts of it restate national law on admission and treatment that a municipality cannot change.

apply.if: If your LGU has a health officer and a Local Health Board
apply.then: you can replicate this by making the mental health board a committee of the health board, with San Roque's members added, so you do not run 2 boards with the same people.

apply.if: If your barangays have active BHWs
apply.then: copy the barangay mental health teams and train them first in psychological first aid and referral before the health center adds services.

apply.if: If your health center has no doctor trained in mental health
apply.then: start with screening, home visits, a helpline and referral, and add the observation room, day care and medicines once staff and supply are in place.

apply.if: If families in your LGU turn first to religious or traditional leaders
apply.then: include them among the community health workers, as San Roque does with faith-based leaders, and train them to refer.

apply.if: If you can budget more than ₱100,000
apply.then: tie the amount to the services you will actually open in the first year, such as medicines and telemedicine sessions.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 17 and s. 480 (municipal health services) instead of RA 7160 s. 17, with RA 11036 as the national law on mental health.

Build the board around the Local Health Board under BLGC s. 114, which includes a Ministry of Health representative, and name the health officer (s. 532) and social welfare officer (s. 537) as its working members.

Replace the Department of Health with the Bangsamoro Ministry of Health in the facility review board and training links, and keep the Philippine Council for Mental Health where national law still gives it a role.
Cite RA 11036 for admission, retention and consent rather than restating them, since a municipal ordinance cannot change those rules and the health center will rarely admit patients.
Fix the numbering of the board's member list and say which NGOs and CSOs sit on it and how they are chosen (BLGC s. 39).
barmm.fits: Municipalities with a health center, active barangay health workers and a health officer or nurse who can lead the program.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Adopting the National Nutrition Council (NNC) Governing Board Resolution No. 1, Series of 2022, Entitled: "Adopting the National Policy on Nutrition in Emergencies, Tasking NNC Governing Board Member Agencies to Ensure the Efficient and Effective Implementation of the Policy, and Tasking the Nutrition Cluster to Formulate the Appropriate Advisories, Guidelines, and Other Materials to Disseminate and Implement the Policy," in the Municipality of San Roque, Northern Samar
ordinances.shortTitle: Nutrition in Emergencies Ordinance of San Roque, Northern Samar
ordinances.summary: Adopts in full the National Nutrition Council's 2022 National Policy on Nutrition in Emergencies for San Roque. It makes the Municipal Nutrition Committee, with the health office and the MDRRMO, write the policy into the municipal nutrition and DRRM plans and send advisories to all barangays, funded from the DRRM fund and nutrition program funds. Its substance is the national policy, which this copy does not attach.
points: Adopts NNC Governing Board Resolution No. 1, Series of 2022, approved on 28 January 2022, which replaced the 2009 national policy on nutrition in emergencies and disasters
The Municipal Nutrition Committee leads, with the Municipal Health Office and the MDRRMO
The policy must be written into the municipal nutrition plan and the DRRM plan
The nutrition committee and the MDRRMO jointly issue advisories, guidelines and teaching materials to all barangays and stakeholders
Funded from the MDRRM fund, municipal nutrition program funds or other available sources
The preamble names children, pregnant and lactating women and the elderly as most at risk in disasters

provisions.title: Why nutrition belongs in disaster planning
provisions.text: Disasters cause food shortages and health crises that hit children, pregnant and lactating women and the elderly hardest, so nutrition management must be part of the municipality's disaster system under its LDRRM Plan, through every phase from prevention to rehabilitation.

provisions.title: The national policy adopted in full
provisions.text: San Roque adopts in full NNC Governing Board Resolution No. 1, Series of 2022, approved on 28 January 2022, which replaced the 2009 national policy on nutrition in emergencies and disasters with the updated National Policy on Nutrition in Emergencies.

provisions.title: The nutrition committee leads
provisions.text: The Municipal Nutrition Committee implements it, with the Municipal Health Office and the MDRRMO.

provisions.title: Written into the municipal plans
provisions.text: The lead offices must integrate the policy into the municipal nutrition plan and the disaster risk reduction and management plan.

provisions.title: Advisories for every barangay
provisions.text: The nutrition committee and the MDRRMO jointly prepare and distribute advisories, guidelines and teaching materials to all barangays and stakeholders on nutrition in emergencies.

provisions.title: Funded from the DRRM and nutrition funds
provisions.text: Funds come from the Municipal DRRM Fund, municipal nutrition program funds or other available sources, under accounting and auditing rules. It takes effect on approval after posting and publication.

ordinances.caveat: The attached pages are the NNC board resolution and its signatures, not the policy itself, so a reader must get the national policy separately to see what the municipality has committed to.

details.effect: Upon approval, after posting and publication

details.enforcers: Municipal Nutrition Committee, with the Municipal Health Office and the MDRRMO
details.funding: MDRRM Fund, municipal nutrition program funds or other available sources

plans it must be written into

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has a nutrition committee and a DRRM plan that do not talk to each other, so feeding and nutrition checks during evacuations are improvised. San Roque's 2025 ordinance is a short adoption: it takes the national policy as is and tells the nutrition committee, health office and DRRM office to build it into their plans. It sets no local rules of its own, so its value depends on the national policy and on the plans that follow.

apply.if: If your LGU has a nutrition action officer and a municipal nutrition committee
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the national policy and naming the committee, the health office and the DRRM office as the leads, as San Roque did.

apply.if: If your DRRM plan has no nutrition section
apply.then: require the nutrition and DRRM plans to carry the policy and set a date for it, which San Roque leaves open.

apply.if: If your LGU often runs evacuation centres or hosts displaced families
apply.then: name those sites in the ordinance so the advisories and the nutrition cluster reach them first.

apply.if: If you want the funding to be clear
apply.then: name the budget lines: the 5% calamity fund and the nutrition allocation the annual budget must carry.

apply.if: If you want more than an adoption
apply.then: add local duties, such as who screens children after a disaster and who reports the results, which San Roque's text does not set.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 129 on the DRRM council and s. 548, which makes the nutrition action officer mobilise the nutrition cluster in disasters and emergencies.

Align the policy with the Bangsamoro Nutrition Commission (BAA No. 83) and the Ministry of Health, and adopt any guidance the Commission has issued on nutrition in emergencies alongside the NNC policy.
Name the funds as BLGC s. 348 does: the 5% lump sum for calamities and the required nutrition allocation.
If your LGU hosts displaced families, link the policy to the council for internally displaced persons (BLGC s. 130, BAA No. 62).
It has no penalties, so post it under BLGC s. 67 rather than the 6-week posting for penal ordinances.
barmm.fits: Any municipality with a nutrition committee and a DRRM office, especially those that often run evacuation centres.

ordinances.title: An Ordinance Mandating the Establishment of a Violence Against Women (VAW) and Their Children Desk in Every Barangay of the Municipality of Remedios T. Romualdez, Agusan del Norte and Providing Its Guidelines, Procedures and Mechanism Thereof and for Other Purposes
ordinances.shortTitle: Barangay VAW Desk Ordinance of Remedios T. Romualdez
ordinances.summary: Requires every barangay in Remedios T. Romualdez, Agusan del Norte, to set up a desk for cases of violence against women and their children in the barangay hall. It says who staffs the desk, what it does, and the step-by-step protocol for a victim who comes in and for a case reported by someone else. The desks are paid for from the barangays' gender and development budget.
points: The punong barangay sets aside a space in the barangay hall with a table, chairs, a separate filing cabinet and a logbook, and keeps cases confidential
The desk is run by a person trained in gender-sensitive handling of cases, preferably a woman kagawad or woman tanod; untrained staff must take basic gender sensitivity and anti-VAW training
The desk has 9 tasks, including helping victims get a Barangay Protection Order, a gender-responsive barangay plan, referrals, and a quarterly report to the DILG field office and the MSWDO
No amicable settlement, mediation, conciliation or arbitration is allowed in VAWC cases
Every case is reported to the police and the MSWDO within 4 hours, and the victim is helped to seek a court protection order within 24 hours of the BPO if she wants one
Rape, trafficking and other cases outside barangay jurisdiction go to the police women and children protection centre or the NBI
Funded from the barangays' gender and development budget of at least 5%

provisions.title: What counts as violence against women
provisions.text: VAW covers any gender-based act causing physical, sexual, psychological or economic harm to women, in the family, the community or by the state, including the acts defined in RA 9208 and RA 9262.

provisions.title: A VAW desk in every barangay hall
provisions.text: Each punong barangay sets aside an area in the barangay hall, or wherever the punong barangay holds office, with a table, chairs, a separate filing cabinet and a logbook, and keeps cases confidential and victims safe.

provisions.title: A trained desk officer, preferably a woman
provisions.text: The punong barangay designates a desk officer trained in gender-sensitive handling of cases, preferably a woman kagawad or woman tanod. Anyone untrained must take basic gender sensitivity training and an orientation on anti-VAW laws.

provisions.title: 9 tasks of the desk
provisions.text: The desk responds to cases, keeps records confidential, helps victims get a Barangay Protection Order and services, drafts a gender-responsive barangay plan, refers cases, leads advocacy, and sends a quarterly report to the DILG field office and the MSWDO.

provisions.title: BPO on the day of filing, no settlement
provisions.text: The punong barangay, or the kagawad on duty, must act at once on a reported incident and issue a BPO on the day of filing. No mediation, conciliation, arbitration or other amicable settlement applies to VAWC cases.

provisions.title: When a victim comes to the barangay
provisions.text: The desk officer gives her a safe, private room, checks if she needs medical care, helps with a gender-sensitive investigation in her language, explains her rights and the BPO, records the case on the national form, and arranges a shelter if she wants one.

provisions.title: Court orders within 24 hours, police within 4
provisions.text: If she wishes, the desk helps her apply for a temporary or permanent protection order at the nearest Family Court within 24 hours of the BPO. Every incident is reported to the PNP and the MSWDO within 4 hours.

provisions.title: When someone else reports a case
provisions.text: The desk verifies the report, with PNP help if needed, arranges a rescue to keep the woman and her children safe, explains the BPO, refers her for medical care and shelter, and records and reports the case within 4 hours.

provisions.title: Rape and trafficking go to the police or NBI
provisions.text: For rape, trafficking in persons and other cases outside barangay jurisdiction, the desk helps the victim file a complaint with the PNP Women and Children Protection Center or the NBI.

provisions.title: Paid from the GAD budget
provisions.text: The desk is charged to the barangay's gender and development budget, at least 5% of its budget, and is included in the annual GAD plan. The ordinance took effect on approval.

ordinances.caveat: The first 5 pages are the provincial board's Resolution No. 166-2014 approving the ordinance, its committee report and the transmittal letter; the ordinance is pages 6 to 10, and the Annex 1 recording form it cites is not attached.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your barangays have no set place or person to receive women and children who report violence, or if cases are still settled at the barangay. Remedios T. Romualdez's 5-page ordinance gives each barangay a desk, a trained desk officer, a clear protocol with time limits and a funding source, and the provincial board found it valid. It names national offices that work differently in BARMM, and its recording form is missing from this copy.

apply.if: If your barangays already have a VAW desk on paper
apply.then: you can replicate this by adopting the step-by-step protocol, the 4-hour report and the quarterly report to the social welfare office, so the desks work the same way everywhere.

apply.if: If your barangays have no woman kagawad or tanod with training
apply.then: start by sending the designated desk officers to basic gender sensitivity and anti-VAW training, as the ordinance requires.

apply.if: If your barangay halls lack a private room
apply.then: set aside a screened corner and a locked cabinet for records, and say where victims may wait safely.

apply.if: If there is no family court or women's shelter nearby
apply.then: name the nearest court and shelter in the ordinance, and say how the desk will get the victim there.

change: Re-cite the desk to BLGC s. 408, which lists the VAW desk among barangay social services, and the municipality's role to its supervision over barangays (s. 37); RA 9262 and the Magna Carta of Women stay as the national law basis.
Keep the ban on settlement and tie it to BLGC s. 436, which excludes VAW cases from the lupon; say the same for settlement by elders or clan leaders.

Send the quarterly reports to the Ministry of the Interior and Local Government's municipal office instead of DILG, and to the social welfare officer (s. 537) and, where there is one, the Local Women's Development Officer (s. 547), with the Bangsamoro Women Commission (BAA No. 8) informed.
Fund it from the 5% GAD budget in BLGC s. 348, and translate the protocol into the local languages (s. 67).
barmm.fits: Any municipality whose barangays have a hall or office and at least one official who can be trained to run the desk.

ordinances.category: Senior citizens and persons with disability
ordinances.title: An Ordinance Creating the Office for the Senior Citizens Affairs (OSCA) Headed by a Senior Citizen in the Municipality of Kitcharao as Mandated by R.A. 9257
ordinances.shortTitle: Office for Senior Citizens Affairs Ordinance of Kitcharao
ordinances.summary: Kitcharao's ordinance creating an Office for Senior Citizens Affairs under the mayor, headed by a senior citizen. It lists the office's functions, from keeping the list of senior citizens and issuing their IDs to monitoring discounts and helping file complaints against establishments that refuse them. It covers residents aged 60 and over.
points: Creates the OSCA under the Office of the Mayor, which supervises its plans and programs
Its head is a senior citizen appointed by the mayor from 3 nominees of the Sangguniang Bayan, for a 3-year term without reappointment
Keeps the list of senior citizens, updated every quarter, and issues IDs free of charge, valid anywhere in the country
Draws up a yearly work program and a list of services senior citizens can provide, and serves as their information and liaison center
Monitors compliance with senior citizen discounts and privileges, reports violating establishments to the mayor, and helps seniors file complaints with the DOJ or the courts
The old MSWD building in Barangay Songkoy is the office; it works with accredited NGOs, POs and barangays

provisions.title: Covers residents aged 60 and over
provisions.text: A senior citizen is any resident citizen of the Philippines at least 60 years old; the office serves them under RA 9257.

provisions.title: Plans and runs a yearly work program
provisions.text: The OSCA plans, implements and monitors yearly work programs and draws up a list of the services senior citizens can provide and need.

provisions.title: Keeps the list of seniors and issues free IDs
provisions.text: It updates the list of senior citizens every quarter and issues IDs free of charge, valid anywhere in the country.

provisions.title: An information and liaison centre
provisions.text: The office serves as the general information and liaison centre for the needs of senior citizens.

provisions.title: Monitors discounts and reports violators
provisions.text: It monitors compliance with the ordinance and national laws, especially senior citizen discounts and privileges, and reports violating establishments to the mayor.

provisions.title: Helps seniors file complaints
provisions.text: It helps senior citizens file complaints against any establishment, institution or agency that refuses their privileges under RA 9257, before the Department of Justice or a court.

provisions.title: Headed by a senior citizen for 3 years
provisions.text: The office is headed by a senior citizen whom the mayor appoints from 3 nominees of the Sangguniang Bayan, for a 3-year term without reappointment.

provisions.title: Under the mayor, in the old MSWD building
provisions.text: The Office of the Mayor supervises the OSCA's plans and programs; its office is the old MSWD building in Barangay Songkoy, and it links with accredited NGOs, POs and barangays.

provisions.title: Takes effect on approval
provisions.text: The ordinance takes effect immediately upon approval.

ordinances.amends: Repeals or modifies inconsistent ordinances, rules and regulations (none named)
ordinances.caveat: Pages 1 to 4 are the provincial board's approving resolution and committee report; the ordinance cites RA 9257 although RA 9994 had amended it in 2010, and sets no budget or staff.

barmm.why: Worth reading if your LGU has no Office for Senior Citizens Affairs, or runs one informally without an ordinance. Kitcharao's is short and lists the core functions: the master list, free IDs, discount monitoring and help with complaints. It is 3 pages long, cites a superseded law, picks the head's nominees in a way that differs from RA 9994, and gives the office no budget or staff.

apply.if: If your LGU already has a senior citizens' federation or association
apply.then: you can replicate this by having the mayor choose the OSCA head from 3 nominees of their general assembly, as RA 9994 provides, rather than from the Sangguniang Bayan.

apply.if: If your social welfare office handles senior citizens today
apply.then: copy the functions list and have that office hand over the master list and ID issuance to the new OSCA, with a vacant room or building as Kitcharao assigned.

apply.if: If establishments in your LGU are refusing senior discounts
apply.then: keep the duties to monitor, report violators to the mayor and help seniors file complaints, and link them to business permit renewal.

apply.if: If your LGU cannot fund a full office yet
apply.then: start with the head, one staff member and the master list, and add the yearly work program once the office has a budget line.

change: Re-cite the basis to BLGC s. 480, which lists the Office of Senior Citizens' Affairs among municipal social services, and to RA 7432 as amended by RA 9257 and RA 9994 as the national law.
Check the head's selection against RA 9994, which has the nominees come from a general assembly of senior citizens' organizations, and allow an extension of the term if needed as that law does.

Name the Bangsamoro Ministry of Social Services and Development and your social welfare officer (BLGC s. 537) as partners, and list senior citizens' organizations among the groups the office works with (s. 39).
Add a budget line and staff; the ordinance creates an office with neither.
Send the ordinance to the provincial board within 3 days of approval if your municipality is in a province (s. 64), as Kitcharao's was.
barmm.fits: Municipalities with an organized senior citizens' association and no ordinance yet establishing the Office for Senior Citizens Affairs.
